Geologic site characterization confirmed that the Columbia River Basalt Group offers a unique
combination of attributes for CO2 storage: thick stacks of reservoir-quality flow tops, laterally
continuous aquitards, newly recognized hyaloclastite reservoirs with exceptional porosity and
reactivity, non-potable and isolated formation waters, and robust structural settings that minimize
leakage risk. Core analyses provided direct evidence of rapid and permanent mineralization.
These findings demonstrate that the Columbia Basin is among the most promising geologic
settings globally for large-scale carbon mineralization storage, and provide the technical
foundation for advancing to stratigraphic test wells and future Class VI demonstration projects.

  Modeling and Simulation
Numerical modeling and simulation were critical for understanding how injected CO2 would
behave in basalt reservoirs over time. Using the STOMP-CO2 simulator, PNNL researchers
integrated geologic data, mineral kinetics, and hydrogeologic parameters to reproduce field-scale
injection at Wallula and extend predictions to commercial scenarios. The modeling program
advanced stepwise: benchmarking against known results, sensitivity testing to identify
controlling processes, calibrating with laboratory and field data, and scenario analysis to assess
storage security and mineralization potential.

 Benchmarking with Wallula Pilot Injection
Initial simulations replicated the 2013 Wallula pilot, which injected approximately 1,000 t of
supercritical CO2 into a Grande Ronde Basalt reservoir (McGrail et al. 2009, 2011, 2014, 2017).
Previous monitoring had shown that approximately 60% of the CO2 mineralized within 2 yr
(White et al. 2020), with nearly all expected to mineralize within a decade. STOMP-CO2
simulations successfully reproduced these outcomes, providing confidence that the model
captured key flow and geochemical processes. Benchmark runs confirmed the multiphase
distribution of injected CO2: a mobile supercritical phase near the wellbore, a dissolved fraction
spreading into formation waters, and carbonate precipitation concentrated in reactive flow tops.

 Sensitivity Analyses and Controlling Processes
Once benchmarked, the model was used to explore how reservoir properties and reaction kinetics
influence storage outcomes. Two key findings emerged:
1) Diffusion controls dissolution rates. Simulations showed that CO2 begins dissolving into
 formation waters immediately upon contact, but the overall rate of dissolution is governed by
 molecular diffusion. Even when other factors such as brine salinity or aqueous species
 concentrations were varied, diffusion remained the dominant control (Figure 124 and Figure
 125).

 218

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 124 (A) CO2 saturation, (B) clinopyroxene concentration, and (C) carbonate concentration in Scenario A at
25 days (the end of injection), 2 yr, and 10 yr after injection started.

 219

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 125 (A) CO2 saturation, (B) clinopyroxene concentration, and (C) carbonate concentration in Scenario B at
25 days (the end of injection), 2 yr, and 10 yr after injection started.
2) Mineral dissolution kinetics drive long-term mineralization. In baseline cases,
 approximately 20% of injected CO2 mineralized over 10 yr (Figure 124). When the
 dissolution rate of clinopyroxene, a primary basalt mineral, was increased by one order of
 magnitude, the extent of mineralization rose dramatically to approximately 90% over the
 same period (Figure 125). This demonstrated that uncertainties in primary mineral reactivity
 translate directly into uncertainty in long-term storage security.

 Reactive Transport Calibration
To reduce uncertainty, a calibration workflow was developed that coupled STOMP-CO2 outputs
with PEST software. This approach allowed multiparameter fitting of model results to field data,
including temporal groundwater chemistry (e.g., Ca, Mg, Fe, Mn concentrations, and pH) and
postinjection pressure responses. The calibrated models achieved reaction networks consistent
with 62% mineralization within 2 yr, aligning with Wallula pilot observations. The remaining
refinements focused on adjusting precipitation rates of secondary minerals such as ankerite and
aragonite to match core observations from postinjection samples.

 220

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 Simulation of Injection Scenarios
Beyond reproducing pilot outcomes, simulations explored injection at commercial scale
(approximately 1 MtCO2/yr). These runs tested different reservoir architectures, injection rates,
and geochemical settings. Results showed
• Plume behavior – Injected CO2 remained confined within target flow tops, spreading laterally
 less than 50 m from the wellbore in 10-year simulations. Dense flow interiors effectively
 limit vertical migration.
• Mineral trapping timeline – All scenarios converged on rapid dissolution followed by
 precipitation. Even conservative cases predicted most injected CO2 would transition into
 mineral phases within decades.
• Impact of glassy/amorphous vs. crystalline basalt – Simulations parameterized with
 amorphous glass data (from lab carbonation tests) yielded faster mineralization than
 crystalline enstatite cases, underscoring the importance of reservoir mineralogy.

 Key Findings
• Rapid permanence – Both modeling and field calibration confirm that CO2 injected into
 basalt reservoirs transitions to stable carbonate minerals within years to decades, ensuring
 permanent storage.
• Critical uncertainties – The rate of primary mineral dissolution (especially clinopyroxene and
 basalt glass) is the main uncertainty influencing predicted mineralization rates.
• Reservoir confinement – Flow interiors act as strong seals, and modeled plumes remained
 tightly confined, reducing risk of leakage.
• Scalability – Simulations demonstrate that mineralization can occur at scales relevant to
 commercial projects, not just pilots, making basalt storage competitive with sedimentary
 basins.

 Risk Assessment
Risk assessment for CO2 storage in basalt reservoirs required addressing both technical risks
(injectivity, mineralization rates, reservoir heterogeneity, and containment) and nontechnical
risks (regulatory pathways, stakeholder acceptance, infrastructure, and long-term liability). The
project advanced risk management through laboratory validation, numerical simulations,
hydrogeologic and geochemical testing, and stakeholder workshops. Together these efforts
established a framework for anticipating, quantifying, and mitigating risks to enable Class VI
permitting and commercial deployment.

 Technical Risks and Mitigation
 Reservoir Heterogeneity
Basalt formations are inherently heterogeneous, with properties varying among porous flow tops,
massive flow interiors, and hyaloclastite facies. This variability poses uncertainty in predicting
injectivity and storage capacity. To mitigate, the project integrated multiple borehole datasets
(Wallula, 100 Circles, K2H, Zillah New Well) into a regional geologic model, providing a more
complete picture of lateral continuity. Stacked reservoir–seal sequences demonstrated that even

 221

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

if one flow top underperforms, neighboring horizons can sustain injection, reducing reliance on
any single interval.

 Injectivity and Capacity Uncertainty
Initial risk centered on whether basalt flow tops could support high injection rates at commercial
scale. Hydraulic tests in the Indian Ridge Member demonstrated transmissivity values greater
than 2,000 mD, confirming robust injectivity. The discovery of hyaloclastite reservoirs with
porosities up to 86% and multi-darcy permeability further reduced injectivity risk, offering high-
capacity injection zones that exceed those typical of sedimentary saline formations.

 Mineralization Rate Uncertainty
The pace of mineralization is critical to long-term containment. Simulations of the Wallula pilot
reproduced approximately 60% mineralization within 2 yr, consistent with core analyses.
Sensitivity tests showed mineralization could range from approximately 20% (conservative
scenario) to approximately 90% (accelerated clinopyroxene dissolution) over 10 yr. These results
identified mineral dissolution kinetics as the key uncertainty. Laboratory experiments on basalt
glass and enstatite helped narrow parameter ranges, and model calibration with groundwater
chemistry (Ca, Mg, Fe, Mn, pH) further improved confidence.

 Containment and Leakage
Risk of upward migration was assessed through structural and hydrogeologic analysis. Anticlinal
structures in the Yakima Fold Belt and thick, undeformed basalt in the Palouse Slope provide
natural confinement (Figure 123). Massive flow interiors serve as aquitards, with hydraulic head
and water-chemistry data confirming minimal vertical connectivity between injection zones and
overlying potable aquifers. Modeled plumes spread less than 50 m from the wellbore over 10 yr,
indicating strong lateral confinement (Figure 124 and Figure 125).

 Nontechnical Risks and Mitigation
 Regulatory Familiarity and Permitting
Basalt reservoirs are novel for US regulators accustomed to sedimentary saline formations. This
introduces risk in Class VI permitting pathways. To mitigate, the project developed a permitting
and cost framework specific to basalt, including definition of Areas of Review (AORs) for 30-
year injections (approximately 14 km radius for 50 MtCO2). Cost of permitting and
characterization was estimated at approximately $1.4/tCO2, demonstrating feasibility within
DOE expectations.

 Stakeholder and Public Acceptance
Public unfamiliarity with CCS and concern about subsurface risks represent significant
roadblocks. Engagement through five workshops (Richland, Ellensburg, Toppenish, Washington,
D.C., and Richland Integrated Mineralization Workshop) brought together more than 120
participants, including Tribal Nations, local governments, nongovernmental organizations
(NGOs), and public groups. Concerns about groundwater safety, pipeline infrastructure, and

 222

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

long-term liability were openly discussed. Input was incorporated into planning, particularly on-
site access and workforce development.

 Economic Risk
Cost competitiveness was another risk. Analyses compared supercritical CO2 injection
(approximately $11.9/tCO2) with aqueous dissolved injection (approximately $23.5/tCO2).
Although both were within the ranges reported for sedimentary saline formations (typically
approximately $8/tCO2 to $20/tCO2 depending on depth, reservoir quality, and monitoring
requirements), supercritical injection offered clear cost advantages, reducing the risk of
economic nonviability. For estimations specific to the Columbia Basin, costs ranged from
$13.3/tCO2 for supercritical CO2 to $24.9/tCO2 for aqueous CO2 injection, placing basalt storage
at the upper end of sedimentary basin costs but with the added advantage of rapid mineralization
and permanent immobilization of injected carbon.

 Long-Term Liability
The permanence of storage is essential for reducing monitoring costs and liability exposure.
Mineralization in basalts provides unique assurance: Once CO2 is converted to solid carbonate, it
cannot migrate. This outcome directly addresses one of the largest risks in sedimentary CCS
projects—postinjection care—by reducing the required monitoring timeframe.

Risk assessment demonstrated that although basalts pose unique uncertainties, especially
regarding heterogeneity and reaction kinetics, these risks are mitigated by their equally unique
advantages: stacked aquifer–seal architecture, rapid mineralization, and natural geochemical
isolation. Technical analyses reduced uncertainty in injectivity and mineralization rates, whereas
nontechnical engagement reduced regulatory and public risks. The combined findings show risks
are manageable and, in some cases, lower than for conventional saline reservoirs, making basalt
storage not only viable but highly attractive for long-term CO2 management.

 Technical/Infrastructure Issues
Although the scientific focus of this project was on geologic suitability and mineralization
kinetics, technical and infrastructure considerations were also evaluated to understand feasibility
of scaling basalt storage from pilot to commercial levels. These considerations included
identifying potential CO2 sources, matching with prospective sinks in the Columbia Basin,
assessing transport and compression needs, and comparing engineering designs for different
injection approaches. This work informed economic assessments and provided a realistic picture
of how a commercial basalt storage project might be deployed in the Pacific Northwest.

 Source–Sink Matching
The Columbia Basin is home to multiple potential point sources of CO2, including natural gas
combined-cycle (NGCC) power plants, industrial facilities, and pulp and paper operations. The
Hermiston Power Project (Hermiston, OR), a 546-MW natural gas–fired facility, was specifically
evaluated as a capture candidate. Its location near the down selected storage sites in the Yakima
Fold Belt and Palouse Slope minimizes transport distance and costs (Figure 123). Analyses
 223

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

assumed post-combustion capture at the power plant, with injection either directly onsite or via
short pipeline routing.

 Injection Scenarios and Compression Needs
Two injection strategies were compared:
• scCO2 injection – requires compression of captured CO2 to pressures greater than 7.4 MPa
 and delivery to depths greater than 800 m. Modeling and cost assessments showed this option
 has lower water requirements, a smaller surface and subsurface footprint, and fewer
 monitoring wells.
• Aqueous dissolved CO2 injection (CO2 (aq)) – requires dissolving CO2 into large volumes of
 water before injection. For a 50-Mt injection scenario, approximately 1.25 Gt of water would
 be required, leading to higher capital costs (more wells, pumps) and higher O&M costs.

 Transport and Pipeline Considerations
Pipeline construction and routing were recognized as key infrastructure elements. Although long-
distance transport was not required for the modeled Hermiston case, regional deployment would
involve building new CO2 pipelines or repurposing existing rights-of-way. Workshops and
stakeholder input highlighted concerns about pipeline safety, permitting, and land use, consistent
with broader CCS infrastructure challenges. Although detailed routing analyses (e.g., using
SimCCS optimization) were not conducted in this project, preliminary cost estimates assumed
short-distance pipelines linking capture facilities to nearby basalt sinks.

 Coupling with Existing Infrastructure
The Columbia Basin has several advantages for infrastructure combination:
• Energy infrastructure is already established in Hermiston and Tri-Cities, with power
 generation, transmission lines, and rail networks.
• Industrial partners (e.g., Boise Cascade pulp mill at Wallula, WA; Packaging Corporation of
 America, headquartered in Lake Forest, IL) have prior engagement in CO2 projects, creating
 opportunities for early adoption.
• Regional geology aligns with infrastructure corridors, meaning many candidate sinks are
 close to existing industrial centers, reducing transport challenges.

 In Situ Critical Mineral Recovery
Recent analyses also suggest that basalt reservoirs hold potential for co-benefits through critical
mineral recovery, particularly titanium (Ti), vanadium (V), and rare earth elements present in
glassy mesostasis phases. During carbonation reactions, dissolution of basalt glass liberates not
only divalent cations (Ca, Mg, Fe, and Mn) that drive carbonate formation but also trace
elements of economic value. Experimental and nanoscale studies have shown that Ti-bearing
oxides and silicates undergo partial alteration in CO2-bearing fluids, releasing Ti and other
critical minerals into solution where it may be recoverable under controlled conditions (Jacobs et
al. 2025; Miller et al. 2025; Murchland et al. 2025; Stanfield et al, 2024). Although the primary
goal of injection is permanent carbon storage, the potential for dual outcomes—CO2
mineralization and critical mineral mobilization through CO2 enhanced mineral recovery (CO2-
 224

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

EMR)—adds value to basalt reservoirs and aligns with US priorities for securing domestic
supplies of strategic materials.

 Site Access and Permitting Logistics
From a logistical standpoint, site access and permitting were considered in preoperational
planning. Candidate sites were chosen in areas with minimal surface hazards (e.g., away from
floodplains or landslide-prone zones) and close to existing roads and utilities. Early engagement
with landowners and Tribal Nations informed site location discussions, whereas regulatory
planning anticipated the requirements of EPA Class VI permitting, including definition of Areas
of Review (AORs), well design standards, and monitoring networks.

Technical and infrastructure assessments confirmed that basalt storage in the Columbia Basin
can be integrated with nearby power and industrial facilities using existing infrastructure
corridors, supplemented by new injection and short pipeline systems. Comparative analysis
showed that supercritical CO2 injection is the most practical and cost-effective option, with
significantly lower water demand and fewer wells than aqueous dissolved injection. These
findings reduce infrastructure uncertainty and demonstrate that basalt storage can be deployed at
commercial scale with realistic engineering and logistical requirements.

  Nontechnical Issues / Scenario Analysis
Beyond technical feasibility, the success of commercial-scale CO2 mineralization projects
depends on addressing nontechnical factors such as property rights, regulatory pathways, public
acceptance, and long-term liability. These issues often determine whether technically sound
projects can be permitted, financed, and sustained. For basalt storage in the Columbia River
Basalt Group (CRBG), the project team evaluated land and pore space ownership, transport and
rights-of-way, water availability, liability frameworks, economics, and outreach activities.
Collectively, these assessments revealed both challenges and opportunities and shaped strategies
for building social license and regulatory readiness.

 Land and Pore Space Ownership
The CRBG spans multiple states, counties, and private landholdings, introducing complexity
around pore space rights. In many US jurisdictions, subsurface pore space is considered part of
the surface estate, although interpretations vary. This uncertainty poses risk for permitting Class
VI injection wells, where landowner agreements are required. To mitigate, the project identified
target areas (Yakima Fold Belt and Palouse Slope) with relatively simple ownership structures,
avoiding urbanized or highly fragmented parcels (Figure 123). Early engagement with
landowners and Tribal Nations emphasized transparent communication about the use of pore
space for long-term carbon storage.

 Transport and Rights-of-Way
Transporting captured CO2 to injection sites requires access to pipeline corridors or the
development of new rights-of-way. Although the Hermiston and Tri-Cities areas already host

 225

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

extensive energy infrastructure, new CO2 pipelines may face siting challenges, including
opposition from landowners or environmental groups. Stakeholders expressed concerns about
pipeline safety, permitting delays, and public disruption. Although detailed routing optimization
(e.g., with SimCCS) was not performed under this project, economic analyses assumed short-
haul transport from local NGCC power plants to basalt sinks. Future work will need to integrate
routing studies, permitting strategies, and right-of-way negotiations into early project planning.

 Water Rights
Injection strategies requiring water, such as dissolved CO2 injection (CO2 (aq)), introduce
significant water rights challenges. For a 50-MtCO2 injection, approximately 1.25 Gt of water
would be needed, placing enormous strain on already contested water resources in the Columbia
Basin. By contrast, supercritical CO2 injection has minimal water demand, making it more
feasible in regions where agricultural and municipal water use dominates. Water scarcity in the
Yakima Valley and Eastern Oregon was flagged by stakeholders as a critical nontechnical issue,
strongly influencing the project team’s preference for supercritical injection pathways.

 Liability and Long-Term Stewardship
A persistent roadblock to CO2 storage projects is uncertainty about long-term liability. In
sedimentary projects, liability often extends for decades postinjection, with operators responsible
for monitoring and potential leakage remediation. Basalt mineralization reduces this burden:
Once CO2 is converted into stable carbonates, leakage pathways are effectively eliminated. This
geochemical permanence could shorten the period of required postinjection site care, reducing
both financial and regulatory liabilities. Nevertheless, clarity is still needed on how liability
would be transferred to state or federal entities once monitoring is complete.

 Economic Assessment
Economic feasibility is central to commercial deployment. Analyses compared supercritical CO2
injection (approximately $11.9/tCO2) with aqueous injection (approximately $23.5/tCO2).
Supercritical injection offered lower capital and operating costs due to reduced water demand,
smaller well fields, and fewer monitoring requirements. Permitting and site characterization costs
added approximately $1.4/tCO2, bringing total levelized storage costs into the range of $13/tCO2
to $25/tCO2. These figures are competitive with sedimentary basin projects, providing
confidence that basalt mineralization can attract investment if regulatory and policy frameworks
support tax credits under Section 45Q of the US Tax Code (Credit…2022) and other incentives.

 Outreach and Engagement
Outreach activities were central to addressing nontechnical risks. Over five workshops were held
in FY22–FY24, engaging more than 120 participants, including Tribal Nations, local
communities, NGOs, industry, and regulators. The Carbon Interactive Workshop (Richland,
WA), the “Big Questions” workshop (Ellensburg, WA), and outreach to Heritage University
(Toppenish, WA) each provided forums for stakeholders to voice priorities and concerns (Figure
126). Issues raised included groundwater protection, pipeline safety, and land use. The project
team emphasized early information sharing and opportunities for student internships and
workforce development to build trust and regional readiness.

 Nontechnical Risks
Key nontechnical risks identified include
• public unfamiliarity with CCS leads to misconceptions about safety,
• opposition to CO2 pipelines due to safety or land use concerns,
• water rights conflicts in regions where dissolved injection would compete with agriculture,

 227

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

• regulatory uncertainty about permitting basalt reservoirs under Class VI, and
• long-term liability frameworks for mineralization-based storage that are not yet tested.
Mitigation strategies included prioritizing supercritical CO2 injection, selecting sites in
structurally stable and less densely populated areas, and conducting extensive outreach. Early
adoption of public feedback was identified as essential to avoiding delays during permitting and
operation.

Nontechnical assessments underscored that public trust, regulatory clarity, and water resource
management are as critical as technical feasibility. By proactively addressing pore space
ownership, rights-of-way, liability, and economic competitiveness, and by engaging stakeholders
in open dialogue, the project reduced roadblocks to future demonstration projects. These efforts
position basalt mineralization storage not only as a technically sound option but also as a socially
and economically viable pathway for large-scale carbon management in the Pacific Northwest.

 Permitting and Regulatory Planning and Progress
 UIC Class VI Permit Planning
The EPA’s Class VI well program governs the injection of CO2 for the purpose of long-term
storage. Although prior Class VI permits have been issued for saline formations, none have yet
been granted for basalts, introducing regulatory uncertainty. To reduce risk, the project team
applied lessons from the Wallula pilot (globally, the only prior basalt injection) and from
sedimentary projects such as FutureGen. Class VI–relevant activities included
• Area of Review (AOR) analysis that used modeled pressure fronts, with a 30-year injection
 of 50 MtCO2 generating a critical pressure radius of approximately 14 km used to delineate
 the AOR (FY23–FY24 modeling outputs);
• Well construction planning that anticipated casing, cementing, and monitoring requirements
 tailored to fractured flow tops and hyaloclastite facies; and
• Reservoir and seal characterization that demonstrated lateral continuity, low vertical
 connectivity, and non-potable groundwater at target depths, prerequisites for Class VI
 approval.
These activities provide the technical foundation for an eventual permit application once a
demonstration site is selected.

 Monitoring, Reporting, and Verification (MRV)
A Class VI permit requires a robust monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) plan to ensure
injected CO2 remains contained. The project prepared for this by integrating
• Reactive transport simulations that were calibrated to field chemistry, which enabled
 predictions of plume extent, mineralization rates, and long-term fate;
• Baseline groundwater chemistry datasets that included iron, manganese, and fluorine
 concentrations, which exceeded potable standards and support non-USDW classification; and

 228

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

• Proposed monitoring strategies that included pressure observation wells, seismic surveys, and
 geochemical sampling, which aligned with Wallula pilot experience.
Together, these elements provide the basis for MRV plans that regulators and stakeholders can
trust.

 45Q Incentive Readiness
Economic viability of basalt storage depends in part on the federal 45Q tax credit, which rewards
secure CO2 storage. The project team evaluated how basalt mineralization fits within 45Q
frameworks. Although current rules were developed for saline and depleted hydrocarbon
reservoirs, the permanence of mineralization offers an even stronger assurance of storage. Cost
assessments ($13/tCO2 to $25/tCO2 for basalt storage in the Columbia Basin) align with 45Q
thresholds, and stakeholder discussions emphasized that early basalt projects should be
prioritized for credit eligibility. Positioning basalt mineralization within 45Q enhances its
competitiveness with sedimentary basin projects.

 Stakeholder and Public Engagement
Because regulatory unfamiliarity with basalt reservoirs represents a risk, stakeholder engagement
was incorporated into regulatory planning. Five workshops between FY22 and FY24—Richland,
WA; Ellensburg, WA; Toppenish, WA; Washington, D.C.; and Richland Integrated
Mineralization Workshop—brought together more than 120 participants, including Tribal
Nations, regulators, DOE officials, and public representatives. These events provided
opportunities to
• explain the permitting process and Class VI requirements;
• address public concerns about groundwater protection, pipeline safety, and site access; and
• build support for early basalt demonstration projects through transparent dialogue.
This engagement not only advanced social license but also gave regulators confidence that public
acceptance was being addressed proactively.

 Other Regulatory Activities
In addition to Class VI planning, the project addressed related regulatory considerations:
• State-level water rights and land use policies, which strongly influence site selection.
• Cross comparison with sedimentary Class VI permits, such as FutureGen and Illinois Basin
 projects, to identify transferable best practices.
• Synergy with DOE’s CarbonSAFE program, which provides a pathway for large-scale
 demonstration and future commercialization.

 Project Findings and Conclusions
The project demonstrated that the Columbia River Basalt Group (CRBG) possesses the geologic,
geochemical, and structural characteristics necessary to support secure, commercial-scale CO2
storage. Site characterization confirmed that flow tops within the Grande Ronde Formation
provide laterally extensive, permeable reservoirs, whereas massive flow interiors act as effective
aquitards. The discovery of basal hyaloclastite deposits as a new reservoir class expanded
 229

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

injection opportunities by revealing zones with extremely high porosity, permeability, and glass
content, which are ideal for both injectivity and rapid mineralization. Hydrogeologic and
geochemical testing further showed that target formations occur well below potable groundwater
and are chemically isolated, strengthening the case for long-term containment.
Modeling and simulation results validated that mineralization occurs on decadal or shorter
timescales, with up to 60% of injected CO2 mineralized within 2 yr at the Wallula pilot site.
Sensitivity analyses highlighted diffusion and mineral dissolution kinetics as the main controls
on long-term outcomes, whereas calibration with groundwater chemistry aligned predictions
with field data. Core analyses provided direct, physical evidence of permanent storage through
the formation of novel carbonate phases, including cation-ordered ankerite and calcian siderite.
These findings demonstrated that basalt storage not only matches but, in some ways, exceeds the
permanence guarantees of sedimentary reservoirs.
Collectively, the project derisked CO2 mineralization in basalts by addressing geologic
uncertainty, validating reactive transport models, and establishing permitting and economic
frameworks. Cost estimates for Columbia Basin storage ($13–25/tCO2) are comparable with
those reported for sedimentary saline formations, but with the added benefit of permanent
mineralization that reduces the need for long-term postinjection monitoring and liability.
Nontechnical risks, such as pore space ownership, pipeline rights-of-way, and stakeholder
acceptance, were proactively managed through workshops, engagement with Tribal Nations and
communities, and development of permitting readiness pathways.
The overall conclusion of the project is that basalts in the Pacific Northwest represent a gigaton-
scale, permanent, and economically competitive storage resource. With both technical feasibility
and stakeholder frameworks now in place, the region is ready to advance to Class VI permitting
and demonstration-scale injection projects. This work positions basalt mineralization as a
cornerstone of carbon management in the western United States and as a globally relevant option
for durable, geologic-scale carbon dioxide removal with potential for coupling with other
subsurface technologies, such as in situ critical mineral recovery.

CCS at the Iron Mountain Iron Mine and Direct
Reduced Iron Processing Plant, Southern Utah
The Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP) Iron Mountain Subsurface
Characterization Focused Project evaluated the technical feasibility of geologic CO2 storage to
support a planned direct-reduced iron (DRI) facility in the Iron Springs District near Cedar City,
UT. The project focused on establishing the feasibility for a storage complex concept in a data-
limited setting, with the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone as the primary storage reservoir and
associated Jurassic–Triassic units and intrusive rock bodies evaluated as sealing units. Work was
structured to (1) assemble and quality-control the critical subsurface datasets needed for storage
assessment, (2) develop a geological model and simulation study, (3) evaluate storage
performance and key containment risks, and (4) define the engineering scope required to close
remaining uncertainties through a dedicated stratigraphic characterization well.
Across the project, partners integrated legacy and newly generated geoscience and engineering
inputs, including well logs and sample-based observations, outcrop and laboratory
measurements, and regional geophysical constraints. Legacy 2D seismic data were reprocessed
using updated velocity modeling to improve structural interpretation, supported by automated
fault detection products where appropriate. New terrestrial gravity data were acquired and
merged with regional datasets to better constrain basin geometry and structural context. These
inputs were incorporated into an iterative geological modeling workflow, progressing from
updated surfaces and interpretations (v2/v3) to a complete stratigraphic sequence model from
surface (digital elevation model [DEM]) through the Moenkopi (v4), with corresponding updates
to petrophysical property representations.
Using the resulting models, the team performed site-scale performance assessment to evaluate
injectivity, pressure evolution, CO2 plume behavior and stabilization trends, and area of review
(AoR) sensitivities under multiple operating scenarios. The project also produced a preliminary
engineering basis for next-phase field work, including a defined scope and budget framework for
a stratigraphic characterization well with coring, logging, and sampling intended to reduce key
uncertainties for future Class VI and 45Q tax credit (Credit…2022) documentation. Collectively,
these outcomes establish a technically grounded foundation for advancing Iron Mountain toward
a field characterization phase and subsequent EPA Class VI storage complex design.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

  Outcomes and Objectives
The CUSP Iron Mountain Subsurface Characterization Focused Project evaluated the feasibility
of geologic CO2 storage associated with a planned DRI facility in the Iron Springs District near
Cedar City, UT. The work concentrated on the Navajo Sandstone and associated formations as a
potential storage complex, with the Carmel and Temple Cap formations and the Three Peaks
quartz monzonite laccolith acting as the confining units. The overarching goals were to assemble
sufficient geologic, petrophysical, and geomechanical information to support a geological model
suitable for dynamic simulation, to characterize key geologic risks such as induced seismicity
and seal integrity, and to prepare the technical and non-technical foundation for eventual Class
VI and 45Q work.
The primary objectives of this proposed project include (1) detailed site characterization and
analysis of storage capacity, risks and economic options for carbon capture, utilization, and
storage (CCUS) at Iron Mountain; (2) developing a plan for drilling a stratigraphic well and/or
acquiring a 3D seismic survey of the area of interest; and (3) comprehensive plans for
assembling Underground Injection Control (UIC) Class VI and 45Q tax credit applications. The
nature and success of these objectives depend explicitly on the target storage formation and its
specific geologic setting.
The target formation for this project is the Navajo Sandstone, with a possible secondary target of
the Kaibab Limestone. The Jurassic-aged Navajo Sandstone is a prolific aquifer south of the Pine
Valley Mountains and oil reservoir in other areas throughout southwestern Utah. At depths
suitable for CO2 storage (> 800 m, to maintain supercritical state), two key reservoir/seal pairs
include (1) the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone (and possibly the overlying Temple Cap Formation)
that is stratigraphically sealed by the heterolithic, mudstone and gypsum-rich Carmel Formation
and, in certain areas, is intruded with several thousand feet of the Three Peaks quartz monzonite
laccolith and (2) the Permian Kaibab Limestone with (potentially) self-sealing intraformational
gypsum layers and overlain by the mudstone-rich Triassic Chinle and Moenkopi Formations.

  Scope of Work
Preliminary analysis suggests that the Navajo Sandstone and/or the Kaibab are both capable of
storing at least 50 million tons of CO2 in the area of Iron Mountain, also known as the Iron
Spring District. Geologic carbon sequestration in these formations in this area is favorable for
several reasons, including the presence of several reservoir/seal pairs at different depth intervals
as mentioned above, which provides potential for multiple targets. Additionally, lack of
hydrocarbons may lower the risk of unavailable pore space or associated overpressures. And,
given that these units are deep (7,000+ ft) but not excessively so translates to relatively low
drilling and injection costs. Ultimately, the project objectives included assessment of
commercial-scale storage potential with nominal risks, with 21 and 50 million tons over 30 yr
evaluated. Additionally, the demonstration of CCUS with an iron-processing plant specifically
has never been attempted to date, and this project would provide a meaningful example for other
iron and steel industry projects coming on line in the next decade.
Key outcomes achieved during the project include:
 1. Integration and quality assurance / quality control (QA/QC) of legacy and newly
 generated datasets, including the ARCO Three Peaks #1 well logs and cuttings, analogue
 233

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 well information, outcrop observations and sampling, petrographic products, laboratory
 petrophysical and geomechanical measurements, and regional geophysical datasets.
 2. Reprocessing and depth imaging of legacy 2D seismic data using updated velocity
 models and reverse-time migration (RTM), followed by automated fault detection to
 improve structural interpretation in areas affected by complex geology.
 3. Acquisition and interpretation of new terrestrial gravity data, merged with regional
 datasets, to constrain basin geometry and the extent of the Three Peaks intrusion and to
 provide independent structural constraints for model building.
 4. Progressive development of a 3D geological model suitable for simulation, including
 iterative updates to formation surfaces and property models as new interpretations and
 measurements became available.
 5. Site-scale performance assessment using numerical simulation and supporting analyses to
 evaluate pressure evolution, injectivity, CO2 plume behavior and stabilization, and AoR
 sensitivities under multiple operating scenarios.
 6. Development of preliminary engineering planning products (scope, basis of estimate, and
 cost framework) for a stratigraphic characterization well and associated coring, logging,
 and sampling program to close key data gaps identified by the subsurface characterization
 and modeling work.”

 CUSP Iron Mountain Team
Project management focused on coordinating a geographically distributed team, managing
budgets and cost-share, and enabling data access critical for geophysical reprocessing and
modeling.
The project was executed by a multi-institutional team that included the University of Utah (UU)
Energy & Geoscience Institute (EGI), Utah Geological Survey (UGS), Oklahoma Geological
Survey (OGS) and the Integrated Core Characterization Center (IC3) laboratory, Los Alamos
National Laboratory (LANL), Carbon Solutions (Saint Paul, MN)/MSU, and state policy
partners. Work began in mid 2022, included a pause related to funding and a subsequent no-cost
extension, and continued through mid 2024.
From project initiation, the management team organized a technical kickoff meeting and field
visit in Cedar City that combined presentations with a tour of the mine and key outcrops of the
Navajo Sandstone and overlying formations. This visit helped align the team on both the
industrial context and the subsurface geology. Routine bi-weekly all-hands meetings were
maintained through most of the project, with alternating geology-focused meetings hosted by
UGS. These meetings were used to track progress across site characterization, laboratory testing,
modeling, and risk assessment, and to avoid duplication of efforts.
A substantial management effort went into enabling LANL to reprocess legacy 2D seismic data
using the Echos processing system (University of Houston, Houston, TX). This required
negotiating and executing a multi-party nondisclosure and data-sharing arrangement among UU,
LANL, Seismax, and the University of Houston so that existing processing flows and velocity
models could be transferred and interrogated. In parallel, the UU team worked with UGS to plan
around budget constraints and a no-cost extension, pausing some work streams (particularly at
UGS) when BP2 funds were exhausted and restarting them once additional support became
available.

Management also developed and maintained standardized quarterly reporting templates, a Gantt
chart, and a final report outline keyed to the Statement of Project Objectives. Toward the end of

  Geologic Site Characterization
The UGS lead the geologic site characterization effort and are in the process of writing a
manuscript that details their work. The following title and abstract are from this in-process
manuscript. Additional information from the project reporting is documented in the following

 Geologic Carbon Storage Potential in the Neck of the Escalante
 Desert, Iron County, UT
The Iron Springs District in southwestern Utah lies at the eastern boundary of the Basin and
Range Province as it transitions into the Colorado Plateau and it is one of the largest iron ore
producing regions in the western United States. In 2022, a local mining company proposed
building a DRI plant to optimize their operations and increase the domestic steel supply. A DRI
plant would also generate approximately 500,000 t CO2 annually, and to reduce the amount of
carbon-rich byproducts released into the atmosphere, a rigorous subsurface characterization
project was conducted under the purview of CUSP (DOE Award DE-FE0031837) to assess the
potential for industrial-scale geologic carbon sequestration in a nearby basin. The approximately
180-km² study area within the Neck of the Escalante Desert comprises north-northeast-trending
basement-cored horst and graben structures that juxtapose thick sequences of Paleozoic and
Mesozoic sedimentary strata and extensive Eocene and younger volcanics, all of which have
been heavily faulted and sometimes cross-cut and intruded by Miocene-age plutonism. This
structural complexity, combined with a lack of data from few local well penetrations, meant
significant uncertainty for geological risk elements like reservoir and seal quality and a
subsurface characterization study was framed to determine the favorability of local subsurface
conditions for geological carbon storage and create reliable data for quantitative reservoir
modeling. Our multidisciplinary workflow integrated new and existing geological and
geophysical control points including reprocessed 2D seismic lines, newly acquired terrestrial
gravity surveys with refined inter-station spacing, petrographic data from local and regional
outcrop exposures representing a range of depositional realms and diagenetic conditions, and
geophysical logs, core, and cuttings from three nearby petroleum exploration wells, particularly
the 1984 ARCO Three Peaks #1 (ATP-1) well. The primary reservoir targeted for CO2 injection
is the approximately 1,500-ft-thick Jurassic Navajo Sandstone that lies entirely in the subsurface
locally at a mean depth of 7,000 ft below ground. In the ATP-1 well, the Navajo Sandstone is
overlain by multiple sealing units including anhydrite-carbonate beds in the Manganese Wash
Member of the Jurassic Temple Cap Formation and gypsiferous shale and limestone of the Co-
Op Creek Member of the Carmel Formation. These sealing units were intruded during the
Oligocene-Miocene (ca. 22 Ma) by the Three Peaks quartz monzonite laccolith, creating a
complex volcano-stratigraphic caprock. Metasomatic fluids generated during laccolith

 235

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

development likely precipitated pore-occluding CaCO3 and CaSO4 in the uppermost Navajo
Sandstone after filtering through anhydrite-carbonate beds in the Manganese Wash Member and
overpressure created during laccolith development created several crosscutting, healed calcite-
filled fracture sets in the Carmel Formation. Yet despite a range of complex conditions where
diagenetic events impacted highly favorable native rock properties, numerical reservoir models
indicate that available pore space in the Navajo Sandstone may sufficiently accommodate the
volumes of CO2 byproducts expected from the planned DRI plant. This study demonstrates how
practical reservoir characterization can improve geologic carbon storage models that require a
detailed understanding of the extent, architecture, and inherent rock properties of subsurface
strata, even in data-poor environments.

 Evaluate Well Logs and Cuttings from Nearby Wells and Determine
 High-Level Reservoir and Seal Properties
The ARCO Three Peaks #1 well provided the primary subsurface control for the Iron Mountain
project. UGS compiled and interpreted digital logs, organized cuttings from the full depth range,
and integrated existing core from key intervals in the Carmel and Kaibab formations.
Stratigraphic interpretation from this well was carried into Petrel (https://www.slb.com/products-
and-services/innovating-in-oil-and-gas/geology-and-geophysics/petrel-geology-and-geophysics-
software) and served as the backbone for the geological model.
To complement the ARCO well, UGS identified an additional analogue well (Delta Federal 23-
44) in the Parowan Gap region, whose cuttings and logs provide constraints on the lateral
variability of the stratigraphy and rock properties near the project area. Cuttings and core
materials from the ARCO well—particularly from the Carmel Formation and the target depth
range for storage and seal units—were distributed to UU and OGS/IC3 for petrophysical and
geomechanical testing.
By early 2024, the project reported Subtask 2.1 as complete: the evaluation of well logs and
cuttings had defined high-level reservoir and seal properties, identified key reservoir and seal
intervals, and provided calibrated 1D property profiles for use in the geological model.

 Evaluate Seal Properties of Nearby Outcrop (e.g., Lithology,
 Porosity, Permeability, Etc.), Including the Jurassic and Cretaceous
 Seal Rocks, and Igneous Intrusive Bodies
Outcrop analogs around Cedar City and Parowan Gap were used to characterize both reservoir
and seal units and to provide physical samples for laboratory testing.
UGS conducted multiple field campaigns to collect oriented core plugs and hand samples from
the Navajo Sandstone, Carmel Formation, Temple Cap Formation, and the Three Peaks quartz
monzonite. Navajo samples included both typical high-quality eolian sandstone and a “siltier”
facies (NAV-6) to represent lower-permeability reservoir or baffle units. Temple Cap samples
were chosen from evaporite-rich layers that may act as caprock or intra-formational seals. The
Three Peaks quartz monzonite samples were collected at and away from its contact with Carmel,
targeting both the intrusive body and contact aureole. These samples were prepared as both 1-
inch oriented core plugs and thin sections to support integrated petrographic, petrophysical, and
mechanical analyses.

 236

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Thin section production was contracted to a commercial lab for both outcrop samples and ARCO
cuttings from the formations of interest. The resulting sections were split between UGS and
OGS/IC3 for petrographic analysis, which identified lithofacies, diagenetic features, and mineral
assemblages controlling porosity, permeability, and sealing potential. UGS used these
petrographic results combined with outcrop observations to refine facies interpretations that feed
into the facies and property modeling components of the geological model.
At OGS/IC3, seal and reservoir samples were subjected to a systematic laboratory program that
included Fourier-transform infrared (FTIR) mineralogical assessment, helium-expansion
porosity, nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) porosity and pore-size distributions, and mercury
intrusion capillary pressure or analogous pore-throat characterization to estimate capillary entry
pressures, tortuosity, and diffusivity. Nanoindentation experiments provided localized Young’s
modulus and hardness for seal units, while scanning electron microscopy documented
microstructural controls on sealing behavior. A subset of seal samples was exposed to
supercritical CO2 for periods of several weeks to evaluate potential chemo-mechanical
degradation, with pre- and post-exposure properties compared.
In parallel, UU’s rock mechanics laboratory conducted triaxial tests on Carmel and Navajo
samples under different fluid conditions (dry, nitrogen-saturated, and planned brine and CO2-
saturated states) to determine strength and failure envelopes and to evaluate the effect of pore
fluid composition on mechanical behavior. Mechanical problems with the triaxial apparatus
delayed some planned tests, but the sample suite and experimental design for both reservoir and
seal units were in place by the end of the project period.
Taken together, these efforts produced a rich dataset of reservoir and seal properties—porosity,
permeability proxies, capillary behavior, elastic moduli, and microstructure—for use in the
geological model, dynamic simulations, and risk assessment.

 Evaluate Storage Potential/Reservoir Properties in Nearby
 Outcrops and Core – Navajo Sandstone and Kaibab Limestone

 Gather Legacy Gravity Data and Collect New Gravity Data to Define
 Subsurface Characteristics and Tie to Seismic and Well Data
To better constrain the geometry of the Three Peaks laccolith and the broader basin structure,
UGS acquired and processed new ground gravity data in the Iron Mountain region. Fieldwork
added 25 new stations in late 2022, bringing the total dataset to more than 200 gravity
measurements. These were merged with existing regional data and aeromagnetic information to
generate complete Bouguer anomaly maps, horizontal gradient maps, and inversion models of
the laccolith body (Figure 127).
By mid 2024, UGS had compiled these products into an ArcPro layer package (Esri 2024) for the
project, including station locations, regional and detailed grids, and contour maps. These
products inform the structural framework of the geological model by constraining the depth and
extent of the intrusive body, as well as highlighting density contrasts that may be associated with
major fault zones and basin geometry.

 Characterization of Faults and Fractures Relevant to Seal Integrity
 and Lateral Compartmentalization
Legacy 2D seismic lines in the Iron Mountain area were reinterpreted and reprocessed to support
the structural component of the geological model and to inform fault-related risk assessments.
OGS interpreted three 2D time-domain seismic sections tied to the ARCO Three Peaks #1 well.
Key reflectors corresponding to the Carmel, Navajo, and Kaibab formations were identified, and
a time–depth relationship was developed using the well log–based velocity information. This
work produced preliminary formation tops and highlighted areas of structural complexity,
especially northwest of the main area of interest.
LANL, after gaining access to the Echos processing system under the negotiated nondisclosure
agreement (NDA), investigated and adapted the original seismic processing flow and developed
new velocity models suitable for prestack depth migration. RTM was applied to selected lines,
significantly improving imaging quality in areas with complex structure.
On these RTM images LANL deployed a nested residual U-Net deep learning workflow for
automatic fault detection. The method successfully mapped faults on key lines and was
subsequently extended with a new architecture capable of detecting high-angle as well as low-
and variable-angle faults. This allowed a more comprehensive mapping of the local fault
network, including elements associated with the Neck of the Desert and Antelope Range fault
systems.
Fault and fracture characterization at the surface, led by UGS, included analysis of LiDAR-
derived fault traces and field observations that documented Quaternary normal faults trending
across the region. These data were integrated with seismic interpretations to identify structures

 238

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

that might intersect the intended storage interval. By early 2024, Subtask 2.5 Characterization of
faults and fractures relevant to seal integrity and lateral compartmentalization, was reported as
complete.
As site characterization transitioned from data acquisition to synthesis, UGS began assembling a
comprehensive Open File Report that integrates well, outcrop, gravity, aeromagnetic, and
seismic interpretation into a coherent description of the Iron Mountain storage complex. Drafting
of this report, and coordination of contributions from UU, OGS, and LANL, was a major focus
of UGS activities in the final year.

 Modeling and Simulation
The modeling and simulation work was carried out by UU, UGS, LANL, and OGS. UGS
performed the seismic well tie work (Task 3.1) and OGS interpreted the three 2-D seismic lines
(Task 3.2). Then using data provided by UGS and OGS, UU and OGS developed the geologic

The UU then performed the CO2 storage assessment (Task 3.4), developed the numerical

 Seismic Well Tie by UGS for Static Model Construction
A time–depth conversion was assembled using available sonic-log data and seismic velocities
from the ARCO Three Peaks #1 well. Three 2D seismic lines (G07601-760-7B, G07601-760-9,
and GSI-SU-13) were purchased from Seismic Exchange (SEI; Houston, TX) that provided raw,
processed, and enhanced post stack migration dataset formats per 2D line. Enhanced stack
migration format contained best visual quality for comparing picked formation tops interpreted
from Van Kooten (1988) along the southwest–northeast trending seismic line G07601-760-9
adjacent to the nearby ARCO Three Peaks #1 well. Geophysical logs (density, sonic, and
gamma), as well as formation tops at depth, from the ARCO Three Peaks #1 well and TWT
amplitude horizons provided by Van Kooten (1988), allowed for creation of a synthetic
checkshot associated with the well. The primary formation tops used for generating a reliable
interval velocity alignment at depth and time were the top of the Three-Peaks monzonite
laccolith, Carmel, Navajo Sandstone, Kaibab, and Redwall Limestone formations. Proceeding
wavelet calibration from density and sonic logs and formation tops, a coherent velocity model
was created for time-depth conversion for further interpretations and sequential forward reservoir
modeling.

 Velocity Modeling and Fault Evaluation by LANL
Subsurface structure imaging and fault detection are essential for site characterization and risk
assessment in geologic carbon storage. In this study, we use 2D surface seismic data acquired at
Iron Mountain, UT, to characterize subsurface structures. The data were collected with vibroseis
sources along three 2D walkaway lines, with a source spacing of approximately 91 m, receiver
spacing of about 45 m, and line lengths ranging from 9 to 15 km. We analyze two of these lines,
Line 7B and Line 9, to construct 2D velocity models using first-arrival travel time tomography
and pre-stack depth migration velocity analysis. RTM with the migration velocity analysis–
updated velocity models produces high-resolution images of the subsurface, and a machine
learning (ML) algorithm is subsequently applied to delineate faults in the migration results.
These analyses provide critical insights into the subsurface structures and support the assessment
of geologic carbon storage feasibility at Iron Mountain.

To mitigate anthropogenic CO2 emissions, researchers are focusing on decarbonizing heavy
industries such as iron production. In conventional processes, iron is refined by reacting iron ore,
 241

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

which contains iron oxides (Fe2O3), with carbon monoxide (CO) to yield pure iron and CO2.
Traditionally, CO is generated by burning coal in a low-oxygen environment or within a blast
furnace. However, this method releases significant amounts of greenhouse gases and other
pollutants into the atmosphere.
In contrast, the DRI process refines iron by reacting iron ore in a reactor vessel with synthesis
gas (syngas), a mixture of CO and H2, produced through the catalytic reforming of CH4 rather
than the combustion of coal. In DRI, iron ore reacts with CO and H2 to produce pure iron, CO2,
and water (Battelle et al. 2024). The resulting CO2 stream is relatively pure and can be dried and
either utilized for industrial applications or permanently stored through geological carbon
sequestration.
To evaluate a potential site for carbon capture and storage (CCS) associated with DRI
production, we characterized the subsurface of a proposed DRI plant in southern Utah using
legacy seismic data acquired in the 1980s. The prospective DRI-CCS field is located in the Iron
Springs District in the southwestern part of Utah. A geologic map of the area, modified from
Blank and Mackin (1967), is presented in Figure 130.

 242

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 130 Geologic map of Iron Mountain, UT, showing Seismic Line 7B (red) and Line 9 (blue). Green dots
indicate wells drilled in the region, and the gray ellipse marks the CO2 injection area of interest. Modified from
Blank and Mackin (1967).
The target formation for CO2 sequestration is the Navajo Sandstone, a Jurassic-aged, porous
sandstone situated at a depth of approximately 1,890 m (6,200 ft) below the surface. Preliminary
studies suggest that this formation has the capacity to store at least 15 million tons of CO2
(Moodie et al. 2022). The Navajo Sandstone is overlain by several potential caprock formations,
including the Jurassic Temple Formation, composed primarily of evaporites, and the Jurassic
Carmel Formation, which consists of mudstones and limestones.
In certain areas of the site, outlined by the red dashed line in Figure 130, the Jurassic Carmel
Formation is intruded by several hundred meters of quartz monzonite laccolith (Rowley and
Barker 1978; van Kooten 1988). A geologic cross-section illustrating these formations is shown
in Figure 131.

 243

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 131 Geologic cross-section from west to east across the Iron Mountain area showing the Jurassic Navajo
Sandstone reservoir layer, the Temple Formation caprock, the Carmel Formation, and the quartz monzonite
intrusion. Modified from Moodie et al. 2022.
To assess the feasibility of CCS for DRI production in this region, we analyzed 2D legacy active
seismic land data acquired along two walkaway lines (shown as red and blue lines in Figure 130)
to characterize subsurface structures. An initial layered velocity model was constructed by
applying a median filter to the sonic slowness log obtained from the Arco Three Peaks #1 well,
located at the northernmost green circle in Figure 130.
First-arrival traveltime tomography (FATT; Leung and Qian 2006; Taillander et al. 2009; Fomel
et al. 2009; Tong 2021) was then applied using the first arrival times of P-waves to refine the
shallow portions (less than 1 km) of the P-wave velocity (Vp) model. Migration velocity analysis
(Liu and Bleistein 1995) was subsequently used to update the deeper sections of the model.
After obtaining the migration velocity analysis–updated Vp models, RTM (McMechan 1983; Fei
et al. 2015) was used to produce pre-stack depth migration images of the subsurface. Finally, a
ML algorithm (Gao 2024) was applied to reduce noise, enhance image resolution, and
automatically detect faults within the migration images.

 Legacy 2D Seismic Data Acquisition and Processing
The 2D legacy seismic data were acquired at Iron Mountain, UT, along three walkaway lines:
7B, 9, and 13. For this study, only Lines 7B and 9 were analyzed because the data quality for
Line 13 was extremely poor, preventing the extraction of any meaningful information. The
limitations of Line 13 will be discussed further in the discussion section. The geometries of Lines
7B and 9 are shown in Figure 132.

 244

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 132 Map showing the location of Line 7B (red) extending from A to A′ and Line 9 (blue) extending from B
to B′
The linear portion of Line 7B (red line) trends northwest–southeast and includes 118 common-
shot gathers, while Line 9 (blue line) trends southwest–northeast and includes approximately 183
shots. For each common-shot gather, up to 96 receiver channels were used for data acquisition.
The shot spacing was approximately 91 m, and the receiver spacing was about 45 m. The data
were sampled at a 2 ms interval, with a total recording time of 3 s.
Following standard preprocessing procedures (Yilmaz 2001), automatic gain control was applied
to attenuate ground roll noise, and a band-pass filter of 3–8–20–25 Hz was used to suppress
high-frequency noise. Two processed mid-spread common-shot gathers from Lines 7B and 9 are
shown in Figure 133. After pre-processing, Vp models were constructed for pre-stack depth
migration.

 Velocity Model Building
To construct the Vp models for migration imaging using the legacy 2D surface seismic data at
Iron Mountain, we first developed an initial layered velocity model based on sonic well log data
from the Arco Three Peaks #1 well and interpreted formation boundaries. The shallow portions
of the Vp model along each 2D walkaway line were then refined using FATT. Following the
FATT update, we performed pre-stack Kirchhoff depth migration and subsequently refined the
deeper parts of the model through migration velocity analysis.
To build the initial layered velocity models, we began with well log data and interpreted
formation boundaries from the Arco Three Peaks #1 well. The well logging data were acquired
by Schlumberger in January 1985, covering measured depths from 16.46 m (54 ft) to 3,761.2 m
(12,340 ft) at 0.1524 m (0.5 ft) intervals. A datum of 1,785 m was used for the velocity models
and migration images, and the depths of the logging data were adjusted to account for elevation
differences between the well and the seismic data reference. Median values were selected within
layer intervals on the compression slowness log to derive the layered Vp velocity profiles.
Constant velocity values were assigned to regions beyond the logged interval, and the resulting
1D velocity profile was used to build the layered initial models down to a depth of 4.5 km. The
median velocity layers and corresponding sonic log velocities are shown in Figure 134, and the
initial Vp models for each walkaway line are presented in Figure 135.

Traveltime tomography was then applied using the first arrivals of P-waves to refine the shallow
portions of the velocity models. After 40 iterations, the traveltime misfit was reduced by more
than 95% for both Lines 7B and 9. The convergence curves for relative misfit, along with
histograms of traveltime misfits before and after tomography, are shown in Figure 136 and
Figure 137, respectively. The updated Vp models after FATT for Lines 7B and 9 are displayed in
Figure 138, showing significant improvements in the shallow regions of the models
(approximately the upper 1 km). These FATT models were then used for migration velocity
analysis.
Following the FATT updates, pre-stack Kirchhoff depth migration was performed along both
walkaway lines using the FATT velocity models to produce pre-stack depth migration images.
Horizons were interpreted from these images, and the velocities between horizons were adjusted
by flattening reflection events on common-image gathers. The final Vp models after migration
velocity analysis are shown in Figure 139. These migration velocity analysis–updated velocity
models were subsequently used in RTM to generate high-resolution subsurface images of the
structural features.

After constructing the velocity models using sonic logging data, FATT, and migration velocity
analysis, and processing the PP reflections, we applied RTM to obtain high-resolution PP images
of the subsurface structures beneath Iron Mountain. Each common-shot gather was migrated
individually, and a spatial taper mask was applied to suppress migration artifacts resulting from
limited source and receiver coverage. The raw PP RTM migration images for each line,
generated using the migration velocity analysis velocity models, are shown in Figure 140.

RTM images, improve spatial resolution, and automatically detect faults. The ML-denoised

 Discussions
We overlaid the velocity models on the ML-denoised migration images, as shown in Figure 143.
From the figure, there is a strong correspondence between the velocity contrasts and the seismic
reflectors. In Figure 143a, the edge of the high-velocity zone aligns closely with the dipping
reflector observed at approximately 1.5 to 0.5 km depth and 2 to 7 km horizontal distance. This
structure corresponds well with the quartz monzonite intrusion identified in the conceptual
geologic cross-section (Figure 131). Furthermore, Figure 143a indicates that our migration
velocity analysis successfully resolved the lower-velocity lithologies surrounding the quartz
monzonite intrusion. The low-velocity region between 0 and 3 km horizontal distance and 1 and
2 km depth is clearly visible in the migration velocity analysis–derived Vp model (Figure 143a),
whereas it was not evident in either the initial layered Vp model (Figure 135a) or the FATT-
updated model (Figure 138a).

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

(red) plotted alongside P-wave velocity (Vp) models for (a) Line 7B extending from A to A′ and (b) Line 9
extending from B to B′
The ML-denoised migration images for Lines 7B and 9 were plotted in 3D at different azimuthal
viewpoints, as shown in Figure 144. From this figure, we observe good continuity and alignment
of reflectors between Lines 7B and 9. Minor variations in reflector positions are likely due to
slight differences in the velocity fields of the two lines, as each line was processed independently
in 2D. For a more complete and accurate characterization of the subsurface structures and fault
systems, a dedicated 3D seismic survey of the region is recommended.

We analyzed two 2D legacy walkaway seismic datasets acquired in the Iron Mountain area of
Utah. Initial Vp models were constructed using sonic log data and subsequently refined through
FATT and migration velocity analysis. RTM was then applied to generate pre-stack depth
migration images of the subsurface. Following RTM, a ML algorithm was used to denoise the
migration images and automatically detect faults.
By overlaying the Vp models on the denoised images, we demonstrated that the boundary of the
quartz monzonite laccolith was successfully resolved along Line 7B. The denoised migration
images from Lines 7B and 9 were also visualized together in 3D, revealing good correspondence
in layer continuity and structural alignment. Minor discrepancies between the two profiles are
attributed to slight variations in the Vp models at corresponding locations.
Overall, the results indicate that the processed 2D seismic data effectively delineate key
subsurface features in the study area. However, to achieve a more detailed and reliable
characterization of the subsurface structures and fault systems, acquisition and analysis of a 3D
seismic survey are recommended.

 Geological Modeling
The geological model with an area of 122.4 mi2 was constructed in Petrel using three legacy 2D
seismic lines, well control from the ARCO Three Peaks #1 well (API 4302130006) and
supporting analyses of outcrop samples. Petrophysical properties were derived primarily from

area, collected under the Rocky Mountain Carbon Capture and Sequestration (RMCCS) project
(DE-FE0001812). Table 26 summarizes the porosity and permeability datasets used for each

The structural framework was developed from the depth-migrated formation surfaces interpreted
in Subtask 3.1. These surfaces include the Three Peaks quartz monzonite laccolith, Carmel
Formation, Navajo Sandstone, Kayenta Formation, Moenave Formation, and Chinle Formation.
These horizons were used to generate a 3D gridded framework, within which the stratigraphy
was discretized into model layers as follows: the laccolith (4 layers), Carmel Formation (5
layers), Navajo Sandstone injection interval (10 layers), Kayenta Formation (4 layers), and
Moenave Formation (2 layers). The resulting grid contains 123 × 128 × 25 cells, for a total of
393,600 active cells, with an average lateral cell dimension of approximately 220 by 200 ft.
Porosity was upscaled to the model grid from neutron and density porosity logs in the ARCO
Three Peaks #1 well, using the arithmetic mean of density porosity and neutron porosity
(porosity = (DPHI + NPHI)/2). Figure 148 shows the porosity distribution in the Navajo
Sandstone and the wells logs in the ARCO Three Peaks well. Permeability was calculated in the
ARCO Three Peaks well from porosity using an industry-standard porosity–permeability
correlation and then upscaled to the model grid. Permeability was populated throughout the
model volume using sequential Gaussian simulation (SGS) with co-kriging to the porosity
volume, applying a spherical variogram with correlation lengths of 12,300 ft × 12,300 ft. Figure
149 shows the permeability distribution in the Navajo Sandstone.

Initial pressure conditions were set using a hydrostatic pressure gradient. The model was
initialized as fully water-saturated (no free-phase CO2 present), with brine salinity set to 20,000
ppm total dissolved solids (TDS). A reference temperature of 160 °F was applied, along with a
Navajo Sandstone reference pressure of 2,462 psi. The compositional fluid description for
subsequent simulation consists of CO2 and water only; however, the initial state of the full model
includes water only (0% CO2).

 CO2 Quality and Quantity
Utah Iron’s proposed DRI facility will produce a concentrated CO2 stream as an inherent
byproduct of reducing iron oxide (magnetite) to metallic iron using a reducing gas composed
primarily of CO and H2. In the shaft furnace, CO and H2 react with oxygen in the ore to form
CO2 and H2O (steam), and the resulting “top gas” also contains variable amounts of unreacted
reducing gas (CO and H2) and other minor constituents depending on plant configuration and
feed gas composition (Midrex Technologies 2018).
The furnace effluent is conditioned upstream of CO2 capture to enable efficient recycle of the
reducing gas. Gas conditioning typically includes cooling (often with direct contact cooling or
heat exchange) and knock-out/separation steps that remove bulk water condensed from the high-
moisture furnace effluent, along with entrained solids. While this front-end conditioning removes

 262

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

a substantial fraction of water, the gas entering the CO2 capture unit remains humid, and
moisture management is a primary design consideration because the reduction reactions generate
water and because cooling/condensation behavior varies with operating conditions (Midrex
Technologies 2018).
CO2 is then separated using an amine-based capture system. In this configuration, CO2 is
selectively absorbed from the conditioned top gas into an aqueous amine solvent, and the CO2-
lean gas (enriched in CO and H2) is recycled back to the shaft furnace as part of the closed-loop
reducing gas circuit. Amine-based capture is a mature post-combustion/industrial separation
approach and is capable of producing a high-purity CO2 product suitable for compression and
geologic storage when paired with standard downstream conditioning (Hack et al. 2022).
A key implication of amine capture is that the CO2 product leaving the regenerator/stripper is
typically saturated with water vapor (and may contain trace solvent carryover), because the
separation process is water-based and the CO2 is liberated at elevated temperature in contact with
aqueous solvent. Accordingly, dehydration is required to produce a CO2 stream that is
compatible with compression, dense-phase transport (if applicable), and injection operations. In
practice, dehydration is commonly implemented in combination with compression: interstage
cooling during multi-stage CO2 compression condenses and removes additional water, followed
by a dedicated dehydration unit to meet the final moisture specification. Dehydration
technologies used in CCUS service commonly include triethylene glycol (TEG) contactors
and/or molecular sieve systems, sometimes in series, with upstream protection (e.g., coalescers
or guard beds) to limit solvent/impurity impacts on the dehydration media (Kemper et al. 2014).
For CO2 transport and injection system integrity, the target water content is typically very low to
minimize corrosion risk and to avoid hydrate-related operability issues under compression and
pipeline/injection conditions. A commonly cited design target for “dry” CO2 in CCUS transport
service is on the order of less than 50 ppmv water, with the final specification set by the chosen
operating pressure–temperature envelope and materials strategy (Cao et al. 2024).
After CO2 capture and dehydration, the conditioned product stream is expected to be a high-
purity, dry CO2 stream ready for compression and sequestration at depth in the Navajo Sandstone
(eolian strata). This study indicates that the Navajo Sandstone in the Iron Springs Mining District
is capable of storing at least 50 million tons of CO2. In terms of supply, based on Utah Iron’s
estimates of unmined ore and planned operations, the project anticipates capturing approximately
750,000 t CO2/yr, with a source lifetime exceeding 30 yr.

 Storage Resource Assessment
A storage resource assessment was completed for the Neck of the Desert area adjacent to the Iron
Springs mining district using the National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL) CO2-
SCREEN tool (Goodman et al. 2020). The assessment area covers 104.4 km² (Figure 150) and
was selected to represent the portion of the Navajo Sandstone storage complex relevant to Utah
Iron’s planned CO2 sequestration project. The CO2-SCREEN workflow was implemented as a
probabilistic (distribution-based) volumetric assessment, with key geologic inputs populated
from the project geological model. Specifically, the model provided the reservoir thickness and
porosity statistics for the Navajo Sandstone, as well as representative pressure and temperature
conditions used to characterize in situ CO2 behavior.

 Dynamic Numerical Simulation
 Simulation Model Development and Setup
A dynamic numerical simulation model was constructed from the geological model and executed
in Eclipse (https://www.slb.com/products-and-services/innovating-in-oil-and-gas/reservoir-
performance/reservoir-simulation/eclipse-reservoir-simulation-software). The simulation domain
covers approximately 22.0 km by 14.4 km and uses the same grid architecture as the geological
model (123 by 128 by 25 cells; 393,600 active cells). The intent of matching the geological and
simulation grids was to minimize grid translation effects and avoid introducing additional
uncertainty from a second upscaling step. Accordingly, porosity and permeability properties
from the geological model were applied directly to the simulation grid.
Relative permeability for the Navajo Sandstone was assigned using core-derived data measured
on Navajo Sandstone samples from the Covenant field by the Rocky Mountain CarbonSAFE
Phase I project (DE-FE0029280; Figure 151).

Figure 151 Relative permeability measured on Navajo Sandstone core from the Covenant oil field
Boundary conditions were specified as open along all lateral model boundaries and closed at the
top and bottom. This configuration approximates laterally extensive flow within the Navajo
Sandstone while restricting vertical mass exchange outside the modeled stratigraphic interval.
The model was initialized under hydrostatic conditions with brine salinity set to 200,000 ppm.
Figure 152 shows the initial pressure distribution at the top of the Navajo Sandstone.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 152 Initial pressure at the top of the Navajo Sandstone

 Injection Scenarios Evaluated
Three candidate injection locations were evaluated (Well #1a, Well #1b, and Well #1c; Figure
152). These sites were selected within the portion of the 2D seismic coverage exhibiting the most
coherent and laterally continuous reflectors, interpreted to indicate well-defined stratigraphy and
favorable storage conditions. Among the three sites, the Well #1a location is associated with the
most continuous and interpretable stratigraphic character.
Four injection scenarios were simulated. All scenarios include 30 yr of active CO2 injection
followed by a 50-yr postinjection site care (PISC) period, for a total simulation duration of 80 yr
(2024–2104). Two injection rates were evaluated at Well #1a, while only the higher rate was
evaluated at Well #1b and Well #1c. The four cases are as follows:
    1.    Well #1a, 36,649 Mscf/d (0.704 Mt CO2/yr), 30-yr injection (21.1 Mt case)
    2.    Well #1a, 81,442.3 Mscf/d (1.56 Mt CO2/yr), 30-yr injection (50 Mt case)
    3.    Well #1b, 81,442.3 Mscf/d (1.56 Mt CO2/yr), 30-yr injection (50 Mt case)
    4.    Well #1c, 81,442.3 Mscf/d (1.56 Mt CO2/yr), 30-yr injection (50 Mt case)

 CO2 Phase Partitioning and Trapping Behavior
CO2 phase behavior in the reservoir is consistent with expectations for deep saline aquifer
storage, with injected CO2 partitioning between a mobile/supercritical phase and a dissolved
phase in brine over time. The dissolved CO2 mass increases throughout both the injection and
post-injection periods (dashed lines in Figure 154), while the mass of supercritical CO2 increases
during injection and then decreases post-injection as dissolution progresses (solid lines in Figure
154).
