 Numerical Modeling Results Conclusion
Across all four scenarios, the modeled Navajo Sandstone injection interval demonstrates
sustained injectivity over 30 yr of injection without pressure-limited rate reduction, and the
 270

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

pressure response remains modest under both the 21.1 and 50 Mt scenarios. Differences among
the three candidate well locations are negligible at the modeled scale, suggesting that injectivity
performance is primarily controlled by the regional reservoir framework and boundary condition
assumptions rather than by local variations among the tested sites. CO2 partitioning indicates
progressive dissolution over time, with approximately 19% of injected CO2 dissolved in the
lower-rate scenario and approximately 16% to 18% dissolved in the higher-rate scenarios by the
end of the 80-yr simulation, consistent with expected trapping evolution in a deep saline aquifer
setting.

 Plume Analysis and AoR Delineation
CO2 plume footprint, plume growth rate, and the EPA Class VI AoR were evaluated to provide
an initial indication of permitting-relevant performance for the modeled injection scenarios.
Plume metrics were derived from the dynamic simulation results (Section 3.5), and AoR
delineations were developed using a hydrostatic underground source of drinking water (USDW)
protection basis consistent with EPA Class VI AoR and corrective action guidance.

 Plume Area Analysis
For all four scenarios, the CO2 plume area expands during the active injection period in an
approximately linear manner (Figure 155). After injection ceases, the plume footprint continues
to grow, but the rate of areal expansion decreases steadily as the plume approaches stabilization.
Consistent with this behavior, the post-injection rate of change falls to less than approximately
2% per year as plume growth tapers and the footprint asymptotically approaches a stable
maximum extent (Figure 155).

 271

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 155 CO2 plume area and change in area through time

Unlike the injectivity and pressure behavior described in Section 3.5, where differences among
the three candidate sites were minor, the plume footprint is strongly site dependent. The lower-
rate, 21.1 Mt scenario produces the smallest plume area, as expected. For the higher-rate (50 Mt)
scenarios, the final plume extent varies materially among Well #1a, Well #1b, and Well #1c,
indicating that local stratigraphic/structural differences and heterogeneity expressed in the model
have an impact on plume migration and areal containment. This finding reinforces the
importance of site selection and local subsurface characterization for plume management and
monitoring design.

To estimate zu (base of USDW), the base of the USDW was assumed to be 200 ft below ground

system that broadly follows topography (Figure 156). The depth to the injection interval (zi) was
computed by subtracting the DEM from the mapped top Navajo Sandstone surface. The reservoir
brine density (ρi) was extracted from the simulation initialization state (time step 0) for
consistency with the model’s fluid and salinity assumptions. The USDW density (ρu) was taken
as the average density of freshwater (62.37 lbm/ft³).

 Allowable Pressure Increase (ΔPu) Field
Using these inputs, an allowable pressure increase field (ΔPu) was calculated and mapped to the
Navajo Sandstone surface (Figure 157). The allowable pressure increase grows toward the head
of the valley nearer to Iron Mountain, reflecting increasing surface elevation while the Navajo
Sandstone remains comparatively flat over the modeled area. From a siting perspective, this
trend is favorable: locating injection closer to Iron Mountain increases the allowable pressure
increase before a USDW-protection threshold is exceeded.

Task 3 integrated legacy 2D seismic interpretation, well control from the ARCO Three Peaks #1
well, petrophysical data from cuttings/core and outcrop analyses, and screening- to simulation-
level modeling to evaluate CO2 storage feasibility in the Navajo Sandstone beneath the Iron
Mountain project area. Collectively, this workflow establishes a technical basis for injection
scenario design and Class VI relevant performance metrics (injectivity, pressure response, plume
footprint, and AoR extent), while also identifying the subsurface uncertainties that most strongly
control storage performance.
Seismic processing and interpretation demonstrate that the legacy 2D datasets can resolve key
structural and stratigraphic features, including imaging of the quartz monzonite laccolith
boundary along the better-quality lines. LANL’s RTM reprocessing and ML-assisted fault
detection further indicate that faults can be mapped on the improved images, supporting ongoing
refinement of the structural understanding; however, the limited 2D geometry and variable data
quality (particularly on Line GSI-SU-13) remain a fundamental constraint on confidently
defining a complete fault framework without additional 3D seismic coverage.
The Petrel geological model (built from the interpreted horizons and available petrophysical
constraints) provided the structural and property framework for screening and dynamic
simulation. CO2-SCREEN results for the 104.4 km² Neck of the Desert assessment area indicate
 283

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

a probabilistic storage resource ranging from 8.78 to 206.73 Mt, with a median (P50) estimate of
54.92 Mt, supporting multi-decade storage of Utah Iron’s anticipated captured CO2 volumes
under most plausible parameter combinations.
Dynamic simulations executed in Eclipse (30 yr injection plus 50 yr PISC) show sustained
injectivity without pressure-limited rate reduction under the modeled assumptions, for both the
anticipated operational-rate case (0.704 Mt/yr; 21.1 Mt total) and higher-rate stress-test cases
(1.56 Mt/yr; approximately 50 Mt total). The modeled pressure response remains modest across
all scenarios, with the maximum well-site pressure increase reaching about 130 psi in the
evaluated cases. CO2 trapping evolution is consistent with expectations for deep saline injection:
dissolution progresses throughout the simulation period, reaching about 19% dissolved in the
lower-rate scenario and between 16% and 18% dissolved in the higher-rate scenarios by the end
of the 80-yr modeled period.
CO2 Plume behavior is characterized by approximately linear areal growth during injection and a
decreasing post-injection growth rate as the plume stabilizes (with postinjection areal growth
declining to less than approximately 2% per year). Unlike the pressure response, which shows
minimal differences among the candidate sites at the modeled scale, final plume footprint is
distinctly site dependent, indicating that well placement and local stratigraphic/structural
variability can influence plume migration and therefore monitoring design.
Under the hydrostatic AoR framework applied here, the operational-rate case (21.1 Mt total
injected) produces no AoR because modeled pressure increases remain below the allowable
pressure increase across the modeled domain, an outcome that is favorable for the planned DRI
capture scale (0.75 Mt/yr). For the higher-rate cases, AoR footprints are present but remain
broadly comparable in magnitude to plume footprints, ranging from 5.30 to 10.58 mi2, with the
maximum AoR extent occurring at the Well #1b location.
Overall, all three sites are excellent candidates for CO2 sequestration of effluent from the
planned DRI plant, a positive picture for CCUS at the Iron Springs mine.

  Risk Assessment
The primary technical focus under Task 4 was induced seismicity risk, particularly related to the
Antelope Range Fault and other Basin-and-Range style normal faults in the vicinity of the
proposed storage complex.
McCormack compiled historical seismicity data and focal mechanisms from regional catalogs,
confirming a normal-fault dominated stress regime consistent with extension in southwestern
Utah. The state of stress at depth was estimated using stress gradients and coefficients from
published relationships, assuming that the least principal stress is near frictional failure and that
pore pressures are initially hydrostatic.
Using these stress models, the team developed probabilistic geomechanical analyses for the
Antelope Range Fault, treating fault dip and depth extent as key uncertain parameters. A Monte
Carlo approach, with multiple realizations over plausible dip scenarios, yielded Coulomb failure
function (CFF) distributions that show the fault system is within roughly 100 psi of frictional
failure under baseline conditions. This result implies that modest perturbations in pore pressure
or stress associated with CO2 injection could, in principle, bring portions of the fault to failure if
they hydraulically communicate with the storage interval.
 284

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The work concluded that induced seismicity risk at Iron Mountain is not prohibitive but is highly
sensitive to the precise geometry and connectivity of major faults, as well as to the true in-situ
stress state. These findings emphasize the importance of improved imaging and characterization
of the Antelope Range Fault and related structures, as well as careful operational planning for
injection rates and pressure management. Subtask 4.1 was reported as complete by early 2024,
with results prepared for publication and for inclusion in the project’s final report.

 Constraining Induced Seismicity Hazard on the Neck of the Desert
 Fault for the Proposed Iron Mountain, Utah, Carbon Sequestration
 Project
As significantly more focus is placed on carbon sequestration as a means to help mitigate the
progression of climate change, the need to adequately characterize an injection target for its
induced seismicity potential becomes more apparent. In the Iron Mountain project in southern
Utah, a single fault is identified in the Neck of the Desert near Iron Mountain. The dip of the
fault is unknown, and the geomechanical stability of the fault (i.e., distribution of CFFs) is highly
dependent upon the dip. For some dips, such as 15°, the hazard from injection is low. For other
dips, such as 75°, the hazard is high. Another key consideration is the depth of penetration of the
fault. Should the fault not penetrate the stress and pressure perturbed region from injection, it
will not be induced to fail. Thus, understanding the dip and the depth of penetration of the fault
will greatly improve our understanding of the likelihood of inducing an earthquake.

The process of reducing iron typically requires heating the ore to high temperatures (>1,000 °F),
but the technique of DRI uses a syngas to catalyze the reduction process at lower temperatures
(Anameric and Kawatra 2007). A byproduct of this reaction is CO2. The Iron Mountain iron
mine in southern Utah will upgrade its reduction facilities to use this process and is actively
seeking an environmentally sound means to dispose of the CO2 waste. Geologic carbon
sequestration has been proposed in the Navajo Sandstone at a depth of roughly 6,300 ft in the
Neck of the Desert near the mine. Federally funded characterization efforts for the subsurface in
the region of interest are being undertaken by a consortium of universities, private industry, and
national labs.
One element of the characterization is the assessment of induced seismicity potential. While
carbon sequestration has yet to induce a damaging earthquake, the largest was possibly a
magnitude 4.4 in the Cogdell oilfield in Texas (Gan and Frohlich 2013; White and Foxall 2016),
the potential exists for more potent events, especially as more projects become funded. To ensure
that the social license to operate subsurface injection projects remains intact, it is essential to do
an initial assessment of the potential for seismicity (Vilarrasa et al. 2019; Templeton et al. 2023).
This paper illustrates the methodology applied to the LiDAR-identified Neck of the Desert fault,
using probabilistic Mohr-Coulomb theory, and demonstrates that the hazard of the fault is highly
dependent on the dip, which is a difficult parameter to constrain.

 Past Seismicity
Prior to initiating injection projects, it is important to examine the seismic activity in the region.
Figure 166 shows the recorded seismic events on instruments from the United States Geological

 285

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Survey between October 1998 and October 2023 (25 yr). In total, there are 831 events in the
region, and they concentrate in the Cedar Valley. To the west, in the Neck of the Desert, there
are fewer events recorded, but seismicity is still present. The inset of Figure 166 shows that the
maximum magnitude event was 4.1 with a magnitude of completion of the catalog of roughly
1.5. The majority of the events have magnitudes below 2.0 although larger events are also
present. Of note as well is the geologically mapped Antelope Range Fault in the western portion
of the study area, which does not appear to have been seismically active in the last 25 yr. The
degree of seismicity present in the Neck of the Desert and the surrounding area, especially the
Cedar Valley, should be considered carefully by the project team as they develop their injection
plan.

Figure 166 A map of the past seismicity in the Neck of the Desert and surrounding regions. The inset shows a
Gutenberg–Richter plot of the 831 events depicted on the map.

 Input Parameters

 Fault Location, Size, and Orientation
The first input parameter of the characterization is the fault geometry. This has been inferred
from LiDAR data collected by the UGS. While it is open to interpretation, the data indicate that a
fault striking at roughly 10 ? cuts through the target location for the injection (Figure 167). We
term this fault the Neck of the Desert fault. Other faults may exist in the region but are not
expressed at the surface. Some researchers have demonstrated that often faults that host large,

 286

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

induced events, such as the Pawnee Mw 5.8 event, are not capable of being detected beforehand
(Brocher et al. 2015; Kolawale et al. 2019). The hazard associated with such faults cannot be
fully mitigated (Templeton et al. 2023), but in the event that there is a large, known fault oriented
close to failure relative to the stress field, the project team needs to be made aware of the hazard.
Should the project proceed, extra efforts must be made to avoid pressurizing the problematic
fault. Therefore, although not every fault can be detected prior to injection, those faults that can
must be scrutinized for their ability to host large earthquakes. Also, the Neck of the Desert fault
appears to transect the proposed injection site, which could be problematic for storage regardless
of seismic potential.

Figure 167 LiDAR data in the region of interest. The black arrows point to the inferred fault studied in this paper.

 287

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The surface trace of the Neck of the Desert fault is several miles long, yet the subsurface
structure is unknown. For the purposes of being conservative, this paper assumes that the fault
reaches to the depth of the Navajo Sandstone (the injection reservoir), the top of which is
roughly 6,290 ft deep. This assumption, however, is critical. Should the depth of penetration of
the fault not reach the region around the injection, it will unlikely host an induced event. Soliva
et al. (2008) indicated that in most normal faults, the surface extent typically is larger when the
depth of penetration is larger. Therefore, the large surface extent of the fault implies a deeper
depth of penetration, but more data is needed before we can ascertain if it reaches the Navajo
Sandstone.
The strike of the fault is roughly 10°, but the dip is unconstrained. Given its location at the edge
of the Basin and Range, it is reasonable to assume that this is a low-angle normal fault (Wernicke
1981), but we do not limit our investigation by this possibility. Instead, we analyze the fault for a
suite of possible dips ranging from 0° to 90°.

 Pore Pressure
There is not sufficient information to determine the pore pressure at depth in the Neck of the
Desert region. Therefore, we make the assumption that the pore pressure is nearly hydrostatically
pressured, which is not always a valid assumption in deep sedimentary formations, but when the
sedimentation rate is slow, hydrostatic conditions are common (Zhang 2011). As a result, we
assume that there is error in our assumption of hydrostatic pore pressure, but not to the degree
that it obfuscates the analysis.

 Coefficient of Friction
Geologic materials have been seen to have coefficients of friction between 0.6 and 0.8 (Dieterich
1972). Other authors have shown coefficients as high as 1.0 (Dieterich and Conrad 1984).
Byerlee (1978) showed that a value of 0.6 describes most materials, so we elect to use this value
as the mean of our distribution for the coefficient of friction.

 Maximum Horizontal Stress Direction
The maximum horizontal principal stress direction is often considered to be a function of
tectonics and physiographic provinces (Zoback and Zoback 1980). In our case, we obtain this
parameter from regional maps (Snee and Zoback 2022). The closest indicators are within roughly
100 mi and agree on a measurement of roughly 40° of azimuth.

 Principal Stresses
The vertical stress is assumed to have a gradient of 1.07 psi/ft. This value is observed in the
Paradox Basin about a hundred miles to the east of the Neck of the Desert (McCormack et al.
2023). The vertical stress is typically measured with density logs, which are not present for this
region. Thus, we need to use the nearby proxy of the Paradox Basin.
The least horizontal principal stress is calculated using frictional faulting equilibrium (Zoback
2007). This calculation assumes the same coefficient of friction of 0.6. The assumption here is
that the stress in the earth cannot fall below the threshold because well-oriented faults will slip,
relaxing the stress. Furthermore, the assumption that the earth is close to critically stressed in

 288

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

most regions (Townend and Zoback 2000) indicates that the least horizontal stress will not
greatly exceed this threshold.
The maximum horizontal principal stress is calculated using Simpson’s coefficient method
(McCormack et al. 2023). This method takes the Simpson’s coefficient from regional maps
(Snee and Zoback 2022) to approximate a lower bound for the maximum horizontal principal
stress by using the pore pressure and the equation of frictional faulting equilibrium for a normal
faulting environment. Normal faulting is essential for this method to work, and in the Neck of the
Desert, the vertical stress appears to be the maximum stress as determined from regional maps.
The model of the stress state that we use is show in Figure 168.

Figure 168 The stress state obtained from the Simpson’s coefficient method.
 The stress state is a model that suffers from the lack of available data. We use hydrostatic pore
pressure, and a Simpson’s coefficient value of 0.6 to obtain this model. If additional data were
available, such as core data, diagnostic fracture injection test data, or image logs, the state of
stress could be more reliably constrained. Nonetheless, this simple model represents the best of
our knowledge, and can be used in the subsequent analyses of the hazard of induced seismicity.

 Methodology
After choosing distributions for the input parameters, the next step in the probabilistic
geomechanics workflow is to sample from each distribution in a Monte Carlo fashion and
propagate the realizations through a geomechanical model (Walsh and Zoback 2016;
McCormack et al. 2022). Figure 169 shows the Mohr circles of this forward propagation on
twenty realizations out of twenty thousand for six scenarios of the dip: uniform, 15°, 30°, 45°,
60°, and 75°. These values are chosen to elucidate the difference in the final distribution of CFFs
that results in different input distributions for the dip. The direction of dip, that is, east or west,
 289

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

was also tested but was found to have a minimal impact. The minimal impact is due to the
similarity between the strike and the direction of maximum horizontal principal stress.

Figure 169 Probabilistic Mohr circles for the six scenarios of dip. a) uniform dip, b) 15 dip, c) 30 dip, d) 45 dip,
e) 60 dip, and f) 75 dip. The bold lines represent the mean values for the stresses and the coefficienct of friction.

 Results
The distributions of the CFFs for each of the six scenarios of dip are shown in Figure 170. There
is a clear dependence of the distributions of the CFFs on the dip. In the case of the uniform dip
ranging from 0° to 90°, the distribution has the highest standard deviation as more possible
orientations are sampled. As the sampling becomes narrower in the subsequent dip distributions,
the resulting distributions of the CFF also become narrower. The lower the mean dip, the lower
the CFF due to the relation between the fault orientation and the stress state, and conversely,
when the mean dip is higher, the hazard is also higher. The mean of the CFF distribution for the
uniform dip input and the 45° dip input is similar because the mean of the uniform distribution is
also 45°. The difference is sampling a narrower normal distribution in the 45° case versus a
wider uniform distribution. We do not analyze a dip of 90° because as a normal fault, it is
unrealistic for the dip to be that high.

 290

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 170 Six distributions of Coulomb failure functions using six different inputs of the dip of the Neck of the
Desert fault

 Discussion
The difference between the CFF distributions for the different mean dips underscores the
importance of constraining this parameter. Seismic surveys, especially 3D surveys, have the
potential to vastly improve our understanding of the orientation of the Neck of the Desert fault
(Gibson et al. 2005; Bahorich and Farmer 1995). Currently, there is substantial work in the
literature to use ML to automatically detect faults in 3D seismic volumes, which may elucidate
additional features that should be analyzed in the same manner as the Neck of the Desert fault
(Li et al. 2022; Bi et al. 2021; Wang et al. 2018).
In addition to seismic surveys, geologic inference can also constrain the orientation of the faults.
Cross sections such as that in Rowley and Barker (1978) can inform which dips are more likely
to be present in the larger faults, such as the Neck of the Desert fault. While geologic inference is
not as reliable as seismic surveys, it is a reasonable first approach to narrow the breadth of the
investigation.
The relative sensitivities of the different input parameters in the model are shown for the uniform
dip distribution in Figure 171. These sensitivities clearly show the importance of the dip, but
other parameters such as the coefficient of friction or the principal stresses also have an impact.

 291

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Additional data will further improve the uncertainty in the input parameters. Specifically,
laboratory tests of friction, in situ measurements of least principal stress, direct borehole
measurements of pore pressure, borehole failures related to the direction of the maximum
horizontal principal stress, as well as a more detailed, site-specific understanding of the
Simpson’s coefficient will all benefit the analysis.

Figure 171 The sensitivity of the Coulomb failure function to each of the input parameters in the uniform
distribution of dip. The dip is the most sensitive.
The hazard associated with the Neck of the Desert fault is dependent on whether or not it reaches
depths of the injection. Around the injection there is a 3D region, which possesses elevated pore
pressures, and around that region, there is another volume, which possesses altered stresses due
to poroelasticity (Detournay and Cheng 1993). If the fault does not interact with these regions,
the hazard is significantly lessened. Also, the fault can only provide a conduit for the escape of
CO2 or migration of brine if it intersects the Navajo Sandstone. Therefore, it is important to
assess the depth of penetration of this major fault.
The major faults are not the only faults that may be induced to fail in the event of the injection of
the CO2. Smaller faults, even so small that they cannot be detected, can also host microseismic
events. In an EOR field in Texas, Qin et al. (2023) showed that the preponderance of earthquakes
were relatively small magnitude and concentrated in certain layers of higher density of fractures.

 292

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Thus, it is important that the subsurface is fully characterized to avoid fractures that may host
microseismicity near the caprock because that could denigrate the integrity of the seal.

Using the available data at the Neck of the Desert proposed carbon sequestration site, we have
detailed the hazard along an identified fault that cuts the proposed injection site. Even in the
event that the fault is not close to failure, it may have implications for the ability to store the
carbon because it may provide a pathway for leakage. A key consideration both in terms of
seismicity and leakage is the depth to which the fault penetrates. Both the depth of penetration
and the dip of the fault are, at present, highly uncertain. The hazard of the fault failing is higher
for higher dips and conversely, lower for lower dips. Further characterization is required to
understand how problematic the Neck of the Desert fault might be for the proposed injection.

  Nontechnical Issues / Scenario Analysis
Task 5 activities addressed pipeline routing, non-technical risks, and the broader policy and
outreach context for Iron Mountain.

Carbon Solutions and MSU used the CostMAP and SimCCS toolchain to explore pipeline
routing between the Utah Iron plant and candidate injection sites. Cost surfaces incorporated land
cover, slope, population density, roads, railways, rivers, transmission lines, and the plant
boundary, and distinguished barriers from potential corridors. An early analysis considered
multiple candidate source–sink combinations and produced optimal pipeline alignments in a
multi-source/multi-sink framework. Subsequent work explicitly incorporated Utah Iron rights-of-
way, testing how strongly weighting these corridors in the cost surface alters the optimal route.
This demonstrated that preferential use of existing rights-of-way can significantly reroute
pipelines in the near-plant vicinity while leaving distal route segments largely unchanged.

The same workflow was then applied to “Plan B” injection sites located north of the primary Iron
Mountain site, including candidate locations in the Escalante Desert and west of Parowan. New
cost surfaces and pipeline routes were generated, and digital well logs were acquired for at least
two of the alternate storage sites to begin evaluating their subsurface suitability. This pipeline-
routing and scenario-analysis framework is designed to be reused and refined in future phases as
additional storage sites or capacity expansion options are considered.

On the policy and regulatory side, the project benefitted from significant progress within the
state of Utah. Earlier legislation established a carbon sequestration liability fund and a pathway
for eventual transfer of long-term liability to the state. During the project period, Utah passed
additional CCS legislation (e.g., a Carbon Capture Amendments bill) that clarified aspects of
long-term liability and financial assurance for Class VI projects. In parallel, the Utah Division of
Oil, Gas and Mining advanced work on a state Class VI rule and preparations for seeking Class
VI primacy from EPA. Project personnel were engaged in these discussions, ensuring that the
technical work at Iron Mountain is aligned with the emerging regulatory framework that will
ultimately govern a Class VI application and 45Q claims.

 293

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Outreach and non-technical risk activities included field trips for the UGS Advisory Board to
Iron Mountain, presentations at scientific conferences (Geological Society of America [GSA],
American Association of Petroleum Geologists [AAPG] Rocky Mountain Section, American
Geophysical Union [AGU], and Seismological Society of America [SSA]), and invited talks on
Utah’s emerging CCS portfolio. These efforts raised awareness of the Iron Mountain project
among scientists, regulators, and the public, and helped position the site within the broader
context of Utah’s decarbonization strategy.

Formal economic assessments and detailed analyses of water rights, land and pore-space
ownership, and long-term liability were largely deferred to future phases, but the groundwork
laid through policy engagement and scenario analysis will facilitate those efforts.

 Transport and Rights of Way
The goal of Subtask 5.1 is to build a cost surface for the vicinity of the Iron Mountain site to
support identifying feasible pipeline transport corridors. Geospatial data was used to assess the
economic viability of pipeline routing. Existing rights of way owned by Utah Iron were
incorporated into the cost surface to reduce the logistical and economic burdens of pipeline
routing. In particular, the team focused on pipeline routes that will transport captured CO2 from
the Iron Mountain capture site to nearby possible sequestration sites. This subtask is a key
component of ensuring the economic and logistical feasibility of the Iron Mountain CCS effort.
To aid the construction of a cost surface to be used in the subsequent economic analysis, the
team performed a preliminary transport and rights of way analysis using CostMAPPRO (Carbon
Solutions 2025a). An area of interest was first identified that includes possible CO2 storage sites
along with the planned CO2 source, Utah Iron (Figure 172).

 Economic Assessment
The goal of Subtask 5.2 is to assess the economic implications of the proposed CCUS project.
During the project, the team focused on exploring the most economically viable routing of CO2
pipelines subject to various assumptions. Economic information related to pipeline routing was
embedded in the cost surface constructed during Subtask 5.1. Cheapest pipeline routes were
identified using SimCCSPRO which implements a shortest path network construction scheme. The
assumptions considered in this analysis included both the weighting of right of way priorities and
contingency storage location planning.
The team explored two different ways of incorporating existing Utah Iron rights of way into the
pipeline routing. The first was to merely add new rights of way to the existing cost surface while
maintaining the weights normally allocated for right of ways. The second was to heavily bias the
cost surface weights to prioritize using right of ways whenever possible. Cost surfaces for both
of these options were generated. To test the effect of the two options on pipeline routing,
cheapest pipeline routes were calculated by SimCCSPRO in the cost surfaces between the
anticipated capture location and the primary targeted storage location. The two paths generated
are seen in Figure 178.

 298

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 178 Optimal pipeline routs through cost surfaces with differing rights of way prioritization
The source location is the circle near the plant boundary shape and the storage location is the
circle to the north. The tan source-to-storage path is the cheapest pipeline route generated
through the cost surface where rights of way carry the default weight. The grey source-to-storage
path is the cheapest pipeline route generated through the cost surface where rights of way are
heavily prioritized. It can be seen that the grey path minimizes the distance travelled off of right
of ways. Note that the jagged nature of the paths is due to the raster nature of the cost surface.
The result of this exercise is to show that the Utah Iron designated right of ways have the
potential to influence pipeline routing.
The team explored pipeline routes to alternate injection sites (Parowan site and Beaver Valley
site) that was identified to the north of the primary injection site. Two new surfaces with a
revised extent, beyond the initial area of interest, to include the new alternate injection sites were
constructed to support this analysis. The first cost surface employed standard weighting
techniques for rights of way prioritization. The second cost surface heavily biased routing to
prioritize the existing rights of way owned by Utah Iron.
These new cost surfaces were used to calculate minimum cost pipeline routes between the
capture location at Utah Iron and the alternate injection sites. Figure 179 shows the pipeline
routes generated by SimCCSPRO, where the purple route is the route that uses standard weighting
of rights of way and the green route is the route that heavily biases routing towards existing
rights of way. The routes differ in the vicinity of Utah Iron, where the existing rights of way are
highly prioritized. Outside of the Utah Iron vicinity, the routes coincide.

The analysis conducted as part of Subtask 5.2 demonstrated that leveraging existing rights of
way could be a critical factor in determining CO2 pipeline transport networks for the project. The
ability to prioritize these corridors could reduce potential delays and logistical challenges
associated with securing new land for pipeline routing. Additionally, the exploration of
alternative storage locations provides a flexible, cost-effective contingency plan, ensuring the
project can remain economically viable even in the face of unforeseen challenges. This is
particularly true given the colocation of pipelines to the two alternate storage locations.

 Site Characterization for Geologic Carbon Storage of CO2 from a Direct
 Reduced Iron Plant
Decarbonizing the industrial sector of our economy to meet climate goals and slow climate
change is a challenging prospect. To meet these goals, industrial plants that process ethanol,
fertilizer, cement, and iron and steel will need to either decarbonize or capture and sequester
their CO2 emissions. The primary objective of this study is decarbonization of iron processing
through DRI with CCS, in place of a traditional blast furnace. Iron ore is reduced to elemental
iron by exposing the ore to a high-temperature (800–1,200 °C) syngas (H2 and CO) in a reactor
vessel. The reaction releases CO2, water, and unreacted syngas. The CO2 and water are separated
and unreacted syngas is recycled back into the reactor. This separation results in a source of low
pressure, wet, nearly pure CO2 that may be dried, compressed, transported and injected for
permanent geologic sequestration or used for other industrial needs.
This analysis is a case study (“focus project”) under the auspices of CUSP (DOE Award DE-
FE0031837). We are assessing the carbon storage potential of local subsurface geology near a
proposed DRI plant in southern Utah. The primary objectives of this focused project include: (1)
rigorous site characterization and analysis of storage capacity, risks and economic options for
CCS, (2) a detailed plan for drilling a stratigraphic well and performing a 3D seismic survey, and
(3) comprehensive plans for assembling UIC Class VI and 45Q tax credit applications. The
targeted reservoir formation is the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone at about a 6,200-ft depth, which is
stratigraphically overlain by potential sealing units of evaporite-rich Jurassic Temple Cap and
limestone/mudstone-dominated Carmel Formations which, in certain areas, were intruded
approximately 22 Ma by several thousand feet of quartz monzonite laccolith. Preliminary
analysis indicate that the Navajo Sandstone in this area is capable of storing at least 15 million
tons of CO2.
A goal of this study is to facilitate decision making needed to implement commercial-scale
geologic carbon storage at a DRI facility. Demonstration of CCS with an iron-processing plant
has not been attempted to date, and a goal is to provide a meaningful example for other iron and
steel plants.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 180 American Geophysical Union (AGU) 2022 poster

 • Project progress was presented at the CUSP Annual Meeting in 2023 in the form of a
 poster highlighting the work done.

• AAPG 2023 conference presentation by UGS

 Basin Analysis and Reservoir Characterization for Subsurface Geologic
 Carbon (CO2) Sequestration Associated with a Direct Reduced Iron Plant,
 Iron County, UT
The Iron Springs district in southwestern Utah is one of the largest iron producing regions in the
western United States. A local mine recently proposed building a DRI plant to optimize their
operations and increase the domestic supply of steel. Funded by the DOE (Award DE-
FE0031837), we are conducting rigorous site characterization to assesses the CO2 sequestration
potential of subsurface geologic strata near the proposed plant to accommodate carbon-rich
byproducts on a commercial scale. The region possesses world-class reservoir/seal packages at
depths suitable for CO2 storage and lacks evidence of an active petroleum system which lowers
the risk of occluded pore space and overpressure, but considerable geologic uncertainty remains
due to complex and poorly constrained subsurface conditions. Our characterization leverages
geological and geophysical data to assess CO2 reservoir and seal quality and drilling hazards.
Primary injection targets lie within eolian sequences of the Jurassic Navajo Sandstone (porosity
15%; permeability 156 mD), overlain by stacked confining units that include anhydrite-carbonate
beds in the Temple Cap Formation (Manganese Wash Member) and gypsiferous shale and
limestone of the Carmel Formation (Co-Op Creek Member), which itself was intruded by the
Three Peaks quartz monzonite. Locally, the Navajo Sandstone lies entirely in the subsurface and
preliminary thin section petrography work on cuttings samples from the ARCO Three Peaks #1
well reveals a range of lithofacies and fabrics that appear promising for CO2 storage. Reservoir
analog data from nearby outcrop exhibit a range of structural and depositional realms rock
mechanics and petrographic data from these locations provide potential end-member values for
reservoir quality. Attribute analysis of reprocessed 2D seismic data indicates laterally continuous
subsurface reflectors and viable structural, stratigraphic, and volcano-stratigraphic trap styles,
suggesting favorable reservoir / seal presence and continuity. A new gravity survey reveals an
intrusive sealing unit with greater volume and more complex geometry than previously
identified. Each of these data inputs will be combined into a geomodel to simulate flow and CO2
storage potential. This study highlights how integrated basin analysis and reservoir
characterization can provide key inputs for site selection and facility design, a first step on the
path toward onsite CO2 sequestration for industrial projects.
• The final project results were presented at the CUSP Annual meeting 2024.
Slides are available on the CUSP website.

 Preliminary Assessment of Possible Stratigraphic Well and
 3D Seismic Survey
Although no stratigraphic test well or 3D seismic survey was drilled or acquired under this
focused project, substantial planning and costing work was completed.
For the 3D seismic survey, the team obtained a detailed proposal from Explor (Calgary, AB) for
a high-density survey of approximately 15 to 16 mi2 north of the mine, using micro-vibrator
source technology and dense receiver and source spacing. The proposed design, with trace
 305

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

density corresponding to roughly 33-ft bin sizes and more than four million traces, would
provide finely resolved images of the upper crustal structure, including the geometry of the
laccolith and major faults, and would be well-suited to both structural interpretation and
advanced fault detection workflows.
In parallel, preliminary engineering and cost estimates were assembled for a stratigraphic test
well located just north of the mine. This work, led by project staff working with multiple
vendors, outlined requirements for rig mobilization, drilling, coring, logging, and laboratory
testing. While no contracts were executed, this bid package provides a ready-to-implement plan
that could be activated in a future CarbonSAFE phase once funding is available.

 Assemble Engineering Design Plans and Budget for Seismic
 Survey(s)
A 3D seismic survey was designed by Explor. The “Iron Mountain 3D Seismic Acquisition
Proposal” is a turnkey acquisition plan for collecting a high-density 3D seismic survey to support
geologic evaluation of CO2 storage potential near the Iron Mountain mining facility (Neck of the
Desert / Iron Springs area), see Figure 182. The proposal scope is a 15.5 mi2 3D survey designed
to address complex near-surface conditions while also attempting to image as deep as
practicable, including requested maximum offsets of approximately 9,000 ft.

Figure 182 Proposed 3D seismic survey acquisition area

 306

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The project setting is characterized as a Basin and Range physiographic/ecological context (EPA
Level III Central Basin and Range, near boundaries with adjacent ecoregions; Level IV
“Woodland and Shrub-Covered Low Mountains”). It notes the southern portion of the survey
area lies on a flat valley plain with ephemeral drainage and good access and is therefore well
suited to efficient high-density vibroseis acquisition.
The recommended acquisition design is an “all-live” high-density 3D geometry (every receiver
records every source point) intended to maximize offset and azimuth distribution and improve
imaging and seismic attribute reliability. Key proposed parameters include receiver line interval
330 ft and receiver station interval 66 ft with source line interval 330 ft and source point interval
66 ft. This would give approximately 20,000 receiver nodes deployed “all live” and
approximately 20,000 vibroseis source points on about a 33 ft × 33 ft bin size fully populated
across azimuths and offsets. The nearest far-offset near-offset on any source point would be 233
ft with an estimated total traces on the order of about 400 million (reported as approximately 10
million traces/km² at all offsets). The proposal indicates single-vibe, single-sweep operations
with independent simultaneous sweeping using nodes, and 24-hour source operations to improve
efficiency.
Operationally, Explor proposes using its IntelliSeis system (a GIS-enabled dashboard and project
hub; Explor) to support survey design, stakeless deployment, near-real-time tracking, QC, and
KPI analytics accessible to the client and stakeholders during execution (Figure 183). The
proposal emphasizes flexibility to adapt to changing field conditions through stakeless methods
and integrated positioning/timing workflows.

 Assemble Engineering Design Plans and Budget for Stratigraphic
 Well
The engineering design basis for the stratigraphic well was established to obtain the subsurface
datasets required to evaluate storage feasibility and to support future characterization and Class
VI permitting. The design integrated drilling, coring, mud logging, and wireline logging
requirements into a single operational program, and then translated that program into a budget
with vendor-backed costs for the major services.
According to project engineering and service-provider quote packages prepared in June and July
2023 (rig, mobilization, drilling bits/fluids, mud logging, coring, and wireline logging), the
stratigraphic well engineering design and budget were assembled to support a deep
characterization well near Iron Mountain with (1) continuous core across target storage and seal
intervals, (2) comprehensive open hole logging and formation testing for reservoir and caprock
evaluation, and (3) cemented casing strings designed to enable safe drilling through the USDW
interval and reliable isolation of deeper sections

 Wellbore Architecture and Drilling Approach
The planned well configuration utilized a staged hole-and-casing architecture to (1) set shallow
conductor casing for near-surface stability, (2) isolate the USDW interval behind cemented
surface casing, and (3) drill deeper intermediate/production-size intervals suitable for coring and
open hole logging. A representative staged design (used for drilling bit estimation and consistent
with the planned deep characterization objective) included: 20-in hole to approximately 120 ft
(roller cone), 12-1/4 in hole to approximately 1,500 ft, 8-1/2 in hole to approximately 8,500 ft,
and 6-1/8-in hole to approximately 12,500 ft (multiple polycrystalline diamond compact [PDC]
bits planned for the deeper intervals). The staged concept was selected specifically to support
large-diameter casing through shallow zones and then maintain a stable borehole at depth that
could be easily logged and cored.

 Rig Selection and Execution Readiness
A trailer-mounted drilling package with deep capacity and a modern top drive system was
selected for budgeting and execution planning. The IronHand Rig 118 package was quoted with
a 25,000-ft depth rating, 750,000-lb hook load, a TDS-11SA top drive, dual F-1600 mud pumps,
and supporting solids-control and tubular-handling equipment. Commercial terms included a
daywork drilling rate and defined standby/mobilization-related conditions, which were rolled
into the drilling cost model used for the budget.

 Coring and Sample Acquisition Program
Continuous core was treated as a primary project deliverable and therefore a primary cost driver.
The coring program was budgeted using a dedicated coring provider, with pricing structured
around (1) core acquisition, (2) core handling, and (3) core processing and ancillary services.
The ProCoring (a division of ProDirectional; Conroe, TX) estimate provided a total coring-
services budget on the order of approximately $0.63 million, comprising a core acquisition
estimate of approximately $0.47 million and core processing of approximately $0.16 million
(with the understanding that final cost scales with final core footage, tool selection, and
downhole conditions). This coring scope was intentionally paired with a mud logging and sample
 308

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

management plan to ensure continuous lithologic description, gas monitoring, and chain-of-
custody documentation for core and cuttings. See Figure 184 for a coring diagram highlighting
the intervals being targeted.

Figure 184 Casing and coring design

 Mud Logging, HSE Spacing, and Operational Controls
Mud logging was included as a continuous safety and characterization function during drilling
and coring operations. The mud logging quote (Suttles Logging; Midland, TX) was structured as
a two-person computerized unit with a daily rate and standard adders (synthetic mud system
charge, communications, lodging, and one-time rig up/down trailer charges), and included
explicit safety placement requirements (e.g., logging unit located at least 100 ft from the
wellbore, flare line, and generators/diesel engines) to support safe operations on location.

 Wireline Logging and Formation Evaluation
Wireline logging was scoped to support reservoir quality, caprock integrity, geomechanics, and
fluid characterization objectives. Because logging suite selection strongly controls total cost,
multiple vendor quotes were obtained. The SLB (formerly Schlumberger; Houston, TX) RFP
package provided section-by-section grand totals (12-1/4-in, 8-1/2-in, and 6-1/8-in intervals) and
optional adders (e.g., certain specialty services). Halliburton (Houston, TX) and Baker Hughes
(Houston, TX) quotes provided alternative toolstring configurations and pricing, including
options that bundle more advanced formation testing and specialty measurements. The budget
consolidated these alternatives into a single “logging / fluid sampling / mini-fracs” line item
sized to capture a comprehensive formation evaluation program rather than a minimal triple-
combo log suite. See Table 35 and Table 36 for the logging plan for the Navajo and Kaibab
intervals respectively.

 Cementing and Zonal Isolation Design
Cementing costs were included explicitly in the budget to cover surface and intermediate casing

documented candidate additive systems (e.g., ThermaLock [Halliburton] / latex options and loss-

consistent with deep intermediate casing requirements and the associated pumping, blending, and
contingency needs typical for the anticipated drilling environment.

the budget included (1) pre-spud civil/site costs (survey, roads/pits, damages/ROW), (2) drilling

 Comprehensive Plan to Prepare and Submit UIC Class VI
 Application
Detailed work on the Class VI application plan (Task 7) was scheduled for later in the broader
CUSP program and did not proceed beyond preliminary planning within this focused project.
However, the technical outputs produced here, geological model, reservoir and seal property
datasets, induced seismicity risk assessment, and pipeline-routing scenarios, were developed
with an eye toward their eventual inclusion in a Class VI permit application.

The concurrent progress in Utah’s regulatory framework and efforts toward Class VI primacy
means that the Iron Mountain site, once fully characterized and modeled, will be well positioned
to move into formal permitting and tax-credit qualification.

The concurrent progress in Utah’s regulatory framework and efforts toward Class VI primacy
means that the Iron Mountain site, once fully characterized and modeled, will be well positioned
to move into formal permitting and tax-credit qualification.

 Integrated Outcomes and Site Readiness
Across its duration, the CUSP Iron Mountain Subsurface Characterization Focused Project
achieved its central objective: to move the Iron Mountain CO2 storage concept from a
reconnaissance-level idea to a technically grounded, partially modeled site with a clear path
toward a future CarbonSAFE Phase II/III.
The project produced a geological model that integrates well, outcrop, gravity, aeromagnetic, and
reprocessed seismic data into a coherent structural framework with facies and property modeling
appropriate for reservoir simulation. It generated a substantial rock-property database for both
reservoir and seal units, including porosity, permeability, capillary pressure, geomechanical
properties, and CO2 reactivity, derived from coordinated UGS, UU, and OGS/IC3 laboratory
programs. Preliminary dynamic simulations demonstrated that plausible injection scenarios of
0.5 to 1.0 Mt/yr over 20 yr yield compact CO2 plumes under the assumed reservoir conditions.
The induced seismicity work showed that major normal faults in the region, particularly the
Antelope Range Fault, may be close to frictional failure, underscoring the need for improved
structural imaging and careful pressure management, but did not reveal any fundamental barriers
to storage. Pipeline-routing and scenario analysis established how CO2 could be transported from
the plant to primary and alternate storage sites while leveraging existing rights-of-way. Policy
and outreach efforts kept the project aligned with an evolving state regulatory environment that
is increasingly supportive of CCUS.
Some key elements, most notably acquisition of a stratigraphic test well and 3D seismic survey,
fully coupled dynamic simulations with pressure and leakage risk analysis, and detailed Class VI
and 45Q plans, remain future work. Nevertheless, the integrated technical, modeling, and non-
technical outputs of this project provided a strong foundation from which a subsequent
CarbonSAFE Phase II project proposal was submitted and accepted by the DOE and is currently
under review. This project provided the key data and technical knowledge to make that
successful proposal a reality and will facilitate permitting and deployment of CO2 storage to
support low-carbon iron production at Iron Mountain.

CCS Hub 2.0 Concept for ONEOK: Infrastructure
Development for Handling of New Gaseous Products
for Natural Gas Liquids Fractionation and Gas
Processing Plants in Kansas and Oklahoma
The project team evaluated the feasibility of carbon capture and storage (CCS) at ONEOK’s
(Tulsa, OK) natural gas liquids (NGL) fractionation facilities in Bushton, KS, and Medford, OK.
In 2020 and 2021, the two sites combined emitted over 500,000 t of CO2 annually. Capturing and
geologically storing this CO2 presents an opportunity to reduce environmental impact, improve
facility economics, and establish eligibility for federal incentives under Section 45Q of the US
Tax Code (Credit…2022).
To support this goal, the team conducted geologic screening to identify subsurface formations
near the Bushton and Medford facilities that may be suitable for long-term CO2 storage. Initial
site assessments were followed by the development of static geocellular models, dynamic
simulations, and infrastructure planning, including conceptual routing for a CO2 transportation
network that considers land use, easements, and proximity to population centers.
Due to changes in site access and infrastructure planning at the Medford facility during the
project period, detailed field activities and site-specific permitting work were concentrated at the
Bushton location. However, preliminary modeling was still conducted for a Medford-area
reservoir based on available data.
Study conclusions:
• ONEOK’s Bushton NGL facility is a promising candidate for CCS development and
 regulatory planning.
• Two potential storage targets were identified at Bushton: the Lansing–Kansas City (LKC)
 and Arbuckle formations.
• Geocellular models were constructed for both Bushton targets, with simulations showing that
 while the LKC may offer secondary injection potential, the Arbuckle formation is more
 favorable as a primary target. Further coordination with nearby oil, gas, and water operators
 will be needed to mitigate potential subsurface interactions.
• A single geocellular model was also developed for the Wilcox–Bromide formation near
 Medford using publicly available and digitized data.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

This work provides a technical foundation for future development of a CO2 transportation and
sequestration facility in Kansas, with a focus on economic feasibility, integration with existing
midstream infrastructure, and alignment with regulatory pathways in Kansas.
Project accomplishments:
• Designed, deployed, and monitored a cost-effective seismic network in central Kansas,
 including the area surrounding the ONEOK Bushton facility.
• Constructed three subsurface geocellular property models: two at Bushton (LKC and
 Arbuckle) and one at Medford (Wilcox–Bromide).
• Conducted multiple simulation cases to assess CO2 injection behavior across modeled
 scenarios.
• Completed a comprehensive subsurface data audit, digitization effort, and integration of
 historical geologic and well data to support model development and risk analysis.

The Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP) Midstream Operator Storage of CO2
(MOSCO2) project aimed to address the annual CO2 production from ONEOK’s NGL
fractionation plants in Bushton, KS, and Medford, OK. The primary objective was to identify
and evaluate suitable subsurface reservoirs for the long-term geologic storage of captured CO2.
This work supports ONEOK’s ability to leverage US Internal Revenue Service (IRS) 45Q tax
credits, improve operational economics, and reduce its environmental footprint.
This technical report summarizes progress toward the primary objective, including reservoir
characterization, geomechanical and seismic risk analyses, dynamic simulation of injection
scenarios, and infrastructure network modeling. The report also includes preliminary work on
temporary on-site CO2 storage and integrated options to support the conceptual design of a CO2
transportation and sequestration facility, with potential future linkage to hydrogen production
emissions.
In 2021, the US Congress introduced the Storing CO2 and Lowering Emissions (SCALE) Act, a
bipartisan initiative designed to expand the deployment of carbon capture technologies and
reduce greenhouse gas emissions (Beck and Ross 2021). The act enhanced the existing Section
45Q tax credit by broadening eligibility criteria and improving financial incentives for CCS
projects. Under the revised provisions, the credit increased to $120/Mt for CO2 removed via
direct air capture and to $75 per ton for CO2 used in enhanced oil recovery (EOR) applications
(Ochu 2021). The legislation also introduced a direct-pay option, allowing developers to receive
the tax credit through annual returns without needing taxable income (Ochu 2021).
These expanded incentives have generated strong interest from industrial operators in pursuing
Class VI injection wells. To secure a Class VI permit, applicants must meet detailed site
characterization, well design, and monitoring requirements defined by the US Environmental
Protection Agency (EPA; EPA 2013). Permitted injection operations are contingent on
maintaining seismic activity below thresholds established through analysis of regional tectonic
setting, historical earthquake records, and baseline monitoring data (Templeton et al. 2022). The
report includes results from initial analyses of these factors.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 Objectives
This project aimed to evaluate the viability of long-term geologic storage of CO2 emissions from
ONEOK’s NGL fractionation plants at Bushton, KS, and Medford, OK, by identifying suitable
subsurface reservoirs near the emitting sites. A key driver was to support ONEOK’s eligibility
for US IRS 45Q tax credits, while simultaneously enhancing operational economics and reducing
environmental impact. In addition to evaluating permanent storage options, the project explored
the feasibility of temporary on-site CO2 storage prior to pipeline transport or injection.

 CCS-Specific Objectives
With the project’s CCS assessment ultimately focusing on the Bushton, KS, facility, the
technical and planning goals included:
1) Evaluate Potential CO2 Storage Reservoirs: Conduct preliminary characterization of
 subsurface formations near the Bushton NGL fractionator to assess their suitability for long-
 term CO2 storage. This included geological screening, early modeling, and petrophysical
 analysis to support future Class VI permitting.
2) Support UIC Class VI Permit Planning: Compile data and develop technical guidance to
 inform a future EPA UIC Class VI application, including site-specific inputs for reservoir
 integrity, injectivity, and area-of-review (AoR) delineation.
3) Assess 45Q Tax Credit Eligibility: Estimate potential CO2 volumes for capture and storage
 to determine whether anticipated emissions meet the threshold for federal tax credit
 qualification under IRS 45Q guidelines.
4) Support Planning for a CO2 Transportation and Sequestration Facility: Develop a
 conceptual design for a CO2 capture and delivery system that integrates emissions from
 multiple sources and supports long-term transport and storage.
5) Analyze Pipeline and Infrastructure Needs: Use SimCCSPRO (Carbon Solutions 2025)
 modeling software to evaluate optimal routing scenarios for new CO2 pipelines, considering
 existing infrastructure, surface constraints, and economic feasibility.
6) Explore Integration with Hydrogen Production: Consider synergies with future hydrogen
 generation facilities in the region, particularly the potential to co-manage CO2 emissions
 streams from multiple industrial sources.

 Scope of Work
This study evaluated the potential for long-term geologic storage of CO2 near ONEOK’s NGL
fractionation plants in Bushton, KS, and Medford, OK. The original project scope included
identification of suitable saline reservoirs, assessment of permitting pathways, and development
of monitoring strategies for CCS implementation.
To support project viability and tax credit eligibility under IRS 45Q, the study also investigated
opportunities to increase CO2 capture volumes, including the potential development of an
integrated capture and delivery system that leverages existing infrastructure, particularly the
NGL pipeline network. Essentially, the study provides a technical basis for establishing a CO2
transportation and sequestration facility.

 Task 2 – High-Level Technical Review
Task 2 provides the foundational technical screening necessary to evaluate the feasibility of CO2
storage at ONEOK’s midstream facilities, focusing on geological integrity, regulatory
compliance, and site-specific data readiness. Led by the KGS, this task integrated geologic,
engineering, risk, and infrastructure expertise across institutional partners, establishing the basis
for simulation, permitting, and risk analysis in subsequent tasks.
Effective CCS site screening requires consideration of both geologic suitability and interaction
with existing subsurface infrastructure (DOE NETL 2017). These factors include:
• Presence of permeable and laterally continuous reservoirs;
• Effective top seals or intraformational barriers to prevent vertical CO2 migration;
• Temperature and pressure conditions exceeding 88 °F and 1,070 psi (supercritical threshold);
• Absence of faults, fractures, or legacy wellbores that could serve as leakage pathways;
• Appropriate formation pressures and stress regimes to minimize induced seismicity;
• Isolation from USDWs;
• Compatibility with existing injection operations;
• Suitability for robust monitoring, reporting, and verification (MRV) systems.
Key deliverables included:
• Compilation and quality assurance/quality control (QA/QC) of subsurface geologic and
 petrophysical datasets;
• Delineation of USDWs and evaluation of salinity gradients;
• Environmental justice (EJ) screening;
• Preliminary AoR delineation to support Class VI permitting.

These outputs directly supported reservoir modeling (Task 3), simulation (Task 4), risk
assessment (Task 5), and permitting strategy (Task 6).

 Bushton, KS, Site
The Bushton study area (Figure 185 ) is located on the southeastern flank of the Central Kansas
Uplift (CKU), where Paleozoic carbonate reservoirs, especially the Arbuckle Formation, are
common (Figure 186). This area benefits from dense well control, existing infrastructure, and
robust production histories. Challenges include legacy wellbores, incomplete records, and
complex subsurface structure.

Figure 185 Bushton study area map

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 186 Initial screening map of the Bushton site, showing the distribution of oil and gas fields and the spatial
extent of Class I and Class II wastewater disposal activity. Significant volumes of water have historically been
injected into the Arbuckle reservoir, informing injectivity and pressure conditions for carbon capture and storage
evaluation.
An initial 3-by-3-mi model was expanded and rotated approximately 35° to define a 5-by-5-mi
area better aligned with regional fracture orientations and less affected by legacy production.
This area captures higher quality logs, maintains proximity to infrastructure, and avoids
interference from high-producing fields and nearby wastewater injection (e.g., by Northern
Natural Gas). Two target reservoirs were selected; their reservoir properties are summarized in
Figure 187:
 1. LKC Group: fractured oomoldic grainstones and packstones, moderate production rates,
 known shoal geometries;
 2. Arbuckle Formation: fractured, karst dolostone with matrix and non-matrix porosity
 systems; permeabilities often exceed 1,000 mD.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 187 Reservoir properties for the two target reservoirs at the Bushton site
Small basement uplifts and irregular Arbuckle weathering contribute to warping of overlying
units and likely influence fracture trends (predominantly NW/SE, consistent with CKU
orientation), affecting both target formations. Regional seals include the Simpson and Douglas
Shales; the Simpson may include interbedded sands that reduce seal quality in structural lows
(Figure 188). The thick, high-quality seals are not expected to be compromised by fractures due
to their ductility and overall thickness.

Figure 188 Bushton area conceptual model
The Bushton site hosts numerous oil and gas wells, most of which terminate in the upper
Arbuckle (UA). Injector wells and a subset of deeper producers penetrate the “Mid Arbuckle,” a
zone with especially high permeability (Figure 188). This distribution complicates AoR and
injectivity due to potential legacy wellbore impacts.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 Medford, OK, Site
The Medford area is located at the southern margin of the Sedgwick Basin in central Grant
County (Figure 189), adjacent to legacy production from the Mississippian Chat, Wilcox, and
Arbuckle formations. Prior activity has included horizontal drilling and injection, though induced
seismicity concerns have curtailed some operations.

Figure 189 Location and satellite image of ONEOK facility at Medford, OK
The OGS provided 128 raster logs and header metadata over a 6-by-6-mi area. KGS digitized ten
wells for Petrel integration, four of which included modern porosity–permeability data.
The Wilcox–Bromide interval was prioritized over the Mississippian Chat based on:
• Stratigraphic thickening toward the Texas Arch, influenced by Ouachita-related subsidence
    (Figure 190);
• Deposition within a distributive system sourced from Canadian Shield clastics with high net-
 to-gross ratios;
• Consistent thickness and quality in distal shoreface sandstones (Figure 191);
• Sufficient well control for preliminary modeling;
• Reduced reservoir pressure from prior production, potentially improving injectivity and
 reducing seismic risk.

Figure 192 Stratigraphy and underground sources of drinking water (USDWs) in Rice County, KS

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The Bromide Formation, part of the Simpson Group, accumulated rapidly in response to
subsidence within a sediment-loaded tectonic basin west of the Nemaha Fault, sometimes
exceeding 250 ft in thickness (Figure 191). It is among the region’s most productive and high-
quality sandstone reservoirs.
The Mississippian Chat showed locally favorable porosity development in the northern part of
the study area. However, that zone had been extensively drilled and included active production,
making it less favorable due to the risk of CO2 intrusion into hydrocarbon streams and higher
abundance of legacy wellbores that could increase leakage risk. In contrast, areas farther south
lacked adequate porosity, likely due to reduced karst development.
The Arbuckle Formation, while technically attractive, was excluded from detailed modeling due
to a limited number of well penetrations in the Medford area and heightened concerns regarding
induced seismicity. This formation lies closer to the Precambrian basement and is intersected by
faults known to be critically stressed. Prior wastewater disposal in the region has been linked to
seismic events, and informal consultation with OGS staff indicated that injection into the
Arbuckle would face significant regulatory obstacles.

 Data Aggregation
KGS conducted data integration and QA/QC, producing:
• 265 digitized log curves from 36 wells, loaded and stretched in Petrel;
• Porosity-permeability data from routine core analyses (RCAs);
• Drill stem test (DST) and falloff test data;
• Type logs and regional well top correlation in both project areas;
• Petrel-ready datasets for use in static modeling (Subtask 3.2), simulation (Task 4), and AoR
 analysis (Subtask 2.4).

 Subtask 2.2 – Delineate Underground Sources of Drinking Water
KGS delineated USDWs at both sites using stratigraphic interpretations and water quality
datasets from KGS and OGS, supplemented by regional brine chemistry and salinity cross-
sections developed for this study.
At the Bushton site, the base of the USDW was placed near the top of the Hutchinson Salt
Member of the Wellington Formation at approximately 950 ft below ground surface (bgs), based
on halite occurrence and salinity increase (Figure 192). Shallower sediments include Holocene
alluvium and eolian deposits, while the Cretaceous Dakota Sandstone forms the base of the
USDW.
At the Medford site, USDWs are associated with Quaternary alluvium and Permian Garber-
Wellington and Chase Groups. Below the Simpson Group, total dissolved solids (TDS) exceeds
10,000 mg/L. The Wilcox–Bromide formation target lies well below and is isolated from these
zones.
These delineations supported reservoir selection and AoR boundaries, ensuring vertical and
lateral isolation from potable aquifers.

 Subtask 2.3 – Review Environmental/Social Justice Considerations
An EJ screening was conducted to assess whether either of the candidate sites are located within
or near disadvantaged communities that could be disproportionately affected by carbon storage
activities (Figure 193A). The analysis followed guidance from the DOE’s Office of Fossil
Energy and Carbon Management (FECM), using the Climate and Economic Justice Screening
Tool (CEJST) and archived EPA EJScreen data (EDGI 2024).
Bushton, KS: Rural Rice County showed no disadvantaged community indicators within 5 mi
(Figure 193B). Air quality and hazard exposure were low, and no Tribal lands were nearby.
Medford, OK: While not classified as disadvantaged, poverty and energy burden indicators
approach threshold levels. No elevated risk indicators were identified within 5 mi (Figure 193C),
but future stakeholder engagement is recommended.

Figure 193 Disadvantaged communities (A) at regional scale, (B) near Bushton, KS, and (C) near Medford, OK.
Nearby Disadvantaged Communities and Tribal Context: Nearby disadvantaged
communities (within 100 mi) were noted for future consideration. These include Hoisington

 334

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 Subtask 2.4–Determine AoR
The work completed for this study is not adequate to rigorously delineate an AoR per current
EPA Class VI Well AoR Evaluation and Corrective Action Guidance. This work is useful as a
preliminary benchmark for injection into a single deterministic subsurface property model;
additional data collection (e.g., seismic, core, post-production formation pressures, etc.) are
highly recommended. While these models are not intended to serve as an EPA-ready AoR, they
demonstrate a viable workflow for future permit application development. All necessary
simulation data for a formal Class VI AoR evaluation are contained within LANL’s model
output files but were not post-processed for regulatory compliance in this study as the underlying
static property is under-constrained and numerous critical assumptions were required (e.g.,
reservoir connectivity within and adjacent to the model; current formation pressure). Additional
technical work is recommended to refine these AoRs, including acquisition of 3D seismic,
advanced logging data, formation pressure measurements, and conventional core from both
storage and seal units. The spatial geometry of modeled plume and pressure behavior aligns with
regional injectivity trends and provides a strong technical foundation for advancing future site
characterization and risk-informed project design. Below is summary of the most relevant
outputs generated from the technical work completed at LANL.
The AoR for a geologic sequestration project is a delineation on a surface map of the region over
which USDWs may be endangered by the injection activity (EPA 2013). This area encompasses
two regions, both of which are determined from computational modeling that accounts for the
characterization of the subsurface site and the thermodynamic, chemical and transport properties
of the fluid phases in the reservoir pore space (40 C.F.R. § 146.84(a) and 40 C.F.R. §
146.84(c)(1); Area…2024). The first region is the areal extent of the CO2 over time, from the
commencement of injection until the CO2 plume (free and dissolved components) movement
ceases. One methodology for determining this region is selecting a cutoff value for the vertically
integrated mass per area (Zhang et al. 2015). The second method uses areal extent of the pressure
within injection reservoir that could result in the upward migration of reservoir fluid into an
overlying USDW as delineated by dynamic simulation model outputs. As with the CO2 plume
region, this region is delineated from the commencement of injection until pressure differentials
sufficient to cause the movement of injected fluids or formation fluids into a USDW cease to
exist (40 C.F.R. § 146.84(c)(1); Area of review…2024).
KGS conducted preliminary AoR analysis for the Bushton site using static and dynamic reservoir
simulation tools. These conceptual models delineate the expected spatial extent of pressure
propagation and CO2 plume migration for two potential injection intervals: the LKC group and
the Arbuckle Formation. Simulations were conducted with STOMP-CO2 and STOMPX-CO2,
incorporating formation-specific parameters such as porosity, permeability, and pressure. For the
LKC reservoir, simulation results indicated limited CO2 plume expansion, primarily due to poor
injectivity and low reservoir pressure. Fracture gradient scenarios of 0.6, 0.7, and 0.8 psi/ft
yielded top-hole pressure limits of approximately 1,740 to 2,750 psi, limiting injection rates
below viable thresholds. As a result, the LKC was assessed to be a marginal candidate for
sustained CO2 injection unless active fracture management strategies are used or legacy fracture
systems allow for diffusion of CO2 plumes and associated pressure fronts. In contrast, the
Arbuckle Formation demonstrated greater injectivity and a broader CO2 plume footprint.
Calibration of permeability inputs was based on historical data from five nearby disposal wells.

 335

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Additional modeling scenarios evaluated three hypothetical injection wells placed in deeper
sections of the Arbuckle not commonly penetrated by existing wells. To support this, KGS
integrated logs from four deep penetrations located approximately 7 mi south of Bushton. These
inputs allowed for conceptual modeling of deep Arbuckle behavior at depths comparable to
legacy Class I injection operations. Although these models are exploratory and cannot yet be
fully validated with site-specific data, they provide valuable insight into the storage potential of
deeper Arbuckle intervals.
Pressure-based AoRs were developed for both intervals, incorporating simulation outputs (see
Task 4) and risk considerations (see Task 5). For the LKC, the AoR reflects the fracture and
karst geometries embedded in the property model (Figure 194). For the Arbuckle Deep (AD)
scenario, the pressure-based footprint was smaller due to favorable reservoir properties,
including thickness, fracture-enhanced porosity, connectivity, and permeability. The maximum
projected extent of both CO2 plume migration and pressure increase was used to define the
preliminary AoRs.
