  Task 3 – Subsurface Studies
Subsurface screening and evaluation for ONEOK facilities in Medford, OK, and Bushton, KS,
were conducted under this CUSP-West focused study. This work represents a preliminary
technical foundation for future site-specific Class VI application development. Establishing a
viable regional CCS hub in the midcontinent will require substantial additional geologic and
engineering assessment. The results frame future work by identifying existing data assets,
technical gaps, and key elements required to reduce subsurface uncertainty.
This relied on publicly available geologic resources, including regional syntheses for Kansas and
Oklahoma (e.g., Bream et al. 2025; Buchanan and Carr 2008; OGS 2021), detailed reservoir-
scale assessments (e.g., Benmadi et al. 2024; Holubnyak and Dubois 2018), and ongoing DOE
Funding Opportunity Announcement (FOA) 2711 work in Kansas. Long-term CO2 storage

 337

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

potential in Kansas aligns, in descending viability: (1) Arbuckle Formation (deep saline aquifer);
(2) younger porous carbonate reservoirs (Mississippian, LKC); and (3) mineralization in
Precambrian mafic rocks of the Midcontinent Rift System.
Existing reservoir distribution and property studies supported model construction and parameter
selection, for example, Byrnes et al. (2010) for the LKC, Franseen et al. (2004) for the Arbuckle,
and Suhm (2016) for the Wilcox–Bromide. Figure 195 maps regional play adequacy relevant to
Bushton (Bream et al. 2025). Probabilistic play evaluation remains recommended to frame value-
of-information (VOI) decisions for new data (seismic, core, wireline) and develop high/low/best-
case scenarios reflecting uncertainty.

Figure 195 Example of two aggregated regional play assessment adequacy maps for Kansas (Bream et al. 2025).
The color bar represents the aggregated chance of adequacy of carbon capture and storage potential for four different
play elements (reservoir presence, reservoir quality, CO 2 phase, and seal). The highlighted counties are Ellsworth
(North) and Rice (South); the ONEOK Bushton facility is about 6.5 mi from the western edge of this county
boundary.
Geocellular models, integrated with dynamic simulation, are essential screening tools. However,
deterministic realizations are non-unique and must be interpreted considering data quality, facies
interpretation, and geologic uncertainty. These models provide representative—not
comprehensive—subsurface scenarios, useful for guiding screening, economic evaluation, and
regulatory planning.
A generalized subsurface workflow, reflective of Class VI application needs, is recommended:
1) Identify, assemble, and assess local subsurface data (see Subtask 3.1).
2) Evaluate regional reservoir/seal properties, including trends in thickness, porosity,
 permeability, salinity, etc.
3) Assess regional existing seismicity (see Subtask 3.5).
4) Evaluate regional and subregional structural influences, including previously recognized
 faults, fault trends, and fracture or geomechanical data obtainable from offset wells, for
 example, published maps, core descriptions, dipole sonic and microresistivity imaging logs
 (see Subtask 3.4).

 338

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

5) Assess subregional dynamic factors (e.g., nearby field production, wastewater injection,
 impact of legacy wellbores for leakage risk).
6) Collect baseline geochemical data to understand impact of CO2 brines on seals, reservoir
 injectivity, and legacy boreholes.
7) Define reasonable property distributions based on available data or analogues.
8) Perform probabilistic assessment of key subsurface field inputs with dependencies (e.g.,
 porosity and permeability).
9) Qualify subsurface parameters by quality and confidence (e.g., Callas et al. 2024).
10) Construct simplified scenario-based subsurface representations that capture at least high-side,
 low-side, and best-estimate cases.
11) Build one or more static geologic models that integrate the available data into viable
 subsurface solutions (see Subtask 3.3).
12) Add static models tied to probabilistic assessment inputs (e.g., P10 porosity), probabilistic
 outputs (e.g., P50 capillary seal capacity), or revised interpretations (e.g., from new wells or
 seismic).
Bushton and Medford illustrate typical midcontinent CCS challenges: well density and reservoir
knowledge coexist with legacy data formats, limited coverage, and proprietary restrictions. This
study generated viable geologic models that support simulation (Task 4) and risk assessment
(Task 5), while defining future refinement paths. The outlook for long-term CO2 storage in
central Kansas remains favorable, though technically complex.

KGS, with support from OGS and Carbon Solutions, compiled subsurface data for Petrel
modeling near Bushton and Medford. The integrated project includes well locations, raster and
digital well logs, stratigraphic correlation picks, core-derived porosity–permeability data, and
type well control. Figure 196 shows the Petrel interface for the Bushton model.

 Bushton Site Data
Two primary target reservoirs were selected: LKC group and Arbuckle Formation, chosen for
supercritical CO2 conditions and data availability. A 5-by-5-mi modeling area includes 40 wells
with raster logs, composed of a mix of legacy suites (e.g., spontaneous potential [SP], gamma ray
[GR], and deep resistivity [RESD]) and more modern log suites (e.g., GR, resistivity, neutron
porosity hydrogen index [NPHI], bulk density [RHOB], and photoelectric factor [Pe]).
Digitization efforts focused on modern logs, resulting in 26 wells with digital logs, and 11 with
complete triple-combo logs (Figure 197). Injector data include cased-hole logs, falloff tests, and
free-water levels. Regional salinity is constrained via the KGS Brine Database and the USGS
Produced Water database. No new seismic data was acquired. Analog data for geologic modeling
were drawn from the Hall-Gurney Field, a DOE-supported CO2-EOR project in the LKC group,
and the Wellington and North Hugoton CCS projects, which are Arbuckle Group
characterization studies.

 Medford Site Data
Two primary target reservoirs were selected: Mississippian Chat and Wilcox–Bromide system.
Over 125 raster logs were provided by OGS; ten wells were digitized by KGS for model
development, including two injector wells. Only four wells contained complete modern log
suites sufficient for porosity and permeability estimation. Most wells were drilled to total depth
above the target Wilcox–Bromide intervals, and no core data from these reservoirs were
available. KGS supported the effort by providing core-derived porosity, permeability, and grain
density data from the Simpson sandstone, which is time-equivalent to the Wilcox–Bromide.
Additionally, one well with DST records was identified through GeoIntegra’s (Denver, CO)
Enverus (Austin, TX) subscription.

 Bushton (KS) Geologic Models
Three Bushton models were created: Lansing–Kansas City (KC2), UA, and AD. The UA model
was discontinued due to poor regional correlation and pressure alignment. The KC2 and AD
models were selected for simulation (Subtask 4.2).

 LKC Static Model
The LKC Group model is shown in Figure 203.

Figure 203 Permeability and petrophysical model for the Lansing–Kansas City Group
Reservoir analogue: Hall-Gurney Field (approximately 25 mi NW), with DOE-supported data
(Byrnes et al. 2010). The best reservoir quality was observed in the upper Kansas City interval.
Progradational shoals displayed high permeability (hundreds of millidarcies) and were
“shingled” over time in depositional patterns comparable to modern Bahamas analogues
(Gonzalez and Eberli 1997). These high-permeability zones are bordered by deeper water
carbonates with lower permeability (tens of millidarcies). Results from the Hall-Gurney CO2
WAG program showed permeability anisotropy aligned NW–SE, interpreted as controlled by
basement-involved fractures and paleotopographic highs.
Well log correlation: Within the study area, stretched raster and digital well logs were used to
create the geologic model zones that honor the Hall-Gurney analogue with compensational and
shingling of shoal systems within the LKC reservoir at Bushton. Over time, the locus of
deposition shifts from the NW corner, to the central area, to the south/southwest portion of the
study area as lateral migration of carbonate shoals fill in the available accommodation space

 346

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

(Figure 204). Similar to the Hall-Gurney reservoir analogue, the porous units (shown as green
bars) are more commonly found in the thicker deposits near the top of coarsening upward
sequences. An interpreted fracture trend was also created for the Bushton study site.

Figure 204 Stacking trends within the Lansing–Kansas City reservoir system. Note that there are significant
thickness variations as interpreted across the study site that could impact connectivity and plume evolution.
Zone model/layering: LKC reservoir zonation and layering was a function of (1) the stratal
framework built for the region and (2) the desire to adequately represent high and lower
permeability intervals that were mappable across some or all of the study area. The result is a 28-
layer model covering approximately 75 ft of section in the upper portion of the Kansas City
Formation (Figure 205). The layers were mapped as conformable and proportional, thus allowing
for pinching and swelling that is expected in the depositional systems. The shingling nature of
sediments in the Bushton LKC study area is comparable to what is observed at Hall-Gurney
field. Each zone contains between 1 and 5 layers, averaging 4.8 to 17.6 ft thick. Proportional
layering was applied and deemed appropriate for the expected stratal geometries.

 347

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 205 Lansing–Kansas City (LKC) modeled zones highlighting thickness variation and proportional layering
applied.
Facies modeling: Using matrix-corrected NPHI porosity and GR as a proxy for clay, three facies
were identified (porous carbonate, tight carbonate, and shale). Vertical Proportion Curves were
built using the vertical variations observed in the 4 pseudo-wells used in this project (Figure
206). Different stratigraphic units contained different facies percentages. Furthermore, lateral
thickness variations commonly resulted in different facies percentages for the same stratigraphic
interval. Vertical proportion curves and layer thickness (i.e., thicker intervals had more high
porosity carbonates) were used to distribute the facies within the model.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Effective porosity: Porosity was upscaled at the wells using an arithmetic mean of the calculated
effective porosity (PHIE) well log. Resulting upscaled porosity values match the PHIE curve
reasonably well as seen in the histogram of well logs vs. upscaled cells (Figure 207).

Figure 207 Effective porosity log and upscaling example from the Donald 44937 well

 349

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Variograms were also used to guide facies distribution in the model (Figure 208). Shales are
interpreted to represent flooding events and have an equal aspect ratio in major and minor
directions. The tight carbonate facies have a moderate major/minor aspect ratio to represent the
more laterally continuous off-shoal facies. Porous carbonate facies have the highest major/minor
aspect ratio compared to other facies due to the linear nature of shoal crests. Default values for
vertical variogram length (100 ft) were used because the fractured nature of this reservoir likely
results in high vertical permeability and/or continuity of permeability systems. The vertical
variogram from shale was derived from the vertical variogram plots and is lower than the other
facies because the high clay content within renders it less likely to fracture.

Figure 208 Lansing–Kansas City (LKC) variograms applied for the three modeled facies
Final PHIE property model trends show similar patterns as those observed in the Hall-Gurney
Field (Figure 209). Shoal bodies within individual zones mostly show higher porosity
distributions; this is most notable in the younger, thicker carbonate shoal bodies.

Figure 209 Lansing–Kansas City (LKC) porosity model. PHIE = effective porosity.

 350

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Permeability values were derived from the core-based porosity-permeability transform at Hall-
Gurney field. The model’s horizontal permeability (Kh) was enhanced to account for non-matrix
pore systems, including fractures and connected vugs, based on production data from Hall-
Gurney field. Vertical permeability (Kv) was set at 30% of Kh, following recommendations from
Battelle’s Midcontinent Storage report (Battelle Memorial Institute 2018). This ratio aligns with
values observed in carbonate reservoirs analyzed by KGS in the Patterson and Wellington CCS
reports.
Production data from Hall-Gurney revealed elevated permeability and reservoir connectivity
along a northwest–southeast axis, suggesting that lineaments identified in seismic data may
represent fracture corridors. Analysis indicates that permeability systems in these reservoirs are
controlled by both depositional geometries and fracture networks. These findings guided
permeability modeling in the Bushton LKC model (Figure 210).

Figure 210 Lansing–Kansas City (LKC) horizontal permeability model
The modeling approach incorporated porosity-permeability transforms from Hall-Gurney and
vertical-to-horizontal permeability ratios from the Battelle Midcontinent Storage study. Similar
to the porosity model, higher permeability streaks were oriented northwest-southeast but with
tighter distribution to simulate the impact of fracture corridors on prograding shoal bodies
extending south-southwest. The resulting permeability model displays northwest-southeast
oriented permeability systems reflecting both depositional geometries and fracture systems.
Note: Future phases of CCS screening will require development of a dual porosity/dual
permeability model for the LKC to account for distinct behaviors of matrix and fracture porosity
systems. This advanced modeling approach requires additional data including 3D seismic,
formation microimager (FMI) data, and conventional core descriptions that were not available
during this study phase.

 AD Static Model Details
After the initial Arbuckle model had been constructed (see section 3.2.4), ONEOK provided
additional well data from wastewater disposal wells in the area. Injection top and base for those

 351

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

wells were deeper than any of the wells used for the initial Arbuckle reservoir modeling (Figure
211). The shallow Arbuckle wells likely penetrate most of the Cotter Dolomite and some of the
Jefferson City Dolomite, but none of the Roubidoux and Gasconade formations. These
formations have been shown to have the best porosity and permeability development in the
Arbuckle Group. As such, it was necessary to pull in wells from offsite that penetrated these
intervals for use as pseudo-wells for the AD static model. The stratigraphy from the shallow
wells was used as a guide in the pseudo-wells, but the stratigraphic tops used were at a lower
resolution to ensure that the entire reservoir section could be modeled efficiently. This highlights
the importance of a stratigraphic well to fully characterize the reservoir and delineate zones for
injection.

impacted by fracturing and karst, as described by Franseen et al. (2004). The KGS researchers
built a simulation model for the Wellington site with stratiform layering, as shown in the figure
above. This concept agrees with similar stratigraphic architecture observed at the Bushton site.

Facies model: Log-based facies for the Arbuckle reservoir were split into the following facies
based on interpreted permeability and clay abundance:
• High perm dolomites – 75 mD+ that likely represent karst intervals, mimetic dolomites in
 prior high energy grainstone or framework deposits
• Moderate perm dolomites - 75 mD>PermXY>5 that likely represent more heavily
 cemented grainstones/packstones or muddy and recrystallized sediments
• Low Perm Dolomite – PermXY<5 mD that likely represents lower energy depositional
 environments (mudstones, wackestones) or very heavily cemented shallow water deposits
• Shales – Vclay >50% that likely represents depositional lows along the Ordovician-Silurian
 carbonate ramp and/or local high level flooding events
Vertical proportion curves were derived from the available log data to guide the relative
abundance of the log facies in each zone (Figure 214). There was significant vertical and lateral
variability in the interpreted facies, though the upper units were generally lower reservoir quality
and the lower units were generally higher reservoir quality. Shales were relatively rare, which is
expected on a high-energy shallow water carbonate ramp with low accommodation space.

Figure 217 Effective porosity model for the Arbuckle Deep geologic model
The final effective porosity model shows general conformance between well logs, upscaled
values at the well, and the conceptual geologic model (Figure 218). The porosity model inherits
the variogram dimensions from facies modeling. Karst and fractures were not explicitly built into
the porosity model but are not likely to significantly impact overall storage volumes. They will
likely impact permeability and are addressed in the permeability model. The Gaussian Random
Function Simulation was used to distribute porosities in the model based on associated values
found in log calculations for each zone. Porosity in karst or heavily fractured zones was not
included in model, as no known karst/fracture zones were encountered in logs evaluated for the
model.

 357

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 218 3D view of the Arbuckle Deep effective porosity model
Permeability: The permeability trends in the model are like those from the porosity model, with
a N35W orientation, but overall magnitude of permeability is higher in the upper 1/3 and lower
half of the model (Figure 219). Water injection rates from Class I water injectors were used to
history match the AD model. Simulation of the early AD static model experienced rapid pressure
rise and required a substantial drop in injection rates to prevent frac gradient from being
exceeded. The permeability was iteratively increased until the model could handle the known
water disposal rates and a 5X permeability multiplier was applied to the static model
permeability properties. Lack of conformance between original perm model and history-matched
permeabilities is attributed to the lack of dual porosity and dual permeability in the model. Future
models should include a discrete fracture network (DFN) and attempt to quantify porosity and
permeability in fractures and brecciated cavern fill in Arbuckle Group. No core available in
study area, so leveraged prior KGS research to derive reasonable Arbuckle perm estimate ICKan
quarterly report by Bidgoli and Dubois (07/07/2018), which contains a core-corrected poro-perm
transform derived from nuclear magnetic resonance (NMR) log measurements. Intervals with Kh
> 75 mD received a 5X boost to match perms seen in ONEOK #4 injector wells. The upscaling
process resulted in a muted impact on permeability boost in some intervals. Core data from the
Hadley-1 well in Bemis Shutts field was used to estimate Kv/Kh ratio of 0.202.

 UA Geologic Model
The Upper Arbuckle Geologic Model represents the first Arbuckle model built for the Bushton

 Medford (OK) Geologic Model
A model of the Wilcox–Bromide sandstones was constructed in an area of central Grant County
that includes the ONEOK facility. The model boundary was positioned to take advantage of
existing well data without being too close to extant Wilcox production in the northern and
southern areas. This would allow for reasonable modeling that included areas with undrilled
potential that would not interfere with ongoing oil and gas operations (Figure 220).

Figure 220 Map showing the area of the Medford subsurface model (red outline) with production wells displayed
with cumulative production in units of barrel of oil equivalent
Model location resulted from prioritization of several goals:
 • Proximity to ONEOK Medford facility
 • Avoiding faulted areas or intervals with high oil and gas production that could lead to
 lower formation pressures, relative permeability issues, etc.
 • “Goldilocks” zone for data needs vs. undrilled potential, resulting in:
 o Sufficient data coverage that permits reservoir seal characterization
 o Undrilled areas that would have comparable reservoir/seal properties but with
 lower leakage potential from legacy boreholes

 Wilcox–Bromide Static Model Details
Reservoir analogue: The Wilcox–Bromide sandstones are part of a larger marine clastic
distributive system that sourced sediments from the Canadian Shield. The Wilcox–Bromide
sandstones produce large volumes of oil and gas within Oklahoma and have some of the best
reservoir quality of all oil and gas reservoirs in the region. For these reasons, we decided to focus
on the Wilcox–Bromide sandstones over the Mississippian Chat reservoirs. These sediments
were funneled into the study area via shelfal clastic systems that existed between structural
highs. Upon entering Oklahoma, these clastic sediments moved beyond the shelf/slope break,
resulting in increased accommodation space and a change in overall depositional style to lobate
turbidite systems. These sediments thicken to the south, where they abruptly terminate against
the Texas Arch that was created by the pre-collision phase of the Ouachita orogeny.
Well log correlation: Raster logs were depth registered to perform the initial stratigraphic
correlation. Available log data indicates a lateral compensational stacking pattern within the
Wilcox-Bromide sandstone. This pattern likely represents high frequency (parasequence scale),
autochthonous sedimentation distributive systems within the broader clastic depositional system.
There is likely minor scouring occurring, but no major erosive events, leading to mostly
conformable sedimentation in the area.
Zone model and layering: Six sand zones with an upper shale-prone zone were correlated and
modeled (Figure 222). There are more wells that penetrate the upper portion of the Wilcox sands
(Wilcox_6 to Wilcox_3) and thus more confidence in the thickness trends in those intervals.
 361

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Nevertheless, all intervals show apparent compensational stacking patterns as sediment filled in
local lows created by turbidite distribute systems nearby. Well clustering and data quality issues
in the raster logs create uncertainty in the reservoir dimensions. As a result, analogues from
Doveton et al. (1990) in Kansas were used as a reference in the geologic model.

Figure 222 Zone model showing 10 wells from NW (left) to the SE (right) within the modeled area
Facies model: The Wilcox-Bromide sandstone likely represents multiple turbidite depositional
sequences, with higher quality sands representing Ta and Tb beds. The lower equality sands
likely represent Tc and Td beds, with shales representing Te beds or pelagic sedimentation. No
clear trend of the high- or low-quality sands was discerned from the available wells, so vertical
proportion curves relied on the average facies abundance across all four wells in the study area
(Figure 223).

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 223 Vertical proportion curves used to distribute each of the 3 facies (high porosity sandstone, low porosity
sandstone, shale) within the Wilcox zone
Effective porosity: Modeled porosity trends compare favorably with those taken from the well
logs or upscaled values (PHIE; Figure 224). Low porosities are less abundant in the model than
in well logs due to upscaling and facies and porosity distributions in the model. The lack of
lower porosities is not expected to have a material impact on the model during simulation.

depths are approximately 3,200 to 3,400 ft below the surface whereas the Wilcox-Bromide sands
in the Medford area are approximately 4,600 to 4,900 ft below the surface (Figure 225).

 Salt Horizons CO2 Storage Evaluation
CO2 sequestration in salt caverns was initially considered as part of this study’s scope but was
ultimately determined to be non-feasible for the Bushton site. This determination was based on
several critical technical and economic constraints identified during preliminary evaluation.
Technical Challenges: The primary technical obstacles include the shallow depth of the
Hutchinson Salt Member near the ONEOK Bushton facility. The salt formation is approximately

 365

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

200 ft thick with the top of salt located around 950 ft below the surface (Figure 226). This
shallow depth presents significant challenges for maintaining CO2 at supercritical conditions,
which typically require greater depths and pressures for effective storage. The Hutchinson Salt
thickness nearest the ONEOK Bushton site is relatively thin and located near the depositional
edge of the evaporitic basin (Figure 226 and Figure 227).

Figure 226 Hutchison salt thickness map for Kansas. From a KU News press release (University of Kansas News
Service 2022).

Figure 227 Maximum extent of Lower Permian evaporite deposits associated with the Blaine Formation, Flower-pot
Shale, Ninnescah Shale unit, and Wellington Formation (Hutchinson Salt Member)

 366

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Additional technical concerns include:
• Risk of salt dissolution and surface subsidence, as evidenced by numerous sinkholes that
 have developed along shallow salt margins from both natural dissolution and wastewater
 disposal activities (Knapp et al. 1989)
• Geomechanical uncertainties regarding the salt’s ability to maintain structural integrity under
 supercritical CO2 conditions
• Potential for induced seismicity and long-term monitoring challenges common to CO2
 sequestration methods (Zhang et al. 2022; Mwakipunda et al. 2024)
Economic and Logistical Considerations: While deeper salt formations in the region could
theoretically overcome some technical limitations, accessing these would require extensive
pipeline infrastructure extending well beyond the existing ONEOK facility network. The
associated capital investment and operational complexity would likely exceed the economic
viability compared to conventional saline aquifer sequestration approaches. Given the
combination of shallow salt depths, geomechanical uncertainties, dissolution risks, and
prohibitive infrastructure requirements, salt cavern CO2 storage was determined to be non-
feasible for this project. The study therefore focused on more technically and economically
viable sequestration options, including saline aquifer storage in deeper formations.

 Subtask 3.3 – Assess CO2 Storage Resources
Accurate evaluation of long-term subsurface CO2 storage potential requires dynamic assessment
of the reservoir to better understand reservoir behavior within the reservoir while injecting at
rates that satisfy project economics. While dynamic modeling results are presented in Task 4,
this subtask focuses on volumetric analysis of the Arbuckle Group to estimate potential CO2
storage resources across central Kansas.
The Arbuckle Group underlies much of the state and has been extensively studied due to its
historical significance as a hydrocarbon reservoir. It is well characterized in most areas and
exhibits significant pore space potential through both primary and secondary porosity (e.g.,
Merriam 1963; Franseen et al. 2004). Although not funded through this CUSP-West study, the
KGS has recently produced a regional model of Arbuckle storage potential (Figure 228), from
which maximum CO2 storage values were derived for each county in the state (e.g., Bream et al.
2025). These volumetric estimates were calculated using mapped formation thicknesses, bulk
rock volume, and average net porosity derived from well log analysis.

 Subtask 3.4 – Geomechanical Assessment
A 1D mechanical earth model (MEM) for the proposed ONEOK, Bushton, Medford CCS site
was constructed. Some petrophysical modeling was incorporated as well to augment previous
petrophysical models generated by the well logging service company. The well data utilized is
located at a site known as the Wellington CCS site, in Ellis County, due to the absence of the
required well log, core, and other data required at the Bushton site. The analog well is located in
the Bemis Shutts oil field, approximately 60 mi from the Bushton site.

Figure 232 Location of the analog study well in relation to the proposed ONEOK Bushton injection site
This work centers on the utilization of well logging data focusing on, but not limited to, the
analysis of the dipole sonic log (Halliburton’s WaveSonic tool) and the density log. These data

 372

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

were taken from the McCord 20H pilot well, a science well that was drilled prior to a horizontal
injection well used in a pilot carbon sequestration study as the injection well.
This work would ultimately provide the basis for microseismic and time-lapse seismic
monitoring, as well as integrate into advanced reservoir simulation models. However, for this
analysis to relate directly to the Bushton site, additional data would have to be acquired in a
project pilot well. This data should include advanced acoustic logs, formation micro-imaging
logs, and core data to undergo triaxial testing, in order to calibrate the 1D model for the Bushton
site and to ensure the most accurate starting point for 3D geomechanical and reservoir flow
simulation modeling.
Although some data is unavailable, the well-bore geomechanics is presented in six sections,
giving a high-level review of areas that would need to be addressed in the event this project
moved forward. The six sections are (1) core analysis, (2) acoustic analysis, (3) petrophysics
analysis, (4) construction of the 1D MEM, (5) integration of geomechanical data with reservoir
flow modeling via coupled geomechanical flow modeling, and (6) structural model.

 Core Analysis
As previously mentioned, no core data exists at the Bushton site. The closest core data available
is in an offset well to the 1D MEM, the KGS 1-32H; these data are discussed in more detail in
section 3.4.5, as they are part of a previous study at the Wellington site. To fully constrain the
MEM, various tests should be performed on core data recovered from a pilot well in the
Arbuckle and additional sealing formations located at Bushton. Tests should include
geochemistry, petrophysical rock properties, and geomechanical rock properties. Stress-strain
curves for both the intended storage formation and seal formations can be derived from triaxial
testing, which would provide insight into the mechanical properties of these formations.
Figure 233 shows a typical stress-strain curve resulting from laboratory testing of core data. The
stress-strain curve has been divided into four regions of geomechanical behavior, chronicling the
increased axial stress during the lab experiment. Region one is defined as concave upward and
results from the closing of microcracks typically introduced during retrieval. Region two
demonstrates the linear stress-strain curve that is typically assumed during the bulk of
geomechanical modeling and flow modeling. The end of the linear portion is the yield strength of
the sample. Region three is concave down, due to the development of new cracks as the result of
the experiment. The maximum load is dictated by the peak of this curve, known as peak strength,
the point at which the sample has failed. Region four occurs post-failure, demonstrating the
residual strength of the sample post-failure. This shows the importance of laboratory testing, as
understanding the end points of these regions and the associated yield strength, peak strength,
and residual strength would allow for calibration of well log data. There are other pertinent
measurements to be derived from these tests as well, such as failure ratio, which not only
facilitate calibration but also allow for the analyst to determine at which state of stress the
formation exists in nature, whether it is in failure (as most unconventional reservoirs),
elastoplastic, or elastic (Bratton 2025). Most workflows assume the formation is linear elastic, as
we will treat the Arbuckle in the upcoming well log analysis.

 373

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 233 Typical stress test on the core for a brittle formation. The strain curve is shown in red as a function of
the applied axial stress. Ultrasonic velocities are shown as green dots. (From Bratton [2025].)
In addition to physical, destructive mechanical testing of the formation samples, sonic
measurements will be made of the core. This will allow the petrophysical analyst to relate the
sonic velocity measurements made at different scales, as the core measurements are much higher
resolution than the log scale, though the log scale is typically more indicative of the in situ
mechanical properties, depending on how the formation is classified. Note the behavior of the
ultrasonic velocities (shown in green) in Figure 233. In this case, the ultrasonic measurements
mimic the stress-strain curve. As a result, this formation may be classified as continuous,
homogeneous, isotropic, linear, elastic. This is an indication that borehole measurements of sonic
velocities will be sensitive to stress. If the sonic velocities did not vary with stress, this indicates
that the sonic velocities will not be sensitive to the state of stress of the formation. If the
formation is stress sensitive, then the sonic velocities will vary with stress loading. Equation 1
shows how compressional (P) and shear (S) waves will change with stress.
                                            ΔVp,s=(Vp,s∂σ)(Δσ) (1)
The first term is the stress sensitivity variable, and the second term is the differential stress
variable. Each term must be greater than zero for us to observe a change in velocity (Bratton
2025).

 Acoustical Analysis
Full waveform sonic log processing is an advanced and complex field, requiring highly
specialized tools and expertise. Modern logs are capable of classifying and differentiating
complex relationships between stress-induced, and intrinsic velocity anisotropy. Understanding
the relationship between the speed of different waves in different directions within the formation
enables the petrophysical analyst to characterize the state of stress in the formation much more
effectively, particularly when understanding the relationship between maximum horizontal and
minimum horizontal stress (Shmax and Shmin).

 374

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

One of tools at the analyst’s disposal is shown in Figure 234. Modern dipole sonic tools measure
not only the P- and S-waves (compressional and shear, respectively) but also the Stonely wave.
All waves are recorded over a wide range of frequencies, as formation and stress anisotropy are
dispersive, or frequency dependent, but formation and stress dispersion will vary independently,
allowing for differentiation between the two (Bratton 2025).

Figure 234 Anisotropy classification based on dispersion. (From Bratton [2025].)
The WaveSonic tool deployed in the McCord 20H, was an early attempt to record all the above
waveforms. Today the WaveSonic tool is a best-in-class sonic evaluation tool, but at the time of
data acquisition of the McCord 20H (2011), the WaveSonic was hampered by hardware
limitations, preventing full characterization of all waveforms. Also, although the data were
recorded, the specialized processing required to separate the wave fields to fully understand the
anisotropy was not performed. These factors limit the use of these data to a strictly isotropic,
linear elastic MEM.

Rock physics–based models, and therefore the resultant geomechanical models, can benefit from

 1D MEM
A MEM is intended to provide the required input data to run a geomechanical simulation. Tom
Bratton (Bratton 2025) summarized the components of the MEM as follows:
“1) a framework model to characterize the structure of the formation including formation
horizons and major faults, 2) a petrophysical model to quantify the lithology, porosity, water
saturation, matrix permeability, and dynamic elastic moduli, 3) a mechanical stratigraphy model
to characterize the stratigraphic column, load bearing facies, and natural and drilling induced
fracture attributes, 4) a rock property model to characterize the static moduli, deformation, yield,
and failure properties of the formation, 5) an overburden model to characterize the vertical
loading, 6) a pore pressure model to quantify the pore pressure, 7) a stress orientation model to
characterize the dip and azimuth of the far-field stresses, and finally 8) a stress magnitude model
to quantify the horizontal loading on the formations.”
A mechanical stratigraphy model was constructed using Schlumberger’s Techlog software (SLP,
formerly Schlumberger; Houston, TX). The approach is based on the cross-plot methods (Herron
et al. 1992).
Rock properties were modeled utilizing standard geomechanical correlations (Figure 235 and
Figure 236). Static Young’s modulus was derived both from the Morales correlation (Morales
and Marcinew 1993) and the Canaday correlation (Canaday 2011) and exhibit a strong match,
the Morales method was utilized for further calculations. The friction angle is derived utilizing
the Plumb correlation (Plumb 1994) while the unconfined compressive strength (UCS) is derived
from the Coates-Denoo correlation (Coates and Denoo 1981).
Figure 235 shows the static moduli, rock strength, and corresponding dipole sonic measurements
for the entirety of the McCord A-20H pilot well. The red curve labeled “AppAni” represents an
apparent anisotropy derived from the shear wave measurements aligned in the X and Y
directions respectively. As previously mentioned, further processing is required to align the shear
waves to the formation fast and slow directions to fully characterize formation and stress
anisotropy. This will further inform the magnitude of minimum and maximum horizontal stress,
as well as characterize the presence of fractures. Figure 236 shows the same data over the depth
interval comprising the proposed injection formation (Arbuckle) and the overlying formations.
There exist some areas of relatively high apparent anisotropy, which will most likely indicate
some formation fracturing in both the Stark and Kansas City formations.

 Seal and Risk Assessment
The potential for injection-induced fault reactivation in the Arbuckle Group reservoir at the
Wellington site was addressed in a previous study incorporating subsurface structural mapping
and stress field conditions related to increased seismicity in the region (Schwab et al. 2017). This
work will be used in addition to the McCord 20H Pilot well-log data as an analog for the
ONEOK Bushton site.

 382

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

To analyze geomechanical caprock integrity concerning CO2 injection and its effects on
subsurface stability at the Wellington site, triaxial tests were conducted in the KGS 1-32 well, an
offset to the McCord A20H Pilot. CO2 injection increases pore pressure, potentially reactivating
fractures or faults. Geomechanical studies are essential to examine fault reactivation potential
and ensure CO2 remains confined. In these studies, three failure modes would be investigated:
new fractures, slippage along faults, and opening of existing fractures.
Subsurface stress fields involve lithostatic and horizontal compressive stresses. Mohr’s Circle
can be used to represent stress states and failure envelopes for fault stability (Mavko et al. 2009).
Effective stress is influenced by pore pressure, which can facilitate fault movement. Future work
would include calibrating the 1D mechanical model in the McCord A20H Pilot to the triaxial
measurements made on core extracted from the KGS 1-32 (Table 43).

The increase in seismic activity in Kansas correlates with brine disposal operations, indicating
that pore fluid pressure is reactivating preexisting faults. This study evaluates the potential for
injection-induced earthquakes in Wellington Field, focusing on subsurface fault mapping and
stress analysis. Kansas has seen a rise in seismicity linked to brine disposal since 2009 with over
100 M3.0+ earthquakes that occurred from 2013 to 2017, with significant events in western
Sumner County. The majority of seismic events are located within the crystalline basement,
suggesting a hydraulic connection with basement faults. A detailed characterization of
subsurface faults utilizing 3D seismic imaging was made at the Wellington site to determine

 383

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

orientations and stresses for assessing induced seismic hazards. A similar study would be
necessary at the proposed Bushton site. These studies will determine which faults are stable. As
an analog, it was determined that at the Wellington site, that faults striking <020° are stable,
while those striking 020° through 049° may be prone to reactivation with increased pore fluid
pressure. At Wellington, the proposed injection volume of 40,000 t was determined unlikely to
reactivate faults at reservoir depths, but higher rates of injection could exceed critical thresholds
in the basement.
The orientation and magnitudes of principal stresses were estimated at Wellington through
analysis of drilling-induced fractures and moment tensor solutions from recent earthquakes. The
study found consistent stress orientations across the region, with significant implications for fault
reactivation potential.
• SHmax estimated at approximately 075°, with no local trends in nodal plane orientation.
•   Stress magnitudes at 1,484 m: Sv = 36.6 MPa, Shmin = 18.4 MPa, SHmax = 31.3–45.9 MPa.
• Stress gradients: Sv = 24 MPa/km, Shmin = 12.4 MPa/km, SHmax = 21–31 MPa/km.
• Pore fluid pressure at 1,484 m is 14.5 MPa.
Slip and dilation tendency analysis assessed the likelihood of fault reactivation by calculating
slip and dilation tendencies based on observed fault geometries and estimated stress states.
Results indicated varying potential for fault slip under different stress conditions.
• Slip tendency values for SS (strike-slip; lateral movement expected) stress state ranged from
    0.46 to 0.01.
• For NS (normal stress; extensional movement expected) stress state, slip tendency values
 were less than 0.34.
• Critical pore fluid pressure changes required for failure ranged from 1.1 MPa to 9.8 MPa,
 depending on the stress state and fault orientation.
• Dilation tendency values were generally low, indicating a higher likelihood of slip over
 dilation.
The study evaluated the potential for fault reactivation in both the Mississippian and Arbuckle
reservoirs, revealing that many faults are moderately oriented for failure under current stress
conditions. The analysis highlighted the influence of pore fluid pressure on fault stability. The
author’s analysis indicated a low likelihood of reactivating faults in the Mississippian and
Arbuckle, but highlighted concerns regarding basement faults. These faults may provide
pathways for pressure changes that could induce seismicity (Schwab et al. 2017). If the injection
reservoirs in the Bushton areas have additional permeability from non-matrix porosity systems
like fractures or karst, this would further decrease the chances of fault or fracture reactivation.

 Structural Model
The structural model, incorporating the static 3D model is documented in section 3.2. A 1D
MEM serves as a calibration point for further coupled geomechanical flow simulation, where
iterative updates are made to the 3D MEM as pore pressure and other stresses evolve during
injection. This represents the final and most comprehensive integration of all data types and
models reviewed thus far.

 384

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 Results and Discussion
We have introduced all the necessary steps to generate a comprehensive, integrated 3D MEM.
This includes core, petrophysical, and well log based geomechanical models as input into a
coupled 3D reservoir/geomechanical flow model. A 1D MEM was created in the nearest offset
well, and a thorough review of previous work incorporating core analysis and fault slip potential
within the intended storage formation (Arbuckle) and overlying sealing rock. Necessary
components are provided here:
• a framework model to characterize the structure of the formation including formation
 horizons and major faults;
• a petrophysical model to quantify the lithology, porosity, water saturation, matrix
 permeability, and dynamic elastic moduli;
• a mechanical stratigraphy model to characterize the stratigraphic column, load bearing facies,
 and natural and drilling induced fracture attributes;
• a rock property model to characterize the static moduli, deformation, yield, and failure
 properties of the formation;
• an overburden model to characterize the vertical loading;
• a pore pressure model to quantify the pore pressure;
• a stress orientation model to characterize the dip and azimuth of the far-field stresses;
• a stress magnitude model to quantify the horizontal loading on the formations.
Recommended further work at the Wellington site includes additional integration of the available
triaxial test in the KGS 1-32H and complete (re)-processing of the sonic data in the McCord
A20H. The integration of the core data will provide calibration to the well-based 1D MEM as
well as set upper and lower bounds for principal horizontal stresses. Reprocessed sonic data will
enable the determination of the stress orientation, and differentiation between stress and fracture
induced anisotropy. These results can further be incorporated into a fully realized, reservoir
coupled, 3D MEM. Risk assessment at the Wellington site was also facilitated through seismic
imaging interpretation of horizons and faults within the formations of interest.
At the Bushton site, core data and modern sonic logs are required to develop a local MEM,
which would be significantly enhanced through integration of a FMI, which provides further
insight into formation stress magnitude and orientation, as well as enabling quantification of pre-
existing faults and fractures. As with the Wellington site, 3D seismic imaging is highly
recommended to realize a full risk assessment of injection induced fault slippage and induced
seismicity.
In summary, the results demonstrate that building a detailed MEM—integrating core, log, and
stress data—is essential for reliably assessing induced seismicity and leakage risk at injection
sites. For Bushton, this means that to ensure safe CO2 or brine injection, similar site-specific data
(core analyses, modern well logs, and especially 3D seismic imaging) are needed to characterize
faults, rock properties, and stress conditions. Applying this approach will allow for targeted risk
assessment of fault reactivation and leakage at Bushton, helping identify safe injection pressures
and minimizing the potential for induced earthquakes or loss of containment. In short, thorough
geomechanical characterization—like what was done at Wellington—is critical before
proceeding with injection operations at Bushton.

 385

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 Subtask 3.5 – Install and Monitor Seismometer Network for Seismic
 Risk Analysis
Induced seismicity in Kansas and Oklahoma has been studied extensively by researchers and
regulatory agencies in both states for more than a decade. Well site monitoring guidelines (EPA
2013; EPA 2018) require that CO2 injection at Class VI wells may proceed only if baseline
seismicity levels are not exceeded. Prior to injection, local monitoring networks must be installed
to establish baseline seismicity levels using historical data and regional tectonic assessments
(Templeton et al. 2022). These networks should be capable of detecting local earthquake
magnitudes of at least M1 and recording all ground motions associated with such events. Once
sequestration begins, projects must adhere to the EPA’s 7-Step protocol and associated traffic
light system for managing induced seismicity risks (Templeton et al. 2022; 40 C.F.R. §
146.94(a); Emergency…2024).
Subtask 3.5 accomplishments:
• Developed and field-tested a low-cost seismic network using the Raspberry Shake 3D (RS-
 3D; Raspberry Shake 2023) seismometers, offering a viable alternative to conventional
 broadband stations. Each station, including peripheral components, cost approximately
 $3,500, substantially lower than commonly used broadband seismometers that cost more than
 $35,000 per station. RS-3D station recordings were validated against broadband seismic
 recordings from regional USGS and KGS networks in Kansas (Proffitt 2024).
• Conducted 11 months of continuous seismic monitoring near the ONEOK Bushton facility
 and established local background seismicity for future seismic risk analysis. The RS-3D
 network detected 440 earthquakes in the state of Kansas and 140 local earthquakes within a
 45-mi (72.4 km) radius of the study site. The RS-3D network revealed local, low-level
 seismicity not reported by the distant USGS and KGS networks (Templeton et al. 2022).

 3.5.1 – Development and Deployment of a Low-Cost Seismic Network
The RS-3D is an all-in-one, plug-and-play seismograph consisting of three electronically
extended 4.5 Hz short period geophone sensors capable of capturing signals down to a 2 second
period (Raspberry Shake 2023). The incorporated computer is the Raspberry Pi 3 – Model B,
which comes with pre-installed Raspberry Shake software, making it ready for immediate use.
This seismometer provides real-time miniSEED data compatible with various seismological
software such as SeisComP (GFZ 2008), Earthworm (USGS 1994; ISTI 2024), ObsPy
(Beyreuther et al. 2010), and SEISAN (Havskov and Ottemöller 1999) (Raspberry Shake 2023).
Five RS-3D seismic stations were constructed and installed at three locations: three co-located at
the ONEOK facility in Bushton, one in Holyrood Cemetery (approximately 6.1 km NW), and
one at the Kansas Wetlands Education Center (approximately 25.3 km SW). Each unit was
installed approximately 2 ft underground in a waterproof enclosure, with an above-ground
system powered by solar panel, 12 V deep cycle battery, and equipped with a Global Positioning
System (GPS) and wireless telemetry components (Figure 241). For detailed description of
station fabrication, refer to Proffitt (2024, Appendix A).

 386

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 241 (left) Raspberry Shake 3D seismometer shown in the waterproof case. (middle) Above ground case
housing station components. (right) A completed seismic station installation at the ONEOK Bushton site. Surface
components housed inside the black tote, antennas for cellular and Global Positioning System (GPS) signals, and a
solar panel to power the components. The polyvinyl chloride (PVC) piping extending above the ground allows
cables connected to the seismometer below ground to reach the tote.
Before field deployment each seismometer was manually configured for continuous data
recording and streaming, and for minimizing network disconnections. Stations were remotely
accessible using the free virtual private network (VPN) service ZeroTier
(https://www.zerotier.com/) safeguarding network data and privacy. Additionally, an in-house
developed script enabled each seismometer to reconnect online in the event of a system reboot.
Remote station access reduced significantly the need for maintenance visits to the network
stations. For a detailed description of the station setup, see Proffitt (2024, Appendix A).
The five RS-3D stations were installed at three locations forming the RS-3D network (Figure
242). The first installation was located at ONEOK facility in Bushton, and consisted of 3 stations
spaced approximately 100 m apart in a N-S orientation. Multiple station deployments at the
ONEOK facility allowed for multiplicity of observations providing nearly uninterrupted
monitoring and confidence in low magnitude recordings at an industrial, noisy site. A second
location was set up in Holyrood cemetery, 6.1 km northwest from the ONEOK facility, and a
third location southwest at the Kansas Wetlands Education Center, 25.3 km away from the
ONEOK facility. Site selection was challenging due to the limited availability of public land and
the few contact points for requesting permission to use private land. The Holyrood location, a
cemetery on the southeast edge of the city limits, proved ideal due to its consistently quiet
environment and regular monitoring lasted 11-months with the exception of a two-week period
in November due to power outage caused by a winter freeze. While the stations at the ONEOK
facility recorded significant operational noise, having multiple stations at this location improved
the signal quality for earthquake detection.

 3.5.2 – Earthquake Data Collection and Analysis
Throughout the project, the use of open-source software for documentation, forums, and
accessibility was maintained. Remote monitoring of the Bushton area began at the KU campus,
where data was collected using a telemetry-based connection for processing and interpretation.
As data was retrieved directly from the stations, it was automatically downloaded in miniSEED
format. The Standard for the Exchange of Earthquake Data (SEED), developed by the USGS and
the Albuquerque Seismic Laboratory, has become the standard for delivering unprocessed
earthquake data to various laboratories (Bormann 2012). The free SEISAN software package
was used for earthquake detection, location, and magnitude calculations. A subsurface seismic
velocity model used in this study was calculated using two well logs (Kinzel well and
Schepmann Trust Well) near the ONEOK facility (Proffit 2024, Appendix C).
For visualization and data compilation, Python (Python Software Foundation, Wilmington DE)
and its extension, ObsPy were used. Python was used to develop an Secure File Transfer
Protocol (SFTP) script that automated the data collection process. The Python script accessed
each station and channel, transferring the data to a specified folder. ObsPy, a Python toolbox for
seismology, was used for waveform analysis and signal detection. The analysis utilized a
recursive STA/LTA (short-term average/long-term average) network trigger, which applies two
moving windows (short-term and long-term) to a continuous data stream to calculate the average
signal power, or signal-to-noise ratio (SNR). For detailed description of data collection and
analysis methods refer to Proffitt (2024, Appendix A).

 3.5.3 – RS-3D Earthquake Data Quality Assessment
Critical information for accurate earthquake detection—such as arrival time, location, and
magnitude—was collected and compared across all three seismic networks (RS-3D, USGS, and
 388

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

KGS; Figure 242). However, the overlap where all three networks recorded the same events was
limited due to differences in coverage area and time constraints.
Continuous monitoring was conducted by the RS-3D network over a period of 11 months (from
May 17, 2023, to April 30, 2024), but the network experienced 15 days in total data loss in
November due to harsh winter conditions causing power outages and animal damage to surface
wiring. Additionally, the USGS network’s spatial coverage in Kansas is limited due to the sparse
distribution of stations within the state.
For the earthquake data comparison, six events that were recorded by all three networks were
analyzed (Table 44 and Figure 243). The earthquakes occurred at least 80 km from the RS-3D
network, classifying them as regional events. Each arrival time from the USGS, RS-3D, and
KGS stations agreed while the magnitudes and epicenters calculated showed some variability
across all three networks (Table 44). Varying magnitudes and earthquake epicenters may be
expected depending on the network location relative to the earthquake, calibration of the user’s
velocity model, response file, and spectral frequency fit. While small differences in magnitude
and epicenter location are observed between the RS-3D and USGS/KGS stations, these
differences are attributed to variations in network geometry and station placement. We note that
the RS-3D station locations are not optimal as they were limited by site availability The
uncertainty in earthquake magnitude and location increased with the distance from the RS-3D
stations. Conversely, seismic events closer to the RS-3D stations were determined with higher
confidence in both location and magnitude.

 Central Kansas Background Seismicity and RS-3D Monitoring
Historically, Kansas experienced relatively low seismicity. Figure 244 summarizes statewide
seismic activity from 1867 to 2018. From 1867 to 1977, only approximately 30 felt earthquakes
were reported. Between 1977 and 2012, a total of 197 earthquakes were recorded by the
statewide network, with fifteen of those having a magnitude of M3 or larger (KGS 2024). The
onset of widespread wastewater disposal activities in the south central and north central part of
the state led to a significant increase in earthquakes from 2013 to 2023 (Figure 244). Very few
earthquakes are reported in the central part of the state near Bushton, as shown in the region near
the RS-3D stations (Figure 245), despite established wastewater disposal operations in the
region. The lack of reported seismicity may be due to the lack of local monitoring networks.
Figure 245 shows the location of seismic stations of the KGS and USGS networks that are
hundreds of kilometers from each other in central Kansas limiting a network’s ability to report
with confidence on small magnitude events. Using the RS-3D network this study compiled an
earthquake catalog from May 17, 2023, through April 30, 2024, documenting 440 earthquakes
across the state of Kansas (Figure 246). Each event was analyzed to determine its epicenter
location and magnitude, with recorded magnitudes ranging from Mw0.7 to Mw4.2. During the
same period, the KGS reported 228 earthquakes with magnitudes between Mw2.0 and Mw4.3.
Meanwhile, the USGS reported 26 events, with magnitudes ranging from Mw1.4 to Mw4.0.
Figure 245 shows the epicenters of each earthquake recorded and its reporting institution. There
was a period of 19 days out of the total 333 days that all RS-3D network seismometers were
down due to a winter storm. The freezing temperatures caused the power convertors from the
deep cycle batteries to the seismometers to stop delivering power to the seismometers. The
number of days without data equals 5.7% of the total monitoring period.

 3.5.5 – RS-3D Earthquake Catalogue of Central Kansas Seismic Activity
Earthquake monitoring in Kansas has historically shown that the central Kansas region is
seismically quiet. However, central Kansas is located on the edge of the CKU and the area has
numerous faults (e.g., Figure 242). Knowing these conditions, the lack of earthquakes in the area
may be due to a lack of local monitoring networks. In Figure 247, all earthquakes reported by the
USGS and KGS are plotted in conjunction with the earthquakes detected from the RS-3D
network. The locations of the RS-3D earthquake epicenters agree with the regional events
reported by the USGS and the KGS while also filling in the central Kansas area that was once
thought to be seismically quiet. Additionally, the epicenter locations within the study area have a
higher confidence in time arrivals, magnitude calculations, and earthquake epicenter locations.

 3.5.6 – Conclusions
This study demonstrated the viability of using low-cost RS-3D seismometers for local seismic
monitoring, particularly in industrial settings requiring continuous monitoring, such as CO2
sequestration and wastewater injection. Given the growing interest in CCS as a strategy to

 394

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

mitigate climate change, efficient and affordable earthquake detection systems are essential to
meet EPA guidelines for managing induced seismicity risks.
The research focused on two primary objectives, a) Developing low-cost seismic stations using
RS-3D seismometers and readily available components (solar panels, wireless modems and
antennas, GPS units, and 12V batteries) and evaluating their performance; and b) Assessing
background seismicity in central Kansas, specifically around the ONEOK facility in Bushton,
Kansas. This region has historically experienced low seismicity, making it an ideal case study for
CO2 sequestration projects.
Over 333 days of continuous data collection, 19 days of data were lost due to a winter storm on
October 27th, which caused all stations to go offline simultaneously. Field investigations
revealed that the $5.00 power converters had frozen during the storm. Use of more robust
components will alleviate the issue. Despite this setback, the RS-3D stations reliably collected
seismic data, detecting small-magnitude earthquakes while maintaining GPS timing and
operating on solar power.
The RS-3D stations proved to be a cost-effective alternative to traditional broadband
seismometers, which are significantly more expensive. At approximately $1,500 per unit, RS-3D
seismometers offer substantial savings while delivering accurate real-time seismic data. The total
cost of each seismic station was approximately $3,500. By integrating GPS timing and utilizing
weather-resistant enclosures and solar panels, the stations achieved continuous operation with
minimal maintenance. The research team processed and analyzed the collected earthquake data
efficiently using open-source software such as SeisAn and ObsPy, validating the RS-3D’s
performance against data from USGS and KGS stations.
While minor discrepancies in magnitude and epicenter location were observed between the RS-
3D and USGS/KGS stations, these differences were attributed to variations in network geometry
and station placement. The uncertainty in earthquake magnitude and location increased with the
distance from the RS-3D stations. Conversely, seismic events closer to the RS-3D stations were
determined with higher confidence in both location and magnitude. This study demonstrated that
RS-3D seismometers could detect seismic events with magnitudes as low as Mw0.7, meeting
EPA requirements for CO2 sequestration operations.
During the monitoring period the RS-3D network identified 140 local earthquakes with
magnitudes ranging from Mw1.5 to Mw2.2. While these earthquakes are too small to be felt by
humans and to be detected reliably by the distant KGS and USGS networks, the RS-3D local
network confirmed the occurrence of low-level seismicity in central Kansas.

 Task 4 – Dynamic Simulation
PNNL participated in the carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) Hub 2.0 Concept for
ONEOK project, led by the KGS for the CUSP-West study, as a consultant and dynamic
reservoir simulation provider. PNNL’s scope on this project was to collaboratively work with the
KGS to model the fate of CO2 injected into selected target project reservoirs. These results were
then passed to LANL for risk analyses with the NRAP tools. Reservoir modeling was completed
with the PNNL-developed STOMP-CO2 and STOMPX-CO2 reservoir simulators. KGS provided
a series of static geologic models to PNNL, which included three storage reservoirs at two sites,
near Bushton, KS and Medford, OK. Two storage reservoirs were considered at the Bushton

 395

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

site—LKC and Arbuckle—and one storage reservoir was considered at the Medford site—
Wilcox-Bromide. Whereas the STOMP-CO2 and STOMPX-CO2 simulators have modeling
capabilities that include geochemistry and geomechanics, neither of these was exercised during
this phase of the project. The static geologic models comprised a structured hexahedral
computational mesh and data concerning the intrinsic permeability, porosity, initial pressure,
initial salinity, and initial pressure at the centroids of each grid cell, in Petrel format.
Unique static geologic models were provided for each storage reservoir, and in the case of the
Bushton, Arbuckle reservoir, two static geologic models were investigated: UA and AD. These
static geologic models, provided as ASCII formatted GRDECL (a Petrel/Eclipse grid file format)
files, were converted to STOMP input format and then combined with other required STOMP
input, such as saturation functions, relative permeability functions, well models, initial
conditions, boundary conditions, and output options to create a simulation model. These models
were then executed with STOMPX-CO2 (i.e., the Message Passing Interface [MPI] parallel
implementation of STOMP-CO2) on PNNL’s supercomputer “constance,” which has 520
compute nodes, each with 24 cores. Constance is being phased out, but when installed in
November 2014, it was ranked 297th on the Top 500 supercomputer list. As the computational
domains were modest in size computations were restricted to single nodes, using either 20 or 24
cores. This technical memo is designed to document the series of simulations executed to model
the fate of CO2 injected into the three reservoirs, located at two sites.

 Saturation Function
Saturation functions relate capillary pressure (i.e., the difference between gas and aqueous
pressure) to aqueous saturation. As parameters for this function were not included in the data
package a representative saturation function was used, based on the Brooks and Corey (1964)
function with the Webb (2000) extension and hysteretic nonwetting fluid entrapment (Figure
251).

 Bushton, KS, Site, UA Reservoir
The static geologic model for the Bushton, KS, site, UA reservoir was provided to PNNL as a
series of four data files, as shown in Table 49. Seven preliminary scenarios were modeled that

 402

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

were directed at establishing the permeability of the reservoir, using the five Class 1 injector
wells as a benchmark. These wells were injecting at a known rate under hydrostatic conditions
from the ground surface. The scenarios labeled cropped used trajectories for these wells that
were restricted in depth to remain above the lower permeability layer in the static geology model,
and those labeled actuals used the actual trajectories, which extended below the low permeability
layer for some wells. These simulations, which were executed for 10 yr, established that a
permeability scaling factor of 5.0 was required to achieve the injection rates for the five Class 1
injectors under hydrostatic pressure conditions. This permeability field was then used in a final
simulation scenario with the five Class 1 injectors and a single Class VI (CO2 injector) injector
well. Simulation times varied with the complexity of the simulation, with shorter times being
associated with the scenarios where the injection well was pressure controlled, yielding injection
rates less than specified, as shown in Table 49. The density range for pure CO2 over the initial
temperature and pressure range of the simulations is shown in Figure 250, as UA at 0.26 psi/ft.

injection was active, in order to mimic the legacy brine disposal into the Arbuckle aquifer in the
region. Then during the next 30 yr, both wastewater and CO2 injection was active. Finally,
during the closing 10 or 60 yr, only wastewater injection was active. Simulation results were
recorded in a series of binary formatted files. The output.bin file contains a record user specified

interval), and well mass injection rate versus time (Figure 269 and Figure 270). The
contours_xxxyr.dat files were used to create color contours of brine and free gas plumes at the
specified plot times (Figure 271 through Figure 273). The implications of these simulation
results will be discussed in Section 4.2.

variables (Table 60) at each time step, and the plot_xxxxxxx.bin files contain a record of user

converted to ASCII formatted files. The output.bin file was converted to output, and the
plot_xxxxxxx.bin files were converted to contours_xxxyr.dat files. The output file was used to
generate plots of forms of integrated CO2 mass, well pressure (top of screened interval), and well
mass injection rate versus time (Figure 260 and Figure 261). The contours_xxxyr.dat files were

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

used to create color contours of brine and free gas plumes at the specified plot times (Figure 262
through Figure 264). The implications of these simulation results will be discussed in Section
4.2.

 Subtask 4.2 – Dynamic Simulations of CO2 Injection Scenarios into
 Saline Storage Reservoirs
A series of numerical simulations were executed with STOMPX-CO2, PNNL developed parallel
reservoir simulator for modeling the fate of CO2 injected into deep saline reservoirs. These
simulations were executed on PNNL’s “constance,” a supercomputer based on the Intel Haswell
CPU architecture and is the generalized system for parallel applications requiring dozens to
thousands of compute cores. The STOMPX-CO2 reservoir simulator is a MPI-based
implementation of STOMP-CO2, which has been benchmarked against problems from two
international code comparison studies: (1) GeoSeq (Pruess et al. 2002), comprising 8 test
problems, and (2) Stuttgart Benchmark Study (Class et al. 2009), comprising 3 test problems.
This series of simulations were designed to provide a preliminary assessment of two sites and
four reservoirs to meet the carbon storage needs of a CCS hub for ONEOK at 0.35 Mt/yr for 30
yr. The sites were located near Bushton, KS, and Medford, OK. At the Bushton, KS, site, three
reservoirs were considered: (1) LKC, (2) UA, and (3) Deep Arbuckle. At the Medford, OK, site,
a single reservoir was considered: (1) Wilcox–Bromide. As with most subsurface modeling
projects, several simulations were executed for each reservoir beyond those reported in this
document. Included in these simulations were those used to conduct auxiliary investigations
(e.g., closed versus open boundaries, neglecting interference from neighboring injectors) and
those that had input errors.
This technical memo was specifically written to document this series of preliminary numerical
simulations, providing a readable log of the data contained in the input and output files for the
reportable simulations completed. This series of simulations are considered preliminary, as they

 426

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

are based on a single realization of the geology and associated petrophysical and transport
properties for each reservoir. Moreover, for most of the simulations completed, the boundary
conditions influenced the simulation results (i.e., pressure field, plume migration behavior), thus
a larger areal computational domain extent is required to avoid this influence. Another context
for which these simulations should be considered preliminary is that of geochemistry. CO2
dissolution in water is dependent on the pressure of the gaseous CO2 and the pH of aqueous
solutions of CO2 is inversely proportional to dissolved CO2 concentration (i.e., higher
concentrations yield lower pH solutions). This yields the potential for dissolution of reservoir
minerals and precipitation of carbonate minerals, potential altering porosity, intrinsic
permeability and other petrophysical properties, including the geomechanical strength of the
rock. Though modeling capabilities for these processes is a capability of the STOMPX-CO2,
simulator geochemical processes were not considered during this study.
As modeled the temperature range of the LKC reservoir is influenced by historical petroleum
industry activities, making it lower than the levels expected for the regional geothermal gradient.
As shown in Figure 250, this creates moderate gas densities (i.e., approximately 600 kg/m3)
under the initial temperature and pressure conditions. The LKC simulations generally showed
injectivity much lower than the specified 0.35 Mt/yr, with the actual injection being dependent
on the injection pressure limit, based on fracturing pressure. A characterization well would
provide opportunities to confirm the reservoir porosity and permeability, including non-matrix
porosity systems like fractures or karst, plus minimum horizontal stress or fracture initiation
pressures.
The static geologic model for the UA reservoir included a low permeability horizon, designed to
separate the Arbuckle formation into two layers. Historical records of injectivity of five
wastewater injectors provided an excellent benchmark for defining the in-situ permeability of the
formation (i.e., combined matrix and fracture permeability). For these simulations, an initial and
boundary condition state of the initial pressure and temperature varying vertically with a
temperature of 97 °F (36.1 °C) and pressure of 1,000 psi (6.89 MPa) imposed at a depth of
3,782.97 ft (1,153 m) bgs. As shown in Figure 250, this yields subcritical-gas CO2 conditions for
the gas with associated low gas densities. The series of UA simulations with the wastewater
injectors established that permeabilities 5 times that of the matrix permeabilities would be
sufficient to show agreement with the historical inject records. During the simulation with
combined injections of wastewater and CO2, however, the low initial pressure yielded large gas-
plume volumes, which was consistent with the density of CO2 for those temperature and pressure
states. These simulations were halted after 15 yr.
Following the investigations with the UA geologic model, the DA static geologic model was
developed, which comprised the entirety of the Arbuckle formation, but did not include a low-
permeability layer. The initial pressure used in the UA models was revised to agree with recent
field measurements. The principal objective for the DA series of simulations was to quantify the
interference in pressure and plume extents between wastewater and CO2 injectors, with the
wastewater plume being a density brine and the CO2 plume being a less dense gas. These
simulations considered three well locations for the CO2 injectors: (1) orthogonal from the trends
of permeability to the wastewater injectors, (2) in line with the trends of permeability to the
wastewater injectors, and (3) amid the wastewater injectors. For all three locations, the CO2
injector was screened at greater depths than those for the wastewater injectors. The third location

 427

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

was selected to determine if the wastewater injections could increase the amount of trapped gas.
Preliminary findings from these simulations indicate that pressure interference between the
wastewater and CO2 injectors is minor due, in part to the density contrasts between the brine
(more dense) and the CO2 (less dense) fluid phase. However, more accurate data concerning the
current state of formation pressure in the Arbuckle is required. Multiple realizations of the static
geologic model well also be required to quantify the uncertainty of the fate of the injected CO2
and AoR over the course of the project.
The MWB reservoir offers advantages of being more remote from other subsurface activities
(i.e., wastewater injections and petroleum production) and is located at the deepest horizon of the
investigated reservoirs. The greater depth means higher temperatures but also higher fluid
pressures, yielding gas densities in the 600 kg/m3 range. The downside to the MWB reservoir is
the lower permeability. Further characterization could indicate a different permeability and pre-
injection stimulations could improve injectivity. Simulations of the MWB considered three
different well locations, but all three simulations showed the CO2 injection well as being
pressure limited with injection rates being well below the target value of 0.35 Mt/yr.

  Task 5 – Risk Assessment
This task summarizes a quantitative risk assessment of CO2 and brine leakage and the potential
impacts on the USDW at the Bushton, KS, ONEOK site. The team developed a workflow to
import pressure and CO2 saturation results obtained by physics-based reservoir simulator
(STOMP) into NRAP Open-Source Integrated Assessment Model (NRAP-Open-IAM;
Vasylkivska et al. 2021). The integrated modeling enabled quantitative assessment of CO2/brine
leakage and aquifer exposure risks. Preliminary 30-yr injection risk modeling in both the
Bushton–LKC and Arbuckle formations suggests low leakage potential within the AoR.
However, modeling limitations—and uncertainties in legacy well sealing and subsurface
faulting—highlight the need for further site characterization.
