 Summary
Among legacy wells that have been drilled in the study domain, wells penetrating to the two
targeted storage formations have been identified. Leakage risk analyses for chosen representative
wells show that the pressure build up and wellbore permeability strongly influence the CO2 and
brine leakage from the reservoir to the USDW.
For LKC formation injection, analysis of chosen representative wells in the reservoir domain
shows there are very small CO2 and brine leakage, and small USDW impact for wells 1, 3, 4, and
5. The percent of CO2 leaked in comparison to the total amount injected is less than 4 × 10-7 %
for the highest potential leaky well. There is no CO2 and brine leakage, and no impact to USDW
on pH and TDS beyond natural background variability for well 2 (API 15159003220000).
For Arbuckle formation injections, analysis of chosen existing wells on the reservoir domain
shows that there is no CO2 and brine leakage and no impact to USDW on pH and TDS beyond
natural background variability for any well.
For this study we take a conservative approach for leakage risk assessment, choosing the legacy
wells that are closest surrounding the injection well to evaluate the highest CO2 and brine
leakage potentials for existing legacy wells. For Class VI well permit application at the ONEOK
site, AoR delineation will confine the leakage risk concerned area. Individual well leakage
situations are different based on each well’s degradation status, more complete wellbore and site
characterization data will help facilitate the site-specific leakage risk assessment accurately.
5.2 Subtask 5.2 – Assess well integrity and seal penetrations. To determine risk for leakage from
storage vessels, seal assessment is necessary in the AoR
Well integrity broadly includes all elements of well construction that are in place to prevent
uncontrolled release of fluids into other formations or the environment. Casing, cement,
wellhead components, and other downhole elements (e.g., sliding sleeves) represent physical
barriers between a producing reservoir and its produced fluids and gases with other permeable
formations penetrated by the wellbore and the surface environment. Carbon sequestration-
specific well integrity considerations and suggestions for additional research needs are
summarized in Iyer et al. (2022); research recommendations of these authors included the
following:
• Improve the availability of existing well construction and inspection data through digitization
 of historical regulatory records.
• Establish quantitative relationships between well information in regulatory databases and
 indicators of leakage risks for use in prioritizing well inspection and remediation efforts.
• Develop and test methods to quantify leakage risk and uncertainty when well attribute data
 are missing.
• Evaluate different mitigation and risk management approaches when leakage risk of legacy
 wells is unacceptable.
• Incorporate improved characterizations of well barrier integrity, leak detectability, and
 mitigation into quantitative risk assessment and management frameworks for improved
 decision support.
As discussed in Subtask 5.1, this study applied a relatively conservative leakage risk assessment
that focused on legacy wells nearest the proposed injection well at the Bushton site and did not

 442

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

include a rigorous well-by-well evaluation for each of the 100+ wells within the AoR. An audit
and evaluation of well integrity at the Medford site was not completed. The approach applied at
the Bushton site was necessary and reviewed with the team during the study for the following
reasons:
• Location of the injection well in the simulation is conceptual
• The static geologic model is under-constrained and lacks a “stratigraphic well” that would
 redefine trends within the model to more properly delineate an AoR.
• Existing drilling, completion, plugging, and status for wells in the model area is variable. A
 thorough evaluation of all wells (including those operated by ONEOK) will be necessary for
 any future carbon sequestration considerations in the area.
• Most wells were drilled prior to 2010 with some approaching 100 yr since their spud date
 (Figure 278 and Figure 279). Newer wells are likely to have better casing and cement;
 however, recent production could decrease formation pressure below pre-production
 conditions which were not assessed during this study.

Figure 278 Map showing spud date by decade for wells in the Bushton area. NOTE: Most wells drilled to the
Arbuckle Group. Data compiled by Enverus (2023); used with permission.

 443

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 279 Map showing wells in the modeled area with current operator (left). Cumulative production by operator
since 2010 (right). Data compiled by Enverus (2023); used with permission.
At the Bushton site an evaluation of well and seal integrity will require analysis of original well
documentation; additionally, a review with the Kansas Corporation Commission (KCC)
regarding historical activity in the area and current operators is recommended. If third party data
aggregation services are utilized (e.g., Enverus), the underlying data must be validated with
documented and publicly available information. As recommended by Iyer et al. (2022), a method
to apply leakage risk and uncertainty where documentation and attributes are unknown will need
to be established as well as strategies for mitigation and risk management where wellbores with
known integrity issues are identified. A detailed vessel and pipeline to the well injection site
(with appropriate leakage/seal evaluation and monitoring) will need to be developed by the
operator of the injection well. As discussed in Subtask 3.2.6, it is not recommended without
additional technical evaluation that salt cavern storage of CO2 be considered at the Bushton site.

 Subtask 5.3 – Prepare a Ranked Matrix of Key Risk Factors for
 Each Seal and Reservoir Horizon AoR Addressing Key Surface and
 Subsurface Issues that Might Affect Injection Viability
This subtask synthesizes the data audit, modeling, and simulation results into a comparative
framework, addressing qualitative subsurface risk profiles relevant to viability, and permitting.
Additionally, it illustrates where additional effort might be invested to reduce subsurface
uncertainty and define the VOI related to collecting new data (e.g., seismic, cased-hole wireline,
new drillwell, etc.). It is inherently a qualitative exercise based on relative quality of the selected
elements. Importantly, it highlights the tradeoff between areas that have reasonable subsurface
datasets (e.g., Bushton Arbuckle) vs. those without (e.g., MWB). At the Bushton site there are
numerous wells with valuable information (top depths, thickness, reservoir properties, etc.) and
offset information (injection and production rates) whereas at the Medford site there are fewer
wells and an under-constrained reservoir system. The Medford site, however, carries
significantly lower seal containment and offset operation risk.
Figure 280 is the summary ranked matrix of the key risk factors that were considered in the
evaluation of the reservoirs, sealing formations, and the USDWs (Kansas only). It is important to
note that in both Kansas and Oklahoma multiple sealing facies exist above the Arbuckle,

 444

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Wilcox–Bromide sandstone, and the LKC systems. The Arbuckle has the advantage in both
states of being deeper, having well characterized reservoir characteristics, and high injectivity.
This evaluation highlights the importance of considering multiple reservoir targets to identify the
best candidate(s) and to consider redundant/backup injection options within injection wells
should initial injection performance prove to be inadequate. It also highlights the importance of
understanding the current formation pressure; specifically for the Bushton site, it is critical to
understand the current regional pressure sources (injection) and sinks (production) that might
cause local perturbations in the system and create unexpected injection plume formation.

Figure 280 Stoplight style risk matrix for each seal and reservoir horizon and area of review (AoR) addressing key
surface and subsurface issues that might affect injection viability. The Kansas underground sources of drinking
water (USDWs) are also included for context.
The AoRs defined in this study are preliminary (see Subtask 2.4 of this report) but highlight the
information density, quality, and availability near the ONEOK operational facilities at Bushton,
KS, and Medford, OK. Future evaluation at either site should benefit from this preliminary work
which has assembled many of the fundamental elements necessary for a successful CCS project.
In particular, it should be noted that the reservoir property modeling (e.g., porosity and
permeability) represent non-unique solutions to the dataset and additional static scenarios could
possibly generate plumes and pressure response quite different than those presented in this
report. The risk from induced seismicity was not included in the risk matrix because neither site
currently has evidence of seismicity above background levels or mapped faults (see Subtask 3.5
of this report). Both Bushton reservoir formations had favorable outcomes in the LANL relative
leakage risk rankings by well and formation with the LKC showing minimal leakage and the
Arbuckle showing none (see Subtask 5.1 of this report).

 445

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 Induced Seismicity
 As outlined in Subtask 3.5, induced seismicity in Kansas and Oklahoma has been studied
extensively by researchers and regulators for over a decade. Kansas historically experienced low
seismicity, with only approximately 30 felt earthquakes between 1867 and 1977. However,
increased saltwater disposal activities since 2000 have been linked to a sharp rise in earthquake
frequency. From 1977 to 2012, more than 200 seismic events were recorded in association with
Arbuckle Group injection. summarizes statewide seismic activity from 1867 to 2018.
Seismic events from 2014 to 2022 are shown in Figure 281, overlaid with mapped fault traces
and newly deployed seismic monitoring stations, including the RS-3D network described in
Subtask 3.5. These observations demonstrate that central Kansas, previously considered
seismically quiet, does exhibit low-magnitude seismic activity detectable with a localized
network.

Figure 281 Induced seismicity in study area is low risk, despite high wastewater injection volumes. (From Fasola et
al. in prep.)
The relationship between elevated pore pressure and induced seismicity is well established
(Langenbruch and Zoback 2016; Rubinstein et al. 2018; Dempsey and Riffault 2019; Chang and
Segall 2016; Zhai et al. 2019; Figure 244). Given these risks, injection into the Arbuckle is
discouraged by the OGS and regional stakeholders. As a result, the Arbuckle was excluded from
dynamic modeling at the Medford site, even though some static characterization was completed.
Simulations instead focused on more geologically favorable intervals, such as the Wilcox–
Bromide system.
While explicit seismicity modeling was not conducted, PNNL’s dynamic simulations evaluated
spatial and temporal pressure changes, including plume overlap and pressure interference
between CO2 and wastewater injectors in the Arbuckle. These are important precursors for
assessing fault reactivation potential. PNNL concluded that further seismic risk evaluation would
require detailed fault mapping and geomechanical modeling, which was beyond the current
project scope.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 Potential Leakage Risk Analysis Using NRAP Tools
To evaluate the potential for CO2 and brine leakage from legacy wells within the AoR, the
NRAP-Open-IAM was used. This toolset incorporates reduced-order models (ROMs) for key
subsurface components, including the reservoir, wellbore, and overlying aquifer systems.
A preliminary AoR containing 69 legacy wells was assessed using pressure and saturation
outputs from STOMP-based reservoir simulations (Task 4). Wellbore integrity was evaluated
using the cemented wellbore ROM, which accounts for well construction, material degradation,
and pressure gradients. Reservoir simulation results Reservoir simulation results for Well1,
located 380 ft west of the CO2 injector, indicated a peak reservoir pressure of approximately 8.5
MPa after 5 yr of injection and a CO2 saturation peak of approximately 32% at year 35 (Figure
282). These values served as inputs to the wellbore ROM. The analysis confirmed that, under
modeled conditions, no significant leakage of CO2 or brine into the USDW occurred, and no
adverse aquifer impacts were observed.

Figure 282 Reservoir pressure (left) and CO2 saturation (right)

 Traffic Light System to Mitigate Induced Seismicity Hazard and Risk
 A structured approach for managing induced seismicity in geologic carbon storage (GCS) has
been recommended by Templeton et al. (2022) and adopted by the EPA as part of Class VI well
permitting requirements (Figure 283). The federal regulations relevant to this process are
codified in 40 C.F.R. § 146.94(a) (Emergency…2024), as part of the Emergency and Remedial
Response Plan, and elaborated in EPA’s Class VI guidance documents.

 447

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 283 The recommended 7-step approach and the adaptive traffic light from the National Risk Association
Partnership in collaboration with Templeton et al. (2022)
Effective risk management requires real-time monitoring of seismic, hydraulic, and operational
parameters. These inputs can trigger pre-defined response levels or inform rapid hazard and risk
assessments that warrant operational changes. Establishing a baseline of local seismicity is a
prerequisite for implementing a site-specific risk management protocol.
As described in Subtask 3.5, a local seismic monitoring network was installed near the Bushton
facility and operated for 11 months. This network provided a new earthquake catalog for
establishing background seismicity and evaluating risk thresholds. It also demonstrated the utility
of low-cost RS-3D instruments for continuous local monitoring in industrial settings.
Although PNNL did not explicitly model induced seismicity, their reservoir simulations did
capture spatial and temporal pressure trends relevant to seismic risk. These included evaluations
of pressure buildup and plume interference with legacy wastewater injection into the Arbuckle.
Such conditions are recognized precursors for fault reactivation.
As concluded by PNNL, a detailed seismic risk assessment would require fault mapping and
mechanical modeling, which exceeded the current project scope. However, their findings helped
define preliminary AoR boundaries and highlighted the sensitivity of model outcomes to initial
pressure distributions, permeability assumptions, and legacy well characteristics (e.g., plugging
methods and construction age).

 Subtask 5.5 – Economic Risk/Feasibility Assessment
Sandia National Laboratories conducted a detailed economic analysis to evaluate the feasibility
of CO2 storage at four proposed injection scenarios near ONEOK’s facilities in Bushton, KS, and
Medford, OK. The study integrated three key methods: (1) technoeconomic analysis (TEA) to
estimate capital expenditures (CAPEX) and operational expenditures (OPEX) and levelized CO2
storage costs (LCOS); (2) cost–benefit analysis (CBA) using Section 45Q tax incentives to
compute net present value (NPV); and (3) evaluation of financial and regulatory risks affecting
project viability.
 448

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The TEA was conducted following methods from Mishra et al. (2025), using both site-specific
data from ONEOK and generalized cost models. The CBA included baseline and sensitivity
scenarios and incorporated key project parameters such as well depth, injection rate, and lifetime.
Economic risk was evaluated by categorizing regulatory, market, financing, and social risks.
The analysis evaluated four proposed CCS sites: Bushton–LKC, Bushton–Upper Arbuckle
(UArb), Bushton–Deep Arbuckle (DArb), and Medford–Wilcox–Bromide (WilBro). Table 64

 Economic Risk Assessment
Sandia’s analysis also identified key financial risks that could affect project feasibility. These are
categorized as follows:

 Regulatory and Policy Risk
The CCS policy landscape remains dynamic. Uncertainty in Section 45Q tax credit duration,
value, and eligibility introduce risk, as many CCS projects rely on full realization of these
incentives for viability. Compliance with monitoring and verification requirements, long-term
liability, and evolving Class VI permitting standards can also increase costs and delay
implementation (EPA 2018).

 Market and Price Risk
Volatile input prices, particularly for compressors, drilling, and electricity, directly affect
CAPEX and OPEX. Between 2021 and 2025, equipment costs rose significantly. As CCS is
energy-intensive, fluctuations in power prices can notably alter LCOS, potentially undermining
economic viability.

 Financing and Interest Rate Risk
All four sites require substantial upfront investment ($8.2M–$35.6M; see techno-economic
results). Large capital requirements combined with uncertain returns reduce investor confidence.
 451

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Interest rate variability further influences project viability; even small increases in borrowing
costs significantly affect NPV in high CAPEX projects with long lifespans.

 Community and Social Licensing Risk
Local community acceptance is critical. Concerns around groundwater protection, induced
seismicity, and long-term site stewardship may delay or block development. Transparent risk
communication, stakeholder engagement, and environmental monitoring are essential to mitigate
opposition and secure social license.

 Conclusion
Based on available site data and the methodology of Mishra et al. (2025), all four proposed
ONEOK wells appear economically feasible. The analysis used conservative assumptions and
focused exclusively on injection-site costs, excluding capture and transportation expenses. NPVs
exceeding $100 million for each site suggest sufficient economic headroom to accommodate
additional upstream costs.
The results should be interpreted as preliminary indicators, not definitive project valuations. TEA
and NPV outputs are sensitive to input assumptions, particularly cost, operational efficiency, and
policy parameters. Improved accuracy in site-specific data will refine future assessments.
Additionally, while the TEA identified economically viable scenarios, it did not include all
financial risks. Sections above outline key uncertainties—regulatory, market, financing, and
community-related—that may influence future project implementation. The accompanying risk
framework provides a tool for CCS developers to evaluate these uncertainties and enhance
financial planning.
This analysis demonstrates that all four ONEOK CCS project sites are technically and
economically promising candidates for development, contingent on further data acquisition,
regulatory alignment, and proactive risk management.

  Task 6 – Infrastructure Network Assessment
Carbon Solutions utilized SimCCSPRO and other supporting tools to assess the infrastructure
network required to transport CO2 from emitting facilities to sites for permanent geological
storage. SimCCSPRO is an economic-engineering, mixed-integer linear programming model that
determines where and how much CO2 to capture, where and how much CO2 to store, and the
pipeline network that connects these point locations. SimCCSPRO utilizes a series of inputs
generated by the other proven software of CO2NCORD (Carbon Solutions 2025d), SCO2TPRO
(Carbon Solutions 2025b), and CostMAP. Together, these software provide estimates for
capturable CO2 emissions and capture costs, estimates for underground CO2 injection capacities
and storage costs, and a weighted cost surface, respectively.

 Subtask 6.1 – Aggregate Infrastructure Data and Build Databases
Carbon Solutions assessed existing infrastructure within the defined region by aggregating
potential sources of CO2 and using the geology characterization provided by the team’s leading
Task 3 and Task 4 to assess storage options. Carbon Solutions used its proprietary software,
CO2NCORD, to determine all the potential CO2 emitters within the AOI before working with
 452

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

industry partner ONEOK to identify which emitters would be included in the analysis.
Ultimately, eight unique facilities across six industries with a total of 12 capturable streams of
CO2 were selected (Figure 284). These facilities have a cumulative amount of 2.1 Mt of
capturable CO2 emissions with capture costs that range from $36.89/tCO2 to $71.13/tCO2.
Capture costs were generated in CO2NCORD using the best available public data, which
includes literature, expert elicitation, and recent reports from NETL (Bennett et al. 2024). These
emitters represent partnership opportunities for ONEOK in developing and deploying a CCS
network in Kansas and represent the entire extent of emitters in the AOI regardless of their
inclusion in final scenarios (Figure 285).

 Subtask 6.2 – Model Pipeline Corridor and Define Surface Facilities
 That Would Be Required to Execute Chosen Design Concepts
CostMAP is used to determine the potential transportation network that connects sources to
storage sites by creating a cost surface that includes a variety of data, such as rights-of-way, land
use changes, population densities, elevation changes, and more. Each layer that is put into
CostMAP is assigned its own routing and cost weights separately. The cost weights are intended
to account for the actual costs of constructing pipelines in each area. Routing weights are
intended to capture non-economic factors such as environmental considerations or important
areas to local communities. The result is both a routing network, that shows where pipelines can
go, and a cost network that provides cost estimates for these potential routes. Keeping routing
and cost separate is important because while one route might have a lower cost, it could pass
through areas that are important to local community or protected lands. Therefore, having
separate routing and cost networks helps to choose the least cost option that includes
environmental, economic, and social factors. These routing and cost weights help to identify
potential barriers, features that prohibit or restrict pipeline deployment like rights-of-ways and
roads.
After routing and cost weights have been chosen, a stepwise process computes the cost of
moving from cell to cell, calculated as the average cost of the corresponding nodes normalized
by the distance needed to travel between nodes (rook vs bishop movement). More details on the
function of CostMAPPRO can be found in Hoover et al. (2019). The result is more realistic
pipeline routing. More details on potential pipeline corridors and surface facilities that would be
involved in capture-transport-storage systems can be found in Subtask 6.3.

 Subtask 6.4 – Identify Potential Business Entry Opportunities
 Related to Nearby Sources or Users of CO2
Through this analysis, several different facilities were consistently deployed across scenarios.
These sites are potential viable candidates for engaging in future business development for CCS.
These facilities include industries such as the oil and gas, ethanol, chemicals manufacturing,
refineries, and food and agriculture. Some industries, like ethanol manufacturing, produce high
purity CO2 streams at a relatively low capture cost. These ethanol facilities, specifically Kansas
Ethanol (Lyons, KS) and PureField Ingredients, could be ideal candidates to be “first-movers” or
support early CCS efforts, highlighting their potential importance to CCS efforts in Kansas.
Additionally, the CHS (Inver Grove Heights, MN) McPherson Refinery (McPherson, KS) has
some of the largest streams of capturable CO2 emissions in the AOI, making it a potentially
important partner for CCS engagement and business development.
There is growing demand for captured CO2 for utilization in applications such as CO2-EOR
operations, chemical manufacturing, and construction efforts. Each of these end uses have the

 463

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

opportunity to be profitable. For example, captured CO2 emissions not only potentially qualify
for the 45Q tax credit for utilization but then has the opportunity to sell these captured emissions
to any of these utilization industries, allowing them to be potentially profitable.
Total CCS costs are between $87.52/tCO2 to $110.22/tCO2, across all scenarios Carbon
Solutions analyzed. It should be noted that this is higher than some CCS policy support such as
45Q which provides $85/tCO2 for CO2 that is captured and permanently sequestered in
underground geologic storage. Nevertheless, the total CCS network cost decreases with an
increasing number of potential sources and the higher the capture target goes. For example, when
considering storage at the Bushton location CCS network costs go from $103.41/tCO2 when only
considering three sources to $88.58/tCO2 when considering eight sources. This trend is reflected
when storage is placed at either of the alternate sites. This reflects the potential for economies of
scale that CCS networks can benefit from when bringing in new sources.
One of the biggest challenges in this region is the rate at which CO2 can be injected. In the
future, there may be opportunities for other industries to join or engage with CCS by utilizing the
existing infrastructure, given that the storage formations can sustain higher injection rates. It is
important to note that additional infrastructure may be needed to connect these nearby sources
(i.e., additional pipeline deployment). The development of a proposed CCS network will reduce
uncertainty and risk that can be associated with CCS, thereby encouraging future nearby sources
to engage with CCS.
In 2022, the US Congress passed the Inflation Reduction Act (IRA; IRA 2022) which, amongst
other things, included updates to the 45Q tax credit to encourage widespread deployment and
development of CCS activities in the United States. This change increased the tax credit from
$50/tCO2 to $85/tCO2 for captured CO2 that is geologically sequestered. Further, this update also
extended the commence construction window for projects to 2033 and allowed for the credit to
be realized after 12 yr after CCS equipment is in place and active (citation). All facilities chosen
in this analysis meet the eligibility criteria for qualified facilities under 45Q, emitting at least
12,500 tCO2, even if they did not feature in the final proposed networks.
These tax credits are transferable, meaning that eligible facilities can elect to sell their credits to
willing buyers. This transferability means there are opportunities for other industries in the
region to participate in CCS especially if they are not initially part of proposed CCS networks.
This also should help with cost sharing between different participants in the proposed CCS
networks.

  Task 7 – Regulatory Outreach and 45Q Preparations
 Subtask 7.1 – Meet With EPA to Discuss UIC Class VI Permit
 Application
The KGS met with EPA Region 7 representatives to discuss the UIC Class VI permit application

therefore interviews with the EPA were conducted solely for Region 7 (Kansas). This section
documents salient information obtained during interviews and provides a framework for a permit
application in Region 7, following guidelines set forth by the EPA (EPA 2013).

 Interview with EPA Region 7
On March 31, 2025, representatives of KGS met with Ben Meissner and Marina Mailer of EPA
Region 7’s Water Division to discuss the Class VI well permitting application process. The
process occurs in four stages, followed by a fifth phase once injection operations are complete:
 i. Phase 1: Pre-construction to determine site suitability
  ii. Phase 2: Permit to construct
 iii. Phase 3: Pre-operations
 a. Verify information provided in the pre-construction phase
 b. Move into an authorization to inject
 iv. Phase 4: Injection Operations
  v. Phase 5: Post-injection site care.

Permit applications are evaluated on the following content:
 i. Site characterization, including a narrative description of the geologic structures,
 hydrogeologic properties, injection and confining zones, and fluid and solid geochemistry
         to meet the requirements of 40 C.F.R. § 146.82(a)(3), (5), (6) (Required…2024) and 40
 C.F.R. § 146.83 (Minimum…2024). Items and data required for the geologic narrative
 are described in Table 64.
 ii. Pre-op testing, well construction
 a. In regions with sufficient well control data, data may be accessed and used
 b. In regions lacking sufficient well control, a stratigraphic test well may be drilled
 to ensure the AoR is adequate for sequestration
 iii. AoR and Corrective Action (Table 65)
 iv. Testing and Monitoring Plan (Table 66)
  v. Plugging Plan. The Well Plugging Plan may be a narrative (sometimes step-by-step)
 description of plugging procedures for the injection well. It may be accompanied by
 schematics and tables. The plan must include the following information:
 a. Tests or measures for determining bottomhole reservoir pressure.
 b. External mechanical integrity testing methods
 c. The type and number of plugs to be used.
 d. The placement of each plug, including the elevation of the top and bottom of each
 plug.
 e. The type, grade, and quantity of material to be used in plugging.
 f. The method of placement of the plugs.
 vi. Emergency and remedial response plan. The Emergency and Remedial Response Plan
 will be a narrative description of local resources and infrastructure, potential emergency
 events and response actions, personnel, and equipment to address USDW endangerment.
 It may be accompanied by maps, illustrations, and tables.
vii. Construction Details.
 Description of the casing and cement. Well schematics (either planned or as-built) that
 show the surface casing and at least one long string casing. The schematics may be
 accompanied by a narrative step-by-step process for installing casing strings, description
 of centralizers, cementing procedures, cement and cement additives. The application may
 also include a narrative description of how the casing and cement will be compatible with

To date, Region 7 has received four Class VI permit applications: two in Kansas, others are in
Nebraska. Primacy will be determined by the States’ goals for the program and whether there is
an industry push to justify entering the primacy process. Applications for primacy will typically
fall to a state’s regulatory agency. It would be advantageous for states pursuing primacy to
partner with the State Geological Survey, given the vast amounts of regional data that surveys
have.
Recommendations for entities interested in applying for a Class VI permit include reviewing all
requirements of the permitting process before beginning the process. EPA’s website contains all
information and lists of required data. It was also recommended that the suitability of well
construction materials be considered, as well as supply chain delays. Applicants should assume 6
to 8 months lead time in securing certain materials. Overall, CCUS is being taken more seriously
and there is interest in moving CCS projects forward with investment by industry.

 Subtask 7.2 – Meet With External Teams That Have Experience
 Applying for EPA–UIC Class VI Permits
KGS met with an external team who has experience applying for EPA–UIC Class VI permits to
discuss the application process. This section documents information obtained during the
interview.

 Interview with Advanced Resources International
On March 25, 2025, representatives of KGS met with Dave Riestenberg and Manoj Valluri of
Advanced Resources International (ARI; Arlington, VA). ARI specializes in global
unconventional gas resources, enhanced recovery, and CO2 storage, with research on these topics
 469

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

dating back to 1980 for the DOE. Over the past two decades, the company has conducted
extensive R&D on shale oil, gas shales, coalbed methane, and tight sands, focusing on geology,
engineering, economics, and environmental impacts worldwide. ARI has also explored CO2
storage opportunities for over 50 power plants and industrial facilities, assessing regional and
site-specific geological feasibility, storage capacity, and project development plans. Since 2022,
ARI has led the application for multiple Class VI injection wells in Kansas, California, Alabama,
Florida, Illinois, Louisiana, Missouri, Texas, and Ohio. The company has also been a consortia
participant on applications for Colorado and Alaska.
ARI has partnered with only one state with primacy over Class VI systems at the time of
application (Louisiana; Texas was close to obtaining primacy at the time of their application).
There is a greater synergy between the EPA and states with primacy during the Class VI
application process, leading to more actionable feedback from the EPA that results in the
application process happening faster. Main differences ARI noted between working with the
EPA versus working with states on Class VI applications include:
• States that have received primacy (i.e., Louisiana, North Dakota, West Virginia, and
 Wyoming) are taking a more careful approach and add local-scale nuances with respect to
 environmental regulation.
• Regulatory bodies are variable due to their experience, established protocols (or lack
 thereof), efficiency, etc. For example, Region 7 (Kansas) has a streamlined system that is
 very efficient, likely related to workload and regulatory environment, and as a result response
 times are very quick.
Efficiency and expediency of the application process is also dependent upon the characteristics
of the geological unit and stratigraphy that proposed injection wells to be penetrated. Application
complexity and time-to-approval can be a function of regionally specific sub-surface traits (e.g.,
seismic activity in the Midwest vs. brine/brackish water in coastal plain states).
ARI noted that, in some regions, there is tension between CCUS and Oil and Gas industries,
though there are advantages to the two industries working together. This tension could be
attributed to a perceived competition for land/subsurface access and use rights, materials and
services. Research consortia such as CUSP-West, in partnership with State Geological Surveys
and private industry could enhance the evaluation of regional sub-surface challenges like
overpressure and seismic activity. By sharing data and coordinating outreach initiatives, they can
collaboratively address risk mitigation, particularly regarding basin-scale concerns and
opportunities. Although private partnerships have seen some success with advancing through tax
credits for carbon storage, most of the work on advancing the industry has benefited from public
partnerships. Pairing public dollars to nudge commercialization would grow the industry.
Near- and mid-term challenges ARI noted for CCUS projects in the United States include:
• Uncertainty around DOE funding availability and timeline
• Stability of incentives and tax credits such as 45Q
• Inflation, potential impact of tariffs on materials and services
• Evolving/developing regulatory environment
• Investor confidence in the global economy
• Supply chain issues
• A lack of certainty in CCS well design requirements
 470

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Despite these challenges, CCS maintains bipartisan political support, provides jobs, and offers an
industry-friendly solution to carbon reduction. States are continuing to pursue primacy and
receiving approval, signaling expansion of the industry. The relatively small size of the CCS
industry has allowed for agility when compared to the oil and gas industry, providing
opportunities for growth across a range of sectors, including finance, manufacturing,
transportation, science, and more.

 Subtask 7.3– Meet With State Environmental and Petroleum
 Regulators
KGS met with state environmental and petroleum regulators to discuss the current regulatory
framework for CO2 injection scenarios. This section summarizes information obtained during the
interview.

 Interview with the Kansas Department of Health and Environment (KDHE)
On April 30, 2025, representatives of KGS met with Sue Funk, Wakil Balumi, and Riley Biel of
the KDHE. KDHE’s Division of Environment protects public health and the environment
through environmental regulatory programs and other programs that remediate contamination,
lessen nonpoint pollution, and evaluate environmental conditions across the state. Included in the
responsibilities of KDHE are regulation of the UIC program. KDHE would work with the KCC
(see section 7.3.2) to establish the process of Kansas pursuing primacy.
The main change needed to facilitate injection scenarios in Kansas is a greater demand for it by
industry. As of the date of the interview, only 2 ethanol plants in Kansas are interested in
primacy. Overall, companies would prefer to deal with the state governments, rather than the
Federal Government, because state governments are familiar with local scale activities and are
more accessible.
If the demand for primacy were to grow in Kansas, the state would model their efforts after other
states that have successfully secured primacy (Wyoming, Texas, Louisiana). These states have
shared with other states their experience with obtaining primacy, which seems to be positive. The
main limitations in Kansas are demand and resources; if the demand was high, the Kansas state
agencies working on obtaining primacy will collaborate to submit the primacy application. If
Kansas were to pursue primacy, KGS, KCC and KDHE have the expertise to write and review
technical submissions for Class VI applications.

 Interview with the KCC
On April 29, 2025, representatives from KGS met with Ryan Hoffman, the director of the KCC.
The KCC regulates five cornerstone industries in the Kansas economy. The Commission has the
responsibility of ensuring that natural gas, electricity, telephone and transportation vendors
provide safe, adequate and reliable services at reasonable rates. The Commission also has the
mandate of assuring that oil and gas producers protect correlative rights and environmental
resources.
At the time of this report, Kansas has not initiated the process to establish state primacy and there
are two UIC Class VI permit applications in Region 7 under review by the EPA.

 471

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The EPA approves and oversees Class VI wells in Kansas. Once an application to drill a Class
VI well is submitted, the EPA will partner with the KCC through the application’s completion.
The current process for drilling new stratigraphic wells involves initial permitting by KCC. New
wells may be drilled as disposal wells and are not initially authorized for injection. Such wells
can be used to determine a site’s suitability for CO2 injection through data collection and
stratigraphic tests to assess, for example, subsurface geological and hydrogeologic
characteristics. Once testing is completed, entities have 90 days to apply for a permit to inject.
During the testing period, it is under the jurisdiction of KCC. Once it is approved for injection,
EPA has oversight of all injection activities.
State primacy generally results in a more efficient and rapid turnaround on applications than
currently occurs when applications are submitted to EPA. Demand for primacy in Kansas is
currently low, but subject to change should industry show more interest. Primacy interests in
Kansas will likely remain stagnant until a utility or major refiner takes the lead and provides the
resources needed to support the application process. The uncertain future of the 45Q tax credit
for carbon capture projects also plays a role in low industry demand. In the meantime, Kansas’
CCS industry is “closely watching and learning” from nearby states such as Nebraska as they
move through the primacy process.
Should the demand for primacy in Kansas increase, KCC sees the KGS as an integral part of the
application team owing to its extensive subsurface modeling and stratigraphic studies of the
Arbuckle Group, a prospective environment for CO2 sequestration. If Kansas were to obtain
primacy, KGS has the in-house expertise to, for example, conduct original site-specific
evaluations and perform technical review in support of applications to the state.
The greatest risks of CO2 injection in Kansas, as with many states, is potential seismic activity
arising from brine injection, and determination of the triggering mechanism of injection-induced
seismicity.

  Task 8 – Technology Transfer
KGS, with contributions from partner organizations, led the technology transfer activities for the
ONEOK-focused CUSP-West study. These efforts aimed to enhance public engagement,
promote technical knowledge-sharing, and disseminate research findings to both scientific and
stakeholder audiences.

 Subtask 8.1 – Maintain Website for Project
A dedicated website for the project is maintained by KGS at https://kgs.ku.edu/kgs-cusp-west.
This online platform serves as a central repository for selected outputs and supporting materials
from the study. It was developed to facilitate transparent access to key technical resources and to
support broader outreach objectives by increasing visibility into the project’s scope, progress,
and outcomes.

 Subtask 8.2 – Public Presentations
Throughout the project, team members presented findings and engaged with professional
communities at a range of scientific meetings. In June 2023, two posters highlighting different
aspects of the study were presented at the Annual CUSP meeting. One provided a general project

 472

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

overview, while the other described the development and implementation of the seismic
monitoring network. The latter was recognized with third place in the student poster category.
Additional dissemination activities included a technical presentation by KGS staff at the
American Association of Petroleum Geologists (AAPG) International Meeting for Applied
Geoscience and Energy (IMAGE) in Houston in August 2023. In September 2024, Brendan
Bream delivered an update on the study during the Annual CUSP-West meeting in Santa Fe,
which served to introduce the KGS team preparing the final technical report. This engagement
continued at the 2025 Annual CUSP-West meeting in Salt Lake City, where Bream presented a
comprehensive summary of the completed study to the broader research community.

 Technical Transfer Short Course
As part of its professional development and technical outreach efforts, KGS organized and
hosted a four-day advanced modeling short course titled STOMPing at the KGS: Subsurface
Simulator from March 17 to 20, 2025 (Fig. 8.1). This course was conducted as part of the
project’s broader objectives to enhance technical capacity related to subsurface energy systems
and carbon storage.

Figure 293 Photos from Kansas Geological Survey technology transfer short course

 473

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The short course engaged 15 participants from the United States and the United Kingdon,
including professionals from Burns & McDonnell (Kansas City, MO) and INTERA (Austin,
TX), KGS researchers, and graduate students from KU. Participants brought expertise from
disciplines spanning engineering, geology, geophysics, and geochemistry. The course was led by
Mark White (PNNL) and Signe White (INTERA), recognized experts in the STOMP simulation
platform.
Course content focused on applied scenario modeling across a diverse range of geologic
processes relevant to carbon management and energy transition, including:
• Geologic carbon sequestration
• Natural gas hydrate production
• Geologic hydrogen systems
• Enhanced oil recovery
• Reactive transport
• Coupled geomechanics
• Hydrothermal systems
• Closed-loop and enhanced geothermal technologies
• Nuclear waste repository performance
• Microbial and biological processes in the subsurface
The course functioned as a pilot for a continuing education series hosted by KGS, designed to
strengthen applied modeling skills in support of CCUS deployment. All participants completed
scenario-based modeling exercises, with content tailored to simulate the kinds of geologic
systems encountered in regional carbon hub development.
KGS coordinated course planning, logistics, and continuing education unit (CEU) certification
internally, with operational support from Brendan Bream and Souvik Bhattacharjee and
coordination by Hannah Horinek. Instruction was delivered through a combination of structured
modules and hands-on sessions, contributing directly to the project’s goal of expanding
simulation expertise among collaborators and external stakeholders.

 Subtask 8.3 – Publications
In addition to presentations and outreach activities, the project generated several technical
publications. Most notably, Hannah Proffitt produced a detailed manual documenting the seismic
network design and associated data workflows developed for the project. This work also formed
the basis of her master’s thesis at KU and was presented at the Geological Society of America
national meeting in 2023.
The thesis, titled Development of Efficient Seismic Networks to Detect Local Earthquakes
(Proffitt 2024), provides a transferable framework for monitoring seismicity in CCS projects and
has informed the broader discussion on best practices for subsurface monitoring. The
combination of technical documentation, academic scholarship, and field implementation
represents a successful integration of research, education, and applied geotechnical development.

Laying the Cornerstones of a Regional Storage Hub in
California
The overarching goal of the California Cornerstone project was to provide foundational
engineering analysis across immediate, near-term, and medium-term time frames to accelerate
the implementation of a shovel-ready project that has the potential to scale and address the 12.3
MtCO2/yr emitted from upstream oil and gas operations in the San Joaquin Valley (SJV), see
Figure 294(a). This represents a first-mover carbon capture and storage (CCS) project on the
Pacific Coast and the involvement of the Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP) to
help establish a pathway for additional projects in California, including a regional storage hub.
The project’s physical location is one of the closest prospective storage sites to the Los Angeles
(LA) Basin. Within the LA Basin any subsurface storage is unlikely due to population density
and seismic activity making the SJV especially interesting.
The area of interest (AOI) for CO2 storage is located in Kern County, CA, in the southern San
Joaquin Basin. Previously, Kim et al. (2023a) found that the southern San Joaquin Basin is a
good location for geological carbon storage (GCS) projects based on geological properties and
technoeconomic aspects. The potential storage site is 50 km west of Bakersfield, CA, as shown

 480

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

in Figure 294(a). Also, the simplified maps of the AOI in 2D and 3D are shown in Figure 294(b)
and Figure 294(c), respectively. The potential CO2 injector is located in the middle of the AOI,
and the existing wellbores and Quaternary faults (QF) are shown in Figure 294(b). In addition,
the historic seismicity near AOI is shown in Figure 294(c).

 (a)

 (b) (c)
Figure 294 (a) Map of CO2 storage opportunities in the San Joaquin Basin and the area of interest (AOI) of this

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The objective was to provide technical and economic analysis to support a first-of-its-kind
capture and storage project aimed at reducing emissions from upstream oil production
operations. Project goals were to (1) leverage low-carbon fuel standard (LCFS) credits and
CUSP technical expertise to move a CCS project in California from concept to permitting to
implementation, (2) add certainty to storage volumes and dynamic storage capacity of relatively
poorly characterized saline formations in the SJV, (3) forge a pathway for others to follow with
similar projects, and (4) lay the foundations of a regional storage hub.
Our previous analysis of capacity in California for CUSP found a storage capacity of 864 MtCO2
in the oil fields of the SJV (Kim et al. 2022). This is a substantial volume but not a large enough
volume to construct a carbon storage hub and to have sufficient storage volume to scale. Our
study also suggested significant potential of saline formations in the SJV that far exceeds the
capacity of oil fields. These saline formations are not well characterized and understood from a
storage engineering perspective. Hence, we have a specific objective to conduct further
evaluation to obtain more certain estimates of saline formation storage capacity and storage rates.
We achieved our goals using 7 tasks with collaboration among team members. The outline of
each task was as follows.
1) Distributed emitters – Identify the spatial locations of steam generators (SGs) in Kern County
 for integration into ArcGIS (Esri 2025), enabling analysis of potential surface infrastructure
 and association of emissions with individual generators to prioritize sources. Conduct a
 techno-economic analysis to assess the value generated from capturing these emissions.
2) Subsurface model – Develop a reservoir model of a typical saline formation in the SJV,
 including key features such as geology, aquifers, permeability, porosity, and capillary
 pressure. The model aligned with Sentinel Peak Resources’ (Englewood, CO) recent
 geological assessment of saline formations and was used to demonstrate the site’s capacity to
 confine effectively CO2.
3) Storage assessment – Evaluate the dynamic CO2 storage capacity over time using reservoir
 simulation to guide injection well operations. Use uncertainty analysis to explore the range of
 possible outcomes.
4) Plume migration – Using the subsurface model, conduct simulation studies incorporating
 uncertainty to predict the transport and fate of the CO2 injected and simulate plume dynamics
 and pressure buildup incorporating uncertainty quantification. Additionally, we evaluate and
 assess an interferometric synthetic aperture radar (InSAR)-based surveillance approach for
 GCS to demonstrate the potential use of satellite images to monitor a CCS project in Kern
 County, CA.
5) Field project – Support the planning, infrastructure development, and monitoring of a field
 project. Use the SimCCSPRO (Carbon Solutions 2025c) toolset to visualize the Sentinel Peak
 Resources project with pipeline routing (using CostMAPPRO [Carbon Solutions 2025a]) and
 evaluate potential well placements and configurations using SCO2TPRO (Carbon Solutions
 2025b) and related tools.
6) Risk assessment – Incorporate reservoir mechanics if needed and simulate deformation of the
 storage formation and conduct a geomechanical risk assessment to establish that proposed
 storage sites(s) are low risk. Also, evaluate the risk of CO2 leakage from existing wellbores.
7) Forward-looking regional scenarios – Consider 2 expansion scenarios: first, capturing and
 storing 90% of emissions from thermal enhanced oil recovery (EOR) SGs in California, and

 482

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 second, developing a regional CO2 storage hub. Use the SimCCSPRO toolset to model both
 scenarios. The regional hub would serve as a CCS complex, helping to launch the CCS
 industry in the SJV and beyond.

 Distributed Emitters
We conducted a comprehensive assessment of CCS opportunities within California’s southern
San Joaquin Basin, in particular Kern County laying the groundwork for a regional storage hub.
The analysis involved a detailed methodology to identify and characterize CO2 emitters and a
thorough techno-economic evaluation to prioritize CCS projects under current and potential
financial incentives. The detailed results in this section are provided in Kim et al. (2023b); see
the Appendix.

 Identification and Selection of CO2 Emitters
We identified the emission sources and spatial locations for oil and gas thermal EOR production
facilities, specifically SGs and combined heat and power (CHP) plants, in Kern County. The
thermal enhanced oil production facilities (SGs and CHP) are shown in Figure 295(a). Also,
additional CO2 emitting regions, throughout Southern California are shown in Figure 295(b).
There are 125 large CO2-emitting facilities (EPA 2021b) in Southern California, with a
significant concentration of oil and gas production operations in Kern County. These facilities
include SGs and CHP systems that support thermal EOR.

A systematic selection process was used to identify candidate sites for carbon capture:
• SGs – We used the California Air Resource Board (CARB 2021a) and California
 Department of Conservation (CA DOC 2021) databases, along with Google Earth (Google,
 Mountain View, CA; https://earth.google.com), to locate thermal EOR sites. A key criterion
 for selection was an annual emission rate of 0.025 MtCO2 or greater. This process resulted in
 the identification of 63 SG sites, which contain approximately 380 individual units.
• CHP Plants – Starting with 1,695 sites from the US Environmental Protection Agency’s
 (EPA’s) Emission & Generation Resource Integrated Database (eGRID) database (EPA
 2021a), we filtered for industrial and independent CHP facilities that produce both power and
 steam for oil and gas production, making them applicable for the LCFS credit. After applying
 an emissions threshold of at least 0.025 MtCO2/yr, our procedure identified 20 CHP sites as
 suitable candidates.

 Capture Cost for Steam Generation and CHP
Previous studies were consulted for greenhouse gas (GHG) capture cost estimates for California
(EFI and Stanford 2020) and the United States as a whole (Abramson et al. 2020; Pilorgé et al.
2020). The capture cost for industrial facilities in California ranged from $58/tCO2 to $131/tCO2
(EFI and Stanford 2020), whereas the capture cost for the United States was reported as
$36/tCO2 to $75/tCO2 (Abramson et al. 2020). It is assumed that the carbon capture facility is an

 484

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

amine-based solvent unit. In particular, the capture cost for a natural gas powerplant, which is an
application similar to CHP, ranged from $53/tCO2 to $63/tCO2 at the national level (Abramson
et al. 2020). The difference in capture cost for CO2 emitters in California was considered related
to specific conditions of operation and maintenance.
Unit capture cost is expressed in Eq. (1). The total capture cost (Capturetotal cost) consists of
capital expenditures (CAPEX) and operating expenditures (OPEX). The OPEX is composed of
operating costs (Cop) and energy costs (CE). A 20-year time period was assumed for economics,
but actual plant lifetime may be longer. The detailed parameters to calculate capture cost are
shown in the Appendix.

The CAPEX included the capture unit and engineering fee. CAPEX were spread over the first 2
years. The operating costs were calculated at 5% of CAPEX for both CHP plants and SGs The
OPEX includes labor, tax, materials, and insurance (EFI and Stanford 2020). The energy cost
(CE) considers both electricity and natural gas expenses. The electricity cost and natural gas costs
are $50/MWh and $3.5/MMBTU, respectively (NPC 2019). Regarding the capture cost of CHP,
there were 3 cases depending on CAPEX and energy costs. The base case was estimated using
the average CAPEX from a previous study (EFI and Stanford 2020). The capture cost for steam
generation assumed parameters identical to CHP except CAPEX and gas consumption. Based on
the capacity of the SG, 50, 62.5, and 85 MMBTU, the retrofit CAPEX costs were determined to
be $7 million, $8.1 million, and $10 million, respectively. The detailed parameters for each case
are in the Supplementary Material.
The estimated capture cost for oil production facilities (CHP and steam generation) is shown in
Figure 296. In particular, the capture cost for CHP has 3 different cases based on the capacity
operation factor. We assumed that the capacity operation factor ranged from 0.6 to 0.9. As the
operation factor increased, the capture cost decreased. The capture cost in Case3 for CHP ranged
from $59.3/tCO2 to $78.0/tCO2. The capture cost of steam generation was estimated based on
emissions per steam generation unit with the capacity operation factor from 0.7 to 0.9. The
capture cost decreases with the increase of capacity operation factor and steam generation
capacity type. The capture cost of steam generation in our model ranges from $57.6/tCO2 to
$74.5/tCO2 depending on the estimated operating conditions of each site. The mean capture cost
for 50, 62.5, and 85 MMBTU steam generation units are $69.0/tCO2, $66.6/tCO2, and
$62.2/tCO2, respectively.

 Identification of Potential Storage Sites
We evaluated and ranked potential CO2 storage sites, considering both saline formations and
hydrocarbon fields in the southern San Joaquin Basin. We used a 3-stage procedure below.
Detailed explanations are found in the Appendix.

• Stage 1 – Geological Screening: Candidate sites were first evaluated against qualifying
 geological thresholds for properties such as depth (>800 m), reservoir thickness (>10 m), and
 permeability (>10 mD) to ensure their suitability for secure, long-term storage.

 486

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

• Stage 2 – Exclusion Zones: We then defined and applied exclusion zones to minimize risk
 and potential land-use conflicts. These zones removed areas based on seismic risk (e.g., a 4-
 km buffer around Quaternary faults), high population density, sensitive habitats, and
 restricted lands.
• Stage 3 – Qualification and Ranking: After removing exclusion zones, the remaining areas
 were evaluated and their storage resource estimates revised. Despite this conservative
 method, the region still showed an estimated storage capacity of 0.45 to 1.15 GtCO2 in
 qualified hydrocarbon fields and 16.6 to 52.0 GtCO2 in saline formations. A scoring system
 using 12 criteria—such as storage capacity, permeability, and seal integrity—was applied to
 identify the most promising sites.

This comprehensive screening and scoring process resulted in the selection of 41 high-priority
storage sites for the techno-economic analysis. These 41 sites, which include 7 hydrocarbon
fields and 34 saline or stacked formations, represent a total storage resource of 5.8 GtCO2.
Finally, Figure 297 shows the 41 target CO2 storage sites in the available saline formations in the
southern San Joaquin Basin.

Figure 297 Prospective CO2 storage sites among available saline formations and hydrocarbon fields. Source: Kim et

 Technoeconomic Analysis
The version of SimCCS used in this study is the temporal model and is different from the
previous version (Middleton et al. 2020). An overview of the SimCCS model is given in the
Supplementary Material. Tax credits are modeled in SimCCS as modifications to capture or
storage costs. If the state-level credit varies based on the source (e.g., LCFS credits), then the
credit is applied to the capture cost as
Total Capture Cost = Raw Capture Cost − Tax Credit (2)

 487

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The LCFS credit was conservatively considered to be $100/tCO2 with a 100% LCFS assumption.
The maximum LCFS credit (2021) price was posted as $221.67 (CARB 2021b). LCFS credits
are only applied for refineries, SGs, CHP plants, and ethanol refineries based on LCFS pathways.
Steam generators, refinery, and hydrogen facilities received 80% of $100/tCO2 LCFS credit. The
ethanol facility receives 100% of the $100/tCO2 LCFS credit. The LCFS percentage of CHP
facilities varied from 50 to 60% based on the contribution of steam generation for oil production
(Supplementary Material, Table S2 in Appendix A-1). The cement and powerplant facility
cannot receive the LCFS credit except Elk Hills powerplant (40% LCFS) that provides electricity
to oil production. In the scenario case study, the LCFS credits used were $70/tCO2, $100/tCO2
and $150/tCO2.
The 45Q tax credit (Section 45Q of the US Tax Code; Credit…2022) was applied to the cost of
storage for the maximum credit period of 12 years. The updated 45Q credit (Credit…2022) for
saline and CO2-EOR fields was $85/tCO2 and $60/tCO2, respectively. The injection cost of CO2
in saline formations and depleted hydrocarbon fields was simply assumed to be $10/tCO2, which
is consistent with previous studies (DOE 2014; Rubin et al. 2015). We note that actual injection
cost of CO2 is variable based on formation depth and injectivity. So, the storage cost per metric
ton of CO2 in saline formations was −$75/tCO2 with the net benefit computed as
Total storage cost = $10 (CO2 injection cost) − $85 (45Q credit) (3)
Regarding the cost of storage for CO2-EOR, we conservatively considered the revenue from the
additional hydrocarbon production as an additional credit. In particular, the cost of CO2 purchase
and recycling price ranges from 25% to 50% of the cost per barrel oil produced at $70/bbl
(NETL 2010). Based on the condition of operation, the revenue generated by CO2 injection and
operation ($/tCO2) was varied. We conservatively assumed revenue of $17.5/tCO2, whereas
another study assumed the revenue from CO2-EOR projects was $15/tCO2 (EFI and Stanford
2020). The storage cost for CO2-EOR fields was estimated as −$67.5/tCO2 with the net benefit
computed as
Total storage cost = $10 (Injection Cost) − $17.5 (Revenue from CO2-EOR) − $60 (45Q credit)
 (4)
The storage cost in CO2-EOR fields needs to be further investigated. In this study, the injection
rate limit for saline formations and hydrocarbon fields was constrained to 2 and 1 MtCO2/yr,
respectively. Also, the pipeline network rights-of-way (ROWs) used existing natural gas and
crude oil pipeline ROWs.
Generally, the SimCCS optimization model operates in 3 modes: (1) CAP, (2) PRICE, and (3)
TIME. SimCCS formulates these optimization models as mixed-integer linear programs
(MILPs). In all modes, SimCCS aims to minimize infrastructure cost subject to various
constraints. Equation (7) represents infrastructure cost as shown below.

 (5)
The objective function contains the capture (𝑉𝑖𝑠 ) and storage (𝑉𝑗𝑤 ) cost data provided to SimCCS
as well as transportation costs calculated from the cost surface (𝛼𝑘𝑐 and 𝛽𝑘𝑐 ). The other variables
in the objective function are decision variables that represent the amount of CO2 captured at a
 488

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

location (𝑎𝑖 ), the amount of CO2 stored at a location (𝑏𝑗 ), the amount of CO2 transported in a
pipeline component (𝑝𝑘𝑐 ), and an indicator for whether or not a pipeline component is
constructed (𝑦𝑘𝑐 ). Further explanation is provided in the Supplementary Material.
The different modes of SimCCS reflect variations in the model as follows.
• CAP Mode – This mode is the model presented but with an additional constraint that forces
 the resulting infrastructure to capture a certain amount of CO2. This mode is used for
 scenarios that target capture amounts. In this study, CAP mode was used to collect and store
 all capturable emissions.
• PRICE Mode – This mode has no constraint requiring the capture of a specific amount of
 CO2. This is possible only with negative costs (or profit) in the system. Therefore,
 infrastructure is deployed only if the cost of the objective function is less than zero.
 Generally, this mode depends on 45Q credit, LCFS credit, or EOR sales profit at a storage
 site. This mode is used to find the profitable scenarios under deployment. We conducted
 several scenarios depending on the variation of credits including the 45Q tax credit, LCFS
 credit, and the capture threshold for the 45Q tax credit.
• TIME Mode – This mode is more complicated than the CAP and PRICE models. The
 project period is broken up into phases and each phase has its own set of cost and capacity
 parameters. Infrastructure for each phase is designed to minimize total project cost, so
 infrastructure that can be shared across phases is prioritized over infrastructure that needs to
 be rebuilt in subsequent phases (Jones and Marples 2023). This mode is used for scenarios in
 which evolution is expected (e.g., tax credit values, capture costs, source and reservoir
 availability, and capture targets change). A simple phasing study was applied to gauge the
 effect of the 45Q credit period using 12-, 16-, and 20-year durations of 45Q.
Table 68 presents the deployment scenarios with different parameters. The current threshold of
capture amount for the 45Q tax credit is 0.0125 MtCO2/yr (industrial emitter) and 0.0185
MtCO2/yr (powerplant). All scenarios operate for 20 years. The base-case scenarios with current
45Q capture thresholds and credit value were used in CAP and PRICE modes. Sensitivity studies
were conducted based upon 45Q credit duration (12, 16, 20 years) and LCFS credit value ($70/t,
$100/t, $150/t). Case studies with the 45Q tax criteria before 2022 are reported in the
Supplementary Material. The all-storage option refers to considering all kinds of storage sites
including CO2-EOR candidate sites.

As discussed above, the CAP mode operates to collect and store all capturable emissions where
PRICE mode finds the profitable individual CCS project under deployment. As a result, the
capturable amount in the PRICE mode shows 22 MtCO2/yr amounting to around 50% of the total
capturable amount (42.7 MtCO2/yr) in the CAP mode. Therefore, the number of storage sites is
less in the PRICE mode. We notice that the total project cost in the CAP mode was profitable
with the 2022 45Q tax credit value.
Figure 316 shows the distribution of capture amount and number of emitters within each
industrial field. In the CAP mode, all capturable emissions (42.7 MtCO2) and emitters (125)
were engaged. In the PRICE mode, the majority of emissions from cement manufacture and
natural gas power plants can not be captured with an economic benefit under the current 45Q tax
credit value except the emissions from Elk Hills natural gas power plant because they are not
LCFS eligible. About 50% of emissions from CHP can be economically captured and stored. The
emissions from ethanol, steam generation, refinery and hydrogen production can be mostly
captured with economic benefit. Note that more than 90% of steam generation emissions and
refinery hydrogen production can be captured and stored with economic benefit because they
receive both the LCFS credit and the 45Q credit.

The sensitivity of 45Q tax credit value assuming a 20-year project lifetime was investigated to

The current 45Q credit is $60/$85/tCO2 for EOR/no-EOR sites. The effect of CO2 capturable
amount on different industries is shown in Figure 318. The current 45Q tax credit with the
assumption of 12 year and 20 year credit life can capture 22 and 31.7 MtCO2/yr, respectively, in
PRICE mode. This results suggests that the current 45Q tax credit lifetime of 12 years is too
short to improve the economic viability of many CCS actions. Unfortunately, the emissions from
cement and powerplant sectors are not captured and stored due to the lack of economic benefit
with a 12 year credit life. Increasing the 45Q credit life increases the capturable amount to 31.7
MtCO2/yr. In this scenario, all emissions from the cement industry can be captured and stored
economically. The greater 45Q credit value ($70/$100/tCO2) with a 12-year credit life leads to
storage amounts (22.9 MtCO2/yr) similar to the current 45Q credit value. The scenario with 20-
year 45Q credit life mostly captures and stores all emissions. This results in 41.3 MtCO2/yr,
which is almost 97% of the total capturable amount (42.7 MtCO2/yr) in the target region. The
carbon capture cost has a critical role within the technoeconomic analysis. The capture cost
should decrease over time with technology innovation to fulfill a carbon neutral economy. The
results from SimCCS showed that carbon capture from some large emitters in natural gas power
plant and cement industries did not have an economic benefit with the current 45Q tax credit
lifetime and the retrofit costs for carbon capture. The target capture cost for these industrial fields
should be less than $40/tCO2 to $50/tCO2 with current tax credit and storage cost. Detailed
analysis of target capture costs and pipeline network construction will be conducted in the future.
An aggressive 45Q tax credit strategy, cost-effective capture units, and optimal pipeline
networks will speed deployment of carbon storage.

 Summary
Steam generation and CHP operations within oil and gas production facilities were identified and
located using public data in and around Kern County. These facilities were selected as eligible
for the LCFS credit if their emissions were equal to or greater than 0.025 MtCO2/yr. The
capturable cumulative GHG emissions from 63 SGs and 20 CHP plants with LCFS applicable
facilities were 8.6 and 2.8 MtCO2/yr, respectively. Additionally, another 42 selected large
emitters in the Kern County vicinity and Southern California were estimated as having
capturable emissions of 42.7 MtCO2/yr. The capture cost for CHP ranged from $59/tCO2 to
$78/tCO2 depending on the operating conditions whereas the capture cost for emissions from
steam generation ranged from $58/tCO2 to $74.5/tCO2 depending on the estimates for each site.
CO2 storage resources were reevaluated and investigated using a 3-stage screening procedure.
Conservative risk exclusion zones were used to increase the security of potential CO2 storage in
geological formations. The exclusion zones consist of risk category (Quaternary fault and
seismic activity), population density, restricted lands, and sensitive ecological habitats. Even
with a significantly conservative approach, the resulting estimated storage resources for
hydrocarbon fields and saline formations were 0.45 to 1.15 GtCO2 and 16.6 to 52.0 (mean 34.3)
GtCO2, respectively. These resources were then scored and storage sites with high and medium
priority scores and greater than 20 MtCO2 storage resource were defined as the target sites for
technoeconomic analysis. All fields passing through screening with exclusion zones have
desirable qualities for storage. In this way, 7 hydrocarbon fields were selected. Among them, 5
fields were CO2-EOR candidates and 2 fields were depleted oil fields only for storage. Also, a

 494

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

total of 34 saline formations including 2 stacked formations were selected. The 41 storage sites
chosen totaled 5.8 GtCO2 of storage resource.
Subsequently, in our study, the 125 emitters in Kern County and Southern California were
connected with 41 prospective storage sites and a regional technoeconomic analysis conducted.
The capture costs for the additional 42 large emitters were adopted from a previous study (EFI
and Stanford 2020). The proposed regional scenarios were conducted to find the optimal CCS
project with proper credit assumptions. Oil and gas production facilities are predicted to break
even or profit under current 45Q tax and LCFS credit conditions. Almost all oil and gas facilities
can receive both credits. The base-case results using CAP and PRICE mode in the SimCCS tool
illustrated that cement manufacture and natural gas power plants do not receive enough credit to
break even. Therefore, there are limitations to deploying CCS projects under the current 45Q and
LCFS credits.

  Subsurface Model
We modeled the pilot-scale CCS site incorporating geomechanics to quantify the rock
deformation at land surface and subsurface. The detailed results in this section are provided in Li
et al. (2024); see the Appendix.

 Overview of CCS Sites
The potential GCS site is located in Kern County in the southern SJV in California. Significant
CO2 emissions exist throughout the region (Kim et al. 2023b). Figure 319(a) shows an overview
of the study area, which is 66.0 square miles (7.08 miles in width and 9.32 miles in height) at the
land surface. The target storage formation is a saline aquifer, and it is around 3,861 ft (1,177 m)
in depth dipping to the west and south. Within this site, a 6-by-6-mile (10-by-10-km) area,
shown as the orange square, is selected to build the subsurface model for numerical simulation.
The blue polygon in Figure 319(a) is the potential land focus area at the early stage of this
project, and we aim to constrain the majority of the injected CO2 within a small area to preserve
the site for future activities. The injection well location is selected according to the injectivity
map (Figure 319(b)). The injectivity is defined as the product of permeability and effective pay
thickness. Figure 319(b) shows that the large injectivity regions are unfortunately out of the land
acquisition area. The injection well is placed at the location of the yellow triangle by considering
the distances to the boundaries of the land focus area and the injectivity potential. The blue
triangles are other candidate injection locations, and they are not selected because they are very
close to the west boundaries of the land focus area. The dashed line in Figure 319(b) shows the
exact land focus area, as shown in Figure 319(a). The green dots in Figure 319(b) are the known
wells in this area, and the star icons represent the other candidate injection sites that were studied
and found to not be as advantageous as the selected site. The identified injection well is 1.56
miles away from the west boundary of the land focus area. There are surface exposures of faults
in this area, and the injection well location is 0.68 miles to the QF1 fault and 1.48 miles to the
QF2 fault.
