The subsurface geological stratigraphy demonstrates subsurface layers in Figure 320. The
subsurface geological stratigraphy is summarized in Figure 320 and is based on well logs. This
given well is about 1.5 km away from the potential injection well. In this work, we mainly focus
on the Etchegoin Formation as our CO2 storage reservoir. In general, the Etchegoin Formation is
around 3,862 ft (1,177 m) in depth and has an average thickness of 2,258 ft (688.2 m). The
Etchegoin Formation also dips to the west with an approximate angle of 9°. This imposes further
challenges for CO2 storage due to the fact that a dipping formation drives CO2 plume migration.
The Etchegoin Formation is modeled with overburden shale layers (SJ shale 1 and SJ shale 2) of
1,912 ft (582.3 m) thickness in total. It also has bottom seal at the depth of 6,120 ft (1,865.4 m).
The Etchegoin Formation has significant potential for CO2 storage. The underground source of
drinking water (USDW) starts in the middle of the San Joaquin Formation (above 1,320 ft [402.3
m] depth).

 496

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 320 Schematic vertical section of geological strata adjacent to the injection well. The middle of the storage
formation is over a mile (1.6 km) deep. Source: Kim et al. (2023a), licensed under CC BY-NC.

One of the site-specific challenges in this work is the heterogeneous storage formation with low-
permeability layers as shown in Figure 304(a). We need to limit CO2 migration while
maximizing the storage amount in this dipping saline formation. In addition, the predefine
injection scheme is shown in Figure 304(b). Annual injection rates peak in 2027 at 1.2 MtCO2/yr
as defined by a potential project. The variable injection rate poses significant challenges for this
GCS case study because the pressure response needs to be managed carefully to avoid fracturing
the storage formation seal and to reduce the risk of leakage. It is necessary to address the
changing injection rate challenge because the imbalance of CO2 supply and demand in the region
may happen (Davis et al. 2011; Naims 2016). This project plans to inject a total amount of 12.3
MtCO2 within 18 years followed by a monitoring period of 100 years after shut-in of the well to
ensure that the CO2 plume becomes stationary.

 497

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 (a) (b)
Figure 304 Site-specific design for the geological carbon storage problem. (a) I–K cross-sectional view (610 ft
[185.9 m] tall by 3,500 ft [1,066.8 m] wide) of the horizontal permeability to demonstrate the heterogeneous storage
formation and (b) Injection schedule for 18 years of injection following the predefined annual rates. Injection in the
lower portions of the storage formation where permeability is lower is judged optimal so that plume migration updip
is limited. Source: Li et al. (2024), licensed under CC BY-NC.
It is important to avoid injection into large permeability channels because the CO2 will be very
mobile and a large areal CO2 plume extent will result. The buoyancy-driven CO2 migration
updip during the postinjection period (after shut-in of the injector) further enlarges the final
plume size. The low-permeability zones, however, are not fully capable of storing large amounts
of CO2 given the pressure buildup constraint. We measure this trade-off quantitatively
throughout the dynamic GCS simulation. The surface exposures of the Quaternary faults in this
site are another challenge we need to tackle. According to the geomechanical analysis and the
state of stress at the project site, we need to be extremely careful about slip on the QF2 fault. The
orientation of the QF2 fault within the stress field, as shown in Figure 294(a), presents an angle
that is not normal or parallel to the regional stress in this area. This suggests that QF2 is of great
interest during the design of the injector and the accompanying response to injection. We control
the pressure increase at the location of the QF2 fault with a large safety margin to avoid fault
activation.

 Numerical Simulation Model
The geological structure of the storage formation is analyzed using well logs in order to interpret
the permeability and porosity distribution. There is a dipping tidal channel in the southwest. The
mud in the northeast region leads to low permeability zones. To model the saline storage
formation, the initial water saturation is set to be 1 and the salinity of the brine is equal to 15,300
ppm. The hydrostatic pressure gradient is set to be 0.47 psi/ft (10.63 kPa/m) and the 2.5 °F
(1.39 °C) geothermal gradient is per 100 ft (30.48 m). The grid block design for the Etchegoin
storage formation is 33 by 33 by 75, as is shown in Figure 322 with red layers. There are 40 extra
layers on top of the storage formation (shown in Figure 322 using blue) serving as the cap rock
to represent the sealing formation. The grid blocks are refined in the area close to the injector to
describe the CO2 plume and migration with greater geospatial resolution. The grid blocks far
away from the injector are very large in order to cover the entire 6 by 6 miles (9.66 by 9.66 km)
area of the model.

 498

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 322 Numerical simulation model set-up in the 6-by-6-mile (9.66-by-9.66 km) study area. Fluid flow occurs
in the storage formation overlain by a caprock (left) and the storage zone is 2-way coupled geomechanically to the
land surface and below the storage formation (right). Source: Li et al. (2024), licensed under CC BY-NC.
The geomechanical model is used to understand rock deformation, stress, and strain change due
to injection. The fluid flow model is 2-way coupled with the geomechanical model to simulate
the case with 18 years of injection following the injection scheme in Figure 304(b). We
simulated a 100-year postinjection period after shut-in. We extended the geomechanical grids
upward with 25 extra layers to fill in the gap between the top surface of the sealing formation
and the land surface. Therefore, we are capable to compute the land surface movement due to
CO2 injection. Figure 322 demonstrates the fluid flow model on the left and the 2-way coupled
geomechanical model on the right.
The storage formation is thin compared with the entire subsurface system in this model. This 2-
way coupled model follows a structure of sandstone–shale–sandstone–shale from top to bottom.
The top sandstone represents the rock from land surface to the sealing formation. The next shale
structure represents the ultra-low permeability cap formation to seal the CO2 storage and prevent
upward motion by buoyancy. The next sandstone rock represents the storage formation, and the
shale rock next to it represents the bottom sealing formation. This structure defines different rock
mechanics characteristics in order to compute the solid deformation. The geomechanical model
assumes that the rock follows elastic deformation because we limit pressure increase due to
injection to avoid plastic deformation or potential rock fractures. The Mohr-Coulomb model is
implemented for rock failure due to the normal and shear stresses in the subsurface system.
The pressure–volume–temperature (PVT) model is summarized in Table 69. The main fluids in
this subsurface system include CO2 and brine. The solubility is modelled according to Henry’s
Law, and the Henry’s Law constant is a function of temperature and pressure. Rock fluid models
include relative permeability and capillary pressure and are shown in Figure 323(a) and Figure
323(b), respectively. Gas relative permeability hysteresis is considered to determine the
imbibition curve as a function of a given drainage curve according to the maximum residual gas
saturation, which is defined to be 0.4. We do not consider any geochemical reactions in this
work.

The geomechanical model is detailed in Table 70 and includes storage and sealing formations as
rock types. The storage formation is represented as sandstone for CO2 sequestration. Sandstone
also describes the rock mechanical properties for the layers from the land surface to the top of
the cap rock seal. The sealing formation represents the cap rock on top of the storage formation,
and it also serves as the bottom seal below the storage formation. The values of Young’s
modulus and Poisson’s ratio come from literature to represent SJV rock conditions (Holstein and
Lake 2007; Sone and Zoback 2013; Molina et al. 2017). The unconfined compressive strength
and friction angle are computed based on the empirical relations from the literature (Horsrud
2001; Chang et al. 2006). The Biot coefficients are close to unity because this model tends to
represent a close-to-perfect coupling effect between pore pressure and the rock frame
(Zimmerman 1990). We model a fully saturated saline aquifer in the subsurface where the
majority of the pore pressure increment is expected to contribute to the effective stress change. In
addition, the pore pressure management is essential for GCS projects, and a large Biot coefficient
allows conservative consideration of pore pressure change effects due to the CO2 injectivity.

A sensitivity analysis of grid block size confirms that there are minimal boundary effects related
to pressure, and hence geomechanics, within the 2-way coupled flow and mechanical simulation.
The unit grid block size ranges from 92.7 by 92.7 by 150 ft (28.3 by 28.3 by 45.7 m) to 183.5 by
183.5 by 150 ft (55.9 by 55.9 by 45.7 m) and further to 374.4 by 374.4 by 150 ft (114.1 by 114.1

 500

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

by 45.7 m) to represent a wide range of dimensions for 3 distinct scenarios. The thickness of the
grid blocks is uniformly 150 ft (45.7 m) in the z-direction because initial results showed
consistent observations for different layer thicknesses of 38, 75, and 150 ft (11.6, 22.9, and 45.7
m). We examine the simulated pressure behavior at the boundary of the site (north of the
injector), and the results show constant pressure with an average CO2 injectivity of around 0.68
Mt/yr. This aligns with assumptions of GCS projects that have a large extent of volume for
subsurface storage. The model size is sufficient for minimal boundary effects related to pressure.
Although we observe marginal differences in results when zoomed into the curves, the accuracy
is well maintained so that we balance the grid block sizes with the simulation runtime. For the
same overall dimension of the model, using a much larger amount of small grid blocks
significantly increases the simulation complexity and expected runtime.

 Storage Assessment & Plume Migration
We evaluate the dynamic storage performance of the Kern County pilot site using the optimized
subsurface model. This engineering assessment simulates realistic CO2 injection and monitoring
periods to measure total storage volume, plume behavior, pressure propagation, and mechanical
integrity under operational constraints.
The in-house toolbox pyCCUS (Li et al. 2024) leverages the base-case numerical model and
facilitates computations efficiently. The capacity of high-performance computing resources
enables parallel computations to accelerate the workflow. The post-processing components
evaluate the dynamic simulation quantitatively and combine all the necessary information
together for analysis, visualization, and validation. The definitions of CO2 plume and pressure
footprint are stated. The well design optimization setup demonstrates one of the applications
using the in-house toolbox to find the best injection well trajectory for this GCS case study. The
detailed results in this section are provided in Li et al. (2024, 2025); see the Appendix.

 pyCCUS
We have developed an in-house toolbox to automate the large number of simulations needed to
analyze GCS outcomes during optimization. This toolbox interacts with the commercial software
CMG (Computer Modelling Group, Calgary, AB; https://www.cmgl.ca) so that the numerical
model is parsed by CMG for computations. Our toolbox extracts the results from CMG for post-
processing and analysis. Figure 324 shows an overview of the workflow with essential
components noted. At the beginning, we need to build the base simulation model. We may also
need the inputs from users as an optional choice if the goal is to drive pyCCUS to create many
reservoir simulation models. For example, users could provide a list of parameters with ranges or
distributions, and the design-of-experiment algorithms in pyCCUS would take over the task of
generating the design-of-experiment setup. Therefore, our toolbox writes a number of simulation
model input files accordingly. This function is applicable for uncertainty quantification or global
sensitivity analysis. In this paper, we implemented a novel module to generate deviated injector
trajectories for optimization. When the numerical simulation models are created according to
user needs, the next step is to run all simulations. The toolbox is capable of deploying the work
in different environments, including the Windows operating system, Linux operating system, and
multiple high-performance computing resources. The toolbox submits all jobs prioritizing
parallel over sequential computations depending on the computational resources allocated.

 501

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The numerical simulation results are extracted from CMG to Python for post-processing and
analysis. The “sanity check” component ensures the success of the simulation and filters out
cases that do not satisfy our settings. For example, the actual injection profile may not be the
same as the predefined injection scheme due to the well bottomhole pressure constraint. For
GCS-specific tasks, we highlighted the 2D and 3D CO2 delineation, CO2 migration distances
with uncertainties, case design optimization, and potential artificial intelligence applications. The
CO2 migration distance and pressure plume are essential information for induced seismicity
analysis and management (Kohli et al. 2023). Additionally, the land surface uplift due to
injectivity could be a significant method to monitor the significant extent of the pressure plume
and is discussed later.
In terms of optimization, pyCCUS is capable of both forward and looped optimization. The
looped optimization is favored when performing a history match using a relatively simple model
because the optimizer needs to learn from previous iterations to propose a better set of values.
Example cases include chemical kinetics history matching with experimental measurements (Li
et al. 2023). In this study, we use forward optimization because it reduces the computational
cost. We are capable of requesting enough computational resources to simulate all cases in
parallel so that the amount of time needed for all cases is the same as the time needed for 1
simulation. If the looped optimization is applied, however, there are at least a few iterations
required for optimization and the total computational cost is expected to be many times larger
than the forward optimization.

outputs. The model demonstrated in the user inputs section (required input) represents a 6-by-6-mile (9.66-by-9.66
km) field model. Source: Li et al. (2024), licensed under CC BY-NC.

 Plume Definition
Plume definition is part of the post-processing of pyCCUS so that we are capable of quantifying
the progress of GCS projects. We delineated the 2D and 3D CO2 plumes according to the CO2
gas saturation of the storage formation. The threshold value is defined to be the irreducible gas

CO2 and then draw the boundary lines. The CO2 plume size is computed by integrating the area
within the boundary of the 2D plume at the land surface. Eq. (6) describes the criterion to

 Well Design Optimization
The injector optimization looks for the best trajectory of the deviated well or vertical well
following the objective function in Eq. (8). The optimization process has 3 goals: (1) minimize
the CO2 plume size at the land surface, (2) minimize the pressure buildup in the storage
formation, and (3) minimize the pressure change at the QF2 fault. The constraints include that
the well location is fixed and the injection schedule is fixed, as shown in Figure 304(a). The loss
function in Eq. (8) computes all 3 goals quantitatively for all cases. The well trajectory is the
only independent variable in this work. To combine all optimization goals in 1 loss function, we
normalize the properties and make the terms dimensionless. The terms are normalized by the
minimum values of the population to quantify how far it is from the best achievable case
regarding each optimization goal as

 (8)
where “injector” represents the independent variable in well design optimization, w1, w2, and
w3 are weighting factors for 3 different aspects, and the default values are all equal to 1/3 to
assign equal weights. The minimum values are known given all simulations finished from the
forward optimization process.
 503

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

We use 4 parameters to describe the injector trajectory in Figure 325. They include depth,
deviation, direction, and perforation length. The depth describes the distance from the land
surface to the center of the injector. The deviation is the angle between the deviated portion of
the well and the direction of gravity. The direction is the angle between the projection of the well
on the land surface and the base direction, which is defined to be positive in the east direction.
The length of perforations controls the total length of the well and perforation length is the
contact area of the injector with the storage formation. The combinations of different values of
these 4 parameters generate many potential injector trajectories. Each trajectory is defined by a
unique set of 4 parameters, and each combination of those parameters describes a unique
injector.

Figure 325 Parameter definition for injector design optimization. (left) Areal view (6 by 6 miles) illustrating depth.
(right) 610 ft (185.9 m) tall by 3,500 ft (1,066.8 m) wide cross section of storage formation with permeability
indicated. Source: Li et al. (2024), licensed under CC BY-NC.
The well depth ranges from 4,100 to 4,900 ft (1,249.7 to 1,493.5 m) due to the subsurface
geometry. Essential test cases show that the CO2 plume migrates beyond the study region if
injected into the large permeability layers. Therefore, we need deeper wells injecting into lower
permeability layers to control the plume size. The deviation angle ranges from 78° to 98° for a
wide spread of the subsurface space. The direction ranges from 0° to 360° to consider all
possible angles for tilt. The perforation length ranges from 80 to 5,000 ft (24.4 to 1,524 m), as
shown in Figure 326(b), including scenarios of both vertical wells that are partially perforated at
the deep layers of the storage formation and deviated horizontal wells. There are more than 800
cases generated for all potential trajectories of the injectors, as shown in Figure 326(a). The
injector location is fixed and the trajectory varies to fulfill the entire potential space of the
storage formation.

 Injector Design Optimization Result
The optimization result for the injector trajectories in Figure 316(a) is shown in Figure 317. This

of the objective function computed using Eq. (3). We reserve the capability for users to assign
different weights in Eq. (3) to multiple aspects of GCS projects. The result shows that it is
possible to further reduce the CO2 plume size, but the pressure buildup tends to be larger. This is
a trade-off for project designers to weigh.

 Dynamic Plume Quantification
The CO2 plume size is quantified in a dynamic manner, and we show the growth vs. time for all
cases in Figure 328(a). The highlighted thick black curve represents the optimal case we
identified based on the objective function. Figure 328 shows that the plume size grows very fast
during the first 5 years of the injection due to the large annual injection rates shown in Figure
304(a). The growth rate tends to drop afterward, but the plume size still increases during the
injection period. After the shut-in, there is no CO2 added to the storage formation, but CO2
migration happens due to the increase of formation pressure and the buoyancy force. The plume
size only increases slightly after injection stops.

Figure 328 CO2 plume size for all injector trajectories. (a) Plume size vs. time (the solid line represents the optimal
case). (b) Histogram distribution of the CO2 plume size after shut-in for all injector design cases. Source: Li et al.
(2024), licensed under CC BY-NC.
Throughout the postinjection period, the plume size tends to be stable and the growth rate
gradually drops to zero. The gray thin curves represent all other cases in this work and we
observe cases following different growth patterns regarding the plume size. This happens
because the heterogeneous rock allows mass transfer at different rates. The histogram in Figure
328(b) shows the optimal case stands at a good position among the entire population of cases.
Although there are cases on the left of the optimal case, they may show a large pressure response
in the subsurface. In addition, some cases show small plume sizes because they do not follow the
injection scheme defined in Figure 304(a). In the numerical simulation, the injection well is

 507

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

constrained from injection rate or bottomhole pressure. If the injector reaches the bottomhole
pressure limit, the numerical model reduces the injection rate, and therefore we see cases with
smaller plume sizes. We filtered out cases not following the injection scheme from further
analysis.
Pressure responses are very important to GCS project development, so we show the distribution
of all cases in Figure 329(a). The optimal case shows that the pressure buildup is less than the
majority of the design cases, and the maximum pressure buildup is 196 psi (1,351.4 kPa). The
average of the cases shows 156-psi (1,075.6 kPa) pressure buildup, with a standard deviation of
11.8 psi (81.4 kPa). The pressure increase is a very important evaluation factor to make sure that
injection does not fracture the rock. In addition, we also care about the pressure response at the
QF2 fault for this specific site. The maximum pressure change along the vertical plane of the
QF2 fault is shown in Figure 319(b). We show the maximum pressure change at each depth to
capture the extreme conditions for safety concerns. The thick black curve represents the optimal
design, and all other cases are represented by gray curves. Figure 329 shows that some cases
have significant pressure change from 3,330 to 3,500 ft (1,005.8 to 1,066.8 m) because the
deviated well tilts to a certain direction in the storage formation that stimulates the pressure
change. It is critical to manage the pressure change along the fault to be uniform to avoid the
possibility of fault slip or leakage risks.

the computed pressure response negligibly. After 2027, both pressure and land uplift decrease

allows pressure dissipation. The redistribution of the CO2 away from the injector after shut-in
leads to a slight continued evolution of the pressure plume and uplift. The pressure and uplift
dynamics still show a strong correlation, and the marginal change in uplift computed after shut-

 Optimal Injector Performance Under Uncertainty
To validate the robust performance of the optimal design, we selected 6 representative cases
among the entire population to quantify uncertainties from injection schemes and geological
realizations. The details of the selected wells are in Table 71. The selected cases represent the
entire population because they are extreme cases regarding CO2 plume size and pressure
responses. In addition, we ensure that the selected wells have diverse directions to span the
majority of the parameter space. In Figure 332(a), we visualize the projection of the injectors to
the land surface, and the wells deviate throughout all directions. Figure 327 highlights all
selected wells to provide an additional perspective for visualization. We design 3 additional
injection schemes to explore the capability of the optimal injector for larger amounts of CO2
injection. The baseline comes from the field in Figure 332(b), and scenarios 1, 2, and 3 are
designed to increase the total amount of injection. Scenario 1 has a total injection amount of 13.9
Mt, showing a 13% increment compared with the baseline. The average injection rate is around
0.77 Mt/yr for 18 years of injection. For Scenario 2, we further increase the average annual
injection rate to 0.91 Mt/yr. It has a total of 16.3 MtCO2 injection, showing a 32.5% increment
compared with the baseline. Scenario 3 is designed to be challenging because the average
injection rate is greater than 1 Mt/yr (injection rate is 1.04 Mt/yr). Scenario 3 injects a total of
18.7 Mt with a 52.0% increase compared with the baseline. We keep the annual injection rates
before 2027 to be the same because the peak injection rate is already large. It appears to be better
to ramp up and then maintain a relatively large annual injection rate as a matter of controlling
risks while increasing the total storage amount.

 Assessment of Spatial Monitoring using InSAR
We evaluate and assess an InSAR-based surveillance approach for GCS to demonstrate the
potential use of satellite images to monitor the potential CCS project site in Kern County, CA.
The scope of work includes identifying appropriate subsurface and surface conditions for project
success and presenting the data recoverable through InSAR. The detailed methods and results in
this section are provided in the published paper in the Appendix.

 Background
InSAR may be cost effective for onshore GCS projects either as a stand-alone solution or in
combination with other techniques. Remote sensing has advantages in observing an extensive
area in real time, and it has been successfully applied for various GCS assets (Zhang et al. 2021).
Under the umbrella of remote sensing, ground-based observation has high resolution and
precision but covers a small area (Zhang et al. 2021). Satellite platforms such as Sentinel-2
provide sufficient resolution (10–60 m) for GCS monitoring (Chen et al. 2019). InSAR measures
surface deformation by tracking phase differences in radar waves, enabling quantification of both
the extent and the magnitude of land displacement. Compared with GPS, it is significantly less
expensive for monitoring large regions (Dzurisin and Lu 2007) and has been successfully applied
to geomorphology, hydrology, natural hazards, and subsurface processes, including steam
stimulation (Maharramov and Zoback 2018) and EOR (Bazargan et al. 2020).
For GCS, the primary challenge is that pressure-induced rock deformation is subtle, because
storage security requires limited pressure buildup. Demonstrating measurable surface uplift and
its correlation with reservoir pressure is therefore critical. As we discussed above, our study
focuses on a 6-by-6-mile (9.66 by 9.66 km) area underlain by a 3,861-ft (1,176.8-m)-deep saline
sandstone aquifer sealed by approximately 1,000 ft (304.8 m) of shale (Kohli et al. 2023; Li et al.
2024). Planned injection will occur below 4,000 ft (1,219.2 m) via a long, deviated well.
Historical InSAR data (2015–2023) from a commercial provider confirm detectable surface
signals (Guilhot et al. 2021). As shown in Figure 336, the project site (outlined in blue) remained
stable before injection, with green-coded regions indicating no surface movement. In contrast,
adjacent red-coded zones represent subsidence from oil production but do not overlap the project
boundary. Five stable reference polygons within the site were selected for quality control. The
flat and stable baseline demonstrated in Figure 336 highlights the site’s suitability for InSAR-
based surveillance during and after CO2 injection.

Figure 337(a) provides the planned CO2 injection schedule for the project. Our simulation can
predict land uplift of approximately 25 mm (Figure 337(b)), which shows a strong correlation
with pressure buildup during injection. Notably, the greatest uplift occurs when the annual CO2
injection rate reaches its peak. This finding demonstrates that surface deformation can serve as
an indirect indicator of subsurface processes and may provide valuable information for
monitoring CO2 storage projects.

To quantify uncertainty, a global sensitivity analysis of the coupled transport–geomechanical
model was performed using distance-based generalized sensitivity analysis (DGSA). DGSA was
selected because it is computationally efficient, accounts for 2-way parameter interactions, and
treats all data points equally. This provides a systematic framework to evaluate how uncertain
parameters collectively affect system response over time. Because land uplift data are complex
and high dimensional, feature extraction methods were applied to identify dominant patterns.
Autoencoders, a neural network approach, were particularly effective in reducing dimensionality
and capturing nonlinear features from uplift images. The encoder compresses input data into a
latent representation, whereas the decoder reconstructs the images, ensuring the essential features
are preserved. Synthetic InSAR observations generated from the model demonstrate how
simulation and remote sensing can be integrated for monitoring. These results establish a
foundation for advanced surveillance strategies, including history-matched model calibration,
inversion-based property estimation, and AI-driven mapping of subsurface processes.
This section proceeds with a description of the numerical simulation methodology followed by
the computation of synthetic InSAR observations from model results. These efforts provide a
foundation for advancing InSAR surveillance in future work, such as calibration of history-
matched models to reduce uncertainty, inversion methods, and AI-based mapping tools that
predict subsurface behavior using InSAR data.

 Methodology
We use the pyCCUS toolbox for massive numerical simulation to compute essential data needed
to understand sensitivity. We sample 500 cases from the parameter space identified, and 2
different types of response data are used for global sensitivity analysis.
DGSA demonstrates strong capability for complex subsurface modelling systems, and we extend
the applicability of DGSA on complex datasets by incorporating principal component analysis
(PCA) and autoencoders. Both PCA and the autoencoders contribute to extract essential features
and reduce dimensionality of the complex response data for clustering.

 Parameter Space and Response Data
To initialize the global sensitivity study, we do Monte Carlo sampling on selected parameters for
numerical simulation to generate the dataset. There are 3 main aspects of the parameters that play
essential roles throughout GCS projects, including rock mechanics, petrophysics, and operational
control. Table 68 indicates the range of parameter values that are from field operators and
literature (Lin et al. 2010; Li et al. 2024). To provide valuable information for this particular site,
we set up the field model as the baseline for sensitivity analysis. The rock mechanics parameters
include the Young’s modulus and Poisson’s ratio as defined in Eq. (10), for both the sealing
formation (shale layers) and the storage formation (sandstone layers).

transverse strain, and 𝜖𝑎𝑥𝑖𝑎𝑙 is axial strain.

The shale layers have low permeability and porosity, and they serve as the sealing formation for
GCS. They are fine grained mudstone under significant compaction at this specific site. In
comparison, the sandstone layers in the saline aquifer show much larger porosity. The Young’s
modulus for shale in Table 68 is assumed to be greater than sandstone for this GCS site (Lin et
al. 2010; Li et al. 2024).
The petrophysical parameters define the porous medium for multiphase flow. We include the
vertical-to-horizontal permeability ratio (kv:kh) to capture differences in vertical and lateral mass
transfer. Permeability and porosity models are derived from well logs across the project area (Li
et al. 2024), and multiple realizations are sampled from prior distributions to remain
geologically-consistent. Relative permeability and capillary pressure functions are held constant
across all cases.
For GCS projects, we mainly care about the injection rate and years of injection. The
combination informs the total amount of CO2 storage in the subsurface. Operational parameters
include injection rate and duration in Table 72, which together define the total CO2 stored. We
sampled 500 cases using uniform distributions and a Latin hypercube algorithm to ensure broad
coverage of parameter space. Simulations were run with the pyCCUS toolbox (Li 2024b) using a
2-way coupled flow–geomechanics model to predict land surface displacement.

directly reflects the magnitude of surface uplift.

simulated outcomes (Figure 337).

 DGSA
DGSA is a computationally efficient sensitivity analysis approach to handle complex response
datasets. The DGSA method classifies the entire experimental sample space into different
clusters, according to the response data or their distance matrix. Next, it computes the distances
of cumulative distribution functions (CDFs) in each cluster to its prior to quantify the variance of
an independent variable to the response. The sensitivity index is described in Eq. (11) as
𝑑𝑖,𝑘 = 𝑑(𝐶𝐷𝐹(𝑋𝑖 ), 𝐶𝐷𝐹(𝑋𝑖 |𝑘))                                                                                   (11a)
 1 𝑑
                      𝑘=1 𝑑𝑞                                                                                     (11b)
 𝑖,𝑘
 𝑞
where Xi is the independent variable, K is the total number of clusters, and 𝑑𝑖,𝑘 is the
bootstrapped CDF distance for quantile q.
DGSA is a way to figure out which factors (such as rock strength or injection rate) matter most
for how the system behaves. It works by grouping all simulation results into clusters that look
similar and then checking how much each parameter changes those groups. If a parameter makes
a big difference, it is considered “sensitive.” This method is efficient for handling very complex

 518

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

datasets because it avoids focusing on just a small part of the data. It also looks at interactions
among parameters, which is important in subsurface systems where multiple factors act together.

 PCA
PCA is a typical method to reduce the dimensionality of a large and complex dataset. In
particular, if the large dataset contains the interrelated variables, which is common for time series
data, PCA is powerful to transform linearly the large dataset to a new set of variables that are
orthogonal to each other (Wold et al. 1987). The new set of variables are the principal
components (PCs) selected to represent the entire raw dataset. Similarly, the raw dataset could be
reconstructed according to the PCs. One of the main steps is to compute the eigen vectors and
eigenvalues of the matrix, because the eigenvalues represent variance. In order to select the top
K PCs, we define the criterion to collect cumulative variance greater than 96%.
To tackle the variable time length challenge, we pad the dataset with zeroes, because land uplift
is expected to drop back to its initial condition as pressure buildup decreases to zero. The
injectivity induced pressure change will dissipate in the storage formation after shut-in of the
injection well. For GCS projects, we assume rock elastic deformation because the rock
mechanical response is carefully monitored to avoid breaking or fracturing the subsurface
storage and sealing formation. The PCA process is shown in Eq. (12).
𝐾 = arg 𝑚𝑖𝑛𝑘 ∑𝑘𝑖=1 𝜆𝑖 ≥ 96%                                                                    (12a)
𝑃𝐶𝑖=1,…..𝑘 = 𝑃𝐶𝐴(𝑀𝑛,−1 )                                                                       (12b)
𝑀𝑛,−1 ∈ 𝑅 𝑛×(−1)                                                                               (12c)
where n is the number of samples, 𝜆𝑖 is the ith eigenvalue of the dataset, 𝑀𝑛,−1 is a 2D matrix
including all samples with land uplift images at all is a 2D matrix including all samples with land
uplift images at all time query steps from the first year until the shut-in. The K PCs for all
samples come from the first K columns of the matrix transformed from PCA. Therefore, the
number of PCs selected is the same for all samples, although they show different time
dimensions due to the injection horizon ranges from 10 to 30 years.

 Autoencoders
Autoencoders are powerful to extract complex nonlinear features from a large dimensional
dataset. Autoencoders are a type of artificial neural network to learn efficient representations of
unlabeled data. They are typically used for dimensionality reduction and feature. Autoencoders
are composed of 2 main components, that are encoder and decoder as shown in Figure 339. They
work by compressing data into a smaller “latent space” (the bottleneck) and then reconstructing
it. If the reconstruction looks very similar to the original, it means the autoencoder has learned
the important features. Unlike PCA, which captures only linear patterns, autoencoders can detect
complex nonlinear relationships. In this study, autoencoders helped identify subtle spatial and
temporal patterns in land uplift images, providing a more powerful tool for feature extraction
compared with PCA.

 519

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 339 Autoencoder structure from raw images to reconstructed images. The latent vector space represents the
feature extracted from raw images with the reduced dimension. Source: Li (2024a), licensed under CC BY-NC.
The loss function of the autoencoder is the mean absolute error (MAE) of outputs (𝑥̂𝑖 ) from the
autoencoder and inputs (𝑥𝑖 ) for all samples, as is shown in Eq. (13)
 1
𝐿𝑜𝑠𝑠 = 𝑛 ∑𝑛𝑖=1|𝑥𝑖 − 𝑥̂𝑖 |                                                                                    (13)
The MAE is less sensitive to outliers compared with mean square error (MSE), and it maintains
the balance among all errors to avoid extra emphasis on large errors (Chai and Draxler 2014;
Chicco et al. 2021). The autoencoder contains 14 layers in both the encoder and the decoder. The
encoder starts with a linear layer to adjust the dimensionality of the data, and a Leaky rectified
linear unit (ReLU) is used to add nonlinearity. Compared with PCA, which is an orthogonal
linear transformation of the dataset to a new coordinate, the autoencoder approach incorporates
nonlinear relationships in its structure for complex datasets. Eq. (14) is an option for the
activation function to describe a nonlinear mapping from inputs to outputs, but the gradient
vanishing problem exists particularly in multilayer structures due to its saturation nature (Tan
and Lim 2019).
 1
𝑆𝑖𝑔𝑚𝑜𝑖𝑑(𝑥) = 1+𝑒 −𝑥                                                                                          (14)
The ReLU function mitigates this concern by providing a linear function for positive input
values. The ReLU dying problem, however, is an issue (Lu et al. 2020) because the neurons from
ReLU output are 0 when input x is less than 0, as is shown in Eq. (15).
𝑅𝑒𝐿𝑈 (𝑥) = 𝑚𝑎𝑥(0, 𝑥)                                                                                         (15)
A Leaky ReLU (shown in Eq. (16), where a = 0.01) is selected as our activation function because
it improves the ReLU and avoids problems with dying. The Leaky ReLU allows a small positive
gradient when the unit is not active, and it solves the problem that the missing values exist in
reconstructed images due to ReLU dying (Xu et al. 2020).
𝐿𝑒𝑎𝑘𝑦 𝑅𝑒𝐿𝑈 (𝑥) = max(𝑎𝑥, 𝑥) (16)
The network has about 93.9 million parameters. Training uses 500 simulation samples, each a 33
× 33 image of land uplift per year. About 8,130 images (85%) are used for training and 1,433
(15%) for validation. We apply the Adam optimizer (Kingma and Ba 2015) with weight decay
10⁻⁸ for stability and learning rate 10⁻⁶. Training runs for 512 epochs until convergence. The

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

bottleneck (latent space) is 8 dimensions, chosen to capture essential features while keeping
model size small.

 Results
We presented and compared PCA feature extraction and Autoencoder features extraction.

 PCA Feature Extraction
The PCA result relies on the cumulative variance of the data to select a few top PCs for further
analysis. In order to maintain the majority of information from the raw dataset in this paper, we
define the criterion to be 96%, meaning that the selected PCs account for at least 96% of the total
variance of the entire dataset. We need at least 8 PCs to maintain over 96% of the cumulative
variance. It also shows that the cumulative variance achieves 100% with at least 18 PCs, which
means that the raw data contains intercorrelations within the matrix. It is essential to validate the
performance of PCs by comparing the reconstructed images with raw images. We compare a
selected reconstructed image with its raw image in order to validate the performance of PCA.
That is, the PCs are capable of collecting all essential information of an image. In Figure 340, the
reconstructed image preserves the shape and magnitude of the land surface uplift, with the
absolute difference in Figure 340(c) below 0.2 mm.

The example is based on the principal component analysis feature extraction method. Source: Li et al. (2025),
licensed under CC BY-NC.

 Autoencoders Feature Extraction
Training an autoencoder is an alternative option to tackle the com plex dataset challenge for
classification. The loss function quantifies differences between input images and output data
from the encoder–decoder structure. We aim to train the autoencoder as an identical function to
enforce the outputs to be the same as inputs. We train the autoencoder model with 512 epochs
and batch size of 32 until the loss function gradually stabilizes. The architecture of the
autoencoders is configured to produce a latent vector space with a dimensionality of 8. We plot
all dimensions to examine their relationships. Overall, we observe no strong correlations among
the illustrated dimensions, indicating that each extracted dimension captures unique patterns
from the complex dataset.
We validate the strength of autoencoders in a similar way, that is to compare reconstructed
images with raw images. We use the same example case (Case10) after 5 years of injection to
 521

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

demonstrate the details of autoencoder performance. The autoencoder learns features of input
images as the latent vectors after the bottleneck layer. A few layers in the encoder part gradually
reduces the dimensionality of raw images to bottleneck layer dimension. The decoder part parses
the latent vectors and reconstructs images as outputs, that are expected to be the same as inputs.
This validates the latent vectors to represent the entire raw dataset with essential features and key
information. The classification step therefore relies on the reduced dimensionality of latent
vectors to group all samples into multiple clusters. In addition, we compute the error of the
reconstructed data compared with its raw images for all samples according to Eq. (17)

We confirm the performance of both PCA and autoencoders according to their histogram
distributions in Figure 341(a) and Figure 341(b), respectively. Although errors are observed, the
maximum errors are both below 0.16 mm, which is accepted for dimensionality reduction. The
autoencoder demonstrates a smaller potential error, compared with PCA; however, the majority
of samples by PCA present good performance. A few cases do have larger errors than cases that
use autoencoders.

The global sensitivity analysis shows both rock mechanics and field operation parameters are
essential to the magnitude of land uplift in Figure 342. The Young’s modulus of the sandstone
storage formation is one of the most important factors because it describes rock deformation
according to the enforced stress in Eq. (10a). Carbon dioxide is injected into the sandstone layers
defined in the numerical simulation model. The injectivity induced pressure buildup leads to
uplift within the storage formation, and uplift therefore propagates toward the land surface. The
injection rate is another significant factor because it leads to pressure buildup directly, assuming
all other conditions are the same. The injection horizon is the parameter nonsensitive to response
1 data, because the number of years of injection does not contribute to maximum land uplift
during the injection period. The response 1 data is the magnitude of the land uplift throughout
 522

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

the lifespan of GCS projects, which is independent of injection horizon. All samples are set to
have constant injection schemes but with different rates. The permeability and porosity models
are very important to the land displacement. These effects, however, are not well reflected in
Figure 342 because our realizations are constrained to follow the prior distributions and patterns
from the field.
The details in Figure 342(b) show sensitivity index by each cluster. Results clearly show that a
cluster may demonstrate statistical significance (a sensitivity of 1) or may not, depending on the
clusters. The overall results are evaluated as the average of sensitivity index for all clusters to be
robust. Cluster 1 in orange shows a very different pattern in terms of the first 2 dimensions. The
CDFs for all parameters within all clusters are shown in Figure 343. The visualization allows
comparison in a qualitative way. For example, the distances of CDFs for sandstone Young’s
modulus and injection rate are significantly larger than other parameters. In comparison, the
CDFs of the injection horizon are very close to each other and they are the least sensitive factor
to the response 1 dataset.

The operational parameters are factors under control for GCS projects, including the injection
rate and injection horizon. The geological parameters describe the subsurface system, that are
intrinsic by nature. They include permeability and porosity fields, reservoir formation models,
and so on. They play essential roles to impact the pressure change by operational parameters, and
the response caused by pressure increase. The response in this work refers to the land
deformation at the surface. We are motivated to quantify the sensitivity index of selected
parameters to pressure change and also the pressure change to our response. Detailed results are
shown in the Appendix.
The global sensitivity analysis successfully displays the factors that influence land movement
most sensitively. It confirms the potential to recover subsurface information according to land
surface displacement. The InSAR satellite is capable of observing land movement with a
resolution of 1 mm/yr thereby validating the possibility of InSAR surveillance for this specific
GCS site. We show the computed synthetic InSAR data in Figure 344, according to a 2-way
coupled reservoir simulation model reported in the methodology of our prior work (Li et al.
2024). The simulation starts in 2023 and continues for 18 years of injection following a specific
injection scheme in Figure 337(a). The annual land displacement rate changes with the injection
of CO2 and it is predicted to peak in 2027 due to the largest annual injection rate. Before 2027,
the land uplifts faster in the southeast area due to the deviated injection well and the increasing
annual injection rates. After 2027, the land uplift rate gradually drops until it shows land
displaces downward due to the declining formation pore pressure. With a lesser injection rate,
the pressure change decreases and therefore the land uplift drops compared with previous years.

 524

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Thereafter, the land displacement rates become negative. The land uplift drops to its initial
condition, and the land displacement rate becomes zero until the end of the injection period. The
simulation results indicate land surface deformation due to the CO2 injection with induced
pressure increment (Li 2024b; Li et al. 2024), whereas the synthetic InSAR images provide a
view in time series to understand the land movements according to injectivity.

 Discussion
This work evaluates the potential use of InSAR time series images as a monitoring tool for a
GCS project. This study evaluates InSAR time series imaging as a monitoring tool for GCS in
Kern County, CA. Numerical simulations reveal a strong correlation between CO2-induced
pressure changes and net surface displacement, confirming that InSAR signals reflect subsurface
processes. A global sensitivity analysis (DGSA) was performed for 2 responses. Response 1 (net
displacement) shows that sandstone Young’s modulus and injection rate are the most sensitive
parameters controlling land uplift. Response 2 (time series InSAR observations) recovers
additional information, with sensitivity extending to sandstone Young’s modulus, injection rate,
and injection horizon. Parameters such as Poisson’s ratio of shale or sandstone and vertical-to-
horizontal permeability ratios are found to be relatively insensitive.
By modeling elastic rock behavior in a saline aquifer, the study avoids scenarios of fracturing
and leakage, although future work should extend to fractured reservoirs. Synthetic InSAR data
successfully recover land deformation signals above background noise, demonstrating
detectability in the project area where surface vegetation and topographic noise are minimal. The
results suggest that InSAR can complement numerical models by providing real-time geospatial
monitoring, reducing uncertainty through history matching, and improving risk management.
Future directions include broader uncertainty quantification and extension to multiple GCS sites

 525

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

to assess global sensitivities. Overall, InSAR shows strong potential as a cost effective, reliable
component of monitoring, measurement, and verification (MMV) strategies for carbon storage
projects.

 Summary
The main challenges of the prospective site include heterogeneous rock properties, a dipping
storage formation, a large peak annual rate of the injection scheme, and the potential existence of
faults in the storage formation. We developed an in-house toolbox, pyCCUS, to automate the
GCS injector-design workflow and address the challenges. The proposed deviated well keeps the
pressure increase in the storage formation as small as possible while meeting the specified
injection rates. It is essential to quantify the trade-off between CO2 plume size and pressure
responses systematically. This workflow standardizes the process from building the 2-way
coupled numerical model for parallel computations to the postprocessing targeting GCS-specific
needs. The workflow therefore optimizes the well trajectory in the subsurface to maximize CO2
storage security and minimize risk.
We demonstrate the work following a risk-averse strategy that reduces risks caused by the
pressure responses in the storage formation and at the fault. The geomechanical model boundary
is confirmed to comply with assumptions, that we have a stable land surface due to the constant
pressure at the edge. We examine the pressure change at the boundary of this model to ensure the
constant pressure condition is valid for all timesteps. The optimal injector demonstrates the
capability to reduce the pressure buildup by 54% while increasing CO2 plume size by only 21%.
The optimal injector is validated by its performance under uncertainties of the injection schemes
and geological realizations compared with selected representative cases. Sensitivity analysis
indicates that the optimal injector is capable of injecting more CO2 while maintaining storage
integrity. The uncertainty analysis from multiple geological realizations offers additional
validation to confirm the robust performance of our optimal injector design. A long, deviated,
injection well benefits this GCS project with maximal storage security and minimal
geomechanical risk.
We successfully detect the historical net surface displacement signals to establish background
signal as the noise level of InSAR. The spatial information together with vertical resolution
satisfy requirements for using InSAR to monitor the plume for this project because the uplift
signal is distinguishable from the background noise. The analysis confirms that the features
learned from these complex response data are sufficient and representative. The global
sensitivity study of the coupled CO2 transport and geomechanical model shows that InSAR
observations are most sensitive to injection rate and storage formation mechanical parameters,
Youngs modulus. The study also suggests that some model parameters could be recovered
reliably from InSAR images.
It is also challenging to monitor GCS projects throughout their lifespan. We identify the clear
correlation between the land surface uplift and the pressure change in the storage formation for
this site. This response indicates the strong potential to monitor subsurface events according to
the signals from land movements. The 2-way coupled flow and mechanical simulation predicts
that the maximum land uplift will be 2.1 cm in 2027, according to the initial model predictions
based on the SJV conditions. Interestingly, this amount of deformation is measurable using

 526

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

satellite observations. The satellite images could provide cost-effective information to monitor
the site spatially in near real time.

  Field Project
Field Project – Assist with preliminary planning, implementation of infrastructure, and
monitoring of a field project. Provide input on well construction that can withstand CO2 contact
over the project lifetime. Apply the SimCCSPRO toolset and scenario analysis to understand how
the SPR project might look with pipelines and how well locations might look.

 Background
Carbon Solutions (Saint Paul, MN) collaborated with Sentinel Peak Resources
(https://sentinelpeakresources.com/) to identify sources of CO2 and to assess the storage potential
and cost of the proposed field project location. Carbon Solutions ran 2 different sets of scenarios
at the field project location. The first set of runs used a “constrained” storage potential, reflecting
the subsurface storage simulations from the SCO2TPRO model. The second set of runs used an
“unconstrained” storage potential, allowing the capture of all available CO2 emissions. Capture
targets depend on available capturable CO2 emissions and storage capacity. Every run uses a
project duration of 30 years and a capital recovery factor (CRF) of 0.1627, which corresponds to
a 10-year financing period and 10% discount rate.

 CO2 Source Selection
Carbon Solutions identified sources of CO2, including SGs based on previous work (Kim et al.
2022), that exist around the proposed storage location within buffer ranges of 10, 20, 30, 40, 50,
and 65 km. For each buffer zone, Carbon Solutions examined the count of facilities and
cumulative capturable CO2 emissions across different industries. For example, in the 20-km
buffer there are 18 different facilities across 5 industrial sectors with total capturable emissions
of 4.89 MtCO2/yr. Additionally, going from a buffer range of 50 to 65 km brings in an additional
15 facilities and 1.26 MtCO2/yr of capturable CO2 emissions.

 Scenario Set Up
Carbon Solutions ran a total of 12 SimCCSPRO runs broken into 2 different sets, 1 group
featuring a “constrained storage capacity,” that is, using the storage capacity produced from
Carbon Solutions’ SCO2TPRO model, and the other group featuring an “unconstrained storage
capacity” where there is sufficient storage to capture all emissions within the 65 km buffer
radius. The proposed field project location identified in earlier tasks was the only storage
location considered. The first run of each scenario set features only distributed SGs as sources of
CO2 emissions. Each subsequent run features the SGs and the differing buffer ranges starting at
20 km going to 65 km. A complete breakdown of the runs can be found in Table 73.

30-year project duration. The cumulative capturable emissions for all SGs are 0.78 MtCO2/yr;
therefore, the deployed CCS networks using only SGs look like the network show on Figure

 Summary
Carbon Solutions was tasked with “assisting with preliminary planning, implementation of
infrastructure, and monitoring of a field project” by applying the SimCCSPRO toolset in a
scenario analysis. Carbon Solutions ran a total of 12 scenarios at the proposed field project
location. One set of scenarios (6 total) used the storage potential generated by SCO2TPRO
whereas the other set of scenarios (6 total) used an unconstrained storage potential that was able
to store the maximum amount of capturable CO2 emissions. Industry types and counts of sources
were adjusted across scenarios using buffer ranges from 10 to 65 km. Results indicate that when
using the SCO2TPRO storage potential, only 1 facility deploys for 5 of the scenarios resulting in
the same network route being deployed. This network has a total cost of approximately $74/tCO2
and a network length of almost 18 km. When using unconstrained storage, total network costs
range from $74/tCO2 to $81/tCO2 with network lengths going from 82 km to approximately 509
km while capturing between 0.79 and 8.83 MtCO2 annually.

  Risk Assessment
We conducted the leakage risk assessment through the existing wellbores and Quaternary faults
with different trajectory scenarios using the NRAP-Open-IAM (NRAP 2023a) tool. Also, we
calculated the probability of induced slip on faults under a range of injection scenarios.

 Leakage Risk Assessment
To ensure the security of a prospective regional storage hub in California’s southern San Joaquin
Basin, we conducted a detailed leakage risk assessment for a potential storage site. This
assessment established a protocol for evaluating potential CO2 leakage through 2 primary
pathways: preexisting, plugged-and-abandoned wellbores and Quaternary faults. The analysis
demonstrates that with an optimized injection strategy, the risk of leakage is negligible,
providing confidence in the long-term security of the site. The detailed results in this section are
provided in Kim et al. (2025); see the Appendix.

 Overview of the Storage Site and Optimized Well Design
The AOI for CO2 storage is located in Kern County, CA, in the southern San Joaquin Basin.
Previously, Kim et al. (2023b) found that the southern San Joaquin Basin is a good location for
GCS projects based on geological properties and technoeconomic aspects. The potential storage
site is 50 km west of Bakersfield, CA, as previously shown in Figure 294(a). The target storage
formation is the Etchegoin sandstone at a depth of about 1,400 m. Detailed information about the
potential storage site and the available capturable CO2 is provided in a previous study (Kim et al.
2023a).
The simplified stratigraphy of the storage formation is shown in Figure 348(a) and used to assess
leakage. The average top of the storage formation is at 1,339 m. There is a shale layer (Shale 1)
that acts as a primary seal in case of upward CO2 movement. The USDW layer is 395 m thick
and starts at a depth of 402.3 m. The potential pathways for leakage including Quaternary faults
(red solid lines) and existing wellbores (black circles) are shown in map view in Figure 348(b).
The domain is 9.7 km by 9.7 km (6 by 6 miles). Wellbores 1, 2, and 3 penetrate the storage
formation. We assume that all faults are vertical and also penetrate the storage formation. The
injector (open circle) is located in the middle of the domain. The operational conditions are 18
years of injection at an average of 0.683 MtCO2/yr, reaching a total stored amount of 12.3
MtCO2. The postinjection monitoring time is taken as 100 years. We assume that the first and
last years of injection are 2023 and 2041, respectively.

 Leakage Risk Assessment Method
The NRAP-Open-IAM tool was used to assess the risk of leakage to the USDW (Lackey et al.
2019; Vasylkivska et al. 2021; NRAP 2023b). Four reduced-order models (ROMs) were used:
Lookup Table Reservoir component, Multisegmented Wellbore component, Fault Flow
component, and Deep Alluvium Aquifer component. The reservoir pressure and CO2 saturation
profiles, were obtained from a 3D reservoir model reported elsewhere (Li et al. 2024) and used in
the Lookup Table Reservoir component model. The optimized deviated well trajectory was
chosen to minimize the overall CO2 plume size, pressure increase on QF2, and pressure buildup
within the storage formation. The detailed explanation of the well design process is found in Li
et al. (2024). QF2 is predicted to be more likely to slip due to the orientation of the maximum
horizontal stress (Kohli et al. 2023), even though it is farther from the injector than QF1. The
optimized case reduces the pressure change by 67% at QF2 compared with a vertical well and
the plume footprint is 12.6 km2 on the land surface 100 years after injection. The footprint on the
land surface decreased by 3% compared with vertical well cases.
Figure 349 shows CO2 plume migration and pressure footprint with pressure buildup for
injection and postinjection periods. The threshold of CO2 saturation was 0.05 as a residual
saturation. Two pressure thresholds were used for the pressure footprint: 1 and 0.2 MPa. The
value of 1 MPa was decided from the threshold pressure (∆𝑃𝑡ℎ𝑟 ) for the critical pressure region
with an estimated brine density of 1,105 kg/m3 computed using Eq. (18) (EPA 2013),
∆𝑃𝑡ℎ𝑟 = 𝑔 × ∆𝑧 × ∆𝜌                                                                                           (18)
where 𝑔 is the gravity constant of 9.81 m/s2, ∆𝑧 (𝑚) is the depth from the bottom of the USDW
layer (403 m) to the top depth of the injection formation (1,339 m), and ∆𝜌 presents the
difference in density for the USDW water and formation brine. The density of USDW water was
taken as 1,000 kg/m³. The alternate 0.2-MPa threshold was used to account for potential
uncertainty in brine density. This value was calculated assuming a brine density of 1,022 kg/m³

 532

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

from Fig. A-1 of Li et al. (2024). These thresholds ensure a robust evaluation of pressure
impacts, their potential effects on the USDW, and the area of review (AoR).
The CO2 plumes are characterized in the years 2027, 2030, 2035, and 2041 during the injection
period (Figure 349(a)) and further to 2090, 2114, and 2142 during the postinjection period as
shown in Figure 349(b). The later periods are needed to understand the migration and plume
growth driven by buoyancy after injector shut-in. In the region of CO2 plume migration, there
were 3 wellbores and 3 QFs (QF1, QF2, and QF4) to be impacted. The pressure plumes are
evaluated during the injection period in the years 2024, 2027, 2030, 2035, 2040, and 2041 for
better visualization. The pressure footprint rapidly increased until 2030 and then decreased
continuously until the end of injection. Figure 349(c) and Figure 349(d) show results with 1- and
0.2-MPa thresholds. Due to the dissipation of pressure during the postinjection period, the
pressure threshold of 1 MPa existed until 2040. For the case of a 0.2-MPa threshold, pressure
dissipated by 2044, Figure 349(e). After injector shut-in, pressure relaxes relatively rapidly in the
subsurface system and the pressure plume tends to dissipate. The delineation of the AoR, based
on a pressure footprint threshold of 0.2 MPa and CO2 plume migration with a residual saturation
of 0.05, is provided in the Supplementary Information of Kim et al. (2025).

effective wellbore permeability was assumed to be 1 to 10 mD based on previous studies
(Lackey et al. 2019; Kim et al. 2023a). We note that the permeability of an intact cemented
wellbore is generally much less than 1 µD and damaged wellbore permeability was reported
between 10 µD and 10 mD (Tao and Bryant 2014). In this AoR, the existing wellbores are all
plugged wellbores with cement according to public data. Therefore, the wellbore permeability is
assumed as a worst case. For the leakage assessment through existing wellbores, we used the

Multisegmented Wellbore Component ROM in the NRAP-Open-IAM tool. The model calculates

wells passing through the overlying stratigraphy into several intervals to simulate a site’s specific
stratigraphic and hydrogeologic properties (Vasylkivska et al. 2021; Baek et al. 2021). The depth
of the injection was 1,420 m. The Deep Alluvium Aquifer Component ROM was used to predict
the changes in underground water if CO2 and brine were to leak out of the storage zone.

Table 76 shows the fault parameters in the leakage risk assessment. In general, fault zones may
serve either as potential CO2 leakage pathways or barriers depending on geological properties
including fracture aperture size, connectivity, lithology, stress state, and so on (Xiao et al. 2024).
There are many studies that show small leakage risk along fault zones (Rinaldi et al. 2014;
Miocic et al. 2019; Guglielmi et al. 2021).
In this study, we use the surface trace of the Quaternary faults and vary both the permeability and
the depth to assess CO2 leakage along faults. Fault permeability is controlled by the effective
fault aperture, which is assumed to vary from 2 × 10−6 to 2.5 × 10−2 m (0.0002 to 2.5 cm) and 2 ×
10−6 to 1 × 10−1 m (0.0002 to 10 cm). In similar CO2 leakage studies, the effective fault aperture

 535

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

varied from 0.1 to 2 mm. Shear displacement was also varied from 0 to 40 mm to predict the
fault’s permeability (Pasala et al. 2013; Huang et al. 2019). We consider various scenarios for
fault depth (403, 1,200, 1,400, and 1,419 m). We assume that the faults are continuous from the
surface to the specific depth. The depth of the injector is set at 1,420 m. Each fault is divided into
4 segments to capture slight changes in orientation. The maximum permeability ratios (CO2 to
brine) of each fault are chosen as 0.6 and 1.5. We use the Fault Flow Component ROM in the
NRAP-Open-IAM tool to calculate leakage rates.

The process to minimize pressure buildup is explained in detail by Li et al. (2024). Figure 350

plume size, pressure buildup, and pressure responses at the QF2 fault region. From a

 Leakage Risk through Existing Wellbores
Based on the worst-case scenario of large wellbore permeability, we found that there was
leakage of CO2 and brine from wellbore 1 and wellbore 2, as shown in Figure 351. To conduct
stochastic simulations, we used Latin hypercube sampling (LHS), a random parameter sampling
method. The primary variables included wellbore permeability, fault effective aperture, and brine
density. The maximum leakage rates of CO2 and brine are 1.24 kg/d and 3.5 × 10−3 kg/d,
respectively, at year 99 from the existing wellbore 1, Figure 351(a). Also, the maximum leakage
rates of CO2 and brine are 7.6 × 10−2 kg/d and 4.8 × 10−4 kg/s, respectively, at year 15 from the
existing wellbore 2, as shown in Figure 351(b). Year 15 corresponds approximately to the
maximum pressure increase. There was no leakage of CO2 and brine from wellbore 3. The
cumulative leakage ratio (CLR) by mass into the USDW per total CO2 injection is defined as
𝐶𝐿𝑅 = 𝑇𝑜𝑡𝑎𝑙 𝑖𝑛𝑗𝑒𝑐𝑡𝑒𝑑 𝐶𝑂 (19)

During the project lifespan of 118 years, the ratio of the cumulative leaked CO2 to the total mass
injected (i.e., cumulative leakage fraction) in the worst-case scenario at wellbore 1 was 2.8 ×
10−6 to 1.23 × 10−5, Figure 351(c). The maximum cumulative CO2 leakage fractions at wellbore
2 were an order of magnitude less than those at wellbore 1. The combined cumulative leakage
fraction of the 2 existing wellbores reaches 1.44 × 10−5 in the worst-case scenario. Therefore, the
leakage ratio was estimated to range from 0.0003% to 0.001% among the total CO2 injection
amounts by mass where cumulative injection is 12.3 MtCO2.

 Leakage through Quaternary Faults
Quaternary faults may also serve as leakage pathways. Figure 352 shows the CO2 and brine
leakage rate on faults with a maximum permeability ratio of 0.6, aperture of 2 × 10−6 to 2.5 ×
10−2 m, and 1,400 m fault depth. In this model, fault aperture serves as the primary input
parameter for controlling fault permeability. Based on the stress conditions within the storage
formation, the fault aperture was recalculated. The fault permeability was subsequently
determined using the updated aperture and calculated according to the ‘Cubic Law’ method
(Durham and Bonner 1994; Renshaw et al. 2000). Based on these fault conditions, we found that
QF1 has the greatest risk of leakage among all faults. The range of the y-axis for each fluid is
identical. At QF1, the maximum leakage rates for CO2 and brine are 2.25 × 10−4 kg/d in year 11
and 7.9 × 10−5 kg/d in year 1, respectively. The rate of brine leakage at QF1 gradually increased
from year 40 because brine was expelled as the CO2 plume migrated. The CO2 leakage rate on

 539

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

QF2 and QF4 are both 1 to 2 orders of magnitude less than those of QF1. At both QF2 and QF4,
the brine leakage rate is greater than the CO2 leakage rate. Nevertheless, the leakage of CO2 and
brine through these faults is found to be negligible compared with the leakage from the existing
wellbores, see Figure 352(d).

 Summary
We assessed the potential for CO2 leakage along preexisting wellbores and Quaternary faults
near a possible CO2 storage site using the NRAP-Open-IAM tool. Both pressure and CO2
saturation profiles are input to NRAP-Open-IAM and were obtained using a 3D reservoir model.
The optimized design of the CO2 injection scenarios from a companion study was selected to
minimize pressure buildup at faults along with a relatively small-sized CO2 plume. This is a key
initial step in minimizing the risk of leakage.
Starting from an optimized injection scenario and making conservative assumptions to obtain a
worst case for leakage, we found that 2 existing wellbores and 2 Quaternary faults (QF1 and
QF2) were the main leakage pathways in the AoR. The maximum leakage rates of CO2 and brine
at wellbore 1, which is closest to the injector, were 1.24 kg/d and 3.5 × 10−3 kg/d, respectively, at
year 99 from the start of injection. Estimated leakage rates from wellbore 2 were 1 order of

 541

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

magnitude less than wellbore 1. The cumulative CO2 leakage, as a percentage of the total
injected mass is estimated to range from 0.0003% to 0.001% for the 118-year project lifetime
through existing wellbores. Therefore, leakage rates for CO2 and brine to the USDW did not
show any change in total dissolved solids (TDS) and pH above background.
Also, leakage along Quaternary faults was obtained with estimated fault parameters. We found
that the maximum CO2 leakage rate of 2.25 × 10−4 kg/d from QF1 is the greatest amount among
all faults because QF1 is the fault closest to the injector. Results showed that CO2 leakage along
Quaternary faults is much less compared with leakage from the existing wellbores. We found
that the leakage through faults was strongly dependent on fault depth, aperture, and relative
permeability, so further characterization of fault properties is needed to predict leakage rates
more accurately.
In addition, we investigated the leakage from wellbores and Quaternary faults based on different
injection well trajectories. The other injection scenarios show different leakage rates due to the
relative position of the injector and existing wellbores. Overall, the ratio of leaked to injected
CO2 remains small and wellbores are the primary means of leakage. We did not find any
significant change in the pH and TDS of the USDW in any scenario.

 Induced Geomechanical Risk Assessment
Our objective was to build a geomechanical model for the prospective storage site and conduct a
seismic hazard assessment to quantify the risk of induced slip on preexisting faults during the
propose to CO2 injection. The detailed results in this section are provided in Kohli et al. (2023);
see the Appendix.
In this study, we take a 3-part approach to evaluating seismic hazard at a candidate site in the
southern San Joaquin Basin of California. First, we build a geomechanical model and evaluate
the stress state on mapped faults near the injection site. We then examine the probability of
induced fault slip due to CO2 injection using random populations of faults and a distribution of
geomechanical parameters. From these analyses, we delineate the pressure conditions minimize
the increase in seismic hazard on preexisting faults, given the spatial extent and magnitude of the
predicted pressure plume. Finally, we characterize the natural patterns of seismicity at the site
and establish criteria for differentiating induced events during the injection storage periods and
for responding to events at different thresholds using a traffic light system.

 Site Characterization
Figure 353 shows stress, seismicity, and fault map for the candidate CO2 injection site.
• Stress state – The region is in a strike-slip faulting environment. The maximum horizontal
 stress (SHmax) is the greatest principal stress, with a consistent northeast–southwest
 orientation across the southern San Joaquin Basin.
• Faults – Eight major preexisting faults from the USGS Quaternary Faults database (USGS
 2024) were identified within a 10-km radius of the proposed injection site. These represent
 risk factors for reactivation during CO2 injection.
• Background seismicity – The prospective site is in an area of relatively low seismic activity
 compared with other parts of the basin. Analysis of a 20-year seismic record established a
 natural background seismicity rate of 0.2 to 0.3 events/mo⁻¹km⁻². Analysis of the regional

 542

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 earthquake catalog revealed a Gutenberg–Richter b-value of approximately 0.7, which is
 typical for California’s Central Valley. The magnitude of catalog completeness is
 approximately M1.7, indicating that the current seismic network does not detect all smaller
 events.

Figure 353 (left) Stress, seismicity, and fault map for the candidate CO 2 injection site. Black lines represent the
orientation of the maximum horizontal stress. Red lines represent faults from the USGS Quaternary Faults database.
Red circles represent historical seismic events and are sized by magnitude. (right) Gutenberg–Richter plot of
historical seismicity at the prospective storage site. Source: Kohli et al. (2023), licensed under CC BY-NC.

 Geomechanical Model
A geomechanical model was built to understand the preexisting stress conditions of the reservoir
and seal units in Figure 354.
• Rock properties – Porosity and permeability data from logs from a nearby vertical well were
 used to estimate the Young’s modulus of the storage reservoir and seal sequence. The
 porosity and permeability of the storage formation are 0.28 to 32 and 1 to 10 mD,
 respectively. Based on core data for similar lithologies, these porosity–permeability values
 correspond to Young’s modulus values approximately 20 to 30 GPa.
• Viscous relaxation model – Young’s modulus and lithologic data were used to estimate the
 variations of the fracture gradient or the minimum horizontal stress, Shmin, with depth due to
 viscous relaxation over geologic time.
• Model results – The storage reservoir is between 4,000 and 6,000 ft (1,219.2 and 1,828.8 m)
 deep and is overlain by a series of shale seal units. The model predicts a slightly lower Shmin
 gradient than frictional equilibrium and shows little to no significant variations in Shmin
 within the storage or seal formations.

 Fault Slip Analysis
The geomechanical model was used to evaluate the potential for induced slip on the Quaternary
faults in Figure 355.
• Mohr-Coulomb analysis – Using the geomechanical model, the conditions for slip on each
 fault was calculated. Faults 2, 7, and 8 were well oriented for slip in the current stress field.
 The analysis indicates that the pressure change due to CO2 injection should be limited to less
 500 psi (3,447.4 kPa) within 2 km of the injector.
• Probabilistic fault slip analysis – To account for geomechanical parameter uncertainty, a
 probabilistic analysis was conducted using Monte Carlo simulations. The probability of slip
 was calculated for each fault as a function of the change in pore pressure. The analysis
 showed that the initial probability of slip for the most hazardous faults is between 0.1 and 0.3
 and increases to over 0.5 if the pore pressure change exceeds 500 psi (3,447.4 kPa).

 3D Visualization of Plume–Fault Interaction
A 3D model was developed to visualize the dynamic interaction among the simulated CO2
plume, the Quaternary faults, and historical seismicity in Figure 356. Only QF1 through QF4 are
impacted by the simulated pressure plume. QF2 is of particular interest because it is the largest
fault segment, it is near the injector, and it is well oriented for slip in strike-slip motion. There is
no geophysical data to constrain the fault structure at depth, so for this analysis it is assumed that
the faults intersect the full thickness storage zone and are vertically dipping. Visualizing the
historical seismicity in 3D shows that the majority of earthquakes in this area occur far below the
storage reservoir in the crystalline basement. There are several events M1-M2 that were located
within the upper and lower seal units, but no events were detected on any of the Quaternary
faults at the depth of the storage reservoir.

 Modeling Effects of CO2 Injection
The results of the 3D hydrological model were used to calculate the impact of CO2 injection on
the probability of fault slip in Figure 357.
• The 3D hydrological model shows how the pressure changes in space and time due to CO2
 injection. At the peak of injection in 2028, pressure was predicted to increase by up to 1,200
 psi (8,273.7 kPa) in the immediate vicinity of the injector. However, increase in pressure on
 the Quaternary faults was significantly lower, reaching a maximum of approximately 400 psi
 (2,757.9 kPa) on QF1 and less than 200 psi (1,379.0 kPa) on other faults.
• The probabilistic fault slip model shows the likelihood of induced seismicity for different
 injection scenarios. Based a distribution of reservoir simulations with different injection
 schemes, the range of probabilities for slip on QF2 is between 0.2 and 0.3. The probability of
 slip changes over time as the pressure plume builds up and then dissipates. This model can be
 used to iteratively improve injection designs to reduce the risk of induced seismicity.
