 Identifying and Responding to Induced Seismicity
Finally, a framework was developed to monitor, identify, and respond to any induced seismicity
due to CO2 injection.
• Identification criteria: Three categories for flagging an event for further review.
 1) Area of interest: Event occurs in a region mechanically influenced by injection.
 2) Seismic characteristics: Event is part of a sequence with anomalous characteristics (e.g.,
 changes in seismicity rate, b-value, or average event depth).
 3) Ground shaking: The event causes felt reports or ground motion exceeding predefined
 thresholds at seismic stations.
• Response protocol: A CO2 storage specific traffic light protocol was developed for the site
 and defines thresholds for action and specific operational responses.

 Summary
Our study highlights the need for detailed, site-specific assessments of induced seismicity risk
for CO2 injection projects in California. In the AOI of the prospective site, mapped faults are not
associated with any located earthquakes suggesting that these faults are not active in the current

 547

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

tectonic regime. However, increasing pore pressure through CO2 injection drives faults closer to
failure and may induce slip if the magnitude and the footprint of the pressure plume are not
controlled. Our geomechanical analysis suggests that the risk of reactivating mapped faults in the
area is low if pressures are kept below 500 psi (3,447.4 kPa) within 1 to 2 km of the injector. The
probabilistic fault slip analysis indicates fault slip may change by up to 20% under the proposed
injection conditions. The greatest risk is presented by well oriented faults within 2 km of the
injector, where pressure changes are greatest and occur relatively rapidly. Sensitivity analysis
indicates that stress magnitudes and orientations are the greatest sources of variability in fault
slip probability, which demonstrates the need for borehole stress measurements at the site.
The risk for induced seismicity under the proposed condition appears to low, but more data are
needed to resolve naturally occurring seismicity in the estimated AOI. Based on our analysis, we
recommend the following strategies to further characterize and mitigate the risk of induced
seismicity at the prospective site:
• Fortify the earthquake catalog by deploying more surface seismic stations around the injector
 and borehole seismic stations in nearby a monitoring well
• Conduct image logs and stress measurements in both the injector and the monitoring well to
 characterize depth variations in stress and locate zones with active faults
• Acquire seismic imaging to identify hidden faults in the subsurface
• Design the permanent monitoring array around the predicted plume footprint
• Take corrective action if the pressure plume extent and magnitude of pressure increase
 deviates from simulation results and adhere to corrective actions proposed in the traffic light
 system

Carbon Solutions ran all forward-looking scenarios for the entire state of California to better
understand what potential buildouts of CCS infrastructure within the state could look like
depending on distributed or hub geologic storage locations. Here distributed storage refers to
using a 50 km by 50 km grid to generate individual storage points. 3 hub storage locations were
selected: the Northern California Tehama County Hub, the Central California San Joaquin
County Hub, and the Southern California Kern County Hub (Kim et al. 2022).

 Results
Figure 358 shows what a CCS network, using all sources of CO2 in California, would look like
when using hub (A) and distributed (B) storage options. The most used hub storage option in the
 548

hub scenario was the Southern California “Kern County” Hub. Furthermore, the overall CCS
network deployment in this scenario splits into 2 main networks, one going from northern to
central California and another that goes from central to southeastern California. The latter
network hub features the Southern California “Kern County” Hub.
The CCS network in Figure 358(a) deploys approximately 5,143 km of pipeline to capture
almost 52 MtCO2/yr for a network total cost of $109/tCO2. The additional pipeline results from
needing to connect farther-away sources with the targeted hub storage locations. This can be
observed when realizing that using hub storage involves an additional 1,785 km of pipeline when
compared with the equivalent distributed storage scenario (Figure 358(b)). This increase in
pipeline deployment results in approximately $7/tCO2 difference in the total CCS network cost
between the 2 scenarios.
Figure 358(b) shows the distributed storage CCS network for California when capturing all
available CO2 emissions (52 MtCO2/yr). This distributed storage network involves the
deployment of 3,359 km of pipeline with a total unit network cost of $102/tCO2. Approximately
80 different individual geologic storage locations are deployed in this run, highlighting how the
least cost option often involves transporting captured CO2 emissions to nearby low cost and high
storage potential options. For example, the unit storage cost for distributed and hub storage is
$6.91/tCO2 and $6.63/tCO2, respectively. Yet the higher total unit cost for hub storage can be
explained by the fact that the difference in unit transportation costs is approximately $7/tCO2, or
in other words the difference in total CCS network cost.

 Summary
Carbon Solutions was tasked with applying the SimCCSPRO toolset to “develop a conceptual
model of how to stimulate regional CCS for more than 50 MtCO2/yr.” To achieve this objective
Carbon Solutions ran 4 scenarios using either hub or distributed storage options. In hub storage
scenarios, Carbon Solutions designated 3 hubs for the state of California while distributed
storage scenarios use the 50-km SCO2TPRO grid of storage locations. Scenarios also featured
either of 2 options for sources: SGs only (8.64 MtCO2/yr) and all sources of CO2 in California
(51.55 MtCO2/yr). Carbon Solutions results indicate that total network costs are lower when
using distributed storage when compared with hub storage. For example, when using all sources
in California the total network costs for hub storage is approximately $109/tCO2 while
distributed storage has a total network cost of $102/tCO2. This is further supported by looking at
network lengths, where distributed storage has a network length of 3,358 km and hub storage has
a network length of 5,143 km.

 Conclusion
The goal of this work is to provide foundational engineering analysis across immediate, near-
term, and medium-term time frames to accelerate the implementation of a shovel-ready project
that has the potential to scale and address the 12.3 MtCO2/year emitted from upstream oil and
gas operations in the SJV. The project’s physical location is one of the closest prospective
storage sites to the LA Basin. Within the LA Basin any subsurface storage is unlikely due to
population density and seismic activity making the SJV especially interesting. The AOI for CO2
storage site is located near 50 km west of Bakersfield, California in the southern San Joaquin
Basin. Previously, Kim et al. (2023b) found that the southern San Joaquin Basin is a good
location for GCS projects based on geological properties and technoeconomic aspects.
The objective is to provide technical and economic analysis to support a first-of-its-kind capture
and storage project aimed at reducing emissions from upstream oil production operations. Project
goals are (1) to leverage LCFS credits and CUSP technical expertise to move a CCS project in
California from concept to permitting to implementation, (2) add certainty to storage volumes
 550

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

and dynamic storage capacity of relatively poorly characterized saline formations in the SJV, (3)
forge a pathway for others to follow with similar projects, and (4) lay the foundations of a
regional storage hub. We intend to achieve our goals using several tasks with collaboration
among team members. The result of each task is as follows.

 1. Emitter Identification and Capture Economics
A detailed inventory identified 63 SGs and 20 CHP plants emitting roughly 11.4 MtCO2 per
year. Capture cost analysis using amine-based systems revealed an average cost of $57/tCO2 to
$78/tCO2, depending on plant type and load factor. Economies of scale significantly improve
capture affordability. Forty-one potential storage sites were screened, yielding an estimated 5.8
GtCO2 capacity.
SimCCS modeling incorporating 45Q and LCFS incentives revealed economic viability for most
EOR facilities (SR and CHP) at $70/tCO2 to $80/tCO2, while power and cement facilities
become competitive only with extended credit durations.

 2. Subsurface Model Characterization
The Etchegoin Formation was selected as the primary pilot target, characterized by a 2.3 km-
deep saline sandstone sealed by around 600 m of shale. Coupled flow-geomechanical
simulations predict that injecting 12.3 MtCO2 over 18 years results in pressure increases below
130 psi and surface uplift under 2 cm, safely below fracture thresholds. The optimal well
geometry analysis using pyCCUS indicates a long, deviated injector minimizes pressure on
nearby faults by over 70% compared with a vertical well, confirming safe operational margins
and improved reservoir performance.

 3. Storage Assessment and Plume Migration
CMG and pyCCUS simulations estimate a stabilized plume footprint of approximately 12 km²
after 100 years. Sensitivity analyses show limited uncertainty impacts, confirming containment
reliability. The optimized design reduces reservoir overpressure by more than half while
maintaining equivalent storage efficiency.

 4. Monitoring via InSAR and Data Analytics
Analysis of Sentinel-1 InSAR data (2015–2023; European Space Agency, Paris, France;
https://www.esa.int/Applications/Observing_the_Earth/Copernicus/Sentinel-1) established a
stable pre-injection baseline. Synthetic deformation modeling predicts 20 to 25 mm of uplift
during injection, consistent with expected pressure buildup. Sensitivity tests identify rock
stiffness and injection rate as key uplift drivers, supporting the use of InSAR-based monitoring
for regulatory compliance and safety assurance.

 5. Infrastructure and Economic Scenarios in Field Project
Using SimCCSPRO, Carbon Solutions evaluated multiple field development scenarios. In a
capacity-limited (“constrained”) case, network costs reached approximately $74/tCO2 with short
pipeline distances, while “unconstrained” cases expanded injection and transport networks up to
509 km with total costs near $81/t. Capture and storage remain the dominant cost drivers. All

 551

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

scenarios fall below the effective 45Q credit value, supporting the economic feasibility of pilot
deployment.

 6. Risk and Seismic Assessment
The leakage assessment with the NRAP-Open-IAM tool demonstrated extremely low leakage
risk—less than or equal to 0.001% of total injected CO2—through both faults and wells.
Probabilistic analyses show fault-slip likelihood below 0.3 when maintaining pressure increases
under 500 psi. Historical seismic data confirms the absence of active faults within the injection
horizon. A traffic-light protocol was developed for operational management of induced
seismicity.

 7. Forward-Looking Regional Scenarios
Statewide simulations comparing centralized (“hub”) and distributed storage architectures found
that distributed networks across Kern, Tehama, and San Joaquin Counties minimize total system
costs. Capturing all industrial emissions (approximately 52 MtCO2/yr) would require
approximately 5,000 km of pipeline infrastructure at $102 to 109/tCO2, while restricting to oil
and gas emitters lowers cost to approximately $75/tCO2. The southern SJV thus emerges as the
most strategic location for initial large-scale deployment.
Finally, we demonstrated that the San Joaquin Basin offers the geologic, economic, and
infrastructural readiness for CCS hub development. The findings confirmed technical feasibility,
low leakage risk, and cost competitiveness under current credit regimes. The integrated
approach—combining advanced modeling, economic optimization, and InSAR monitoring—lays
the foundation for a pilot project and a scalable statewide CO2 storage network.

 Carbon Solutions’ Contributions
Carbon Solutions primarily supported work on the California Focused Project by applying its
SimCCSPRO toolset to support the following tasks:
• Task 6 – Field Project Assessment
• Task 9 – Forward Looking Scenarios
To begin with, Carbon Solutions identified all sources of CO2 around the proposed project field
site at buffer ranges from 20 km to 50 km with one additional buffer of 65 km considered. In the
20 km buffer there are 18 unique facilities from five different industrial sectors with total annual
capturable emissions of 4.89 MtCO2. When going from the 50 km buffer to the 65 km buffer
adds an additional 15 facilities with 1.26 MtCO2/yr in capturable CO2 emissions.

Carbon Solutions also ran four forward looking scenarios to evaluate hub or distributed storage
as a foundation for future CCS networks in California. Ultimately, these scenarios indicated that
regardless of what sources are being used, CCS networks that use distributed storage are always
less expensive than the corresponding CCS networks that use hub storage. For example, when
capturing CO2 from all sources in California, the distributed storage CCS network has a total cost
of $102/tCO2 while the hub storage CCS network has a total cost of $109/tCO2. There are
notable differences in amounts of pipeline deployed with hub storage adding almost 1,800 km of
additional CO2 pipeline deployment (see Table 4 on page 27).

Feasibility Study on a Potential CCUS Project in
Colorado: CO2 Capture from a Refinery and
Sequestration in the Denver–Julesburg (DJ) Basin
This study evaluates the feasibility of storing over 50 MtCO2 within a 30-yr period in southern
Colorado. The target for injection is the 7,000 ft (2,134 m)-deep Lyons saline aquifer formation,
with the overlying alternating layers of anhydrite and shale serving as seals. Geological static
models were constructed using seismic, well log and core data, followed by fluid flow modeling
to understand the CO2 injection strategy, saturation distribution and plume size. The results
indicate that approximately 60 MtCO2 can be injected with 2 wells into the formation over 30 yr,
with 85% of the CO2 existing in a supercritical phase during the injection stage. After 70 yr of
shut-in, about 30% of the injected CO2 becomes immobilized due to hysteresis. Seismic data
shows no faulting within the injection and seal formations, and no legacy wells penetrate the

 561

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Lyons formation within the study area, which reduces the risks of fault slippage and leakage
through legacy wells. However, the small dip angle of the structure may present challenges to
CO2 plume containment, highlighting the importance of implementing strategies such as
enhanced monitoring systems, detailed geomechanical modeling, and plume migration
simulations to mitigate and better understand potential risks. This study offers early insights into
carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) potential in southern Colorado using seismic and
limited data, and will ultimately provide valuable guidance for future implementation of CO2
injection in the region.

CCUS has emerged as a pivotal technology in the global effort to mitigate climate change by
reducing CO2 emissions from industrial sources. As the world seeks to transition to a low-carbon
economy, CCUS offers a pathway to capture CO2 before it reaches the atmosphere, either
repurposing it for industrial applications or permanently storing it underground (e.g., Metz et al.
2005; Lal 2008; Orr 2018). Geological CO2 sequestration, a key component of CCUS, involves
the long-term storage of captured CO2 in deep subsurface formations. This method is particularly
promising due to its potential to store large quantities of CO2 securely and sustainably, thereby
playing a critical role in achieving net-zero emissions targets (e.g., Page et al. 2020; McCulloch
2021).
Deep saline aquifers—also known as deep saline formations—are porous rock units saturated
with non-potable brine and are considered optimal reservoirs for geological CO2 storage due to
their vast capacity and widespread availability (SPE 2017; Page et al. 2020). The sequestration
process involves injecting CO2 into these deep underground formations, where it is stored
through various mechanisms (Metz et al. 2005), including structural and stratigraphic trapping by
impermeable cap rocks, residual trapping in pore spaces, solubility trapping as CO2 dissolves
into saline water, and mineral trapping where CO2 reacts with minerals to form stable carbonates.
However, effective deployment of large-scale CO2 storage also requires careful evaluation of
potential risks—such as leakage through faults or legacy wells, pressure-induced fault
reactivation, and long-term monitoring challenges. These factors can significantly influence
storage integrity, regulatory approval (e.g., Class VI permitting), and public confidence.
Therefore, in addition to evaluating storage capacity and plume behavior, this study also assesses
site-specific containment risks and monitoring feasibility using geologic, geophysical, and
reservoir simulation data. The focus on a southern Colorado site offers new insights into the
viability of CO2 sequestration in this underexplored region.
Globally, several commercial CCUS projects have been successfully implemented,
demonstrating the viability of this technology at scale. Notable examples include the Sleipner
project in Norway, which has been operated since 1996 (e.g., Chadwick et al. 2004, 2010), the
Quest project in Canada, operated by Shell (London, UK) since 2015 (e.g., Duong et al. 2019;
Brown et al. 2023), and the Gorgon project in Australia, led by Chevron (Houston, TX) since
2019 (e.g., Trupp et al. 2021; Quinn 2022). In the United States, several large-scale projects are
underway, many as part of the US Department of Energy (DOE) Carbon Storage Assurance
Facility Enterprise (CarbonSAFE) program, further contributing to the growing momentum of
CCUS deployment (Sullivan et al. 2020; DOE 2024). These projects require the storage of over
50 MtCO2 over a 30-yr period. Examples include the storage of 3.2 MtCO2 annually in central

 562

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

North Dakota (Peck et al. 2019), the sequestration of 6 to 7 MtCO2 yearly in northwest New
Mexico over 30 yr (Ampomah et al. 2022), and the accelerated deployment of CCUS at coal-
based power plants with CO2 storage in Wyoming’s Powder River Basin (McLaughlin et al.
2019). Based on the analysis of Young et al. (2007) and Ning et al. (2025), Colorado is a state
with significant potential for geological CO2 sequestration.
The goal of this study is to assess the feasibility of storing CO2 in a deep saline aquifer of
southern Colorado and to lay the groundwork for future commercial-scale CCUS projects. In
alignment with the DOE’s commercial-scale CCUS project requirements, the study aims to
explore the potential to sequester more than 50 MtCO2 over 30 yr. To achieve this, the geological
properties of the Lyons saline aquifer and its overlying confining units are first characterized,
followed by dynamic reservoir simulations to evaluate plume migration, pressure buildup, and
CO2 phase behavior. In addition to assessing storage capacity, this study also evaluates key
containment risks, including legacy well integrity, fault reactivation potential, and the feasibility
of seismic monitoring, based on available geological and geophysical data. These considerations
are critical for site selection, permitting, and the design of long-term monitoring strategies in
future CCUS applications.

  Study Area
Colorado hosts numerous industrial facilities and is underlain by extensive geologic formations
with significant potential for CO2 storage (Figure 364). In 2021, Colorado emitted a total of 85.4
MtCO2, representing 1.7% of the total US emissions (EIA 2024). In response to escalating
climate concerns, Colorado aims for a 50% reduction in greenhouse gas emissions by 2030 and
achieving net-zero emissions by 2050 compared to its 2005 levels, positioning CCUS as a
critical strategy in meeting these goals (Colorado Energy Office 2024).

Figure 364 The leading CO2 emission facilities, potential storage basins, and CO2 pipelines in Colorado. Coal-fired
power plants are excluded as they are scheduled for retirement by 2034.

 563

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Deep saline formations that have been identified as potential CO2 storage units in Colorado
include the Fountain, Weber, Morrison, Entrada, Lyons, and Dakota formations, which are
distributed across several basins, including the Denver–Julesburg (DJ), Piceance, San Juan, and
Sand Wash basins, in the state (Figure 364). Assuming a storage efficiency factor of 1%, the
total estimated storage resource for deep saline aquifers in Colorado is approximately 152 billion
metric tons (Young et al. 2007). Notably, the Lyons formation in southern Colorado is estimated
to have a storage resource of 876 Mt, making it a prime candidate for the target injection zone in
this study. Our study area focuses on a 50-square-mile (130-square-km) area in southern
Colorado, located in El Paso County (Figure 364), where several large emission facilities are
situated nearby.

  Stratigraphic Column of the DJ Basin
The area for this study is located on the west edge of the DJ Basin, which is highly asymmetric
and serves as Colorado's principal oil and gas producing region, accounting for 80% of the state's
crude oil output. Bounded by the Front Range thrusts to the west and gradually shallowing
towards the east, the basin's axis extends north to south parallel to the Front Range (Figure 365).
Predominantly, the Cretaceous rock layers, including the Niobrara, Codell, and Dakota
formations, are concentrated in the Wattenberg field just north of Denver and are key to the
majority of the basin's hydrocarbon production.

Figure 365 The stratigraphic column of the Denver–Julesburg Basin west (modified from Nelson and Santus [2011]
and Young et al. [2007]) following the west-east cross-section A–A’. This section intersects the southwest portion of
the Wattenberg gas field. The red-shaded area indicates the approximate location of gas accumulation in the Codell-
Niobrara and Dakota intervals.
Several studies have explored the potential for carbon sequestration in the DJ Basin, evaluating
formations like Lyons and Fountain as possible deep saline aquifers for carbon storage (e.g.,
Young et al. 2007; Drake et al. 2014). While the Fountain Formation has been identified as a
 564

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

potential CO2 storage unit at the state level, in the specific study area it transitions from a
favorable outcrop sandstone to a tighter, less permeable limestone toward the east, suggesting
limited suitability for storage at this location. Consequently, this study concentrates on assessing
the Permian Lyons Sandstone's suitability for CO2 injection, particularly within the southwestern
part of the basin, or El Paso County in Colorado. Notably, the eastern sections of the Lyons
formation are active oil-producing zones; however, these do not overlap with our targeted
western region designated for CO2 storage. The Lyons sandstone is primarily composed of quartz
and feldspar, with depths ranging from approximately 2,000 ft (610 m) in the east to 10,000 ft
(3,048 m) at the basin's axis (Garbarini and Veal 1968). The formation exhibits a porosity range
of 4.4% to 26.1% and permeability between 0.1 and 88 mD (Levandowski et al. 1973). It is
widely distributed across the DJ Basin, with thicknesses varying from less than 25 ft (8 m) to
over 250 ft (76 m; Sonnenberg et al. 2024).

  Static Modeling Construction from Post-Stack Seismic
 Property Distribution
To model CO2 injection accurately, the structural surfaces extracted from the seismic data must
be populated with the physical properties of the deep saline aquifer, specifically porosity and
permeability. These properties are crucial as porosity has a direct relationship with acoustic
impedance, whereas permeability can be exponentially correlated to porosity within a formation.
Figure 366 shows the seal and formation in the study area. The saline aquifer, between 7,316 ft
(2,230 m) and 7,448 ft (2,270 m), is indicated by the interval with minimal separation between
porosity (POR) and density log (RHOB), indicating a clean formation. The variance maps on the
right side of Figure 366, derived from post-stack seismic data, indicate no faulting in either the
upper or lower anhydrite layers. Seismic variance is a discontinuity attribute that highlights
changes in reflection amplitude and continuity; high variance values typically indicate structural
features such as faults or fractures, whereas low variance values reflect continuous, undisturbed
strata.

 565

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 366 Gamma ray (GR), caliper (CALIPER), sonic (SON), density (RHOB), porosity (POR), and resistivity
(RES) logs through the saline aquifer, over burden, and under burden formations. Depth is shown in ft. GR,
CALIPER, and SON logs are color-coded by lithology as interpreted from the logs: red for anhydrite, yellow for
sandstone, and brown for shales. POR (blue) and RHOB (red) are plotted together, with gray shading between them.
Variance attribute for Anhydrite is derived from post-stack seismic volumes and shown on right.
The static model building process begins with the calculation of acoustic impedance for the
seismic volume through a post-stack seismic inversion. This model-based inversion involves
building a low-frequency initial (background) model from seismic horizons and well data, which
correlates to the seismic horizons within the volume. Acoustic impedance from the well is
propagated throughout the seismic volume, using multiple horizons as guides. The statistically
estimated wavelet in the inversion zone and the initial model is then used to generate acoustic
impedances and synthetic seismic data, which is compared to the original seismic data (Herman
2024). The inversion process iteratively updates the acoustic impedances in order to minimize
the residual differences between the synthetic and field data, leading to the final acoustic
impedance model.
This inverted acoustic impedance model is then correlated to porosity and lithology using well-
log information. Two wells were utilized in this study: Well A, penetrating the Lyons formation
but located 30 miles (48.3 km) outside the 3D seismic area, and Well B, situated within the 3D
seismic but lacking the depth necessary to provide properties of the Lyons formation. The P-
impedance vs porosity cross-plot from Well A for the Lyons formation shown in Figure 367. In
this particular case, since there is no fluid change, no pressure change, and no facies change, the
seismic impedance is mostly impacted by porosity changes. Using this linear relationship, the P-
impedance obtained from the post-stack seismic inversion is transformed into porosity. The
average porosity value was seen to be 13%. Subsequently, porosity was transformed into
permeability using operator-derived empirical relationships and core testing, yielding an average
horizontal permeability of 80 mD. Vertical permeability is lower than horizontal permeability,
with a horizontal-to-vertical ratio of 17:1, as indicated by core measurements.

 566

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 367 Cross-plot of P-impedance with porosity in Lyons formation from well log. Color Scale is depth (m). A
linear trend is used to calculate porosity values from P-impedance inversion values.

 Static Model Construction
The static geological model was constructed using four key seismic horizons: the top of the
Lyons Formation, the top and bottom of the saline aquifer interval, and the top of the Fountain
Formation. These horizons define a model framework composed of 15 layers, which were
selected to adequately represent the vertical heterogeneity of the geologic units. The horizontal
grid consists of 132 × 138 cells, covering the area of interest with approximately one-quarter
million total grid blocks. Each grid cell has a horizontal resolution of approximately 330 ft (100
m), and vertical thicknesses ranging from 10 ft (3 m) to 25 ft (8 m), depending on the local
stratigraphy.
Seismic-to-depth conversion was performed using calibrated interval velocities and time-depth
relationships derived from Well A, which lies approximately 30 miles outside the 3D seismic
area. These relationships were used to tie the interpreted seismic horizons to depth and to convert
post-stack seismic inversion results from time to depth domain. Porosity and permeability values
were estimated by correlating acoustic impedance from the inversion volume with well log data
and core-derived empirical relationships. Specifically, porosity was estimated using a linear
relationship with P-impedance from Well A, and permeability was derived using a porosity-
permeability transform calibrated to core data.

 567

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Each grid cell was populated with porosity, horizontal permeability, and vertical permeability
values, with a horizontal-to-vertical permeability ratio of 17:1 based on core analysis. The
resulting static model was then exported to the dynamic simulator for fluid flow analysis.
This static model is based on a single well (Well A) located outside the seismic volume, and
Well B within the seismic survey does not reach the Lyons Formation. Therefore, key
petrophysical properties such as porosity and permeability rely on extrapolation from an analog
location. Additionally, the model is derived from post-stack seismic inversion, which has
inherent resolution and vertical smearing limitations. These factors introduce uncertainty into the
property distribution, particularly in the absence of local well control and core validation. The
current model should be viewed as a first-order approximation to support feasibility assessment.
Future site-specific characterization, including a stratigraphic test well, will be critical for model
refinement and validation.

  Fluid Flow Modeling
 Fluid Model Setup
CO2 injection modeling within the saline aquifers was conducted using the reservoir simulation
software Computer Modelling Group Generalized Equation-of-State Model (CMG-GEM;
https://www.cmgl.ca/solutions/software/gem/). The static model served as the input, with fluid-
related parameters incorporated to estimate the CO2 saturation distribution and pressure change
within the reservoir. A closed boundary condition was used to represent a conservative pressure
buildup scenario, given the absence of reliable data on lateral pressure communication.
The Lyons Formation, situated at a depth of approximately 7,000 ft (2,134 m), has an aquifer
thickness of 150 ft (46 m), with a temperature of 161 °F (71.1 °C) and a pressure of 1,800 psi
(12.4 MPa). This reservoir pressure was determined from drill stem test (DST) data using shut-in
pressure measurements. These reservoir conditions allow the injected CO2 to exist in a
supercritical state. According to US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) guidelines, the
injection pressure cannot exceed 90% of the fracture pressure of the injection zone (EPA 2008),
which places the maximum allowable injection pressure in the study area at 3,400 psi (23.4
MPa). The fracture gradient was calculated using poroelastic equations based on mechanical
rock properties derived from compressional and shear sonic logs, along with density log data.
Lyons formation is naturally underpressured (0.26 psi/ft pressure gradient), which offers a
substantial pressure buffer that enhances injectivity and allows for large-volume storage before
approaching geomechanical limits. The low formation pressure permits high CO2 injection rates
at relatively modest wellhead pressures, with reduced risk of exceeding fracture pressure or
compromising caprock integrity. Moreover, the presence of long-standing underpressure often
implies an effective, intact sealing unit that has prevented fluid equilibration over geologic time,
enhancing storage security (Neuzil 1995). Importantly, the low baseline stress state reduces the
likelihood of fault reactivation or induced seismicity during injection. Together, these
characteristics make naturally underpressured saline aquifers compelling targets for CO2
sequestration, though careful site-specific characterization is essential to quantify plume
behavior and long-term containment.

 568

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The simulation was conducted in two phases: a 30-yr injection period followed by a 70-yr shut-
in period. During the injection phase, two vertical wells were used, each injecting at a rate of 1.2
MtCO2 annually. The injectors were strategically placed at the northern and southern sites of the
study area to mitigate localized pressure buildup (Figure 368). As Layers 3-10 are the aquifer
layers, the perforations for both injectors are set at Layer 10 to model the upward migration of
the CO2 plume.

Figure 368 a) Top view of the study area, where warmer colors indicate higher porosity. The northern site exhibits
relatively higher porosity compared to the southern side. Two injection wells are positioned at the northern and
southern parts of the study area; b) a 3D view of the reservoir model with vertical exaggeration by a factor of 56; c)
a side view of the model, showing 15 vertical layers. There is no structural trapping in this study due to the low dip
angle of about 1%.
When CO2 is injected into a deep saline aquifer formation, four primary trapping mechanisms
are typically considered: structural trapping, mineral trapping, solubility trapping, and residual
trapping. In this study, the first two mechanisms are neglected because there is no structural trap
present in the study area (Figure 368), and the Lyons formation consists of over 95% quartz,
which does not react with CO2 under normal conditions. The latter two mechanisms, however,
are considered. Solubility trapping involves the dissolution of CO2 in water, forming aqueous
ions such as HCO3- and CO32-. Residual trapping occurs due to hysteresis; after CO2 injection
ceases, CO2 at the leading edge of the plume continues to displace water through a drainage
process, while water displaces CO2 in an imbibition process at the trailing edge. This imbibition
process leads to the trapping of CO2. To account for this, the study modifies the relative
permeability curves to simulate the hysteresis effect, resulting in the immobilization of a residual
CO2 trail behind the plume.

 CO2 Saturation Distribution
The CO2 saturation distribution across various layers at Year 30 and Year 100 of CO2 injection is
illustrated in Figure 369. CO2 is injected through Layer 10, and the lateral and upward migration

 569

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

of the CO2 plume can be observed. Notably, the plume sizes in the shallower layers (e.g., Layer
1) are larger compared to deeper layers (e.g., Figure 369a vs. Figure 369c). When comparing the
two injectors, Injector#1 exhibits a larger plume size in Layer 1 (4-mile diameter for Injector#1
vs. 2.5-mile diameter for Injector#2), whereas in Layer 10, Injector#2 shows a larger plume size
(1.8-mile diameter for Injector#2 vs. 1.5-mile diameter for Injector#1) (Figure 369a vs. Figure
369c). This difference is likely due to the higher porosity and permeability in the northern area
compared to the south, resulting in faster CO2 upward migration in the northern well, Injector#1.
Additionally, when comparing the CO2 plume size at Year 100 with that at Year 30, it is evident
that CO2 continues to migrate upward, resulting in a larger plume size and higher CO2 saturation
in the top layer over time (Figure 369a vs. Figure 369d). Note that the maximum simulated CO2
saturation is approximately 0.6, reflecting moderate injectivity and upward migration in a
formation with limited vertical permeability and conservative trapping assumptions, which could
result in broader lateral plume distribution, slower CO2 accumulation, and reduced localized
peak saturation.

Figure 369 CO2 saturation distribution across various layers at Year 30 and Year 100. Panels a through c represent
the CO2 saturation at Year 30 (end of injection), and panels d through f present the saturation at Year 100 (after a
70-yr shut-in). CO2 was injected through Layer 10, leading to significant lateral and upward migration. The color
scale represents CO2 saturation, with warm color indicating higher saturation levels. The observed plume geometry
reflects the influence of the closed boundary condition, which limits lateral migration and results in more confined
plume shapes.

 CO2 Component Inventory
In addition to estimating the CO2 plume, it is crucial to evaluate the distribution of injected CO2
among its various phases. The phase distribution of injected CO2 was modeled using the
compositional simulator CMG-GEM, which applies an equation-of-state (EOS) approach to
simulate multiphase fluid behavior. The simulator distinguishes between supercritical and

 570

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

dissolved CO2 based on local pressure and temperature conditions. Supercritical CO2 is tracked
as a separate phase, while solubility trapping is modeled through CO2 dissolution into brine.
Residual trapping is incorporated by applying hysteresis to the relative permeability curves,
allowing for the immobilization of CO2 following injection. The simulator outputs mass
distributions of each phase over time, enabling quantification of mobile, dissolved, and
immobilized CO2.
Figure 370a) illustrates the CO2 inventory over the 30-yr injection period, showing that
approximately 85% of the injected CO2 exists in a supercritical phase, while the remaining
portion is dissolved in water. Figure 370b) depicts the amount of immobile CO2 that becomes
trapped due to hysteresis, occurring only during the shut-in period. It reveals that 18 out of the 60
Mt of total injected CO2, or 30%, becomes immobile, while the remaining CO2 pools beneath a
low-dip seal. The low dip angle in this study area (as shown in Figure 368) may reduce the
effectiveness of structural trapping, making lateral plume migration more likely. While this does
not imply an immediate risk of leakage, it underscores the importance of incorporating
monitoring strategies and further geomechanical analysis to ensure long-term containment.

Figure 370 Distribution of injected CO2 among different phases over time. Panel a shows the CO 2 inventory during
the 30-yr injection period, with approximately 85% of the injected CO 2 existing in a supercritical phase and the
remaining CO2 dissolved in water; panel b illustrates the immobile CO2 trapped due to hysteresis during the shut-in
period, where around 18 Mt of the total injected CO2 becomes immobile. The low dip angle of the study area
suggests a potential for lateral CO2 migration, increasing the risk of plume containment.

 CO2 Pressure Distribution
Understanding pressure distribution during and after CO2 injection is critical for evaluating
reservoir integrity and containment performance. Given the closed-boundary condition used in
this study, pressure buildup is expected to be conservative, with limited lateral pressure
dissipation. Figure 371a) illustrates the simulated pressure distribution in Layer 3 at Year 30,
immediately after injection ends, while Figure 371b) shows the pressure evolution over a 100-yr
period at the grid cell corresponding to Injector #1. At the end of injection, the maximum
pressure at this location reaches approximately 21 MPa (3,046 psi), remaining about 10% below
the maximum allowable injection pressure of 3,400 psi. This peak pressure represents the
conservative behavior imposed by the closed system model, as pressure dissipation into
surrounding formations is not permitted. Following shut-in, reservoir pressure gradually declines

 571

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

due to equilibration within the system, stabilizing around 18.8 MPa (approximately 2,730 psi)
after 100 yr. This trend suggests that, despite the lack of pressure relief boundaries, long-term
containment within the Lyons Formation remains within acceptable limits under the modeled
scenario.

Figure 371 a) Pressure distribution in Layer 3 at Year 30, immediately after injection ends. b) Pressure changes over
100 yr near Injector #1. The maximum simulated pressure is approximately 21 MPa (3,046 psi), remaining
approximately 10% below the maximum allowable injection pressure of 3,400 psi.

  Risk Evaluation and Discussion
 Confining System Evaluation
The Lyons Formation is overlain by the Lykins Formation, which serves as the primary
confining system and is composed of alternating layers of anhydrite and shale (Young et al. 2007;
Herman 2024). These sealing units are observed both in outcrop and in subsurface datasets
across the basin and appear laterally continuous at the regional scale. In the study area, well log
data (Figure 366) confirm the presence of multiple overlying seal intervals characterized by very
low porosity, consistent with their role as effective vertical flow barriers.
The anhydrite beds, which dominate the seal, are associated with low gamma ray (GR), low
sonic (SON), near-zero porosity (POR), high density (RHOB), and high resistivity (RES)
responses—log signatures indicative of dense, non-permeable lithologies (Herman 2024). These
anhydrite units are interbedded with shale layers that also exhibit low porosity, further enhancing
the sealing effectiveness. The vertical thickness of the composite sealing interval is
approximately 100 ft, providing a significant barrier to vertical CO2 migration and contributing
to capillary entry pressure.
In addition to petrophysical characteristics, structural integrity of the seal was assessed using
variance attribute maps extracted from 3D seismic data (Figure 3, right panels). These maps
reveal no evidence of faulting within the upper or lower anhydrite intervals, indicating that the
confining system is structurally intact at seismic scale. Variance anomalies observed are

 572

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

interpreted as minor vertical heterogeneities, likely associated with depositional or diagenetic
features, rather than through-going faults or fractures.
Based on the combination of well log data, stratigraphic thickness, and seismic variance analysis,
the overburden above the Lyons Formation demonstrates the properties of an effective confining
system. Each layer appears laterally continuous and shows no indication of transmissive features
or structural discontinuities. Therefore, the risk of vertical leakage through the confining system
is considered low within the study area.

 Fault Confinement and Induced Seismicity Potential
Identifying faults in the study area is essential to evaluating both the potential for CO2 migration
through structural discontinuities and the risk of stress-induced fault reactivation. Seismic
variance analysis across the stratigraphic column, from the Niobrara Formation to the basement,
indicates that all identified seismic-scale faults are confined above the Dakota Formation (Figure
9). The Niobrara contains a well-developed system of décollement-style faults (Figure 9b), but
fault frequency decreases with depth. No faults were identified that offset the Lyons Formation
or its overlying confining units based on the resolution of the available seismic data.

Figure 372 a) 3D view of faults in the 3D seismic survey. Horizon tops are labeled and color-coded. No faulting is
observed between the top of the Dakota and the basement, except for the one fault (green-colored) in the basement
shown in the bottom right; b-d) The variance map of various layers indicates that the fault system intersects with
shallower formations, such as the Niobrara and Codell, while deeper formations show no evidence of faulting.
While no faults intersect the injection interval, the potential for pressure-induced fault activation
must still be considered. While this indicates that fault activation or new fracturing is unlikely
under the modeled conditions, it does not rule out the possibility that elevated pore pressures
could reactivate undetected or basement-rooted faults under specific geological or operational
scenarios. Notably, a sequence of induced seismic events associated with fluid injection into the
Lyons Formation was reported in the northern DJ Basin (GWPC 2015), highlighting the need for
site-specific stress evaluation. In contrast, our study area is located in the southern DJ Basin in
the El Paso County, where the Precambrian basement lies at approximately 13,000 ft (4,000 m)
depth. With the Lyons Formation situated at around 7,000 feet, this results in a vertical

 573

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

separation of about 6,000 ft from the basement—providing a substantial buffer from basement-
rooted faults. Nevertheless, ongoing monitoring and further geomechanical analysis, including
data from a planned stratigraphic well, will be critical to fully assess the potential for fault
activation under site-specific conditions.

 Legacy Wells Leakage Risk
The primary risks associated with legacy wells arise from their potential to act as conduits for
CO2 migration out of the injection zone—either into underground sources of drinking water
(USDWs), such as the Fox Hills and Arapahoe formations (approximately 600 ft or 183 m
depth), or ultimately to the surface. These risks are not confined to wells within the immediate
CO2 plume, but may extend across the entire area of review (AoR), where elevated reservoir
pressure can mobilize fluids along compromised wellbores.
The DJ Basin contains thousands of legacy oil and gas wells, many of which were drilled
decades ago under less stringent standards. While most of these wells do not penetrate the Lyons
Formation in the immediate study area, their presence at the regional scale must be considered in
long-term storage risk assessments. Within the 3D seismic survey boundary, no legacy wells are
known to intersect the Lyons Formation, based on a thorough review of public well data.
Consequently, leakage risk from legacy wells is considered low within the modeled domain, but
may require further evaluation when defining the regulatory AoR.
Additionally, the static model was constructed with limited well control in the Lyons
Formation—only one well (Well A) penetrates the formation and lies approximately 30 miles
(48.3 km) outside the seismic volume. This limitation contributes to uncertainty in both
structural interpretation and petrophysical calibration, and it reinforces the need for further site
characterization, including a stratigraphic test well.
The primary well-related risks in this study are therefore associated with new injection and
monitoring wells, which will be designed and constructed in accordance with Class VI
requirements. These standards—enforced during the permitting process—mandate best practices
in well siting, casing, cementing, and long-term monitoring, thereby significantly reducing the
potential for CO2 leakage through engineered wellbores.

 Seismic Monitoring Feasibility
With the construction of a static and dynamic model, rock physics relationships can be used to
estimate if a time-lapse seismic monitoring signal can be detected for this study. For this
purpose, fluid changes on P- and S-impedance are calculated using Gassmann fluid substitution
for sandstone using water and CO2 fluid properties, temperature and pore pressure to calculate
saturated bulk modulus and density. Stress changes on bulk and shear modulus are calculated
using pressure sensitivity from dry core testing on Lyons sandstone. Rock physics properties of
the Lyons sandstone, fluid properties at reservoir temperature and pore pressure of the water and
CO2, and stress changes with changes in pore pressure are used to calculate changes in saturated
bulk modulus, shear modulus and density and used to calculate changes P- and S-impedance at
each grid point of the dynamic model. Figure 10 shows these changes from pre-injection baseline
(all water) to after 30 yr of CO2 injection. The modeling shows that up to a 4% change in P-
impedance can be expected. It would be important to compare this to the expected time-lapse
noise level from seismic data acquisition to understand if monitoring will be successful. The
 574

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

change in P- or S-impedance with stress is observed to be very small or undetectable, based on
core measurements from Well A located approximately 30 miles from the study area, assuming
those measurements are representative of in-situ conditions in the modeled location.

Figure 373 Precent change in P-impedance vs S-impedance from pre-injection to 30 yr of injection. A maximum of
4% change in P-impedance can be expected where CO2 has replaced water. This reservoir is not seen to be very
sensitive to stress changes provided the core measurements are representative of the field. This analysis supports
feasibility for 4D seismic monitoring primarily driven by saturation effects.
The time-lapse impedance changes can be computed field wide, convolved with the wavelet
estimated for the reservoir from seismic field data, and converted to industry standard seismic
amplitude-versus-offset (AVO) products of intercept (I) and gradient (G). Here the time-lapse
intercept and gradient AVO parameters after 30 yr of injection were calculated, as shown in
Figure 11. CO2 saturated zones are clearly seen as decreases in both intercept and gradient. The
center of each plume, where there is higher CO2 saturation and the plume is thicker,
demonstrates a greater decrease in I and G. Nearing the edge of the plume, change in I and G
drops until reaching zero. Outside the plume, there is a small positive difference caused by a
small increase in bulk modulus and density, and subsequently P-impedance in the pore fluid
from increased pore pressure. In the center of each plume there is a zone where this trend is not
observed, and there is less change in I and G. Located at the injection points, these correspond to

 575

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

the highest saturation of CO2 in the plume and the highest pore pressure and is more apparent in
the change in G.

Figure 374 Cross-sectional view of time-lapse seismic attribute response after 30 yr of CO2 injection. The top panel
shows changes in intercept (ΔI), and the bottom panel shows changes in gradient (ΔG). These amplitude-versus-
offset (AVO) attributes reflect changes in acoustic properties due to CO 2 saturation. The maximum decreases in ΔI
and ΔG correspond to the plume tops, indicating potential detectability with properly designed 4D surface seismic
monitoring. Inset map shows the seismic line orientation used for cross-section extraction.
Next, the seismic repeatability requirement was analyzed utilizing normalized root mean square
(NRMS) measure between the baseline and monitor surveys to understand the time-lapse seismic
signal level (Calvert 2005). NRMS is calculated for the base and 30-yr monitor and for the base
and 100-yr monitor. The NRMS cross sections of these synthetic modeled plumes can be seen in
Figure 12. In the reservoir region we observe an average NRMS value of 15%. Based on
published NRMS data from various fields (Calvert 2005), a maximum range of 16.4 ft (5 m) to
32.8 ft (10 m) position difference between shot and receiver locations for baseline and monitor
data will be required to observe the reservoir time-lapse signal. On land, the repeatability
between the baseline and monitor survey may need to be even better or less than 16.4 ft (5 m).

 576

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 375 Normalized root mean square (NRMS) calculated between the base and 30-yr monitor (top). NRMS
calculated between the base and 100-yr monitor (bottom). NRMS is used to quantify the repeatability of seismic
surveys and the detectability of CO2 plume signals. Values in the reservoir interval average around 15%, with
localized zones exceeding 20% to 30%, suggesting that time-lapse signal detectability is achievable with acquisition
repeatability better than 16.4 ft (5 m), as recommended in published 4D seismic monitoring studies.

 Conclusions and Future Work
This study evaluates the feasibility of commercial-scale CO2 sequestration in the Lyons saline
aquifer in El Paso County, southern Colorado, using geological modeling, reservoir simulation,
and containment risk assessment. Based on the current dataset, the following conclusions can be
drawn:
• Storage feasibility: Simulation results indicate that approximately 60 MtCO2 can be injected
 over 30 yr using two vertical wells. During injection, 85% of the CO2 remains in a
 supercritical state, and after a 70-yr shut-in period, about 30% becomes immobilized via
 residual trapping. These findings support the technical viability of long-term storage in this
 formation under modeled conditions.
• Reservoir suitability: The Lyons Formation exhibits favorable reservoir depth, porosity,
 permeability, and multiple overlying confining units, making it a promising target for CO2
 injection in the study area.
• Containment assessment: Within the study area, containment risk is considered low,
 supported by the absence of seismically visible faults intersecting the injection zone and the
 lack of legacy wells penetrating the Lyons Formation. However, this conclusion is specific to
 the modeled area and should not be generalized to the broader region.
• Plume containment risk: The primary site-specific risk is the low structural dip of the
 formation, which limits structural trapping and may enhance lateral plume migration. For
 improved containment, anticlinal or low-dip regions may be more favorable.
• Monitoring feasibility: The detectability of CO2 plume development using surface seismic
 methods presents a challenge, given the relatively small changes in impedance. This

 577

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 monitoring risk may be mitigated through the use of high-repeatability seismic acquisition
 (<5 m offset) and deployment of 3D vertical seismic profile (VSP) systems. This has direct
 implications for monitoring design and regulatory compliance under Class VI standards.
While the current results demonstrate the potential suitability of the Lyons Formation, they are
based on limited site data. To reduce uncertainty and advance toward project deployment, the
following actions are recommended:
• Site characterization: Drill a stratigraphic test well to collect well logs, core data, fluid
 properties, and pressure measurements to improve understanding of reservoir and caprock
 behavior.
• Model refinement: Use newly acquired data to refine static and dynamic models, verify
 assumptions related to permeability, stress distribution, and seal integrity, and improve
 confidence in plume evolution and pressure buildup predictions.
• Boundary condition validation: Incorporate more realistic regional boundary conditions
 based on pressure communication data to evaluate regional flow behavior, plume migration,
 AoR definition, and containment risks under more representative field conditions.
• Monitoring strategy development: Conduct detailed monitoring feasibility analysis to define
 appropriate acquisition geometries, frequency, and resolution requirements for surface and
 borehole seismic data—ensuring regulatory alignment and early detection capability.
These steps will strengthen the technical basis for a Class VI permit application, support risk-
based project design, and inform best practices for safe and effective CO2 storage in
underexplored areas of southern Colorado.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Targa Resources (Formerly Lucid Energy Delaware)
Acid Gas Injection Project
In 2022, the New Mexico Tech Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP) team
partnered with Lucid Energy (Dallas, TX) to permit an acid gas injection (AGI) well for their
Red Hills site in New Mexico. The effort was partially funded by the CUSP project. The goal of
the project was to identify a subsurface geological formation to inject acid gas (CO2 and H2S),
captured during sour natural gas treatment. The acid gas is compressed and injected in the
formation.
The CUSP team prepared a “Permit to Inject” application (C-108). Preparation of the permit
application involved building a geological model, well log analysis, and geophysical
interpretation. Members of the team attended the New Mexico Oil Conservation Division
(NMOCD) hearing as expert witnesses. Lucid Energy was granted the permit. The well was
drilled and completed according to the plan.
The CUSP team supported Lucid Energy’s engineers and drillers in developing (1) core
collection and analysis programs, (2) a well logging program, and (3) a well design.
Based on the successful completion of the focused project, Targa Resources (Houston, TX)
awarded New Mexico Tech’s Petroleum Recovery Center (PRRC) several permitting projects as
well as several monitoring, reporting, and verification projects.

Carbon Solutions’ Contributions to Focused Projects
Carbon Solutions (Saint Paul, MN) provided support across five different Carbon Utilization and
Storage Partnership (CUSP) focused projects by providing detailed information on transport,
capture, and storage in support of carbon capture and storage (CCS) infrastructure assessment.
This was done by applying the SimCCSPRO toolset (Carbon Solutions 2025d) to meet project
specific needs. Carbon Solutions support the Subtask 4.5 deliverable Report: Focused Scenario
Analysis results on Candidate Sites in the CUSP Region submitted in 2024.
The following section summarizes Carbon Solutions efforts for each focused project.

 Subtask 4.5.2 – Regional-Scale Assessment of CO2
 Geological Storage in Sedimentary Basin Geothermal
 Reservoirs of Nevada
Carbon Solutions provided a preliminary assessment of subsurface sedimentary geothermal
potential in support of the Nevada focused project. The 10 km SCO2TPRO (Carbon Solutions
2025c) geospatial dataset was integrated with geothermal data to identify areas favorable for
deep sedimentary basin CO2 plume geothermal (CPG) geologic storage for northern Nevada. A
sedimentary geothermal potential was developed based on combining the following variables:
• Sedimentary valley fill thickness
• Geothermal temperature gradient
• Fault activity or no-fault activity

 581

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

See Figure 376 for a map of the areas identified.

Figure 376 Regional-scale sedimentary basin geothermal reservoirs in northern Nevada
Through this work it was identified that the Black Rock sedimentary basin had the highest
sedimentary geothermal potential of all evaluated basins. Furthermore, the Black Rock
sedimentary basin is the largest of the basins evaluated with an area of 912 km2. This work is
based on the assumption that all the properties of the saline formations, identified from well logs,
are vertically and laterally continuous throughout the Black Rock sedimentary basin. A detailed
view of the geothermal potential for the Black Rock sedimentary basin can be seen in Figure
377.

 582

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 377 Sedimentary geothermal potential rating for the Black Rock sedimentary basin
The aggregated data, in conjunction with temperature gradient data, was then run through the
SCO2TPRO tool to generate estimated greenfield levelized costs of electricity (LCOEs) for CPG
development. LCOE values were calculated using the following assumptions: a 95% power plant
capacity factor, A capital recovery factor of 5.2%, and annual operation and maintenance (O&M)
costs of 5.5% of specific capital costs. The objective was to identify the lowest-cost power
generation sectors of the Black Rock sedimentary basin. This analysis highlighted that large parts
of the basin have the potential for low-cost CPG power generation with most of the basin having
estimated LCOEs of less than $90/MWh.

To begin with, Carbon Solutions identified all sources of CO2 around the proposed project field

Carbon Solutions also ran four forward looking scenarios to evaluate hub or distributed storage
as a foundation for future CCS networks in California. Ultimately, these scenarios indicated that
regardless of what sources are being used, CCS networks that use distributed storage are always
less expensive than the corresponding CCS networks that use hub storage. For example, when
capturing CO2 from all sources in California, the distributed storage CCS network has a total cost
of $102/tCO2 while the hub storage CCS network has a total cost of $109/tCO2. There are
notable differences in amounts of pipeline deployed with hub storage adding almost 1,800 km of
additional CO2 pipeline deployment (see Table 4 on page 27).

  Subtask 4.5.4 – From Site to State: Design of an Integrated
  CCUS Operation in a Complex Geological Structure in
  Osage County, Oklahoma
Carbon Solutions supported the Oklahoma focused project by applying its SimCCSPRO toolset to
evaluate a carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) roadmap for Oklahoma that features
stacked storage. Data on subsurface geology was provided at a county-level resolution using
open-hole logs analyzed at Oklahoma University. Carbon Solutions applied its CO2NCORD tool
to determine capturable emissions and capture costs from facilities in Oklahoma.
Through collaboration with project partners, Carbon Solutions ran 32 distinct scenarios,
separated into two distinct sets. The first set of scenarios (16) featured CO2 storage in any county
with geologic CO2 storage resources, while the second set of scenarios (16) featured CO2 storage
in any county with geologic CO2 storage resources and existing CO2-enhanced oil recovery
(CO2-EOR) operations. The second set of scenarios simulates the conditions for stacked storage
without directly modeling the unique subsurface geology. Figure 387 shows the estimated
storage cost for each county and those counties with existing CO2-EOR projects.

Figure 387 Estimated geologic CO2 storage costs ($/tCO2) for high and low reservoir parameters in the Arbuckle
and Simpson formation. Counties with existing CO2-enhanced oil recovery (CO2-EOR) operations are indicated by
the black triangles. Source: Miranda et al. (2023).

 592

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Once all input data had been collected all 32 scenarios were run using SimCCSPRO. Results
indicate that counties with existing CO2-EOR operations do not coincide with the lowest storage
cost. Further, total CCUS network costs are higher when limiting storage to only those counties
with geologic CO2 storage and existing CO2-EOR operations. This could be explained by
increase in pipeline transports costs, as more pipelines are needed to connect sources to counties
that simulate the conditions for stacked storage. In meeting task objectives, Carbon Solutions
identified those counties most deployed across all 32 scenarios, indicating those counties that
might serve as starting points for CCUS networks in Oklahoma based on stacked storage (Figure
387). An outcome of Carbon Solutions work on the Oklahoma focused project is the publication
Miranda et al. (2023).

  Subtask 4.5.5 – Iron Mountain Subsurface Characterization
Carbon Solutions provided support for this focused project specifically for Subtask 5.2 Transport
and Rights-of-Way. During the first quarter of the focused project, Carbon Solutions took the
project area of interest (AOI) and applied its CostMAPPRO tool (Carbon Solutions 2025b) to
generate a cost surface for estimating costs associated with pipeline routing (Figure 388).

Figure 388 CO2 pipeline cost surface generated by CostMAPPRO for the project area of interest
During subsequent quarters the Carbon Solutions team investigated ways to integrate known
Utah Iron (Iron County, UT) rights-of-way into the cost surface. The first method was to add the
existing rights-of-way to the existing cost surface while maintaining default weighting values.
The second method was to lower the weighting values for the existing rights-of-way to “bias” the
cost surface into prioritizing the existing infrastructure whenever possible. Both options were
made available for future CCS infrastructure assessments when using SimCCSPRO.
This methodology was followed for additional cost surfaces that were generated to consider an
alternate injection site. This alternate cost surface was used in SimCCSPRO to generate pipeline
routes (Figure 389).

Part III – State-by-State Summaries
Arizona
Since 2008, the Arizona Geological Survey (AZGS) has participated in Carbon Capture,
Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) research funded by the US Department of Energy (DOE). These
projects include the Southwest Regional Partnership on Carbon Sequestration (SECARB), the
West Coast Regional Carbon Sequestration Partnership (WESTCARB), and the Rocky Mountain
Carbon Capture and Storage (RMCCS) project. In 2020, AZGS was awarded funding to continue
this research as part of the Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP) West, a 4-yr-long
DOE grant led by the Petroleum Recovery Research Center at the New Mexico Institute of
Mining and Technology (PRRC-NMT). CUSP West is a 13-state and 3-national-lab coalition of
academic and institutional partners whose purpose is to advance existing carbon capture,
utilization, and storage research and development.
As part of CUSP West, AZGS conducted a statewide sedimentary basin data review and data
analyses to locate, catalogue, analyze, and rank subsurface geologic resources that can be used
for long-term carbon sequestration and utilization. The scope of work required data collection,
analysis, and inter-agency/state coordination in five tasks: (1) increase resolution of CCUS
resource potential for all sedimentary basins (updated from Spencer [2011]), (2) catalogue CO2
emissions point-source data, (3) map existing infrastructure pipeline rights-of-way (ROWs), (4)
data assessment and synthesis of sedimentary basins, and (5) technology/data transfer and
dissemination. Participation in multiple CUSP working groups with state partners was extremely
helpful in sharing information, strategies, and much more towards meeting CUSP’s objectives,
milestones, and deliverables. Importantly, CUSP work fostered partnerships with industry
stakeholders, including major power companies, carbon storage facility operators, and Arizona’s
major power and water utilities.
Four deliverables were produced: (1) a statewide map of the sedimentary basins ranked based on
their potential to store CO2 (Figure 390); (2) subsurface data tables shared with the CUSP group
for input into SCO2TPRO (Sequestration of CO2 Tool; Carbon Solutions 2025) and a regional
CUSP database and the DOE’s Energy Data eXchange (EDX) deliverable (Figure 390); (3) an
outreach tool in the form of a web-based ArcGIS Story Map (AZGS 2022) about CCUS,
highlighting basin architecture of sedimentary basins with increased storage potential; and (4) a
publicly available Arizona Subsurface Viewer web map (AZGS 2025) of the subsurface storage
resources in Arizona for outreach and knowledge transfer.

CUSP West had several positive impacts on Arizona’s outlook for CCUS and related synergies.
During CUSP, Arizona received Underground Injection Control (UIC) primacy and is pursuing
regulatory pore space legislation. NMT and AZGS engaged with industry and utilities in south-
central Arizona that resulted in a separately funded focused evaluation of the Harquahala Basin
(Wilson et al. 2024). Results of this feasibility study led to a successful $9M DOE CarbonSAFE
II award. Also, during CUSP, AZGS was awarded funding to lead a $1M DOE project to
characterize mafic rock resources for CO2 mineralization from Direct Air Capture of CO2, in
partnership with Northern Arizona University and Arizona State University. CUSP also led to
two additional projects: CUSP Four Corners Regional Initiative (led by NMT), and the
Southwest Regional Direct Air Capture Hub (led by Arizona State University), both of which
AZGS is a subrecipient. The CUSP West Initiative put Arizona in a stronger position to leverage
its subsurface resources for CCUS and synergistic energy-related efforts. Beyond CUSP, AZGS
will continue to pursue collection of new data and development of new subsurface storage
(CCUS and other gases) and energy-resilient opportunities such as geothermal through the state
government and its stakeholders to attract industry and workforce to the state.

California
As state’s effort, we examined and investigated CO2 storage potential, CO2 emission sources,
capture costs, potential right-of-way for CO2 pipelines in California. The results demonstrate that
California has sufficient geological capacity to store hundreds of years for industrial emissions at
a current trend.
The statewide assessment, however, did not include comprehensive techno-economic analysis.
Instead, such analyses were performed for selected Focused Project regions. Our study, titled
Laying the Cornerstones of a Regional Storage Hub in California, serves as one of these Focused
Projects. Detailed methodologies and case-specific results are provided in the “Distributed
Emitters” section of the Focused Project report.
Additionally, we used the NRAP-Open-IAM tool (Vasylkivska et al. 2021) to assess the leakage
risk through the existing wellbores and Quaternary faults within the potential CO2 storage site in
our Focused Project in Kern County. The corresponding methods and case-specific results for
leakage assessment are found in ‘Risk assessment’ section of the Focused Project report.

  Subtask 3.1.2 – Update Geologic Data for Carbon Capture,
  Utilization, and Storage (CCUS) Assessment
 California CO2 Storage Estimates and Potential Storage Sites
 Screening Methodology for CO2 Storage Sites
Previous studies of CO2 storage resource in California examined oil and gas fields as well as
saline formations (Downey and Clinkenbeard 2011; USGS 2013; NETL 2015a, 2015b; Long et
al. 2018; Teletzke et al. 2018; Baker et al. 2020). The mean CO2 saline formation storage
estimates from USGS (2013) and the National Carbon Sequestration Database and Geographic
Information System (NATCARB; NETL 2015a) are 90.5 GtCO2 and 147.6 GtCO2, respectively.
In addition, a recent study that re-examined saline formations suggested the mean storage
resource is at least 69.1 GtCO2 in California (EFI and Stanford 2020). Baker et al. (2020)
evaluated selected saline formations and hydrocarbon fields for geological carbon storage in the
Sacramento and southern San Joaquin basins. The estimated CO2 storage resources for only 4
formations in the southern San Joaquin basin ranged from 14.1 to 56.4 GtCO2. Therefore, we
examined both hydrocarbon reservoirs and saline formations were considered as CO2 storage
sites. We used a three-stage procedure to screen potential CO2 storage site.
In the first stage, geological properties were applied to select qualified sites from the result of
previous studies. Table 81 shows the qualifying thresholds based on geological properties. A
detailed description and discussion of storage optimization parameters is given elsewhere (Kim
et al. 2022). Parameters except reservoir thickness are identical to the previous study. Here, the
minimum reservoir thickness, 10 m, is taken as identical to (Ramirez et al. 2010). Previously, we
used a minimum reservoir thickness of 3 m. As risk minimization parameters, both salinity and
 599

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

top seal thickness were only applied to saline formations. The top seal thickness of hydrocarbon
formations was not found in public databases; however, a hydrocarbon accumulation indicates
the presence of a seal, in most cases. The water in hydrocarbon reservoirs is typically not suitable
for drinking or for agricultural purposes without significant treatment; hence, all water in oil
reservoirs is assumed to be unsuitable for these purposes. Additionally, offshore sites were
eliminated because they are not eligible for the low-carbon fuel standard (LCFS) credit.
 Table 81 Qualifying thresholds for storage sites in this study. Modified from Callas
 et al. (2022) and Kim et al. (2022).
 Category Geological parameter Qualifying threshold
 Storage Storage resource (high estimate) > 3 MtCO2 (OG field)
 optimization Depth (to top of formation) > 800 m
 Permeability > 10 mD (mean)
 Porosity > 10% (mean)
 Reservoir Thickness Target one layer, > 10 m
 Risk Secondary confining Exist secondary confining unit
 minimization Salinity > 10,000 ppm (TDS): Saline formation only
 Top seal thickness > 25 m: Saline formation only
 Others Offshore location Consider only onshore location
In the second stage, the exclusion zones were developed using four different categories as
detailed in Table 82 (Kim et al. 2022). Risk categories include quaternary faults and seismically
active regions. Risk categories include Quaternary faults and seismically active regions. A 2 km-
wide buffer zone was applied to each side (total 4 km width) of Quaternary faults. Due to the use
of publicly available data, there are, potentially, undetected faults and an incomplete seismicity
catalogue. Site specific risk assessment is also needed (Kim et al. 2023). Seismicity buffer zones
were assigned depending on the magnitude (M) of historical earthquakes. A 10 km diameter
buffer was used for magnitude greater than 5 whereas a 5 km diameter buffer zone was used for
magnitude less than 5. Active hydrocarbon fields consider exclusion zones as well. These fields
are assumed to be mainly used for CO2-enhanced oil recovery (EOR). Both non-active
hydrocarbon fields and saline formations considered all categories including risk, population
density, restricted lands, and sensitive zone/habitats as total exclusion zones.

In the third stage, the exclusion zones were subtracted from the identified hydrocarbon fields or
saline formations from the first stage to obtain available storage sites. The fraction of available
storage area of each original site (first stage) was multiplied by the CO2 storage resource
estimate from previous studies. In this way, new CO2 storage resource estimates were computed.
These potential CO2 storage sites were prioritized with a scoring system.

 Potential CO2 Storage Estimates
Initially, we conducted the state-level CO2 storage estimate for hydrocarbon field and saline
formation with a 3-stage procedure. As a result, 61 potential oil & gas fields were selected with
an estimated storage resource of 1.0 to 2.0 GtCO2. These sites include 21 CO2-EOR sites, mainly
located in the southern San Joaquin, southern Sacramento, and Ventura Basins (Kim et al. 2022).
This storage resource of 61 potential sites is sufficient for 26 to 50 yr of storage with an injection
rate of 42.5 MtCO /year. This storage rate amounts to 10% of California GHG emissions
 2

averaged over 2018 and 2019.
Saline formations showed greater total storage potential than oil & gas fields as we expected. We
analyzed the state-wide geological datasets for the storage site on 50 km by 50 km grid cells. The
original assigned number of grid cells (50 km by 50 km) in California was 193. The number of
focus grid cells in the potential CO2 storage formations decreased to 48 grid cells. We collected
data on storage formations including depth, pressure, storage thickness, permeability, porosity,
temperature, temperature gradient, and storage estimated capacity (P10, P50, P90). The
estimated storage capacity ranged from 52 GtCO2 to 168 GtCO2 before considering the exclusion
criteria (in stage 1). After considering the exclusion criteria (stage 2), the final optimal estimate
storage capacity in stage 3 ranged from 34 GtCO2 to 104 GtCO2 in California in Figure 391. In
addition, we provided the potential 100 storage sites including EOR, depleted, stacked, and
saline formations, total mean capacity around 37 GtCO2.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 391 Available CO2 storage formation in California using a 3-stage procedure
The southern San Joaquin Basin, which hosts the Focused Project’s primary region, was
examined in detail to evaluate its potential for CO2 storage using a 3-stage procedure (Kim et al.
2023). Conservative risk exclusion zones were employed to increase the security of potential
CO2 storage in geological formations. The exclusion zones consist of risk category (Quaternary
fault and seismic activity), population density, restricted lands, and sensitive ecological habitats.
Even with a significantly conservative approach, the resulting estimated storage resources for
hydrocarbon fields and saline formations were 0.45 - 1.15 GtCO2 and 16.6 – 52.0 (mean 34.3)
GtCO2, respectively. These resources were then scored and storage sites with high/medium
priority scores and greater than 20 MtCO2 storage resource were defined as the target sites for
technoeconomic analysis. All fields passing through screening with exclusion zones have
desirable qualities for storage. In this way, 7 hydrocarbon fields were selected. Among them, 5
fields were CO2-EOR candidates and 2 fields were depleted oil fields only for storage. Also, a
total of 34 saline formations including 2 stacked formations were selected. The 41 storage sites
chosen totaled 5.8 GtCO2 of storage resource (see Figure 392).

  Subtask 3.1.4 – Gather and Catalogue CO2 Emissions
 California CO2 Emission Sources
The California Air Resources Board (CARB) reports annual emissions from greenhouse gas
(GHG) generating activities statewide in 2018 of 425.3 Mt of CO2 equivalent (MtCO2e; CARB
2020). This amount is similar to 2017 levels and is 6 MtCO2e below the 2020 GHG target limit
of 431 MtCO2e for California (CARB 2019, 2020). Among GHG emissions, CO2 makes up
about 81% of the total in the United States (EPA 2020a). California GHG emissions were around
6.4% of the United States total of 6,677 MtCO2e in 2018 (EPA 2020a). California contributes
about 1% of global emissions. Figure 393 shows the distribution of all GHG emissions in
California by economic sector including transportation, industrial, electricity, commercial, and so
on in 2018 expressed as CO2 equivalent to account for the differing global warming potentials
among GHG (CARB 2020).

Industrial and electricity sector GHG emissions tend to occur from relatively large point sources.
Hence, we focus on these two sectors that account for 39% or 166 MtCO2e/year of emissions.
Solutions to reduce emissions or capture emissions from these sources are important to meeting
California’s climate goals in a timely and cost-effective manner (EFI and Stanford 2020).
