  CO2 Capture Costs by Industrial Sector in California
We examined and adopted CO2 capture costs for six different industries and power sectors in
Table 81 (EFI and Stanford 2020). This data can be used to assess technoeconomic analysis for
CO2 storage projects for large-scale emission sources. Table 84 shows average and range of CO2
capture costs by different sectors (EFI and Stanford 2020). The CO2 capture cost varies
significantly depending on the purity of the emission stream, composition of the flue gas, and
energy intensity of the capture process. Higher CO2 concentrations significantly reduce capture
cost. For example, ethanol fermentation streams are nearly pure CO2 (approximately 100%),
requiring minimal separation effort, while natural-gas-fired power plants (NGCC) and CHP units
have dilute CO2 streams (7–10%), which demand larger absorber columns, higher solvent
circulation rates, and more regeneration energy.

Additionally, we conservatively estimated the capture costs for EOR facilities—specifically

those for SG systems ranged from $57.6 to $74.5/tCO2, depending on the operating conditions at
each site. Detailed methodologies and site-specific results are presented in ‘Distributed emitters’
section of the Focused Project report.

Nevada
A preliminary and regional assessment of the potential for CO2 storage within a variety of
geological settings was previously performed for the State of Nevada (Price et al. 2005). This
assessment, however, was performed without oil and gas well log information. An assessment of
using enhanced oil recovery (EOR) for CO2 geological storage at existing oil fields in Nevada
was also performed that used site-specific oil and well gas well logs to evaluate the favorability
of EOR in the state (LaPointe et al. 2007). Saline formations were previously assessed as having
the best potential for CO2 geological storage in Nevada compared to other capacities, such as
EOR and chemical reactions with mafic and ultramafic rocks (Price et al. 2005; LaPointe et al.
2007; Sturmer et al. 2007).
The role of the Nevada Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP) West project was to
leverage previous assessments of CO2 geological storage in the state, as well as perform a more
detailed assessment of CO2 geological storage in saline formations using oil and gas well log
information. The Desert Research Institute (DRI; Reno, NV) participated in CUSP West

 610

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

activities and was led by Steven Bacon, PhD, P.G., C.E.G. The DRI team members also included
Jay Arnone, PhD, Richard Jasoni, PhD, Rish Parashar, PhD, and Jessica Larsen. Included in this
report are details of state-level accomplishments for the State of Nevada that are directly related
to specific subtasks related to Tasks 2 and 3 of the CUSP West project.

 Task 2 – Addressing Key Technical Challenges
 Task 2.1 – Expand Characterization of Stacked and Unconventional
 Storage
Nevada CUSP West activities included the identification of five deep sedimentary basins with
stacked saline formations in northern Nevada that have the potential to be sites for CO2
geological storage based on the evaluation of oil and gas well log data. Additional activities
included the completion of a focused project to assess the potential of using CO2 geological
storage in sedimentary basin geothermal reservoirs (see Part II Focused Project section and
report in Appendix).

 Task 2.2 – Develop Collaborations to Integrate and Validate Key
 Technologies to Optimize Storage and Reduce Uncertainty in
 Storage Permanence and Integrity
The DRI team developed new collaborations through the focused project. The focused project
team included collaboration between Steven Bacon (PI) and Rishi Parashar of DRI and Jonathan
Ogland-Hand (Co-PI), Jeff Bennett, and Richard Middleton of Carbon Solutions (Saint Paul,
MN).

 Task 3 – Facilitating Data Collection, Sharing, and Analysis
 Task 3.1 – Engaging with National Laboratories
The DRI team had several email discussions at the beginning of the project with Lianjie Huang
of Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL) regarding potential collaborations with his group
and operators at the Patua Geothermal Power Plant in Fernley, NV, where they are evaluating the
use of CO2 as a fracking fluid to enhance heat generation and transfer. Possible joint work was
internally discussed with the DRI team to include developing a near-surface CO2 monitoring
network near the injection well site to potentially measure CO2 leakage. The overall goals of this
specific research effort would be to better understand the spatiotemporal patterns of leaked CO2
during injection and post injection, that in turn, could be used provide insight on how geothermal
systems potentially store CO2. Ultimately, this effort would be performed in anticipation for
when supercritical CO2 is used as a geothermal working fluid for geological storage in the future
(e.g., focused project). Furthermore, the research effort would also provide information to
evaluate if this type of CO2 monitoring approach is feasible in quantifying CO2 leakage across all
carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) technologies.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 Task 3.1.1 – Identify Data Requirements & Needs
Deep well-log data in Nevada are limited given the relatively low potential for oil and gas
resources in the state (e.g., Price et al. 2005). Early exploration of oil and gas resources across
Nevada and continued development of a few small oil fields in the eastern part of the state have
resulted in up to 1,125 well logs in the Nevada Bureau of Mines and Geology oil and gas well
information database. The DRI team initially screened 300 well logs from the database based on
the criteria of well logs having depths greater than 800 m (Figure 395). A subset of 30 well logs
was further screened for further evaluation based on well sites located outside the regionally
extensive and deep fresh-groundwater aquifer system of eastern-southeastern Nevada that is an
important resource for native habitats and water supply in the southern parts of the state
(Sweetkind et al. 2011; Figure 395).

Figure 395 Map showing the location of oil and gas wells deeper than 800 m and the extent of the regional, deep
fresh-groundwater aquifer in Nevada (e.g., Price et al. 2005; Sweetkind et al. 2011). The location of well logs
evaluated and analyzed by Desert Research Institute (DRI) outside of the deep fresh-groundwater aquifer, along
with the network of existing natural gas pipelines are also shown.

 612

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Lithologic and geophysical logs from the 30 well sites were evaluated to identify data
deficiencies. Of the 30 well logs, only nine logs contained the minimum required data to assess
the potential for stacked saline formations at each well site based on the CUSP screening
parameters for the SCO2T (Sequestration of CO2 Tool; Middleton et al. 2020) database. The
required data in our analysis included a lithologic log, bottom-hole temperature, and geophysical
wire logs of gamma ray, long-normal resistivity, and neutron porosity.

 Task 3.1.2 – Update Geologic Data for CCUS Assessment
Saline formations were targeted for CO2 geologic storage in north-northwestern Nevada. Nine
well sites were evaluated based on meeting screening criteria and minimum requirements of oil
and gas well logs for the SCO2T database (Figure 395). Geophysical wire logs from the nine
wells were digitized using Neuralog Pro software (https://www.neuralog.com) before analysis.
Gamma ray data were used to verify general grain size in combination with lithologic logs to
characterize rock type. Salinity and intrinsic permeability of formations were estimated from
resistivity and neutron porosity wire logs, along with temperature gradient based on a variety of
analytical solutions and methods commonly used to estimate the quality of groundwater and
permeability of aquifers (e.g., Jorgensen 1989; Hudson 1996; USBR 2019). Analytical solutions
were derived and resulting analyses were performed using MATLAB
(https://www.mathworks.com/products/matlab.html) programming language (see Nevada
Appendix).
The analysis of the nine well logs yielded five candidate well sites that have the hydrogeologic
properties favorable for CO2 storage in stacked saline formations with salinities greater than
3,000 mg/L per the CUSP screening parameters (Figure 396). The stacked saline formations of
the five well sites have reservoir thicknesses ranging from 61 to 122 m, mean depths ranging
from 1,040 to 2,010 m, porosity ranging from 0.22 to 0.38, and salinity greater than 3,000 mg/L,
averaging around 10,000 mg/L. The lithology of the saline formations consists of Tertiary
sedimentary basin fill composed mostly of sandstone, siltstone/claystone, limestone with
tuffaceous layers and Miocene basalt (see 50-km SCO2T geologic input database).

 613

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 396 Map showing the location of oil and gas wells deeper than 800 m and the logs digitized and analyzed by
DRI. Of the nine well sites analyzed, five sites were identified as having characteristics that could potentially
support CO2 geologic storage in stacked saline formations (red stars). The API numbers for each well, the network
of existing natural gas pipelines, and the extent of the regional fresh-groundwater aquifer are also shown.
The area of saline reservoirs was estimated at 2-km resolution using geospatial datasets that
show depth to basement from gravity surveys (Ponce 2004; Price et al. 2005) and mapped
Quaternary faults (USGS/NBMG 2016). Depth to pre-Cenozoic rock was used to define the base
of sedimentary basins given a lack of multiple wells at the five candidate CO2 storage sites. The
basement dataset was reclassified to limit areas within sedimentary basins with depths greater
than 800 m. Following the approach of Price et al. (2005), we further reduced the basement
dataset by not including areas near Quaternary faults in order to limit CO2 leakage along shear
zones by including setbacks of 2 km on both sides of normal faults and 1 km on both sides of
strike slip faults (Figure 397).

 614

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 397 Map showing the location of sedimentary basins with depths greater than 800 m (0.8 km) and
Quaternary faults with 2-km setbacks on normal faults and 1-km setbacks on strike slip faults.
The areal extent of identified stacked saline formations at well sites were extrapolated across the
entire sedimentary basin to include areas with depths greater than 800 m and outside fault
setbacks. Additional refinement of basin area was determined from the spatial extent of
sedimentary fill thickness between the depths of identified stacked saline formations. The five
sedimentary basins that meet the criteria of having deep well log information and acceptable
CUSP screening parameters include from west to east: Black Rock, Fallon, Tuscarora,
Humboldt, and Pine Valley. The area and associated aquifer properties of each sedimentary basin
were included in the 50-km SCO2T geology input database. The five-candidate geological CO2
storage sites are also located relatively close to the network of existing natural gas pipelines in
northern Nevada (Figure 398).

 Task 3.1.3 – Update Underground Source of Drinking Water (USDW) Data
 from All Public Sources
The extent of the regional and deep fresh-groundwater aquifer system in south-southeastern

 Task 3.1.4 – Gather and Catalog CO2 Emissions (Point) Source Database
Carbon dioxide point source data for Nevada were collected from the US Environmental
Protection Agency (EPA) Facility Level Information on Greenhouse Gases Tool (FLIGHT)
database (EPA 2025), the US Energy Information Administration (EIA) database (EIA 2025),
information about NV Energy-owned generating resources on the NV Energy website (NV

Energy 2025). Carbon dioxide source data collected during the project period includes: CO2
source site name, latitude and longitude of the site, CO2 source type, number of CO2 streams,
total CO2 emitted (Mt CO2/yr, site owner name, site operator name, county, and state (all data
were cataloged into the “Partner_Site_Selection_Database.xlsx” spreadsheet).
A total of 20 CO2 point sources from power, minerals, and chemical plants were identified near
Reno and Elko in the northern part of the state and Las Vegas in the southern part. Assessment of
point source quantities included identifying CO2 point sources that emitted greater than 0.100
Mt/yr. Total emissions in Nevada were greater than 100 Mt/yr in 2019, where the highest
emissions were centered near Las Vegas in southern Nevada (Figure 399).

The major point sources of CO2 emissions in northern Nevada are located relatively close to the

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 Summary and Conclusions
Previous assessments of Nevada’s CO2 geological storage potential identified saline formations
as the most promising option, but were limited by a lack of supporting oil and gas well-log data.
Under the Nevada CUSP West project, the DRI expanded upon these earlier assessments by
conducting a more detailed evaluation using available oil and well log information. Led by
Steven Bacon, PhD, P.G., C.E.G., the DRI team focused their efforts on Tasks 2 and 3 of the
CUSP project, which centered on identifying and characterizing stacked saline formations for
long-term CO2 storage.
Because Nevada has limited oil and gas resources, only 1,125 well logs exist statewide, and just
300 wells exceed depths of 800 m. After screening for hydrogeologic suitability and avoidance
of major freshwater aquifer systems, only 30 wells were examined in detail, and nine contained
sufficient data for full analysis using SCO2T screening parameters. Digitized geophysical logs,
including gamma ray, resistivity, and neutron porosity were used to estimate lithology, porosity,
salinity, and intrinsic permeability. Of these wells, five sites demonstrated favorable reservoir
properties for CO2 storage in saline formations composed of Tertiary sedimentary and volcanic
rocks having thicknesses of 61 to 122 m, depths of 1,040 to 2,010 m, porosity of 0.22 to 0.38,
and salinities greater than 3,000 mg/L, averaging approximately 10,000 mg/L.
The areas of the five candidate sites, located in the Black Rock, Fallon, Tuscarora, Humboldt,
and Pine Valley sedimentary basins, were mapped using depth-to-basement geophysical and
fault-location datasets, incorporating setbacks to minimize leakage risks. Twenty CO2 emission
point sources were identified statewide, with over 100 Mt CO2 emitted in 2019, primarily near
Reno and Elko in the northern parts, and Las Vegas in the southern part of Nevada. The
candidate sites are near existing natural gas pipeline infrastructure and major CO2 point sources,
improving their potential economic viability. The proximity of point sources and existing
infrastructure to the five candidate CO2 storage sites provides a potential carbon capture
utilization and storage capability for northern Nevada that was unidentified in previous CO2
geologic storage assessments.

New Mexico / West Texas
The overall project objective is to implement a regional initiative to accelerate onshore carbon
capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) technology deployment in the western region of the
United States. The Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP), covering all or parts of
13 states, consists of organizations throughout the western United States including academia,
government agencies, national laboratories, and industry.

 619

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

CUSP will coordinate the capabilities and experience of the diverse organizations to accelerate
CCUS deployment by performing four key activities: (1) addressing key technical challenges (2)
facilitating data collection, sharing, and analysis; (3) evaluating regional infrastructure; and (4)
promoting regional technology transfer.
The project scope of work encompasses data collection and synthesis, data analysis, modeling,
and scenario development to support more rapid implementation of commercial-scale CCUS.
There is an emphasis on collaborative efforts, knowledge dissemination and technology transfer
that will engage and inform stakeholders with the data and knowledge necessary to undertake
CCUS projects throughout the region. The project’s activities span the western United States
with data collection efforts but will identify and focus on specific areas that exhibit higher
commercial CCUS deployment readiness or that have promise but also pose specific
surmountable challenges requiring more detailed examination.

 San Juan Basin
The San Juan Basin is an asymmetric structural depression covering approximately 21,600
square miles of the east-central Colorado Plateau area in northwestern New Mexico,
southwestern Colorado, a small portion of northeastern Arizona, and southeastern Utah (Figure
400). It was formed during the Late Cretaceous to Eocene age Laramide Orogeny, which
occurred approximately 75 to 35 Ma (Dickinson and Snyder 1978). Strata in the basin reaches a
maximum thickness of 14,000 ft and consists primarily of sedimentary and igneous rocks
ranging in age from Devonian to Lower Tertiary. Faulting is prevalent along the basin margins
and in the northeastern, southeastern, and south-central portions of the San Juan Basin.

 620

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 400 Structural elements within the San Juan Basin area

 Tectonics
The tectonic evolution of the San Juan Basin began by at least the late Paleozoic Period
following Precambrian metamorphism, deformation, erosion, and subsequent burial. There is
little evidence to suggest a structural depression existed during the Precambrian. Recurrent
tectonism adjacent to the present-day San Juan Basin began during the late Paleozoic and
extended through Mesozoic Periods, forming the building blocks of the future San Juan, Zuni,
Defiance, and Nacimiento uplifts. Although minor deformation and uplift occurred throughout
most of the Mesozoic, the San Juan Basin began to resemble its current configuration during the
Laramide Period (Cooper and Lorenz 2020).

 621

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The Hogback monocline, a feature that bounds the northwestern limit of the central San Juan
Basin, was initiated during the early Laramide orogeny (Figure 400 and Figure 401). Other
bordering uplifts, including the Defiance to the southwest, the Zuni to the south, the San Juan to
the north, and the Nacimiento to the east, were recurrently active during both the Paleozoic and
Mesozoic periods; however, these uplifts were far more pronounced during late Cretaceous and
the earliest phase of the Eocene Laramide Orogeny (Kelley 1951). Based on the distribution of
post-Cretaceous sediments, uplift of the outer rim areas was localized during the earliest phase of
the Laramide Orogeny and gradually spread to the inner rim of the basin during the later phase
that concluded by the end of the Eocene (Kelley 1951).
Middle and late Tertiary deposits unconformably rest on much older strata, including wide
regions of Precambrian rocks exposed in the cores of some of the earlier uplifts. By the Pliocene,
both the San Juan Basin and Colorado Plateau were uplifted, resulting in drainages developing to
both the east and west of the continental divide. These drainages incised into the basin filling
sediments and removing much of the late and middle Tertiary deposits from the central portion
of the basin (Kelley 1951).

 Structure
The interior of the basin consists of strata that exhibits a gentle, regional dip with numerous
tectonic features that surround the perimeter of the basin, separating it from the Colorado
Plateau. These tectonic features played a predominant role in generating the present basin
configuration. The major structural features adjacent to and within the San Juan Basin are
categorized into three types: large uplifts, low structural arches and embayments, and monoclines
(Figure 400). The Nacimiento fault, on the eastern margin of the basin, resulted in Precambrian
granite being uplifted to the east. It is an example of a fault determining a basin boundary. The
Defiance and Nutria monoclines are also clear basin-bounding features. Features like the Gallup
and Acoma sags form less distinct boundaries where the San Juan Basin merges across structural
saddles with adjacent basins or embayments (Kernodle 1995). The major structural features
bounding the San Juan Basin.

 Stratigraphy
The San Juan Basin contains a thick sequence of sedimentary and igneous rock ranging from the
Precambrian to the Tertiary Period with the largest section deposited from Pennsylvanian Period
to the Tertiary Period. The maximum thickness of the San Juan sedimentary sequence is
approximately 14,400 ft within the central basin region (Figure 400). Figure 402 from Craigg
(2001) presents the stratigraphic framework and nomenclature of the San Juan Basin. Figure 403
presents the stratigraphic framework and nomenclature for the San Juan Basin. Figure 404 is the
type log for the San Juan Basin from New Mexico Tech’s (NMT) CarbonSAFE Strat Test Well
#1. Table 86 provides a list of the formations, rock types, depositional environments, and
resources.

  Delaware Basin
The Permian Basin, the largest hydrocarbon producing area in the United States, contains the
Delaware and Midland Basins. The Delaware Basin, the larger of the two, is found in
southeastern New Mexico and western Texas (Figure 472). Sediments in the area date back to
the Cambrian Bliss Sandstone (Broadhead 2017; Figure 473) and overlay Precambrian granites.
These late Cambrian transgressive sandstones were the initial deposits within (Figure 474 a
shallow marine sea that covered most of North America and Greenland. With continued down
warping or sea-level rise, a broad, relatively shallow marine basin formed: the proto-Tobosa
Basin. The Ellenburger Formation (0–1,000 ft) is dominated by dolostones and limestones that

 697

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

were deposited on a restricted carbonate shelves (Broadhead 2017; Loucks and Kerans 2019).
Tectonic activity near the end of Ellenburger deposition resulted in subaerial exposure and
karstification of these carbonates which increased the unit’s overall porosity and permeability.

 Delaware
 Basin

Figure 472 Location of the Delaware Basin with respect to Permian physiographic features (modified from Ward et
al. [1986] and Scholle et al. [2007])

 698

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 473 General stratigraphic chart for southeastern New Mexico (modified from Broadhead [2017])

 699

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 474 A subsidence chart from Reeves County, Texas showing the timing of development of the Tobosa and
Delaware basins during Paleozoic deposition (from Ewing [2019])
During Middle to Upper Ordovician time, the seas once again covered the area and deposited the
carbonates, sandstones and shales of, first, the Simpson Group (0–1,000 ft) and then the Montoya
Formation (0–600 ft). This is the time when the Tobosa Basin formed due to the Pedernal Uplift
and development of the Texas Arch (Figure 475; Harrington 2019) shedding Precambrian
crystalline clasts into the basin. Reservoirs in New Mexico are typically within the shoreline
sandstones (Broadhead 2017). Another subaerial exposure and karstification event followed the
deposition of the Simpson Group. The Montoya Formation marked a return to dominantly
carbonate sedimentation with minor siliciclastic sedimentation within the Tobosa Basin
(Broadhead 2017; Harrington and Ruppel 2019). Like the Ellenburger and Simpson carbonates,
the subaerial exposure event at the end of Montoya deposition resulted in karstification.

Silurio-Devonian formations consist of the Upper Ordovician to Lower Silurian Fusselman
Formation (0–1,500 ft), the Upper Silurian to Lower Devonian Wristen Group (0–1,400 ft), and
the Lower Devonian Thirtyone Formation (0–250 ft). The Fusselman Formation are shallow-
marine platform deposits of dolostones and limestones (Broadhead 2017; Ruppel 2019b).
Subaerial exposure and karstification associated with another unconformity at top of the
Fusselman Formation as well as intraformational exposure events created brecciated fabrics,
widespread dolomitization, and solution-enlarged pores and fractures (Broadhead 2017). The
Wristen and Thirtyone units appear to be conformable. The Wristen Group consists of tidal to
high-energy platform margin carbonate deposits of dolostones, limestones, and cherts with minor
siliciclastics (Broadhead 2017; Ruppel et al. 2020a). The Thirtyone Formation is present in the
southeastern corner of New Mexico and appears to be either removed by erosion or not deposited
(Figure 476). It is shelfal carbonate with varying amounts of chert nodules and represents the last
carbonate deposition in the area during Devonian time (Ruppel et al. 2020a).

Figure 476 A subcrop map of the Thirtyone and Woodford formations. The Woodford (brown) lies unconformably
on top of the Wristen Group where there is no Thirtyone sediments (yellow). Diagram is from Ruppel et al. (2020a).

 702

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The Siluro-Devonian units are saltwater injection zones within the Delaware Basin and are
typically dolomitized, shallow marine limestones that have secondary porosity produced by
subaerial exposure, karstification and later fracturing/faulting.
The Devonian Woodford Shale, an un-named Mississippian limestone, and the Upper
Mississippian Barnett Shale are seals for the underlying Siluro-Devonian strata. While the
Mississippian recrystallized limestones have minor porosity and permeability, the Woodford and
Barnett shales have extremely low porosity and permeability and would be effective barriers to
upward migration of acid gas out of the injection zone. The Woodford Shale (0–300 ft) ranges
from an organic-rich argillaceous mudstones with abundant siliceous microfossils to organic-
poor argillaceous mudstones (Ruppel et al. 2020b). The Woodford sediments represent stratified
deeper marine basinal deposits with its organic content being a function of the oxygenation
within the bottom waters; the more anoxic the waters, the higher the organic content.
The Mississippian strata within the northern Delaware Basin consists of an un-named carbonate
member and the Barnett Shale and unconformably overlies the Woodford Shale. The lower
Mississippian limestone (0–800 ft) are mostly carbonate mudstones with minor argillaceous
mudstones and cherts. These units were deposited on a Mississippian ramp/shelf and have mostly
been overlooked because of the reservoirs limited size. Where the units have undergone
karstification, porosity may approach 4% to 9% (Broadhead 2017), otherwise it is tight. The
Barnett Shale (0–400 ft) unconformably overlies the Lower Mississippian carbonates and
consists of Upper Mississippian carbonates deposited on a shelf to basinal, siliciclastic deposits
(the Barnett Shale). Within part of the basin, there is at least one tongue of Chesterian limestone
within the Barnett Shale and numerous sandstone/siltstone interbeds within the mudstone
deposits.
Pennsylvanian sedimentation in the area is influenced by glacio-eustatic sea-level cycles
producing numerous shallowing upward cycles within the rock record; the intensity and number
of cycles increase upward in the Pennsylvanian section. The cycles normally start with a sea-
level rise that drowns the platform and deposits marine mudstones. As sea-level starts to fall, the
platform becomes shallower and deposition switches to marine carbonates and coastal
siliciclastic sediments. Finally, as the seas withdraw from the area, the platform is exposed
causing subaerial diagenesis and the deposition terrestrial mudstones, siltstones, and sandstones
in alluvial fan to fluvial deposits. This is followed by the next cycle of sea-level rise and
drowning of the platform.
Lower Pennsylvanian units consist of the Morrow and Atoka formations. The Morrow Formation
(0–2,000 ft) within the northern Delaware Basin was deposited as part of a deepening upward
cycle with depositional environments ranging from fluvial/deltaic deposits at the base, sourced
from the crystalline rocks of the Pedernal Uplift to the northwest, to high-energy, near-shore
coastal sandstones and deeper and/or low-energy mudstones (Broadhead 2017; Wright 2020).
The Atoka Formation (0–500 ft) was deposited during another sea-level transgression within the
area. Within the area, the Atoka sediments are dominated by siliciclastic sediments, and
depositional environments range from fluvial/deltas, shoreline to near-shore coastal barrier bar
systems to occasional shallow-marine carbonates (Broadhead 2017; Wright 2020).
Middle Pennsylvanian units consist of the Strawn group (an informal name used by industry).
Strawn sediments (250–1,000 ft) within the area consists of marine sediments that range from

 703

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

ramp carbonates, containing patch reefs, and marine sandstone bars to deeper marine shales
(Broadhead 2017).
Upper Pennsylvanian Canyon (0–1,200 ft) and Cisco (0–500 ft) group deposits are dominated by
marine, carbonate-ramp deposits and basinal, anoxic, organic-rich shales.
Deformation, folding and high-angle faulting, associated with the Upper Pennsylvanian/Early
Permian Ouachita Orogeny, created the Permian Basin and its two sub-basins, the Midland and
Delaware basins (King 1948; Hills 1984), the Northwest Shelf, and the Central Basin Platform
(CBP; Figure 475, Figure 477, and Figure 478). The Early Permian and older rocks have been
fractured, faulted, and folded during this period of deformation and basin formation resulting in
the deposition of the Wolfcamp and truncation of Wolfcampian and older units (Figure 477).

Figure 477 Cross section through the western Central Basin Platform showing the structural relationship between
the Pennsylvanian and older units and Permian strata (modified from Ward et al. [1986]; from Scholle et al. [2007])

 704

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 478 Reconstruction of southwestern United States about 278 Ma. The Midland Basin (MB), Delaware Basin
(DB), and Orogrande Basin (OB) were the main depositional centers at that time (Scholle et al. 2020a).
The Wolfcampian Hueco Group is informally known as the Wolfcamp and this terminology will
be used in this document. The Wolfcamp Group (approximately 400 ft on the Northwest Shelf,
greater than 2,000 ft in the Delaware Basin) consists of shelf margin deposits ranging from
barrier reefs and fore slope deposits, bioherms, shallow-water carbonate and sandstone shoals,
and basinal carbonate mudstones (Broadhead 2017; Fu et al. 2020).
Differential sedimentation, continual subsidence, and glacial eustasy impacted Permian
sedimentation after Wolfcamp deposition and produced carbonate shelves around the edges of
deep sub-basins. Within the Delaware Basin, this subsidence resulted in deposition of roughly
12,000 ft of siliciclastics, carbonates, and evaporites (King 1945). Eustatic sea-level changes and
differential sedimentation, played an important role in the distribution of sediments/facies within
the Permian Basin. During sea-level lowstands, thousands of feet of siliciclastic sediments
bypassed the shelves and were deposited in the basin. Scattered, thin sandstones and siltstones as
well as fracture and pore filling sands found up on the shelves correlate to those lowstands.
During sea-level highstands, thick sequences of carbonates were deposited by a “carbonate
factory” on the shelf and shelf edge. Carbonate debris beds shedding off the shelf margin were
transported into the basin (Wilson 1972; Scholle et al. 2007). Individual debris flows thinned
substantially from the margin to the basin center (from hundreds of feet to feet).
Unconformably overlying the Hueco Group is the Abo Formation (700–1,400 ft). Abo deposits
range from carbonate grainstone banks and buildups along the Northwest Shelf margin and
shallow-marine carbonates to the northwest of the margin. Further back on the margin, the
backreef sediments grade into intertidal carbonates to siliciclastic-rich sabkha red beds to eolian
and fluvial deposits closer to the Sierra Grande and Uncompahgre uplifts (Broadhead 2017;
Ruppel 2020a). Sediments basinward of the Abo margin are equivalent to the lower Bone Spring
Formation. The Yeso Formation (1,500–2,500 ft), like the Abo Formation, consists of carbonate
banks and buildups along the Abo margin, which is roughly in the same area, just south of
Dagger Draw. Unlike Abo sediments, the Yeso Formation contains more siliciclastic sediments
associated with eolian, sabkha, and tidal flat facies (Ruppel 2020a). The Yeso shelf sandstones

 705

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

are commonly subdivided into the Drinkard, Tubb, Blinebry, Paddock members (from base to
top of section). The Yeso Formation is equivalent to the upper Bone Spring Formation.
Overlying the Yeso, are the clean, white eolian sandstones of the Glorietta Formation. It is a key
marker bed in the region, both on the surface and subsurface. Within the basin, it is equivalent to
the Lower Brushy Canyon Formation of the Delaware Mountain Group.
The Guadalupian San Andres Formation (600–1,600 ft) and Artesia Group (greater than 1,800 ft)
reflect the change in the shelf margin from a distally steepened ramp to a well-developed barrier
reef complex at the end carbonate deposition within the Delaware Basin. The individual
highstand carbonate units are separated by lowstand sandstones/siltstones that moved out over
the exposed shelf. The San Andres Formation consists of supratidal to sandy subtidal carbonates
and banks deposited a distally steepened ramp. Within the San Andres Formation, several
periods of subaerial exposure have been identified that have resulted in karstification and
pervasive dolomitization of the unit. Within the Delaware Basin, it is equivalent to the Brushy
and lower Cherry Canyon Formations.
The Artesia Group (Grayburg, Queen, Seven Rivers, Yates, and Tansill formations, ascending
order) is equivalent to Capitan Limestone, the Guadalupian barrier/fringing reef facies. Within
the basin, the Artesia Group is equivalent to the upper Cherry and Bell Canyon formations. The
Queen and Yates formations contain more sandstones than the Grayburg, Seven Rivers, and
Tansill formations. The Artesia units and the shelf edge equivalent Capitan reef sediments
represent the time when the carbonate factory was at its greatest productivity with the shelf
margin/Capitan reef prograding nearly 6 miles into the basin (Scholle et al. 2007). The Artesia
Group sediments were deposited in back-reef, shallow marine to supratidal/evaporite
environments. Like the San Andres Formation, the individual formations were periodically
exposed during lowstands.
The final stage of Permian deposition on the Northwest Shelf consists of the Ochoan/Lopingian
Salado Formation (greater than 2,800 ft; Nance 2020). Within the basin, the Castile Formation, a
thick sequence (total thickness approximately 1,800 ft; Scholle et al. 2007) of cyclic laminae of
deep-water gypsum/anhydrite interbedded with calcite and organics, formed due to the restriction
of marine waters flowing into the basin. Gypsum/anhydrite laminae precipitated during
evaporative conditions, and the calcite and organic-rich horizons were a result of seasonal
“freshening” of the basin waters by both marine and freshwaters. Unlike the Castile Formation,
the Salado Formation is a relatively shallow water evaporite deposit. Halite, sylvite, anhydrite,
gypsum, and numerous potash minerals were precipitated. The Rustler Formation (500 ft; Nance
2020) consists of gypsum/anhydrite, a few magnesitic and dolomitic limestone horizons, and red
beds. These are mostly shallow marginal marine deposits and represents the last Permian marine
deposits in the Delaware Basin. The Rustler Formation was followed by terrestrial sabkha red
beds of the Dewey Lake Formation (approximately 350 ft; Nance 2020), ending Permian
deposition in the area.
Beginning early in the Triassic, uplift and the breakup of Pangea resulted in another regional
unconformity and the deposition of non-marine, alluvial Triassic sediments (Santa Rosa
Sandstone and Chinle Formation). They are unconformably overlain by Cenozoic alluvium
(which is present at the surface). Cenozoic Basin and Range tectonics resulted in the current
configuration of the region and reactivated numerous Paleozoic faults.

 Structure
The Delaware Basin is surrounded by the CBP on the east, the San Simon Channel that separates
the CBP and the Northwest Shelf, the Diablo Platform to the southwest and west, the Hovey and
Sheffield channels to the south (Figure 479).

 Stratigraphy
 Cambrian to Precambrian

 Bliss Sandstone
The oldest sedimentary unit in the basin is the Cambrian Bliss Sandstone (Broadhead 2017;
Figure 482), which overlies Precambrian granites. These late Cambrian transgressive sandstones
were the initial deposits from a shallow marine sea that covered most of North America and
Greenland. With continued down warping and/or sea-level rise, a broad, relatively shallow
marine basin formed. The Bliss Sandstone and the underlying crystalline Precambrian rocks are
potential lower seals. Porosity and permeability data indicates that in shallower wells, the Bliss is
an aquifer. In deeper wells, the compactional history and potential diagenetic alteration, the Bliss
sandstones and associated granitic debris (from weathering of the basement rock) are probably
relatively tight.

Figure 482 Depositional environments for the bliss Sandstone to early Ellenburger in the proto-Tobosa basin (from
Loucks and Kerans [2019])

 Ordovician

 Ellenburger Group
The Ordovician Ellenburger Group is comprised of dolomites and limestones. These sediments
were deposited in subtropical to tropical belt of shallow-water platform carbonates that covered
most of what is now North America and Greenland. The carbonates in the Permian Basin area
have been extensively altered by later diagenesis that includes several intervals of exposure and

 710

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

karstification, dolomitization, and fracturing and faulting during later tectonic events (Figure
483).

Figure 483 Depositional model for the Ellenburger Group deposits. The diagram shows a sequence of transgressive
sandstones (Bliss Sandstone, yellow) to carbonates (panels A through C) followed by a regressive sequence (panels
C and D) with exposure and karstification in Panel D (from Loucks and Kerans [2019]).
Within the Ellenburger Group strata, the upper and middle section typically has the highest
porosity and permeability due to karsting and cave development as well as later faulting and
fracturing (Figure 484). Late diagenesis plays an important role in porosity destruction and
resurrection. Based on work by Loucks (2016), the best karst-related porosity is to the east of the
Bull Moose area, whereas the Bull Moose area is in the zone of porosity due to tectonically
controlled faulting and fracturing. Porosity and permeability in the Ellenburger section can vary
greatly due to the above considerations (Loucks and Kerans 2019).

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

  A) B)
Figure 484 Karst development. A) Cave development in the upper Ellenburger rocks and their potential impact to
produce porosity and permeability (from Loucks and Kerans [2019]). B) Zones of potential porosity creation: karst
related (blue), fault and fracture (green) and enhanced primary porosity (orange; Loucks 2016).

 Simpson Group
The deposits of the Simpson Group represent a regional transgression after the unconformity at
the end of Ellenburger deposition. This group is a thick sequence of carbonates, sandstones, and
shales (approximately 1,000 ft) which has a depocenter roughly equivalent to the Delaware
Basin/Tobosa Basin. There are several transgressive/regressive cycles within the section, but
only the transgressive sandstone sections have significant porosity. The rest of the section
typically consists of mud-rich carbonates and shales. Within the sandstones (particularly the
McKee Sandstone member), well logs indicate porosity averages around 15%.

 Montoya Group
The Montoya deposits are dominated by shallow-water, ramp limestones that were deposited in
the Tobosa Basin (Figure 485). Like the Ellenburger Group, the porosity within the Montoya
Group is dependent on depositional environment and diagenesis. The higher energy
environments tend to have better initial porosity than the low-energy environments. Compaction
destroys the porosity, and dolomitization produces secondary porosity. Based on the well logs,
the average porosity is approximately 3%, with scattered zones over 5%. The probable average
permeability is probably less than 1 mD, but fracturing may enhance it.

 712

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 485 Tectonic features during development of the Tobosa and Permian Basins during Late Mississippian time
(Ewing 2019)

 Ordovician – Silurian

 Fusselman Formation
The Fusselman Formation is a shallow-water carbonate system that was deposited in the Tobosa
Basin. In the Delaware Basin, the Fusselman thickens to around 1,000 ft of high-energy
packstones to grainstones. Like the Montoya Group, these high-energy sediments started out
with the best primary porosity, but diagenesis usually has decreased both the porosity and
permeability unless impacted by exposure and dissolution. Based on well logs, the porosity
averages around 2%. Reported permeability for shallower sections range from 0.001 to 10 mD
(Ruppel 2019b).

 Lower Devonian – Silurian

 Thirtyone and Wristen Formations
Underlying the Woodford Shale are the interbedded dolomites and dolomitic limestones of the
Devonian Thirtyone Formation and the Silurian Wristen Group, collectively referred to as the
Siluro-Devonian section. Unlike the Fusselman, Montoya and Ellenburger carbonates, these
deposits represent deposition in deeper waters. These deposits range from deep ramp mudstones
and wackestones, to chert- and sponge/radiolarian-rich hemipelagic mudstones
(Wristen/Thirtyone) to outer ramp packstones (Figure 486; Ruppel et al. 2020a, 2020b). Porosity
and permeability in the Wristen are limited in the main body of the unit (1–2%), but exposure
events and carbonate dissolution can improve the porosity (approximately 5%). Within Thirtyone

 713

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

deposits, the chert-rich hemipelagic deposits maintain the best porosity (up to 40%, up to 80
mD), while the limestones have less than 7% porosity and less than 1 mD of permeability
(Ruppel et al. 2020a).

 Upper Devonian

 Woodford Shale
Within the Permian Basin, the Upper Devonian Woodford Shale serves as a seal to hydrocarbon
migration out of Devonian and older units (Wright 1979). In combination with the Mississippian
section, it makes an excellent seal for potential injection. The Woodford Shale is laterally
continuous, organic- and shale-rich, siliceous (radiolarians) mudstone. The porosity that occurs
in the Woodford Shale is usually micro-porosity associated with organic material and not
connected (i.e., low permeability). Porosity can reach as much as 10% (Jarvie et al. 2001), but it
averages around 1% with very low permeabilities.

 Mississippian

 Mississippian Limestone
The Lower Mississippian limestone (an informal name) is a dark colored, deep marine limestone
with minor cherts and shales (Figure 487). In parts of the Delaware Basin, there is a second
carbonate tongue informally known as the Chesterian limestone. Known production from this
limestone consists of one to two well plays that normally have poor porosity (4–9%) and
permeability (Broadhead 2017) in New Mexico and a few isolated fields in the shallow water,
high-energy limestones in Texas.

 715

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 487 Map showing the distribution of platform carbonates of the Mississippian limestone and basin
siliciclastic sediments of the Barnett Shale (from Ruppel et al. [2020c])

 Barnett Shale
The Barnett Shale is a widespread, dark, organic shale with very low porosity and permeability
(Figure 487). Overall, the Mississippian units would be good seals in preventing upward fluid
movement through the section.

 Pennsylvanian

 Morrow Formation
The Morrow Formation consists mainly of shale-dominated grading upward to sandstone-
dominated strata as you move upward through the section. In parts of the basin, the sequence is

 716

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

capped by oolitic limestones. The Morrow sediments were deposited within the basin as part of
several transgressive (shales)/regressive cycles during Morrowan time. They represent deposition
in deltas, shoreface, shallow to deeper water platform environments, basinal shales and
submarine fans (Figure 488). The main reservoirs are within the sandstone lenses with porosities
from 5% to 8% (Broadhead 2017).

Figure 488 Paleodepositional map of Morrowan sedimentation (from Wright [2020])

 Atoka Formation
Atokan units are dominated deltaic and shoreface deposits formed during a transgression, with
occasional carbonate buildups (Figure 489; Broadhead 2017; Wright 2020). The Permian Basin
starts forming during Atokan time (Wright 2020) with the deposition basin forming in the area of
the Midland Basin. Gas production dominates production in the Atoka Formation with porosities
ranging from 8% to 12% (Broadhead 2017).

 717

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 489 Paleodepositional map of Atokan sedimentation (from Wright [2020])

 Strawn Group
Desmoinesian sedimentation consists of the Strawn Group. A second depositional low develops
in the area of the Delaware Basin. Within the Delaware Basin, the Strawn sediments are
dominated by limestones and sandstones deposited on a ramp (Figure 490) to basinal sediments
in the Texas part of the basin. The limestones consist of patch reefs encased by shales (during a
later transgression). A second depositional low develops in the area of the Delaware Basin.
Reservoirs are common in the patch reefs of coralline algae and foraminiferal packstones and
have porosities of approximately 10% and high permeabilities (Broadhead 2017).

 718

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 490 Paleodepositional map of Desmoinesian sedimentation (from Wright [2020])

 Canyon Formation
The Canyon Formation comprise Missourian sedimentation, respectively. This is the time period
of active tectonism and the completion of the Permian Basin formation (Figure 491). The
sediments range from basinal, organic-rich shales and siltstones, basin to platform carbonates,
and clastic deltaics and submarine fans. Phylloid algae mounds and bioclastic packstones are the
major reservoirs within these sediments. They have porosities up to 15%, mostly secondary
porosity.

 719

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 491 Paleodepositional map of Missourian sedimentation (from Wright [2020])

 Cisco Formation
The Ancestral Rocky Mountain deformation and the Ouachita Orogeny, starting in Late
Pennsylvanian (Missourian) and going through Wolfcampian time, resulted in the formation of
the Delaware and Midland basins. This produced changes in the shelf to basin margin throughout
Pennsylvanian time. The Cisco Formation consists of interbedded carbonates, sandstones, and
shales. Deeper marine sediments were dominated by organic-rich shales, the shelf edge was
dominated by fusulinid-rich Syringopora-phylloid algal bioherms and carbonate grainstone
shoals, and the platform shelf, which shallows northward, progressively changing from marine
backreef and lagoonal deposits to subtidal deposits with increasing amounts of sandstone that
was sourced from the Pedernal Uplift (Figure 492; Scholle et al. 2007; Broadhead 2017). The
Cisco Formation is one of several highly productive zones in the Delaware Basin. The nearby
Dagger Draw field has produced more than 70 billion barrels of oil. Oil production with Dagger
Draw and Tatum field is restricted mostly to the platform-edge carbonate bioherms and, to a
lesser extent, the high-energy carbonate grainstones. The bioherms have seen variable amounts
of dolomitization, dissolution, and secondary porosity development. Productive zones typically
have porosities that range from 7% to 12% (Broadhead 2017). The interbedded shales, interior
platform carbonates and sandstones have minimal porosity.

 720

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 492 Paleodepositional map of Virgilian sedimentation (from Wright [2020])

 Permian

 Wolfcampian Rocks
Wolfcamp/Hueco Group
Wolfcampian rocks in the Delaware Basin area have been assigned to the Hueco Group, but they
are informally called the “Wolfcamp.” The Wolfcamp was deposited on shelf margin during a
time of high-frequency, high-amplitude sea-level fluctuations (Fu et al. 2020). The shelf deposits
range from low-energy lagoonal/subtidal mudstones/wackestones to high-energy
packstone/grainstone shoals (Figure 493). Along the shelf margin, phylloid algal bioherms
(boundstones) rim the shelf margin. On many of the bioherms, oolitic grainstones occur as caps
and were deposited in a very high-energy environment (Scholle et al. 2007). On the foreslope
and proximal basin margin, shelf detritus makes up most of the sediments. In more distal areas
within the basin, carbonate- and radiolarian-rich mudstones and shales were deposited.

 721

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 493 Paleodepositional environments within the Permian Basin area during late Wolfcampian deposition
(from Fu et al. [2020])
Within the Wolfcamp strata, carbonate horizons are made up of foraminiferal-phylloid algal
mounds and associated debris beds. Because of their location on the shelf edge, the location and
size of the mounds are impacted by sea-level fluctuations that dominate most of Pennsylvanian
and Permian deposition. Foraminiferal-algal mounds build up during sea-level highstands, and
during lowstands, these mounds are reworked and redeposited in debris fans surrounding the
mounds and into the basin (Figure 494). The positioning and size of the mounds is controlled by
the accommodation space created during sea-level highstands. During lowstands, the mounds
become exposed, undergoing both physical and chemical diagenesis and forming debris beds
around the mounds.

 722

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 494 A depositional model for the Wolfcamp sediments in the Delaware Basin
Wolfcamp reservoirs have porosities average approximately 7% to 10% and occur mainly in the
reef margin facies (Broadhead 2017). During the Ouachita Orogeny, faults and compression
produced uplift in the east forming the CBP and folding resulting in the formation of the
Northwest Shelf and the Delaware Basin. This deformation resulted in the erosion on the CBP of
lower Paleozoic units (down to the Ordovician strata). Within the basin, Wolfcamp sediments
were partially eroded on fault block and fold highs and redeposited in topographic lows. By the
end of Wolfcamp sedimentation, most of the faulting had ceased, but down warping of the basins
continued.

 Leonardian/Cisuralian Rocks
Bone Spring Formation/Abo, and Yeso Group/Victorio Peak Formations
Leonardian strata consists of the Abo Formation and Yeso Group on the CBP, the Victorio Peak
Formation on the Northwest Shelf, and the Bone Spring Formation within the Delaware Basin.
Both the Abo, Yeso and Bone Springs formations are prolific producers with the Delaware Basin
area. The highstand deposits of the Abo and Yeso formations consist of dolomitized fringing
barrier reef boundstones at the shelf break and dolomitized backreef deposits that grade into
dolomitized and anhydrite-bearing tidal flat and supratidal deposits to red bed sabkha and
fluvial/deltaic sandstone and shale deposits to the north (Figure 495 and Figure 496). The
lowstand deposits consist of eolian and fluvial deposits on the platform and turbidites going out
into the basin and breaking up the Bone Spring carbonates. The main Abo reservoirs are in
dolomitized reefal facies and have porosity ranging from 5% to 15% (Broadhead 2017). The
fine-grained backreef deposits act as both lateral and vertical seals, produced by changing sea
levels and migration of the facies across the shelf.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 495 Detailed Leonardian paleodepositional environment for the Permian Basin during sea-level lowstands
(c) and highstands (d) from Nance and Hamlin (2020)

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 496 Depositional environments for sea-level highstand (a) and lowstand (b) times from Nance and Hamlin
(2020)
The Bone Spring Formation is the basin equivalent to the Abo and overlying Yeso formations.
Bone Spring sediments are characterized by >3,000 ft of basin-deposited carbonate and
siliciclastic sediments. The Bone Spring Formation is more carbonate rich than the Delaware
Mountain Group and consists of rockfalls, debris flows, and submarine fans deposited during
sea-level highstand periods and widespread carbonate deposition. Sandstone turbidites and
submarine fan complexes move sandstones out into the basin during sea-level lowstands, when
the carbonate factory has been shut down up on the shelf and siliciclastic sands move across the
shelf.
The Bone Spring Formation contains both conventional and unconventional fields within the
Delaware Basin in both the sandstone-rich and carbonate-rich facies. Most of these plays usually
occur within toe-of-slope carbonate and siliciclastic deposits or the turbidite facies in the deeper

 725

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

sections of the basin (Nance and Hamlin 2020). The upper most Bone Spring is usually dense
carbonate mudstone with limited porosity and low porosity. Carbonate debris derived from the
shelf Bone Spring reservoirs are dominated by turbidite sandstones with porosities averaging
between 7% and 20% (Broadhead 2017).

 Guadalupian Rocks
Delaware Mountain Group/San Andres and Grayburg Formations
Like the Leonardian section, sea-level fluctuations and tectonics played a major role on the
depositional environments on the shelf, slope and basin deposits. On the shelves, the highstand
deposits range from seaward to shoreward: fringing reefs on the edge of the platform, to subtidal
carbonate deposits, to barrier island facies, to lagoonal dolomites and evaporites to sabkha sand,
dolomites and evaporites (Figure 497 to Figure 500). During sea-level lowstand deposition, the
shelves are dominated by clastic deposition: eolian, fluvial and sabkha sands and evaporites.
These high frequency sea-level cycles on the shelves resulted in thick carbonate cycles during
periods when the carbonate factory was active (highstands) separated by exposure surfaces with
thin to very thin sandstones (lowstands).

Figure 497 Relationship between the backreef, basin and later basin fill during Guadalupian deposition

systems within the Delaware Basin. A) A diagrammatic representation of sea-level variations impact on deposition.
B) Model showing basin-wide depositional patterns during lowstand and highstand periods (from Scholle et al.
[2007]).

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

B. Lower San Andres deposits, C. Middle San Andres deposits, and D. Upper San Andres deposits (from Kerans and
Ruppel [2020]).

 728

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 500 Upper Guadalupian Grayburg formation depositional environments. From Kerans and Ruppel (2020).
Sediments of the Delaware Mountain Group (descending, Bell Canyon, Cherry Canyon, and
Brushy Canyon formations) are marine units that represent deposition within the Delaware
Basin. Despite being within a basin that continuously had water in it, sea level fluctuations and
tectonism had as much of an impact on these deposits as it did on the shelves. Lowstand deposits
in the basin are associated with submarine canyons that incise the carbonate platform that
surrounds most of the Delaware Basin. Low stand depositional environments include submarine
fan complexes that encircle the Delaware Basin margin. These submarine canyons that incised
the carbonate platform margin produced complexes of submarine fans consisting of turbidite
channels, splays, and levee/overbank deposits (Figure 501).

 729

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 501 A diagram of typical Delaware Mountain Group basinal siliciclastic deposition patterns (from Nance
[2020]). The channel and splay sandstones have the best porosity, but some of the siltstones also have potential as
injection zones.
Additionally, debris flows and density currents formed units that went far out into the basin.
These isolated coarse-grained to boulder-sized carbonate debris flows and grain falls within the
lowstand clastic sediments likely resulted from erosion and failure of the carbonate shelf margin
during sea-level lowstands or slope failure due to tectonic activity (earthquakes).
Density current deposits resulted from stratified basin waters. The basal waters were likely
stratified and so dense, that turbidity flows containing sands, silts and clays were unable to
displace those bottom waters and instead flowed out over the density interface (Figure 502).
Eventually, the entrained sediments would settle out in a constant rain of sediment forming
laminated deposits with little evidence of traction (bottom flowing) deposition.

 730

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 502 Harms (1974) density overflow model explains the deposition of laminated siliciclastic sediments in the
Delaware Basin. Low density sand-bearing fluids flow over the top of dense, saline brines at the bottom of the basin.
The sands gradually drop out as the flow loses velocity creating uniform, finely laminated deposits (from Scholle et
al. [2007]).
Unlike the shelves, the basin deposits contain very thick, siliciclastic lowstand sequences that are
interbedded with thin, highstand deep-water limestones and mudstones. These deposits are
thickest around the edge (toe-of-slope) of the basin and thin to the basin center (Figure 498). The
limestones are dark, finely crystalline, radiolarian-rich micrites to biomicrites. These highstand
deposits are a combination of suspension and pelagic sediments that also thin towards the basin
center. These relatively thin units are time equivalent to the massive highstand carbonate
deposits on the shelf.
The top of the Guadalupian Series is the Lamar Limestone, which is the source of hydrocarbons
found in underlying Delaware Sand (an upper member of the Bell Canyon Formation). The Bell
Canyon Formation is roughly 1,000 ft thick in the Red Hills area and contains numerous turbidite
input points around the basin margin (Figure 503). During Bell Canyon deposition, the relative
importance of discrete sand sources varied (Giesen and Scholle 1990), creating network of
channel and levee deposits that also varied in their size and position within the basin. Based on
well log analyses, the Bell Canyon 2 and 3 had the thickest sand deposits.

 731

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 503 These maps of Bell Canyon Formation were created by measuring sandstone thicknesses on well logs in
four regionally correlatable intervals (from Giesen and Scholle [1990]). The red circle on the last map surrounds the
Red Hills area.
Like the Bell Canyon and Brushy Canyon formations, the Cherry Canyon Formation is
approximately 1,300 ft thick and contains numerous turbidite source points. Unlike the Bell
Canyon and Brushy Canyon deposits, the channel deposits are not as large (Giesen and Scholle
1990), and the source of the sands appears to be dominantly from the eastern margin (Figure
504). Cherry Canyon 1 and 5 have the best channel development and the thickest sands. Overall,
the Cherry Canyon Formation, on outcrop, is less influenced by traction current deposition than
the rest of the Delaware Mountain Group deposits and is more influenced by sedimentation by
density overflow currents (Figure 502). The Brushy Canyon has notably more discrete channel
deposits and coarser sands than the Cherry Canyon and Bell Canyon. The Brushy Canyon
Formation is approximately 1,500 ft thick.

 732

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 504 These maps of Cherry Canyon Formation were created by measuring sandstone thicknesses on well logs
in five regionally correlatable intervals (from Giesen and Scholle [1990]). Unlike the Bell Canyon sandstones, the
Cherry Canyon sands are thinner and contain fewer channels. The red circle on the last map surrounds the Red Hills
area.
Within the Delaware Mountain Group, the Bell Canyon and Cherry Canyon have the best
porosity (averaging 15–25% within channel/splay sandstones) and permeability (averaging 2–13
mD) than the Brushy Canyon (approximately 14% porosity, an <3 mD; Ge et al. 2022; Smye et
al. 2021).

 Ochoan Rocks
Castile, Salado, and Rustler Formations
The youngest of the Permian sediments, the Ochoan- or Lopingian-aged deposits, consists of
evaporites, carbonates, and red beds. The Castile Formation is made of cyclic laminae of deep-
water gypsum/anhydrite beds interlaminated with calcite and organics. This basin-occurring unit

 733

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

can be up to 1,800 ft thick. The Castile evaporites were followed by the Salado Formation
(approximately 1,500 ft thick). The Salado Formation is a shallow water evaporite deposit, when
compared to the Castile Formation, and consists of halite, sylvite, anhydrite, gypsum, and
numerous potash/bittern minerals. Salado deposits fill the basin and lap onto the older Permian
shelf deposits. The Rustler Formation (up to 500 ft; Nance 2020) consists of gypsum/anhydrite, a
few magnesitic and dolomitic limestone horizons, and red beds. These are mostly shallow
marginal marine deposits and represents the last Permian marine deposits in the Delaware Basin.
The Ochoan evaporitic units are superb seals (usually <1% porosity and <0.01 mD permeability)
and are the reason that the Permian Basin is such a hydrocarbon-rich region despite its less than
promising total organic carbon (TOC) content.

 Geologic Model
The model developed for the Delaware Basin area includes over 2,280 wells (Figure 505). The
tops for each well were handpicked for all the formations present in the logs (Figure 506 and
Figure 507). A database was built in S&P Kingdom that includes well header information,
formation tops, bottom hole temperatures, and calculated geothermal gradients.

  Bravo Dome
The Bravo Dome area was another area selected for detailed mapping for the CUSP project.
Bravo Dome is a large natural CO2 gas field that has been utilized for many years (since the
1930s) for refrigeration and carbonation of drinks; later (1980s), this area was developed for
enhanced oil recovery (EOR) CO2 flooding projects in the Permian Basin. The wells produce
98% to 99% CO2 gas from the main reservoirs (Broadhead 2017). While the exact limits of the
field are yet to be determined (Broadhead 2017), mapping of the area to understand the

 772

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

stratigraphic and structural trapping mechanism can provide opportunities in the future as wells
become depleted, adding potential sequestration opportunities.

 Background Geology
Bravo Dome Field is a large domal feature in northeastern New Mexico (Figure 543). It is
located between the Sierra Grande uplift, Dalhart Basin and the Tucumcari Basin. Like the
Permian Basin region, Bravo Dome formed during the Ouachita Orogeny and the formation of
Pangea. This Pennsylvanian to Permian event eroded the structural highs to Precambrian
volcanic and metamorphic rocks (such as the CBP). Younger deposits (pre-Pennsylvanian) occur
off the structural highs in the basins.

 773

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 543 Location of Bravo Dome, New Mexico (from Broadhead [2017])
The Wolfcampian Abo Formation is the first unit to cover the highs, followed by the Tubb
Sandstone (Figure 544). The Tubb Sandstone, the main CO2 reservoir within the field, is part of
the lower Yeso Formation. It ranges from 100 to 450 ft thick throughout most of the area.
Overlying the Tubb Sandstone, the Cimarron Anhydrite is a thin (approximately 15 ft) anhydrite
layer that seals the Tubb Sandstone. There is upward leakage of the CO2 where faults cut the

 774

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

anhydrite (Broadhead 2017). This CO2 has migrated up section into other permeable sandstones
(Santa Rosa Sandstone).

Figure 544 Stratigraphic column from Broadhead (2019). Between the Abo and Precambrian units, there are other
units present in the off-structure areas.
The upper Yeso Formation consists of interbedded sandstone, siltstone, shale, carbonate, and
anhydrite. Overlying the Yeso Formation, the Glorieta Sandstone, a white fine-grained, shallow
marine sandstone, contains minor amounts of CO2. The Glorieta Sandstone grades upward into
the dolomite and anhydrite of the sabkha to shallow marine carbonates of the San Andres
Formation. The clastics of the Bernal Formation is the final Permian deposits within the area.
Like the Glorieta Sandstones, it has minor CO2 resources.
The Triassic Santa Rosa Sandstone are alluvial and fluvial sandstones that are next major
reservoir for CO2 in the area. The shales of the overlying Chinle Formation provide an excellent
seal to prevent upward gas migration.
The Jurassic Entrada Sandstone and the Cretaceous Dakota Sandstones are visible in some of the
wells.

 775

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

  SCO2TPRO Geologic Data
CUSP used the SCO2TPRO tool to rapidly characterize large areas of saline storage for carbon
sequestration. Geologic parameters utilized by the include: depth (m), net thickness (m), porosity
(fraction), permeability (mD), pressure (MPa), temperature (℃), and area (km2). The center
point of each 50 by 50 km grid was use to populate the data. For data-rich states like New
Mexico, this was a simplification of the data. Future models might include a finer grid size.
Appendix C provides the geologic information utilized to develop the New Mexico maps (Figure
559 to Figure 563). The outputs for the grid include injection rates, reservoir storage capacities,
plume dimensions, and injection costs. Storage capacities represent how much CO2 could be
stored using multiple hypothetical wells within the grid cell.

Oklahoma
The Oklahoma Geological Survey (OGS) assisted University of Oklahoma (OU) PI Professor
Rouzbeh Moghanloo with the CUSP activities related to Oklahoma. On behalf of the State of
Oklahoma, Moghanloo presented at the annual CUSP meeting in 2022 and 2023. OGS activities
included presenting state updates at the 2024 and 2025 CUSP annual meetings, working with the
Oklahoma Secretary of Energy and the Environment on state legislation for carbon management
(a prerequisite for Class VI primacy), and contributing to focused projects. One focused project,
“From Site to State: Design of an Integrated CCS Operation in a Complex Geological Structure
in Osage County, Oklahoma,” was led by Moghanloo and is discussed in this report by Benmadi
Milad. The other focused projects are the Utah Iron Mountain project and the Kansas–Oklahoma
ONEOK project, discussed in this report by Nathan Moodie (“CCS at the Iron Mountain Iron
Mine and Direct Reduced Iron Processing Plant, Southern Utah”) and Brendan Bream
(“Infrastructure Development for Handling of New Gaseous Products for Natural Gas Liquids
Fractionation and Gas Processing Plants in Kansas and Oklahoma”), respectively. Lastly, Ming
Suriamin (of the OGS) contributed OGS data to the SCO2T database. Moghanloo coauthored the
publication by Miranda et al. (2023) that described an economic model for carbon capture and
storage (CCS) deployment in Oklahoma using geologic data provided by a third party (not
OGS).

viability of stacked storage. Greenh Gases Sci Technol. 13(6):763–779. doi:10.1002/ghg.2244

 Oklahoma Geological Survey Carbon Capture, Utilization,
 and Storage Curriculum
Carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) deployment depends on local community
support (NETL 2017), but over a third of American adults are unfamiliar with this technology

 797

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

(Bedle et al. 2024). Accelerating CCUS technology deployment in the Western Region therefore
requires an informed citizenry and a prepared workforce.
In 2023, the Oklahoma Geological Survey (OGS; https://www.ou.edu/ogs, accessed December 2,
2025), a Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP) partner and agency representing
Oklahoma, received US Department of Energy (DOE) funding from the Regional Initiative to
Accelerate CCUS Deployment: Technical Assistance for Large-Scale Data Gathering, Analysis,
Sharing, and Engagement (DOE-FOA-0002799). The 2-yr project, “Oklahoma Geological
Survey coordination of mid-continent carbon management” (DE-FE0032374), began in early
2024 and included a required plan for community and stakeholder engagement (Hayman et al.
2023). The project also promised coordination and collaboration with regional initiatives like
CUSP.
Throughout 2024, the OGS Education and Outreach team developed outreach activities for
different stakeholder groups, including academia, state and federal agencies, industry partners,
Tribal Nations, K-12 teachers, K-12 students, special interest groups, and the public. These
efforts included informational materials about CCUS and cutting-edge projects in Oklahoma and
creation of a professional development curriculum. These materials are freely available to the
public via the OGS website and are shared with CUSP and other regional partners for
dissemination.
Prior to January of 2025, the OGS Education and Outreach team collaborated with OGS research
scientists on other teams, including Energy Geoscience, the Seismic Network, and the Oklahoma
Petroleum Information Center (OPIC) to develop a series of hands-on activities to demonstrate
the carbon capture and storage (CCS) processes. Unique to OGS, the CCS Challenge invited
visitors to choose a geological storage site for carbon dioxide. Participants overlayed simplified
subsurface data maps of a single county and applied four main criteria necessary for safe carbon
storage to choose the best underground reservoir. First deployed at the Women in STEAM
Conference on October 8, 2024, and again on October 26, 2024, at the Oklahoma Mineral and
Gem Show, this display engaged more than 2,500 Oklahomans and began to create new
connections with local industry partners.
Following these successful deployments, the OGS Education and Outreach team began to
develop a curriculum guide for a planned teacher workshop in February 2025. Using the
activities from the interactive CCS display as a jumping point to create “Carbon Capture,
Utilization, and Storage: A Crash Course for Teachers, Students, and Communities.”
In accordance with best practices, this curriculum provides information using simple, accurate,
and direct language (Atkinson et al. 2024), models (Otto and Gross 2021) and multiple means of
visualization to aid understanding (Greenberg and Gavreau 2014). In a commitment to
maintaining transparency and public trust, the OGS Education and Outreach team prioritized
clear explanations of common CCS project motivations (Szizybalski et al. 2014). Rather than
prescribing research questions, the team promotes using data resources to investigate locally
relevant questions (Young and Sacuta 2014). Finally, the OGS Education and Outreach team
focused on activities that facilitate connection and perspective-sharing among community
members to empower local decision-making (Sacuta et al. 2017; Wade and Greenberg 2009).
In December 2024, the OGS hosted a workshop, “Building Foundations for Carbon Capture and
Storage in Oklahoma.” This workshop gathered a group of approximately 50 industry and

 798

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

technical professionals to facilitate communication among industry partners, state and federal
agencies, and representatives from Tribal Nations. The workshop focused specifically on
creating meaningful discussion about Class VI wells and CCS in Oklahoma. A brief presentation
of the interactive CCS display and future professional development curriculum was met with
enthusiasm from several workshop attendees, including representatives of CUSP.
In accordance with new direction from the DOE in late January 2025, and in alignment with
Executive Orders, the OGS Education and Outreach team suspended all work on, and use of
community engagement efforts related to the OGS project. After additional instruction and
clarification from the DOE and given interest from industry partners and regional initiatives,
including CUSP, the OGS Education and Outreach team resumed completion of the CCUS
curriculum to provide resources promoting an informed citizenry and workforce development for
the CCUS/enhanced oil recovery (EOR) economic sectors.
Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage: A Crash Course for Teachers, Students, and
Communities is in its final stages of development. Currently at 86 pages, the final page count is
projected to fall at or around 100 pages, divided into seven main chapters. Within each chapter
are three main sections: presentation slides, a topic overview, and a resource and activity
overview, followed by activity instructions and materials. Upon completion, this resource will be
hosted at https://www.ou.edu/ogs/education/teacherresources (accessed December 2, 2025).
An expanded table of contents summarizes the curriculum content in more detail.

 Climate Change is a Problem

How is your community affected by climate change?

Weather and climate are defined and predictability of each is discussed.

• Use a graph of annual yearly temperature in Oklahoma to inspire observation and
 questioning.
• Ask long-term residents in your community about childhood recollections of weather
 patterns.
• Use public data collections to investigate questions about changes in local weather patterns
 important or interesting to the individual.

 CO2 Holds the Sun’s Energy

What is the relationship between carbon dioxide and climate change?

 799

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Identifies chemical properties of carbon dioxide, gases comprising Earth’s atmosphere, and
atmospheric absorption and reflection of solar energy. Introduces carbon dioxide as a byproduct
of combustion while focusing on the societal benefits of burning fuels for energy. Ends by
connecting carbon dioxide, atmospheric energy, and weather patterns.

• Make observations and ask questions about a graph of atmospheric carbon dioxide and
 emissions from the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA).
• Observe properties of carbon dioxide, especially density.
• Explore relationships between temperature and gases in a contained system.

 CO2 Management Solutions Exist

How can we lower the amount of carbon dioxide in the atmosphere?

Discusses open and closed systems, simplifying Earth’s complex systems using models, and
natural carbon cycles. Defines “NetZero” and briefly introduces reduction and removal as carbon
management methods. Identifies sources of carbon dioxide beyond burning fuels and the highly
unlikely nature of complete decarbonization.

• Follow the pathway of a carbon molecule using a kinesthetic model of the carbon cycle.
• Analyze the message of a figure explaining the idea of NetZero.
• Explore resources to evaluate or create a local Priority Climate Action Plan.

 Carbon Capture, Utilization, and Storage Removes CO2 from the
 Atmosphere

What is carbon capture, utilization, and storage?

Clarifies terminology associated with carbon management, explains sources of carbon dioxide,
scaling innovation for commercial use, and lists multiple solutions for carbon capture. Outlines
the process of compressing carbon dioxide and identifies transportation methods for captured
carbon dioxide, and commercial uses for carbon dioxide.

• Assemble a model CCUS facility.

 800

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

• Investigate compression as a property of gases.
• Explore Oklahoma’s legacy of contributions to CCUS innovation through historic news
 articles.

 Storing CO2 Comes with Risks

How can we watch for and protect against potential problems from CCUS?

Identifies potential risks associated with CCUS in four main categories: environmental,
technical, economic, and social. Underscores the risks OGS has the capacity and expertise to
investigate and publish data for public use. Defines monitoring and mitigation, pointing out
Oklahoma’s Seismic Network, extensive subsurface data repository, and methods used to create
models to identify potential storage reservoirs.

• Brainstorm a list of potential risks of storing or transporting carbon dioxide within the
 community.
• Find and interpret data from the Oklahoma Seismic Network.
• Train AI to detect earthquakes in a dataset from the Oklahoma Seismic Network.

 Oklahoma Can Store CO2 Underground

What are the characteristics of a good storage site for carbon dioxide?

Reviews four main criteria of a good geologic storage reservoir for carbon dioxide: a thick layer
of porous rock to hold CO2 with a layer of caprock on top to trap CO2, at a depth at least 800
meters (½ a mile deep) so compressed CO2 remains a supercritical liquid, in an area with few
earthquakes to prevent CO2 leaks.

• Test the porosity and permeability of different types of rocks.
• Calculate reservoir storage capacity using data from OGS models.
• Choose a potential storage site using maps of areas underground that meet the required
 criteria for a good storage reservoir.

 Teams of People Work on CCUS

Who works on carbon capture and storage projects?

Identifies major career pathways within CCUS stakeholder groups, particularly academia and
research labs, associated industries, and regulatory agencies.

• Use local and regional career exploration resources to research CCUS-related career
 opportunities.
• Chart CCUS career pathways and navigate job announcements
• Interview a local CCUS professional.
