Washington
The overall objective of the Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP) Regional
Initiative was to accelerate onshore carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS) technology
deployment in the Western United States. The Washington State Geological Survey (WGS)
supported this objective by accomplishing the following:
• Digitization of oil and gas (O&G) well logs to Log ASCII Standard (LAS) format
• Sequestration of CO2 Tool (SCO2T; Middleton et al. 2020) reservoir input data deliverable
• Salinity data collection from O&G wells
• Provided CCUS information to industry in Washington State
• Answered public inquiries on CCUS
• Gathered and shared state geologic data with National Laboratories
• Answered state agency policy and regulatory inquiries on CCUS
• Summarized point source emissions data to identify high potential sources for sequestration
The following summarizes the timeline of WGS work on CUSP that produced these
accomplishments, organized by Statement of Project Objectives task.

October through December 2021 – We presented the BECCS business model to DNR executive
management in preparation for the Yale CCL presentation to the Commissioner of Public Lands
(CPL). The CPL is a statewide elected official in Washington State, responsible for managing
state land. Since there is no income tax in Washington State, this is a significant position with
respect to state revenue. BECCS is an important model in Washington State because biomass
energy is integrated with wildfire mitigation (forest thinning projects) and the timber business
(mill waste). The BECCS model proposes a market for forest thinning projects (slash is currently
managed using controlled burns, which contributes to CO2 emissions) and mill waste while also
assisting the state with wildfire mitigation by improving overgrown forest health. In addition to
managing revenue from state lands, DNR is also the state firefighting agency. We helped
facilitate a meeting between the Yale Carbon Containment Lab and the CPL. We met with Drax
Group (also pursuing a BECCS model) in collaboration with DNR executive policy advisors,
including the Chief Resilience Officer. These meetings also involved the state uplands leasing
and forest resources divisions of the DNR.
January through March 2022 – ECY had a vacancy for their UIC coordinator for several months
at the end of 2021. We met with the Water Quality Program manager who oversees the UIC
program to discuss primacy. He said ECY was interested in applying for primacy. However, he
said it would take approximately 18 months to get legislation written. Legislation would have to
align with legislative sessions (long session in odd numbered years, e.g., January–April 2023;
short session in even numbered years, e.g., January–February 2024). After legislation passes
(written into law called the Revised Code of Washington [RCW]), it would take 12–24 months

 814

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

for an agency to write up the rules (Washington Administrative Code [WAC]) based on the
RCW. Therefore, we expect that ECY cannot obtain primacy for another 4 yr from January 2022,
at the earliest. Once ECY obtains primacy there will be a period of hiring and training before the
agency is equipped to permit UIC Class VI wells. As of 2025, ECY has taken no action on UIC
Class VI primacy.
In the meantime, the EPA will permit these wells. They have two staff members for this task in
Region 10 (PNW). Neither of them have permitted a Class VI well before. No agency has
permitted a Class VI well for basalt anywhere in the United States. The only basalt CO2 injection
well (Wallula, WA, in 2009) was permitted as a Class V. It was considered an experimental well,
and Class VI does not exist in the RCW. The last time the RCW was updated was before Class
VI existed.
Separate from permitting, there is the issue of credit offset program rule-making, administered
by a separate ECY division. In the 2021 Washington State legislative session, both cap and trade
(called cap and invest in Washington State and commonly referred to by the name of the act:
Climate Commitment Act [CCA]) and LCFS legislation (called CFS in Washington State)
passed, and two separate teams at ECY for CCA and CFS are working on rule-making (WAC
writing) for these laws. We met with the CCA and CFS groups to ensure that geologic carbon
sequestration is included where applicable in the credit offset program rule-making. This is a
forest-focused state, and we do not want geological carbon sequestration to be sidelined. ECY is
largely following California state protocols, which include geologic carbon sequestration.
Washington has two kinds of legislative sessions that start in January of each year: regular
sessions in odd years are 105 days, and short sessions in even years are 60 days. We monitor
bills related to carbon sequestration. The bills we followed this session were as follows:
• SB 5910: hydrogen incentives. This bill does not directly affect carbon sequestration.
 However, it excludes incentives for hydrogen produced from steam reformation, including
 reformation of hydrocarbons. Hydrogen is a byproduct of BECCS and could be marketed to
 assist a BECCS project economics. While the BECCS process produces hydrogen through
 steam reformation, biomass is not fossil fuel. If a BECCS project proceeds, we will have to
 clarify with rule-makers at the Department of Commerce to determine whether BECCS will
 be eligible for H2 incentives.
• SB 5961: biochar incentives. This bill does not directly affect geologic carbon sequestration
 but I receive a lot of inquiries about it as the state’s carbon sequestration geologist.
• SB 5842: modifications to the 2021 CCA. This bill does not directly affect geologic carbon
 sequestration.
This quarter we met with Assistant Attorneys General (AAGs) for DNR to introduce CUSP to
them and explain carbon sequestration. These AAGs will be responsible in the future for dealing
with CCUS leases. We explained the concept and uncertainties of pore space ownership to them.
April through June 2022 – We attended ECY rule-making meetings for CCA and Clean Fuel

trade, or cap and invest as they are branding it in Washington State, and Clean Fuels Standard,
which is LCFS in California) will go into effect in Washington State on January 1, 2023.

With respect to Task 2.3, DNR PSLD clarified, for the first time, that they are proceeding under
the assumption that pore space belongs to the surface estate. The legal analogy for this is that
RCW 78.60.040 (geothermal sui generis) is analogous to CO2 injection. The geothermal law
states that since geothermal resources are neither a mineral nor a water right, they belong to the
surface estate. This position is still an assumption, and there is currently no move at the state
level to codify pore space ownership in statute. There are no state agency positions held on
amalgamating pooling at this time. We also monitored pre-filed bills for CCUS and emissions
reduction content for the upcoming state legislative session (January–April 2023). Although
there is legislative language regarding amendments to recent (2021–2022) emissions legislation,

 Capture Technologies for Several Major Types of Point Sources
Power Plants
The power industry accounts for a substantial share of total emissions. Generating electricity
accounts for 28.5% of all CO2 emissions in the United States and has increased by 7% since
2020 (EPA 2023). The main way to reduce the electricity-generating sector's footprint is through
carbon capture. Power plants have a wide array of carbon capture technologies that can be used
across different power generation processes. However, all the carbon capture technologies can be
broadly defined into three groups: precombustion, postcombustion, and oxyfuel combustion.
Each of these technologies captures CO2 from the process stream for sequestration or utilization.
Precombustion capture reduces the amount of CO2 emitted from the process before combustion
of fossil fuels is complete. Some notable capture technologies that utilize precombustion capture
are hydrogen membrane reforming (HMR), sorption-enhanced water–gas shift (SEWGS), and

 820

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

integrated gasification combined cycle (IGCC). HMR, via the water–gas shift reaction, mixes the
fuel in a water-rich environment to produce hydrogen and CO. That flue gas is then mixed with a
water–gas shift reaction, which converts CO and water into hydrogen and CO2. Overall, this
changes the fuel when burned to hydrogen, which can be used as fuel, and CO2. You can add a
sorption element to the end of the water–gas shift reaction (Goel et al. 2019). That system is
called the SEWGS reaction. In SEWGS, hydrogen is separated from CO2, which is then
sequestered. The remaining CO is cooled to complete the shift reaction, which is then captured
using an amine. The gas is heated before being fed into the turbine. SEWGS is expensive due to
the many heating and cooling processes. The gasification process converts low-value fuels with
many impurities into high-value syngas. The method achieves this through a gasifier and a shift
reaction, which remove impurities and produce syngas. Syngas reduces carbon emissions by
burning cleaners through the gasification process.
Postcombustion capture is a process that reduces the amount of CO2 released to the atmosphere
after combustion. The primary post-combustion capture method is adsorption. Adsorption is a
fluid-solid interaction and is different from absorption. To maximize adsorption, you want to
maximize the surface area of the solid in which the solvent will sit. When the flue gas passes
through the solvent, it reacts chemically, but it can be regenerated using temperature or pressure
swings. Alkanolamine solvents are the most used technology and include monoethanolamine
(MEA), diethanolamine (DEA), methyldiethanolamine (MDEA), and others. They are effective
due to their high versatility and the ability to remove low concentrations of CO2. The primary
and secondary amines react directly with CO2, while the tertiary amine structure supports
hydrolysis and the reaction (Goel et al. 2019). These solutions are expensive to regenerate for
reuse due to their high energy requirements. Another process used is the carbonate process, in
which the flue gas reacts with an aqueous potassium carbonate solution to form KHCO3, with the
CO2 separated. This process is beneficial because K2CO3 reacts with other harmful gases, but it
requires a remarkably high partial pressure to operate (Goel et al. 2019). Finally, the chilled NH3
process can be used where the crux is to chill the flue gas to increase the CO2 concentration
while decreasing the volume. You then run the gas through an adsorber running with a chemical
solvent (MEA). The high CO2 concentration enables the process to be effective, separating CO2
while minimizing NH3 exposure (Goel et al. 2019). The disadvantage is that this process has
much higher corrosivity on the system.
Finally, oxyfuel combustion uses a process that increases the oxygen concentration in the
combustion chamber while reducing nitrogen to enable a complete reaction. Extra oxygen is
pulled into the system to create an oxygen-rich environment. An air separation unit (ASU)
creates an oxygen-rich environment by separating nitrogen from air. This helps to reduce the
amount of NOx and SOx produced by the reaction while increasing the amount of CO2. This is
beneficial as it can be directly sequestered.
Cement
The cement industry produced 41.3 Mt CO2 in 2021, an increase of 0.5 Mt from 2020. The
demand for cement is heavily reliant on the construction industry and their access to funding.
This trend is evident in the decrease in cement production between 2006 and 2009, driven by the
economic recession. However, since 2009, emissions from cement production have increased by
40% (EPA 2023).

 821

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Creating cement is a complex process that involves multiple reactions. To start, limestone or
CaCO3 is heated in a kiln to high temperatures to produce CaO, or lime, a process known as
calcination. Calcination occurs in a calcinator and produces CO2 as a byproduct. The feverish
temperatures also require a high energy demand, which creates substantial indirect CO2
emissions in the electric power industry. The calcination process enables unique carbon-capture
processes to be observed. The main technologies used are amine absorbers, sodium hydroxide
processes, chilled NH3, and calcium looping.
Adsorption by amine is an effective way to capture carbon in most processes. The flue gas
generated by the chemical reactions during cement manufacturing is captured using amine
solutions. Amine solutions capture CO2 in the flue gas via a chemical reaction. The amines can
regenerate under pressure or at high temperature, each requiring substantial energy.
Additionally, the sodium hydroxide process can be used. The sodium hydroxide process uses
NaOH to react with the flue gas from the cement plant. This reaction produces NaHCO3 (baking
soda) while reducing CO2 emissions. Also, due to v, additional compounds can be created and
sold, such as bleach and hydrochloric acid.
The chilled ammonia process (CAP) was developed to capture carbon from low-concentration
flue gas streams and works much like amine capture. NH3 acts as a liquid solvent, adsorbing the
low concentration of CO2. CAP can be regenerated by utilizing elevated temperatures. To make
this more efficient, the excess heat produced by the cement plant can be used for regeneration.
Finally, calcium looping utilizes calcium in its carbonate and oxide forms to reversibly react with
CO2. This reaction occurs in the carbonator, turning CO2 and CaO into Ca(HCO3)2, which is fed
into the calciner. The calciner heats Ca(HCO3)2, producing a rich gas of pure CO2 that can then
be sequestered or utilized.
Iron & Steel
The emissions produced by the iron and steel industry have remained constant over time,
hovering at 38.8 Mt CO2 from 2017 to 2021 (EPA 2023). The main factors influencing change
are the amount of steel produced, and the number of processes used at the specific plant.
However, over time, modern technologies have implemented the process to make it more
efficient or to recycle steel. Out of the 101 steel plants within the United States, 29% were basic
oxygen furnaces (BOFs) while 71% were electric arc furnaces (EAFs; EPA 2023). In the history
of steel making, BOFs are king. Basic oxygen furnaces draw oxygen into the molten iron to
reduce its carbon content, converting the iron ore into low-carbon steel. EAFs use scrap steel as
their primary input, heating it with electric arcs to reshape it for commercial use. EAFs require a
lower energy output, which, combined with the use of steel scrap as an input, has made it the
dominant process.
Iron and steel production utilizes many processes in unison to reach its final output. Each of
these processes generates emissions. The largest source of emissions is the furnace, either a BOF
or an EAF, due to the high energy input. Additionally, coke production and sinter plant use
contribute to the plant's emissions. The use of all these processes and their individual gas flows
makes it hard to implement a single capture technology. However, technologies focused on
reducing furnace emissions will be the primary focus, as the heating process is the sector's major
contributor.

 822

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

The iron and steel industry uses coal and limestone to remove impurities. However, the reactions
that cut off oxygen from the iron oxides and remove impurities also produce CO2, along with
additional heating and energy requirements. However, because limestone is used, the carbon
capture processes are much the same as those in the cement industry. Amine-based absorption is
often used because the excess heat from the furnace can be used for regeneration. Also, calcium
looping is again used due to limestone in the process.
Petrochemical Production
The petrochemical industry emitted 33.6 Mt of CO2 in 2021, an 11% increase from 2020, when it
emitted 30.1 Mt. Emissions from the petrochemical industry have increased by 53% since 1990,
mainly due to the production of ethylene and methanol (EPA 2023). Petrochemicals are
chemicals derived from petroleum or natural gas inputs. The petrochemical industry is broadly
defined by the large volumes of chemicals it produces. Each production will have a different
process, leading to different capture technologies being effective. However, ethylene and
methanol are the two petrochemicals that emit the most.
Ethylene is widely used in the plastics industry and is incorporated into polymers such as
polyvinyl chloride (PVC), polyethylene, ethylene oxide, and many others. The dominant method
of producing ethylene is through steam cracking natural gas and other feedstocks. After the
steam cracking process, ethylene undergoes direct chlorination and oxychlorination. Direct
oxidation of ethylene is the main source of CO2, as are the emissions from the combustion units.

Part IV – National Laboratories
Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL)
This report presents a suite of technical analyses conducted by LANL as part of the Carbon
Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP) West project to support regional-scale planning and
risk assessment for geologic carbon storage (GCS) across multiple western US states. The work
integrates advanced modeling tools from the National Risk Assessment Partnership (NRAP),
infrastructure optimization using Scalable Infrastructure Model for Carbon Capture and Storage
(SimCCS), geologic risk quantification, and seismic characterization to evaluate the feasibility,
safety, and readiness of emerging CO2 storage opportunities. These efforts provide a consistent
and scientifically grounded framework for assessing GCS performance under diverse geological,
operational, and socio-environmental conditions.
In Task 1, NRAP-Open-IAM (Vasylkivska et al. 2021) was applied to evaluate potential CO2
and brine leakage risks for candidate storage sites in Kansas, California, Colorado, and
Oklahoma. By linking reservoir simulation outputs with reduced-order models (ROMs) for
wellbore leakage and aquifer response, the system-level analyses showed that predicted leakage
rates are generally small and do not produce measurable impacts on underground sources of
drinking water (USDWs). Across all case studies, only limited CO2 or brine migration occurred
through selected legacy wells, and cumulative leakage remained orders of magnitude below
levels of concern, demonstrating that each site exhibits low leakage risk under the modeled
conditions.
Task 2 used the SimCCS optimization platform to examine phase-based CO2 transport network
development in the Four Corners region. The analysis quantified how environmental justice (EJ)
constraints, specifically, avoiding disadvantaged and tribal communities, affect pipeline routing,
network length, and system-wide costs. Results show that enforcing EJ constraints increases
pipeline length by 4 to 11% across development phases and raises transport and storage costs,
but the overall system remains economically viable under current tax credits. These findings
highlight the importance of integrating community considerations into early-stage carbon capture
and storage (CCS) infrastructure design.
In Task 3, LANL developed and demonstrated methods for incorporating geologic risk factors
into regional readiness indices (RRIs). Two key risks were examined: induced seismicity,
represented through capacity multipliers limiting allowable injection volumes, and leakage risk
from legacy wells, represented through well-density-dependent storage cost adjustments. Both
risk types were shown to significantly influence optimal pipeline routing and storage-site
selection, underscoring the need to incorporate geologic and operational risks directly into
regional CCS planning frameworks.
Finally, Task 4 focused on subsurface characterization at Iron Mountain, Utah, using legacy 2D
seismic data. Through traveltime tomography, migration velocity analysis (MVA), reverse-time
migration (RTM), and machine-learning-based fault detection, high-resolution images of
subsurface structures were generated to assess the suitability of deep formations for CO2 storage
associated with direct reduced iron (DRI) production. The results delineate key stratigraphic and
structural features, including the geometry of the Navajo Sandstone reservoir and overlying

 824

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

caprocks, and identify faults that may influence storage integrity, thereby providing essential
inputs for future site evaluation.
Overall, the combined results of Tasks 1 through 4 demonstrate that the western US region
contains promising and diverse opportunities for GCS deployment, but that successful and
responsible implementation requires integrating geologic risk assessment, infrastructure
optimization, and detailed subsurface characterization. The tools and workflows presented in this
report offer a scalable framework to support ongoing CCS planning and regulatory readiness
across the region.

 Task 1 – Apply NRAP Tools to Assess Geologic Risks
This work was conducted as part of the effort under “Subtask 3.2 – Apply NRAP Tools to Assess
Geologic Risks” in the CUSP main project and Kansas Focused Project. This task evaluates
potential geologic risks associated with CO2 storage across multiple candidate sites in the
western United States as part of the CUSP project. The primary objective is to quantify the
likelihood and consequences of CO2 and brine leakage from deep geologic storage reservoirs
into overlying USDWs or the atmosphere. To support this effort, LANL applies the NRAP-
Open-IAM framework—a flexible, system-level modeling tool designed to translate site
characterization data and detailed reservoir simulations into probabilistic assessments of whole-
system risk (Vasylkivska et al. 2022). Through this task, NRAP tools are used to analyze a
variety of geological settings, wellbore conditions, and injection scenarios for Kansas,
California, Colorado, and Oklahoma case studies, enabling consistent comparison of leakage
behavior and potential impacts across all sites.
NRAP-Open-IAM is a modular integrated assessment model (IAM) developed by the US
Department of Energy’s NRAP to support rapid yet scientifically defensible evaluations of CO2
storage system performance. The framework links ROMs representing key subsurface
components—including reservoir pressure and plume migration, wellbore leakage pathways, and
USDW aquifer response—into a computationally efficient system model capable of running
thousands of simulations to explore parameter uncertainty. By coupling site-specific simulation
outputs (e.g., pressure and CO2 saturation from the Computer Modelling Group [CMG;
https://www.cmgl.ca/solutions/software/gem/] or Subsurface Transport Over Multiple Phases
[STOMP; White et al. 2012]) with NRAP’s component ROMs, NRAP-Open-IAM provides a
consistent and transparent method for screening potential storage sites, identifying influential
parameters, and estimating probabilistic leakage risks.
The overall NRAP workflow is illustrated in Figure 565, which outlines the five-step approach
used to predict whole-system risk performance. Step 1 divides the geologic storage system into
discrete components, such as reservoir, wellbore, and aquifer units. Step 2 develops detailed
component models for each subsystem, calibrated and validated against laboratory experiments
and field data. Step 3 transforms these detailed physics-based models into efficient ROMs that
accurately replicate component behavior while enabling rapid computation. Step 4 links the
ROMs within an IAM, allowing system-level interactions and feedbacks to be simulated. Finally,
Step 5 exercises the full-model framework to explore system performance and evaluate CO2 and
brine leakage risks across a wide range of operational and geologic uncertainties. This structured,
hierarchical approach enables NRAP-Open-IAM to provide rigorous, site-specific risk insights
while maintaining computational efficiency suitable for broad regional assessments.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 565 The National Risk Assessment Partnership’s approach for rapid prediction of whole-system risk
performance

 Subtask 1.1 – Kansas Case Study
This subtask summarizes risk analysis of potential CO2 and brine leakage and their impact on the
USDW at the Kansas ONEOK (ONEOK is headquartered at Tulsa, OK) site. This work is
supported by the CUSP West focused study project ONEOK. A workflow was developed
importing pressure and CO2 saturation results obtained by physics-based reservoir simulator
(STOMP) into NRAP Integrated Assessment Model (NRAP-Open-IAM). Quantitative risk
assessment of CO2 and brine leakage, and their aquifer impact was carried out. Preliminary
leakage risk analysis for 30-yr injection into two targeted storage formations (Bushton-LKC,
Arbuckle) shows promising results with minimal leakages in the concerned domain area.
Following component models of the NRAP-Open-IAM system model were included for this
study: Stratigraphy for the vertical structure of the system, Lookup Table Reservoir for
heterogeneous CO2 storage reservoir, Wellbore component for potential leaky wells, FutureGen2
Aquifer component for USDW. The numerical simulations for this analysis consider an
approximately 37,000 by 37,000 ft2 area with wells penetrating to two storage formations.
Injection well locations and existing wells penetrating each targeted storage formation in the
domain are identified. The legacy wells closely surrounding injection wells are chosen for
leakage risk analysis for this study (Table 88). There are 69 existing wells penetrating the
concerned domain area for LKC formation, and 124 existing wells for Arbuckle storage
formation. Figure 566a and Figure 566b show the locations of injection well and existing wells
that penetrate the CO2 injection formation for the two targeted storage reservoir, respectively.

 Subtask 1.3 – Colorado Case Study
This effort is part of the CUSP main project with data provided by Colorado School of Mines.
This subtask presents a preliminary assessment of CO2 and brine leakage risks for a potential
geologic CO2 storage site in Colorado. Using NRAP-Open-IAM (v2.7.2), the analysis evaluates
potential leakage through a selected legacy production well located near the proposed injection
location. The study integrates reservoir pressure and CO2 saturation outputs from CMG
simulations with ROMs representing the wellbore system and an overlying carbonate USDW
aquifer. The primary objective is to quantify the magnitude, timing, and uncertainty associated
with potential leakage to shallow groundwater and the atmosphere under a 130-yr simulation
period, including 30 yr of injection followed by 100 yr of postinjection site care (PISC).
Figure 586 summarizes the stratigraphic configuration and the modeled storage domain. The

from 0.1 to 8 mD. The CO2 injection well is positioned at the center of this domain, with a
constant injection rate of 1 Mt CO2/yr during the 30-yr injection period. Among the 15 existing
wells (4 vertical and 11 horizontal) that penetrate the reservoir interval, a single legacy well—
Prod_v1, located approximately 348 m from the injector—was selected for detailed leakage risk
evaluation due to its proximity and potential to represent a worst-case leakage pathway.

 Task 2 – Evaluating Regional Infrastructure: Four Corners

This effort is part of the “Subtask 4.1 – Catalog, Map, and Evaluate Extant and Near-Term CO2
Distribution Network” in the CUSP main project. This task evaluates regional CO2 transport and
storage infrastructure in the Four Corners region using the SimCCS optimization framework
(Chen et al. 2024). The analysis focuses on phase-based pipeline network development and
quantifies how EJ constraints influence pipeline routing, total network distance, and system-wide
costs. By comparing scenarios with and without restrictions that prevent pipelines from crossing
disadvantaged or tribal communities, the study reveals how incorporating EJ considerations
affects capture, transport, energy consumption, and storage costs. Results indicate that EJ
constraints consistently increase overall pipeline length and system costs, demonstrating the
importance of explicit socioeconomic considerations in CO2 infrastructure planning.

 SimCCS Introduction
SimCCS is an optimization platform designed to identify cost-effective, large-scale CO2 capture,
transport, and storage infrastructures across a region. It integrates spatial data, engineering
constraints, and economic parameters to generate optimized solutions for pipeline routing,
facility siting, and storage allocation. The model simultaneously determines:
• The optimal set of point sources to implement CO2 capture
• The pipeline network topology and phasing strategy
• CO2 flow and capacity requirements across the network
• Storage site selection and injection allocation
SimCCS uses a mixed-integer linear programming (MILP) formulation that balances system-
wide cost minimization with user-defined constraints. These constraints may include land-use
restrictions, terrain, rights-of-way, community impacts, phase-wise infrastructure development,
or regulatory boundaries. The tool is therefore well suited for evaluating emerging CCS
regions—such as Four Corners—where infrastructure must be planned holistically to integrate
multiple emitters and storage sites within a diverse social and environmental landscape.
In this task, SimCCS is applied to examine the impact of EJ constraints on CO2 pipeline
development. Specifically, the model is used to compare optimized buildouts that allow pipelines
to cross disadvantaged or tribal communities versus those that exclude such routes. This
comparison isolates the effects of EJ considerations on routing feasibility, pipeline length, and
overall system costs.

 Four Corners Case Study
To evaluate how EJ constraints influence CO2 infrastructure planning, SimCCS was used to
generate optimized pipeline networks for three sequential development phases that represent

 851

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

progressively larger volumes of CO2 becoming capturable and transported across the region,
culminating in approximately 66.4 Mt/yr CO2 capture in Phase 3. For each phase, the model was
run both with and without routing restrictions. In the constrained scenario, pipeline segments are
prohibited from crossing census-defined disadvantaged communities and tribal lands, requiring
the system to reroute infrastructure around these protected areas. Figure 595 and Figure 596
summarize the resulting pipeline networks for all phases: Figure 595 shows the optimized Phase
1 through 3 routes without EJ restrictions, whereas Figure 596 presents the corresponding
networks when constraints are applied. A comparison between the two sets of results shows that
EJ constraints systematically increase total pipeline length—by 10.8% in Phase 1, 4.5% in Phase
2, and 7.5% in Phase 3—reflecting the additional distance required to circumvent restricted
zones as CO2 capture volumes scale upward. These longer pipeline corridors directly translate
into higher CO2 transport-related construction, operation and maintenance (O&M), and energy
costs, and some storage costs also increase due to shifts in CO2 allocation among injection sites.
Table 91 provides a detailed cost breakdown for Phase 3, illustrating consistent increases in
construction, O&M, energy, and storage categories when EJ constraints are enforced.

 (a) Phase 1 (b) Phase 2 (c) Phase 3

The Phase 3 cost results highlight how EJ routing constraints affect both CO2 transport and
storage economics in the Four Corners region. Because construction, O&M, and energy costs in
Table 91 all represent transport-related costs, the increase in pipeline length from 5,198.65 km

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

(without EJ constraints) to 5,589.99 km (with constraints) directly drives higher transport
expenditures. Specifically, construction cost rises from $0.04/tCO2 to $0.07/tCO2, while
transport O&M cost increases from $0.08/tCO2 to $0.11/tCO2. Energy cost shows the largest
relative change among the transport components, increasing from $0.49/tCO2 to $0.71/tCO2 due
to greater compression requirements and frictional losses along the longer pipeline routes.
Storage costs also increase slightly, from $4.76/tCO2 to $4.94/tCO2, reflecting changes in
injection allocation once routing detours are imposed. In contrast, capture costs remain
unchanged at $48.89/tCO2 because they are independent of pipeline routing. With an updated tax
credit of $80/tCO2, these results collectively demonstrate that while EJ constraints introduce
measurable increases in transport and storage costs, the system remains economically favorable
overall, and the added expense represents a manageable tradeoff for incorporating social-equity
considerations into regional CCS infrastructure planning.

SimCCS modeling for the Four Corners region shows that incorporating EJ constraints has a
clear and measurable impact on CO2 transport network design and associated infrastructure
costs. Requiring pipelines to avoid disadvantaged and tribal communities consistently increases
total pipeline length across all development phases, which in turn raises transport-related
expenses—including construction, O&M, and energy costs—because longer and less direct
routes require more materials, increased maintenance, and greater compression power. Storage
costs also increase modestly as CO2 injection patterns shift to accommodate changes in transport
routing, while capture costs remain unaffected. Even with these cost increases, the system
remains economically favorable under the updated $80/tCO2 tax credit, demonstrating that EJ
considerations can be integrated without compromising the viability of regional CCS
development. Overall, the results highlight the importance of SimCCS as a decision-support tool
for balancing cost efficiency with social-equity objectives, enabling the design of CO2
infrastructure networks that are both technically optimized and aligned with broader community
and environmental priorities.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

  Task 3 – Develop RRIs
This task is part of “Subtask 4.6 – Develop Regional Readiness Indices” in the CUSP main
project. In this task, we investigated two types of storage site risks—induced seismicity risk and
leakage risk of the storage site—on regional pipeline network routing. For the first type of risk,
we introduced a “capacity multiplier” for each storage site to limit the maximum cumulative CO2
injection volume, thus, mitigating potential induced seismicity. As for the second type of risk,
considering the leakage potential due to the presence of legacy wells penetrating a storage
formation, it becomes necessary to implement corrective action (such as well cleaning and well
plugging) and ensure the safety of CO2 injection operations. The two risk factors evaluated in
Task 3—induced seismicity and leakage risk associated with legacy wells—directly impact
regional readiness for large-scale CO2 storage. Induced seismicity risk limits the effective
storage capacity that can be safely utilized, which in turn alters pipeline routing, flow allocation,
and overall infrastructure design. Similarly, leakage risk increases storage cost due to required
corrective actions and can change which storage sites are economically viable. These risks
influence the technical, economic, and regulatory feasibility of deploying regional CO2 transport
and storage networks, making them essential components of the RRIs.

 Impact of Induced Seismicity Risk on Pipeline Routing
The risk for induced seismicity increases with the cumulation of the amount of CO2 injected for
geologic CO2 storage operation. To reduce this risk, it is recommended to limit the maximum
volume of CO2 injection. In this subtask, we first performed experiments using Sequestration of
CO2 Tool (SCO2T; Middleton et al. 2020) tool to understand the correlation between CO2
injectivity and a predefined “safety factor”, which is the ratio of actual CO2 injection pressure
and the maximum allowable injection pressure (90% of formation fracture pressure). A larger
safety factor indicates a higher CO2 injection pressure is allowed for the geologic CO2 storage
operation. We found that CO2 injectivity is almost linearly correlated with the safety factor, that
is, the higher safety factor corresponds to a higher CO2 injectivity. Based on this observation, we
incorporate a capacity multiplier (equal to or less than one) into our modeling. Specially, we first
adjust the maximum CO2 storage capacity by multiplying the capacity multiplier (equivalent to
safety factor) and next use the adjusted storage capacity for pipeline design using SimCCS tool.
To test and evaluate this, we designed a simple hypothetical case study as shown in Figure 597.
This case is in the western region of Colorado and comprises 8 CO2 sources and 4 CO2 storage
sites. The entire CCS project lasts for 20 yr, and the optimization was conducted using our newly
developed temporal modeling capability in SimCCS. The maximum CO2 capture amount is 20.8
Mt CO2/yr from the 8 sources. For this subtask, the maximum CO2 storage capacity for K1 to K4
is 150, 300, 200, and 200 Mt, respectively. We designed four scenarios as presented in Table 92.
Specifically, we set the capacity multiplier to 1.0 for all four storage sites in Run 1. Starting from
Run 2, we gradually reduced the capacity multipliers for K1 and K2 to simulate the increased
risk of induced seismicity, while keeping the capacity multipliers for K3 and K4 unchanged.

The optimization results are shown in Figure 597. For Run 1, the captured CO2 (130 Mt) from
sources S3, S4, and S6 are transported to K1, which is below the CO2 storage capacity of K1
(150 Mt). Similarly, the 286 Mt captured CO2 from the remaining sources is transported to K2
for storage. Again, this amount is below the CO2 storage capacity of K1 (300 Mt). For Run 2,
because the capacity multipliers for K1 and K2 are reduced to 0.9, thus, the corresponding CO2
storage capacities become 135 and 270 Mt, respectively. As shown in Figure 597(b), the updated
storage capacity of K1 still meets the storage capacity requirement, therefore, no change is
necessary for the lower portion of the pipeline network. However, the updated capacity of K2
(270 Mt) due to the risk of induced seismicity is below the cumulative capture amount at S1, S2,
S5, S7, and S8 (286 Mt), therefore, K3 is used as a secondary storage site to store 16 Mt CO2.
We can see that a pipeline is modeled to be constructed to connect S1 and K3. Similar
observations can be found in the remaining runs. In Runs 3 and 4, the CO2 storage capacities for
K1 and K2 are further reduced to simulate a higher risk for induced seismicity. The storage site
K1 no longer meets the required storage capacity, therefore the additional CO2 from S3, S4, and
S6 has to be transported to K3.

 Impact of Leakage Risk on Pipeline Routing
In this subtask, we developed an approach to take into account the risk of increase in storage cost
due to the presence of legacy wells and potential leakage risk. A brownfield generally has a
larger number of legacy wells than a greenfield. After a detailed analysis using SimCCS’ storage
model SCO2T tool, we found that the CO2 storage cost can be impacted by the corrective action
cost for legacy wells at a given storage site. Thus, we used well density (with the unit of
wells/mile2) as one parameter to describe the number of wells. A higher well density indicates
more legacy well penetrating a storage site. Here, well density for a greenfield is equal to 0
wells/mile2 because there are no existing legacy wells penetrating the site. In our previous
simulations, we assumed that the well density is 0.25 wells/mile2. According to SLB’s (formerly
Schlumberger; London, UK) field experience, the suggested minimum distance between two
wells is 900 ft, which corresponds to a well density of 34.4 wells/mile2, which was chosen as the
largest legacy well density if we consider CO2 storage in a brownfield.
In this subtask, we investigated the impact of legacy well density on storage cost (see Figure
598) based on the National Carbon Sequestration Database and Geographic Information System
(NATCARB) database with 314 saline storage formations. Scenario 2 corresponding to legacy
well density of 0.25 wells/mile2, is our base scenario for comparison. Scenario 1 is assumed to be
a greenfield with a well density of 0 wells/mile2. The well density for Scenarios 3 to 6 is 1, 10,
20, and 34.4 wells/mile2, respectively. Clearly, as well density increases, the overall CO2 storage
cost increases. Compared with the base scenario, there is a cost reduction of 1.74% for
greenfield. If the well density is increased from 0.25 to 1 well/mile2, the cost increases by 5.23%
compared to the base scenario. The highest increase in cost can be found for Scenario 6 when the
well density is 34.4 wells/mile2 (maximum allowable legacy well density). This analysis
indicates that well density (i.e., the number of legacy wells) has a big impact on the final storage
cost due to the cost of potential corrective actions for the legacy wells.

The final optimized pipeline routes from our SimCCS modeling are presented in Figure 599.
Clearly, for Run 1 (see in Figure 599(a)), the captured CO2 from sources S1, S2, S5, S7, and S8
are transported to K2 for storage. K1 is used to store the captured CO2 from the remaining three
sources. For Run 2 in Figure 599(b), because the well density of K1 and K2 increases to 1
well/mile2, the corresponding storage costs also increase. In particular, the storage cost of K2
becomes 7.295 instead of 6.663 $/tCO2. The higher storage cost makes the actual CO2 storage

cost of K2 increases to 9.63 $/tCO2 for Run 3. It is not economically feasible to store CO2 in K2
for these scenarios. Therefore, the lowest cost site, i.e., K3 (6.66 $/tCO2) is selected for CO2
storage. As shown in Figure 599(c), a new pipeline network is optimized to connect CO2 sources
to K3.

The results of Task 3 show that both induced seismicity risk and leakage risk associated with
legacy wells significantly influence regional readiness for CO2 storage by altering effective
storage capacity, storage cost, and optimized pipeline routing. When seismicity-related capacity
multipliers reduce the usable volume at a storage site, SimCCS shifts CO2 flows to alternative
sites, resulting in new pipeline connections and higher system costs. Likewise, increased leakage
risk—represented through higher legacy well densities—raises corrective-action costs and can
render certain storage sites uneconomic, prompting rerouting of CO2 to lower-risk formations
even if they lie farther from major emission sources. These findings demonstrate that geologic
risk factors shape the technical and economic feasibility of regional CO2 transport and storage
systems, and therefore need to be incorporated directly into RRIs to accurately assess a region’s
preparedness for large-scale CCS deployment.

  Task 4 – Characterizing Subsurface Structures for GCS at
  Iron Mountain in Utah
This effort is part of Utah focused project “CCS at the Iron Mountain Iron Mine and Direct
Reduced Iron Processing Plant, Southern Utah”. Subsurface structure imaging and fault detection
are essential for site characterization and risk assessment in GCS. In this study, we use 2D
surface seismic data acquired at Iron Mountain, Utah, USA, to characterize subsurface structures.
The data were collected with Vibroseis sources along three 2D walkaway lines, with a source
spacing of approximately 91 m, receiver spacing of about 45 m, and line lengths ranging from 9
to 15 km. We analyze two of these lines, Line 7B and Line 9, to construct 2D velocity models
using first-arrival traveltime tomography (FATT) and pre-stack depth MVA. RTM with the
MVA-updated velocity models produces high-resolution images of the subsurface, and a
machine learning algorithm is subsequently applied to delineate faults in the migration results.
These analyses provide critical insights into the subsurface structures and support the assessment
of GCS feasibility at Iron Mountain.

To mitigate anthropogenic CO2 emissions, researchers are focusing on decarbonizing heavy
industries such as iron production. In conventional processes, iron is refined by reacting iron ore,
which contains iron oxides (Fe2O₃), with carbon monoxide (CO) to yield pure iron and CO2.
Traditionally, CO is generated by burning coal in a low-oxygen environment or within a blast
furnace. However, this method releases significant amounts of greenhouse gases and other
pollutants into the atmosphere.
In contrast, the DRI process refines iron by reacting iron ore in a reactor vessel with synthesis
gas (syngas), a mixture of CO and hydrogen (H2), produced through the catalytic reforming of
methane (CH₄) rather than the combustion of coal. In DRI, iron ore reacts with CO and H2 to
produce pure iron, CO2, and water (Battle et al. 2024). The resulting CO2 stream is relatively
pure and can be dried and either utilized for industrial applications or permanently stored through
geological carbon sequestration.
To evaluate a potential site for CCS associated with DRI production, we characterized the
subsurface of a proposed DRI plant in southern Utah using legacy seismic data acquired in the
 858

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

1980s. The prospective DRI-CCS field is located in the Iron Springs District in the southwestern
part of Utah. A geologic map of the area, modified from Blank and Mackin (1967), is presented
in Figure 600.

Figure 600 Geologic map of Iron Mountain, Utah, showing Seismic Line 7B (red) and Line 9 (blue). Green dots
indicate wells drilled in the region, and the gray ellipse marks the CO 2 injection area of interest. Modified from
Blank and Mackin (1967).
The target formation for CO2 sequestration is the Navajo Sandstone, a Jurassic-aged, porous
sandstone situated at a depth of approximately 1,890 m (6,200 ft) below the surface. Preliminary
studies suggest that this formation has the capacity to store at least 15 million tons of CO2
(Moodie et al. 2022). The Navajo Sandstone is overlain by several potential caprock formations,
including the Jurassic Temple Formation, composed primarily of evaporites, and the Jurassic
Carmel Formation, which consists of mudstones and limestones.

 859

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

In certain areas of the site, outlined by the red dashed line in Figure 600, the Jurassic Carmel
Formation is intruded by several hundred meters of quartz monzonite laccolith (Rowley and
Barker 1978; van Kooten 1988). A geologic cross-section illustrating these formations is shown
in Figure 601.

Figure 601 Geologic cross-section from west to east across the Iron Mountain area showing the Jurassic Navajo
Sandstone reservoir layer, the Temple Formation caprock, the Carmel Formation, and the quartz monzonite
intrusion. Modified from Moodie et al. 2022.
To assess the feasibility of CCS for DRI production in this region, we analyzed 2D legacy active
seismic land data acquired along two walkaway lines (shown as red and blue lines in Figure 600)
to characterize subsurface structures. An initial layered velocity model was constructed by
applying a median filter to the sonic slowness log obtained from the Arco Three Peaks #1 well,
located at the northernmost green circle in Figure 600.
FATT (Leung and Qian 2006; Taillandier et al. 2009; Fomel et al. 2009; Tong 2021) was then
applied using the first arrival times of P-waves to refine the shallow portions (less than 1 km) of
the P-wave velocity (Vp) model. MVA (Liu and Bleistein 1995) was subsequently used to
update the deeper sections of the model.
After obtaining the MVA-updated Vp models, RTM (McMechan 1983; Fei et al. 2015) was
employed to produce pre-stack depth migration images of the subsurface. Finally, a machine
learning algorithm (Gao 2024) was applied to reduce noise, enhance image resolution, and
automatically detect faults within the migration images.

 Legacy 2D Seismic Data Acquisition and Processing
The 2D legacy seismic data were acquired at Iron Mountain, Utah, along three walkaway lines:
7B, 9, and 13. For this study, only Lines 7B and 9 were analyzed because the data quality for
Line 13 was extremely poor, preventing the extraction of any meaningful information. The
limitations of Line 13 will be discussed further in the discussion section. The geometries of Lines
7B and 9 are shown in Figure 602.

 860

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 602 Map showing the location of Line 7B (red) extending from A to A’ and Line 9 (blue) extending from B
to B’
The linear portion of Line 7B (red line) trends northwest–southeast and includes 118 common-
shot gathers, while Line 9 (blue line) trends southwest–northeast and includes approximately 183
shots. For each common-shot gather, up to 96 receiver channels were used for data acquisition.
The shot spacing was approximately 91 m, and the receiver spacing was about 45 m. The data
were sampled at a 2-ms interval, with a total recording time of 3 s.
Following standard pre-processing procedures (Yilmaz 2001), automatic gain control was
applied to attenuate ground roll noise, and a band-pass filter of 3–8–20–25 Hz was used to
suppress high-frequency noise. Two processed mid-spread common-shot gathers from Lines 7B
and 9 are shown in Figure 603. After preprocessing, Vp models were constructed for pre-stack
depth migration.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 603 Two mid-spread common-shot gathers for (a) Line 7B and (b) Line 9 after applying automatic gain
control and band-pass filtering from 3–8–20–25 Hz

 Velocity Model Building
To construct the Vp models for migration imaging using the legacy 2D surface seismic data at
Iron Mountain, we first developed an initial layered velocity model based on sonic well log data
from the Arco Three Peaks #1 well and interpreted formation boundaries. The shallow portions
of the Vp model along each 2D walkaway line were then refined using FATT. Following the
FATT update, we performed pre-stack Kirchhoff depth migration and subsequently refined the
deeper parts of the model through MVA.
To build the initial layered velocity models, we began with well log data and interpreted
formation boundaries from the Arco Three Peaks #1 well. The well logging data were acquired
by Schlumberger in January 1985, covering measured depths from 16.46 m (54 ft) to 3,761.2 m
(12,340 ft) at 0.1524 m (0.5 ft) intervals. A datum of 1,785 m was used for the velocity models
and migration images, and the depths of the logging data were adjusted to account for elevation
differences between the well and the seismic data reference. Median values were selected within
layer intervals on the compression slowness log to derive the layered Vp velocity profiles.
Constant velocity values were assigned to regions beyond the logged interval, and the resulting
1D velocity profile was used to build the layered initial models down to a depth of 4.5 km. The
median velocity layers and corresponding sonic log velocities are shown in Figure 604, and the
initial Vp models for each walkaway line are presented in Figure 605.

Traveltime tomography was then applied using the first arrivals of P-waves to refine the shallow
portions of the velocity models. After 40 iterations, the traveltime misfit was reduced by more
than 95% for both Lines 7B and 9. The convergence curves for relative misfit, along with
histograms of traveltime misfits before and after tomography, are shown in Figure 606 and
Figure 607, respectively. The updated Vp models after FATT for Lines 7B and 9 are displayed in
Figure 608, showing significant improvements in the shallow regions of the models
(approximately the upper 1 km). These FATT models were then used for MVA.

Following the FATT updates, pre-stack Kirchhoff depth migration was performed along both

 Results of Reverse-Time Migration and Fault Detection
After constructing the velocity models using sonic logging data, FATT, and MVA, and
processing the PP reflections, we applied RTM to obtain high-resolution PP images of the
subsurface structures beneath Iron Mountain. Each common-shot gather was migrated
individually, and a spatial taper mask was applied to suppress migration artifacts resulting from
limited source and receiver coverage. The raw PP RTM migration images for each line,
generated using the MVA velocity models, are shown in Figure 610.

To further enhance the imaging results, we employed a multitask machine learning (ML)
approach to denoise the RTM images, improve spatial resolution, and automatically detect faults.
The ML-denoised RTM images for Lines 7B and 9 are shown in Figure 611. Compared to the
raw RTM images, the denoised results reveal greater structural detail, with reflectors appearing
more continuous and better defined, particularly along the edges of the profiles where the raw
images exhibited smiling artifacts.

 Discussions
We overlaid the velocity models on the ML denoised migration images, as shown in Figure 613.
From the figure, there is a strong correspondence between the velocity contrasts and the seismic
reflectors. In Figure 613a, the edge of the high-velocity zone aligns closely with the dipping
reflector observed at approximately 1.5 to 0.5 km depth and 2 to 7 km horizontal distance. This
structure corresponds well with the quartz monzonite intrusion identified in the conceptual
geologic cross-section (Figure 601). Furthermore, Figure 613a indicates that our MVA
successfully resolved the lower-velocity lithologies surrounding the quartz monzonite intrusion.
The low-velocity region between 0 and 3 km horizontal distance and between 1 and 2 km depth
is clearly visible in the MVA-derived Vp model (Figure 613a), whereas it was not evident in
either the initial layered Vp model (Figure 607a) or the FATT-updated model (Figure 608a).

 871

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 613 Machine learning (ML) denoised reverse-time migration (RTM) images with automatically detected
faults (red) plotted alongside P-wave velocity (Vp) models for (a) Line 7B extending from A to A’ and (b) Line 9
extending from B to B’
The ML-denoised migration images for Lines 7B and 9 were plotted in 3D at different azimuthal
viewpoints, as shown in Figure 614. From this figure, we observe good continuity and alignment
of reflectors between Lines 7B and 9. Minor variations in reflector positions are likely due to
slight differences in the velocity fields of the two lines, as each line was processed independently
in 2D. For a more complete and accurate characterization of the subsurface structures and fault
systems, a dedicated 3D seismic survey of the region is recommended.

 872

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 614 3D plot of migration images for Line 7B extending from A to A’ and Line 9 extending from B to B’,
viewed from multiple azimuth angles
As mentioned in previous sections, Line 13 was excluded from the main analysis due to poor
data quality. A common-shot gather from Line 13 is shown in Figure 615. In contrast to the
gathers from Lines 7B (Figure 615a) and 9 (Figure 615b), where distinct parabolic reflection
patterns are visible, no clear reflections are observed in the Line 13 data. Instead, the data are
dominated by strong ringing noise. We attempted to remove this noise using Wiener
deconvolution; however, this approach did not yield any usable signal.

 873

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 615 Common-shot gather from Line 13. In comparison with data from Lines 7B and 9, no clear reflections
are observed. The dataset is also heavily contaminated by strong ringing noise, which obscures coherent seismic
signals.
FATT was performed using the first-arrival picks from Line 13 and the initial layered Vp model.
Unlike the successful convergence observed for Lines 7B and 9, the FATT results for Line 13
did not converge satisfactorily. The relative convergence curve, along with traveltime misfit
histograms before and after tomography, are shown in Figure 616. After FATT, the traveltime
misfits for Lines 7B and 9 are centered near zero, while those for Line 13 exhibit a systematic
bias toward negative misfit values, indicating poor model fitting.

 874

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 616 (a) Relative traveltime misfit convergence curve, (b) histogram of traveltime misfits before tomography,
and (c) histogram of traveltime misfits after 40 iterations for Line 13
RTM was applied to the processed Line 13 data using the FATT velocity model, and the
resulting image is shown in Figure 617. Unlike the raw RTM images of Lines 7B and 9 (Figure
610), the RTM result for Line 13 shows no coherent reflectors corresponding to the major
formations. As a result, we were unable to identify and pick any horizons to perform MVA for
this line. Due to these limitations in data quality and processing, Line 13 was excluded from
further analysis.

 875

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 617 (a) Relative traveltime misfit convergence curve, (b) histogram of traveltime misfits before tomography,
and (c) histogram of traveltime misfits after 40 iterations for Line 13

We analyzed two 2D legacy walkaway seismic datasets acquired in the Iron Mountain area of
Utah. Initial Vp models were constructed using sonic log data and subsequently refined through
FATT and MVA. RTM was then applied to generate pre-stack depth migration images of the
subsurface. Following RTM, a ML algorithm was used to denoise the migration images and
automatically detect faults.
By overlaying the Vp models on the denoised images, we demonstrated that the boundary of the
quartz monzonite laccolith was successfully resolved along Line 7B. The denoised migration
images from Lines 7B and 9 were also visualized together in 3D, revealing good correspondence
in layer continuity and structural alignment. Minor discrepancies between the two profiles are
attributed to slight variations in the Vp models at corresponding locations.
Overall, the results indicate that the processed 2D seismic data effectively delineates key
subsurface features in the study area. However, to achieve a more detailed and reliable
characterization of the subsurface structures and fault systems, acquisition and analysis of a 3D
seismic survey are recommended.

 Subtask 4.4 – Economic Assessment
• SNL developed the blueprint for cost-benefit analysis of carbon, capture utilization and
 storage projects
• SNL developed a framework for TEA of CCUS project
• SNL scaled up the framework and demonstrated regional cost analysis focusing on the
 Permian basin Region
• SNL also developed and demonstrated investigating the implications of Section 45 Q tax
 credits on economic feasibility of CCUS projects.

 Technoeconomic Analysis
The TEA framework SNL developed allows looking into the major cost drivers of CCUS, cost
minimization achieved through optimization in system component(s), as well as the levelized
cost of hydrogen storage under various scenarios. The framework consists of the following:
1. Scoping (project boundaries, capture‐transport‐storage scenarios)
2. Metric specification (capital expenditures [CAPEX] categories—site characterization, area of
 review (AoR) studies, well construction, compressor/pipeline infrastructure,
 monitoring/permit costs; operating expenditures (OPEX) categories – compressor operations
 and maintenance (O&M) cost, well O&M cost, fixed O&M costs, and other costs)
3. Analysis design (levelized costs calculation using CAPEX, capital‐recovery‐factor, and
 OPEX; mapping key CAPEX/OPEX drivers; and sensitivity analysis)
The demonstration of the framework is available in the report and published paper (see the
Reports and Products section below).

 Cost–Benefit Analysis and Evaluation of Implication of 45Q Tax Credits
For this task, SNL developed a TEA method, evaluated the economic feasibility of carbon
capture and storage (CCS) at the acid gas injection (AGI) wells, and assessed the implication of
tax credits under Section 45Q of the US Tax Code (Credit…2022) for CCS at the AGIs. We
included the following additional components on the TEA framework discussed under the
Technoeconomic Analysis section.
1. Discounted‐cash‐flow modeling; net present value (NPV), internal rate of return (IRR), and
 Benefit Cost Ratio
2. Integration of costs and benefits (45Q tax‐credit revenues) into NPV, IRR, and benefit:cost
 outputs.
All formulas and data tables are built into Excel templates that partners can adapt to local inputs.
This standardized model gives all partners a transparent, consistent way to compare CCUS
projects—across technologies, geologies, and policy scenarios—reducing uncertainty and
guiding strategic investment and permitting decisions.
The following is the abstract from our scientific journal article publication (Mishra et al., 2025;
see Section Report and Products for the full reference):
CCUS is an important pathway for meeting climate mitigation goals. While the economic
viability of CCUS is well understood, previous studies do not evaluate the economic feasibility
of CCS in the Permian Basin specifically regarding the new Section 45Q tax credits. We
developed a TEA method, evaluated the economic feasibility of CCS at the AGI wells, and
assessed the implication of Section 45Q tax credits for CCS at the AGIs. We find that the
compressors, well depth, and the permit and monitoring costs drive the facility costs.
Compressors are the predominant contributors to capital and operating expenditure driving the
levelized cost of CO2 storage. Strategic cost reduction measures identified include (1) sourcing
of low-cost electricity and (2) optimizing operational efficiency in well operations. In evaluating
the impact of the tax credits on CCS projects, facility scale proved decisive. We found that
facilities with an annual injection rate exceeding 10,000 Mt storage capacity demonstrate
economic viability contingent upon the procurement of inputs at the least cost. The new
construction of AGI wells was found to be economically viable at a storage capacity of 100,000
Mt. The basin is heavily focused on CCUS (tax credit – $65/Mt CO2), which overshadows CCS
($85/Mt CO2) opportunities. Balancing the dual objectives of CCS and CCUS requires planning
and coordination for optimal resource and pore space utilization to attain the basin’s
decarbonization potential. We also found that CCS on AGI is a lower cost CCS option as
compared to CCS on other industries.

 Future Work and Connections to Other Energy Applications – Support for
 Geothermal, Hydrogen, and Critical Metals and Rare Earths
SNL’s CUSP economic‐assessment—built around modular Excel workbooks for cost–benefit
and discounted cash flow (DCF) analyses—can be directly adapted to other subsurface resource
applications. Building on this, we have refined a TEA and economic feasibility analysis working
with an industry partner on a separate project. We also developed and published on TEA and
economic feasibility analysis of underground hydrogen storage on a separate project.
Furthermore, the Python-based TEA algorithms we developed are easily adaptable to TEA of
carbon, hydrogen and other sub-surface cost-analysis. By applying geothermal-specific inputs
(e.g., well‐drilling and stimulation costs, plant‐capacity factors), hydrogen‐production
parameters (e.g., deep‐drill and separation expenditures, storage‐cavern economics), or critical‐
metal and rare-earth recovery metrics (e.g., mining, processing, and adsorbent‐regeneration
costs), and defining parallel benefit streams (e.g., power sales, hydrogen revenues, rare‐earth
commodity values), the user could generate levelized‐cost, NPV, IRR, and sensitivity reports
across any of these domains. This cross‐sector reuse ensures transparent, apples‐to‐apples
economic comparisons, streamlining investment and policy decisions in geothermal, hydrogen,
and critical-mineral projects.

Part V – Working Groups
Economics Working Group
The goal of the Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP) Economics Working Group
is to develop and maintain a consistent cost–benefit framework—defining cost and benefit
categories, calibrating assumptions, and assembling capture‐cost and emissions datasets—to
underpin CUSP techno‐economic and cost‐benefit analyses. Its members include Sandia
National Laboratories (SNL), New Mexico Tech, Carbon Solutions (Saint Paul, MN), The
University of Texas Permian Basin, Montana State University, Kansas Geological Survey,
Stanford University, University of Utah, and University of Wyoming.
We hosted bimonthly meetings and facilitated discussions on economics of carbon capture,
transport, utilization, and storage with this working group. We involved interested members from
this working group in reports and peer-reviewed papers to recognize and attribute their
contributions. The Economics Working Group collaboratively created materials pertaining to
Economic Analysis of Geologic Carbon Sequestration establishing a clear, methodology for
scoping projects. In parallel, the group built a shared CO2 capture‐cost and emissions database—
harmonizing US Environmental Protection Agency (EPA) Greenhouse Gas Reporting Program
(GHGRP; EPA [year accessed]) data with partner inventories and standardizing formats—to feed
into the partnership’s analysis. Sandia conducted a literature review and provided results on the
capture costs to Carbon Solutions. The major deliverables led by SNL pertaining to this working
group are the Blueprint for economic analysis of carbon capture, utilization, and storage (CCUS)
and the journal article (Mishra et al., 2025) in International Journal of GHG control mentioned
above.

 Targa Resources (Formerly Lucid Energy Delaware) Acid
 Gas Injection Project
 Economic Risk–Related Objectives and Desired Outcomes
Economic assessment objectives included Developing a site‐specific technoeconomic method for
converting Targa’s (Houston, TX) Red Hills acid gas injection (AGI) wells to Underground
Injection Control (UIC) Class VI CO2 storage, capturing all capital and operating cost
components.

 Economic Assessment
A detailed techno‐economic model was constructed for the Red Hills AGI carbon capture and
storage (CCS) project. We developed detailed capital expenditures (CAPEX) calculation method
by disaggregating capital costs into site characterization, area‐of‐review and corrective action,
injection‐well construction, compressor/pipeline infrastructure, and monitoring/permitting
categories, then aggregating these into the total capital cost (TCC). Operating expenses—
including compressor electricity and water, well operations and maintenance (O&M), and
postinjection monitoring—were computed and added to LTCC to yield the levelized cost of CO2
storage per metric ton. The annualized CAPEX and operating expenditures (OPEX) per year

 884

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

were used to calculate the total annual cost which was then divided by annual injection amount
to calculate CCS cost ($/metric ton). We worked closely with the industry partner and shared our
method, variables, literature-based data, equations used, and the assumptions made for the
techno-economic analysis (TEA). The TEA results were shared with the industry partner.

 CCS Hub 2.0 Concept for ONEOK: Infrastructure
 Development for Handling of New Gaseous Products for
 Natural Gas Liquids Fractionation and Gas Processing
 Plants in Kansas and Oklahoma
 Economic Risk–Related Objectives and Outcomes
Objectives for economic risk-related assessment includes:
• Quantify site‐level economics (CAPEX, OPEX, levelized cost) and benefits (45Q revenues
 under Section 45Q of the US Tax Code [Credit…2022]) for ONEOK’s (Tulsa, OK) four
 injection wells under baseline, low‐cost, and high‐cost scenarios.
• Assess key economic risk categories—regulatory/policy, market/price, financing/interest‐
 rate, and community/social‐licensing—and identify mitigation strategies.
• Develop tailored guidance for Class VI permitting and 45Q compliance to streamline EPA
 and Internal Revenue Service (IRS) applications.
Intended outcomes include delivering standardized cost‐and‐benefit metrics for each injection
site, a ranked economic‐risk matrix to guide mitigation strategies, and a clear permitting and
financing roadmap to support ONEOK’s CCS Hub development.

 Risk Assessment
Economic risk assessment identifies and quantifies the key uncertainties that could undermine
project viability. For the ONEOK sites, this project’s analysis groups these into four categories—
regulatory and policy risk, market and price risk, financing and interest‐rate risk, and community
and social‐licensing risk—and applies scenario and sensitivity analyses to measure each
category’s potential impact on project net present value (NPV) and benefit:cost ratios.

 Economic Assessment
SNL conducted economic analysis to support the overarching goal of the project, which is to
identify potential carbon dioxide (CO2) reservoirs for long-term saline storage in the area
surrounding ONEOK natural gas liquids fractionation plants near Bushton, KS, and Medford,
OK, as well as several gas processing plants in Oklahoma that emit approximately 1 Mt of CO2
per annum. SNL submitted a report on economic risk/feasibility assessment, which was included
in the ONEOK report compiled and submitted by Brendan Bream (Kansas Geological Survey).
We used a three-pronged approach for this task. First, we calculated the costs of CO2
sequestration at the identified sites; second, we calculated the cost benefit ratio of sequestration
projects; and finally, we evaluated the economic risks of the project. We followed the TEA and
cost: benefit analysis methods discussed in Mishra et al. (2025) to calculate the cost of CO2
storage at identified ONEOK sites and for the economic feasibility analysis of the CCS projects.

 885

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

We identified and discussed the factors of economic risk and discussed the potential impacts on
the projects’ economic viability.
The TEA conducted for the ONEOK site demonstrates that the total capital and operational costs
associated with CO2 injection are highly dependent on well depth, equipment selection, and site-
specific geological conditions. The estimated levelized cost of CO2 storage provides a useful
benchmark for evaluating the economic feasibility of the proposed ONEOK carbon sequestration
projects. The levelized cost of CO2 storage calculated for the Bushton-LKC, Bushton-UArb,
Buston-DArb, and Medford- WilBro sites are, respectively, $10.92 (9.08–12.76), $11.01 (9.17–
12.85), $10.86 (9.02–12.69) and $11.13 (9.29–12.96) per metric ton CO2. The cost–benefit and
NPV analysis shows that all 4 of these wells are likely to be economically feasible, at least at the
injection site level.
Economic risks associated with CCS projects are categorized as Regulatory and policy risks,
market and price risks, financing and interest rate risks, and public licensing risk. The
uncertainty in the continuation as well as the period (number of years), quantity (dollar value),
and eligibility of CCS project for Section 45Q tax credits introduces economic risks for CCS
projects. Under high-cost scenario combined with high pressure difference and depth, CCS
projects are profitable only when Section 45Q Tax credits are fully realized. Finance risk is
another major risk because CCS projects require large upfront capital. Our calculation shows that
Bushton LKC requires $4.1 million to $16.4 million, Bushton UArb $4.2 million to $17 million,
Bushton DArb $9 million to $35.6 million, and Medford $4.3 million to $17 million (for details,
please refer ONEOK report). When financial returns are uncertain and the investment amounts
are large investment, investors’ confidence decreases. This adds to the financing risk. Similarly,
interest rates fluctuations add risks by affecting the costs of borrowing. For large investment
CCS projects, a small change in interest rate can impact the economic viability of the project,
specifically if the debt-to-equity ratio is higher. Another major risk factor is market conditions.
Inflation led increase in costs of equipment and inputs affect the capital expenses as well as the
operational expenses thereby increasing the economic risks of CCS projects. The high-cost items
such as the costs of compressors, costs of drilling, increased significantly from 2021 to 2025.
Because CCS is energy heavy process, cost per kilowatt-hour for instance can significantly affect
the levelized cost of CO2 storage. A higher cost of storage could convert a CCS project into an
economically unviable project.
