Analytics Working Group
The Analytics Working Group served as the computational and decision-support engine of the
Carbon Utilization and Storage Partnership (CUSP), providing the modeling consistency, data
preparation, and methodological innovation that underpinned many of CUSP’s technical
deliverables. Unlike subtasks focused on a single basin, state, or technology, the Analytics
Working Group worked across the entire CUSP region and spanned multiple subtasks, ensuring
that the data, modeling assumptions, and scenario analyses used by partners were aligned and
reproducible.
The group was led by Montana State University and strongly supported by Carbon Solutions
(Saint Paul, MN), Los Alamos National Laboratory (LANL), Pacific Northwest National
Laboratory (PNNL), and state partners from California, Kansas, Washington, Colorado, Utah,
New Mexico, Arizona, and Nevada. This diverse membership allowed the group to combine
algorithmic expertise with local data knowledge, producing analyses that were both technically
rigorous and grounded in regional priorities.
Over the course of 5 years, the group’s objectives evolved in a natural progression. In the early
stages, the primary focus was supporting data collection: Defining what SimCCS (Middleton et
al. 2020b) requires as input, creating data templates and cost curve specifications, and working
directly with state partners to identify, validate, and format emissions and storage data. This
foundational work transitioned into scenario analysis for subregions of the CUSP footprint,
beginning with Kansas and eventually including California, Nevada, Oklahoma, and the Four
Corners. In these studies, the group developed optimized carbon capture and storage (CCS)
network designs under a variety of capture targets, credit values, and routing constraints. In later
years, the group focused on regional synthesis, producing readiness indices and geospatial
mapping products that quantified each state’s relative potential for CCS deployment.
Throughout the project, the Analytics Working Group contributed to or led several key subtasks,
including:
• Subtask 3.1.1 – Identify data requirements for SimCCS modeling.
• Subtask 3.1.4 – Gather and catalog CO2 emissions (point source) databases, assisting states
 with data curation.
• Subtask 4.5 – Focused scenario analysis, executing hundreds of SimCCS runs across CUSP-
 wide states and multistate regions.
• Subtask 5.1 – Development of regional readiness indices and mapping products.
These contributions were not limited to applied modeling. The group also developed new
algorithms and formulations for multiphased buildout planning, robust design under storage
uncertainty, repair-aware network design, and genetic algorithms for national-scale optimization.
Many of these advances were peer-reviewed and published, ensuring they will continue to
benefit the CCS community beyond the life of CUSP.
The outputs of the Analytics Working Group—cleaned datasets, reproducible scenarios,
technical reports, open-source model improvements, and geospatial products—position the
CUSP region for risk-aware, cost-effective CCS deployment. By addressing uncertainty, scaling
challenges, and the need for phased infrastructure rollouts, this work supports the US

 887

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Department of Energy (DOE)’s long-term carbon management goals and helps de-risk early
infrastructure investment decisions.

 Report Organization
This report documents the Analytics Working Group’s contributions in detail, presenting each
phase of work in the chronological order in which it was undertaken over the life of the project.
Phase 1 describes the early data and scenario guidance efforts that laid the foundation for
consistent modeling across states. Phase 2 summarizes the regional scenario analyses, including
Kansas, California, Nevada, Oklahoma, Utah, and the Four Corners region, with detailed results
tables and figures. Phase 3 presents the group’s model development contributions, including
mathematical formulations, experimental setups, and case study findings. Phase 4 covers the
readiness indices and mapping work that synthesized insights into region-wide metrics. The
report concludes with cross-cutting lessons learned and overarching Analytics Working Group
contributions and results.

 Phase 1 – Foundational Data and Scenario Guidance
The initial phase of the Analytics Working Group’s work focused on establishing a consistent
foundation for CCS modeling across the CUSP region. Before full-scale scenario analyses could
be undertaken, it was necessary to standardize data formats, ensure coverage of all major
emissions sources and candidate storage locations, and align state partners on what SimCCS
requires to generate meaningful optimization results.

 Defining Data Requirements
A comprehensive specification of SimCCS data requirements was developed and distributed to
all CUSP partners. This specification detailed the minimum data needed to construct a valid
scenario, including
• Point-source data: Location coordinates, annual CO2 emissions (Mt/year), fixed and variable
 capture costs, and maximum capture capacity.
• Storage site data: Location, estimated capacity, injectivity (where available), fixed
 development cost, and variable injection cost.
• Transport network data: Candidate pipeline corridors, cost–capacity curves for each diameter
 class, and right-of-way constraints.
• Economic and policy data: 45Q credit values (under Section 45Q of the US Tax Code
 [Credit…2022]) and escalation schedules, Low Carbon Fuel Standard (LCFS) credit values,
 and assumptions about enhanced oil recovery (EOR) revenue.
Templates were provided in comma-separated values (CSV) and shapefile formats, along with
guidance for quality control and unit consistency. These templates ensured that data collected by
different states could be merged into larger regional studies without reformatting.

 Partner Engagement and Education
The group conducted early webinars and presentations for state partners to explain how SimCCS
uses input data to produce optimized infrastructure designs. These sessions demonstrated the

 888

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

three primary optimization modes available in SimCCS—CAP (minimum-cost capture of a
specified quantity), PRICE (profit-maximizing under a credit value), and TIME (minimum cost
subject to a fixed duration of injection)—and showed how pipeline routing cost surfaces are
generated. Special emphasis was placed on the importance of accurate cost curves and site
characterizations, since these directly influence which sources and sinks are selected in an
optimal solution.

 Scenario Typology and Planning Guidance
To ensure comparability across states and regions, the Analytics Working Group developed a
scenario typology that categorized potential analyses into a set of common archetypes. Example
categories included
• Baseline CAP scenarios: capturing all emissions from selected industries at least cost.
• Profit-maximizing PRICE scenarios: determining which subset of emissions can be captured
 economically under current or projected credit levels.
• Sensitivity runs: varying storage capacities, cost multipliers, and credit levels to identify
 thresholds and breakpoints.
• Phased buildout scenarios: modeling infrastructure expansion over multiple decades to reflect
 realistic project sequencing.
The scenario planning guidance also addressed how to incorporate special considerations such as
environmental justice (by adding spatial avoidance constraints), routing preferences (by
weighting existing rights-of-way), and storage reliability (by including multiple candidate
reservoirs to provide redundancy).

 Phase 2 – Scenario Development and Evaluation
Throughout the CUSP project, the Analytics Working Group conducted focused scenario
analysis of CUSP sub-regions encompassing local objectives and constraints. Data for the
scenario analyses presented in this report were collected by CUSP partners, leveraging regional
expertise in geology, energy infrastructure, and emissions data. These focused scenario analyses
described in this section focus on evaluating the geological storage capacity, CO2 capture
potential, and transport infrastructure required to implement CCS projects at scale. Each region
presents unique challenges and opportunities, shaped by local industrial emissions, geological
formations, and existing infrastructure. By systematically analyzing these factors, the Analytics
Working Group aimed to provide critical insights into how CCS can be deployed in a cost-
effective and technically viable manner to help meet regional and national climate goals.
A critical tool in these analyses is SimCCS, an optimization software specifically designed to
model the deployment of CCS infrastructure. SimCCS integrates geospatial, economic, and
technical data to develop optimal strategies for CCS project design. It does so by solving a
mixed-integer linear program (MILP) problem that seeks to minimize overall project costs while
adhering to constraints such as pipeline capacities, capture limits, and storage availability.
SimCCS is flexible and can simulate multiple scenarios, allowing for variations in tax credits,
capture rates, and infrastructure requirements. The tool’s ability to model dynamic, multiphase
projects makes it invaluable for identifying optimal CCS solutions across diverse geographic and
industrial landscapes, as demonstrated in the scenario analyses for the CUSP region. Input data

 889

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

to parameterize SimCCS is provided by CO2NCORD (CO2 capture; Carbon Solutions 2025),
CostMAP (CO2 pipeline routing; Hoover et al. 2020), and SCO2T (CO2 storage; Middleton et al.
2020a).
The data used for these scenario analyses encompass a wide array of factors, including regional
CO2 emissions, geological assessments of potential storage sites, and the availability of pipeline
routes for transporting CO2. The studies focus on key industrial emitters, such as power plants,
refineries, and natural gas facilities, alongside potential storage sites in saline formations,
hydrocarbon fields, and EOR fields. For each site, the analyses explore different scenarios to
capture both the technical feasibility and economic viability of CCS projects under varying
conditions, such as differing 45Q tax credit values and project timeframes.
In the following subsections, the report presents the findings for each CUSP region, highlighting
the specific results of the scenario analyses conducted. These findings provide actionable
insights for developing large-scale CCS infrastructure across the Western United States,
addressing both the economic challenges and environmental benefits of reducing CO2 emissions
through geological storage.

 California: San Joaquin Basin CCS Opportunities
The Southern San Joaquin Basin in California offers significant promise for the deployment of
CCS projects primarily due to its rich geological formations and proximity to large industrial
CO2 sources, as presented in Figure 618 (Kim et al. 2023, Appendix A). The CCS potential of
this region has been a major focus during the CUSP project, particularly in assessing the
economic viability and logistical feasibility of capturing CO2 from a variety of industrial sources
and storing it in the subsurface. This analysis encompasses both saline formations and
hydrocarbon fields, providing insights into the different types of storage sites and the challenges
and opportunities that face CCS adoption in California.

 890

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 618 SimCCS solution for one scenario in the California study covering various emission industries and tax
credits for an explicitly determined capture amount

 Source Types and CO2 Emitters
The industrial landscape of California presents a diverse array of CO2 sources, making it a prime
candidate for large-scale CCS deployment. In the Southern San Joaquin Basin, major CO2
sources include combined heat and power (CHP) plants, refineries, cement production facilities,
and natural gas-fired power plants. CHP systems are particularly relevant in this region due to
their simultaneous production of electricity and steam, which makes them eligible for
California’s LCFS credits.
The study identified capturable emissions from various sectors across Kern County and Southern
California, focusing on linking these sources to storage sites. In particular, thermal EOR
operations in Kern County are responsible for a large proportion of the region’s industrial CO2
emissions. The annual greenhouse gas emissions from oil and gas production operations in Kern
County averaged 12.3 MtCO2 between 2018 and 2019, making it a critical focus for CCS
initiatives. The study also analyzed emissions from cogeneration plants, cement facilities, and
hydrogen production plants, mapping these sources to storage locations based on the proximity
and capture feasibility.

 Case Studies and Technoeconomic Scenarios
Several case studies were performed to explore different scenarios for CO2 capture and storage in
the Southern San Joaquin Basin. SimCCS was used to evaluate the cost and infrastructure needs
under various scenarios, focusing on both the 45Q tax credit and the LCFS credits as key
financial incentives.

 891

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

One key case study explored the impact of the 45Q tax credit, which was modeled to provide
$85/MtCO2 stored in saline formations and $60/Mt for CO2 stored in EOR fields. This scenario
showed that the Southern San Joaquin Basin is an economically viable CCS hub, with costs for
capturing and transporting CO2 remaining within feasible ranges due to the credit availability
and high storage capacity of both saline formations and hydrocarbon fields. Another case study
examined the volatility of LCFS credits, which have fluctuated between $65/Mt and $150/Mt,
and how this affects the financial viability of CCS deployment. These credits were found to be
crucial for enhancing the economic returns from capturing emissions at CHP plants, oil and gas
facilities, and refineries.

 Seismic Fault Avoidance and Geologic Considerations
California’s complex geology requires careful planning when designing CCS infrastructure,
particularly in regions prone to seismic activity. One of the major technical challenges identified
in the study was the need to avoid seismic faults when routing CO2 pipelines and selecting
storage sites. The Southern San Joaquin Basin contains several active fault systems, and the
study employed detailed seismic risk assessments to ensure that CO2 storage locations and
transport routes are not compromised by seismic activity.
The study used seismic fault data in conjunction with SimCCS to map out optimal pipeline
routes that minimize the risk of fault-induced damage. This involved creating buffer zones
around known fault lines and avoiding areas with high seismic hazard potential when planning
storage and pipeline infrastructure. By incorporating these factors into the SimCCS model, the
study ensured that both short-term operational safety and long-term storage integrity would be
maintained.

  Conclusions and Recommendations
The Southern San Joaquin Basin was identified as a key regional hub for CCS due to its large
storage capacity, favorable proximity to CO2 sources, and the financial incentives provided by
both state and federal programs. The study concluded that with proper investment in CO2 capture
infrastructure, supported by the 45Q and LCFS credits, the region could feasibly store large
quantities of CO2 in both saline formations and hydrocarbon fields, making it a critical part of
California’s strategy to achieve net-zero emissions.
One of the key findings was the importance of phased deployment, allowing the infrastructure to
grow over time as more CO2 emitters are linked to the storage sites. This phased approach
reduces initial capital expenditures and spreads out the costs of building pipelines and storage
facilities. The study also highlighted the need for continued monitoring of seismic risks, as well
as further investigation into the long-term storage capabilities of the region’s saline formations.

 Nevada: Resilience for CCS Networks in the Face of Uncertainty
The Nevada study investigated a critical aspect of CCS infrastructure: how to manage the risk of
storage reservoir underperformance (or failure) in CCS networks. The challenge in CCS systems
is not only to capture and transport CO2 efficiently but also to ensure that storage reservoirs can
reliably sequester CO2 over the long term. This study modeled CCS infrastructure as a flow
network, presented in Figure 619, where CO2 sources, storage reservoirs (sinks), and pipelines

 892

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

are represented as edges in the graph. The research specifically explored scenarios in which
storage reservoirs (represented as edges) fail, examining how such failures impact the overall
cost and functionality of the CCS network. This analysis is particularly important in regions like
Nevada, where CO2 storage sites may be located far from industrial sources, and any failure in
storage capacity could disrupt the entire system.

Figure 619 Carbon capture and storage data for the Nevada study consisting of sources (circles), sinks (squares),
and possible pipeline routes (edges). The arrow indicates the sink that fails in the evaluated scenario.

 CO2 Sources and Storage Sites in Nevada
Nevada’s industrial landscape presents several key CO2 emission sources, primarily from power
plants, natural gas facilities, and industrial manufacturing processes such as cement production.
These emissions need to be captured and transported to distant storage sites. The vast distances
between CO2 emitters and potential storage reservoirs make Nevada an ideal case study for
exploring how reservoir failures impact CCS networks.
The study identified several candidate storage reservoirs in Nevada and surrounding regions,
each with different capacities and characteristics. These storage sites, often located in saline
formations, serve as the “sinks” in the modeled flow network. The success of the CCS network
depends on the reliability of these sinks to store CO2 without operational issues such as capacity
overruns, injectivity failures, or other disruptions that might prevent CO2 injection.

 Modeling Reservoir Failures in CCS Networks
A core focus of the Nevada study was modeling the potential failure of storage reservoirs within
the CCS flow network. In this context, a reservoir failure is not a physical pipeline failure but
rather an unexpected inability of the storage site to continue sequestering CO2, either due to
 893

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

reaching capacity limits or operational difficulties with CO2 injection. The study used a fixed-
charge network flow (FCNF) model to represent the CCS infrastructure, where CO2 sources,
pipelines, and storage reservoirs are all modeled as edges. The failure scenarios specifically
considered the edges representing storage reservoirs, allowing the study to simulate what
happens when a storage reservoir can no longer accept CO2.
The optimization model developed in the study aimed to find the most cost-effective flow of CO2
through the network, ensuring that captured CO2 is transported to available storage reservoirs. In
failure scenarios, if a reservoir edge fails (i.e., the storage site is unable to sequester additional
CO2), the network must reroute the CO2 to other available storage sites, increasing the transport
distance and costs. This rerouting represents “repairing” the network, where additional costs are
incurred due to the need to use alternative storage reservoirs that might be farther away or more
expensive to access.
The study’s multi-objective optimization framework provided a Pareto front of solutions,
allowing decision-makers to evaluate the trade-offs between minimizing initial infrastructure
costs and the costs of rerouting CO2 in the event of reservoir failures. This approach is
particularly important in regions like Nevada, where storage sites might be sparse and located far
from emission sources, making rerouting CO2 a potentially costly endeavor.

 Key Findings: Balancing Infrastructure and Failure Costs
The results of the Nevada study highlighted the significant impact that reservoir failures can have
on the overall cost and efficiency of CCS networks. The study found that while the initial
infrastructure costs could be minimized by optimizing the CO2 flow to the nearest and most cost-
effective storage sites, this strategy left the network vulnerable to failures. In scenarios where a
storage reservoir reached capacity or experienced operational issues, the costs of rerouting CO2
to alternative storage sites were substantial.
The analysis showed that building more resilient networks, which incorporate additional storage
reservoirs and redundancy, could reduce the long-term costs associated with reservoir failures.
By investing in infrastructure that allows for multiple storage options, the network can more
easily adapt to failures without significant cost increases. This is particularly relevant for
Nevada, where the geographical distances between storage sites and CO2 emitters make the
rerouting of CO2 a major cost driver in failure scenarios.
Moreover, the study identified critical reservoir edges—those storage locations whose failure
would cause the most disruption to the network. By focusing additional investment on these
critical edges, operators can mitigate the risk of costly rerouting and ensure more consistent CCS
operations. This finding suggests that future CCS development in Nevada should prioritize
storage reservoirs that offer both capacity and operational reliability, while also considering
redundancy in storage options.

 Conclusions and Infrastructure Recommendations
The Nevada study concluded that while optimizing initial CCS infrastructure is important, it is
equally crucial to build networks that are resilient to storage reservoir failures. In regions like
Nevada, where storage sites may be far from CO2 emission sources, the cost of rerouting CO2 in
the event of a reservoir failure can be high, potentially undermining the economic viability of the

 894

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

CCS project. The study recommended investing in additional storage reservoirs and building
redundancy into the network to reduce the risks associated with these failures.
Additionally, the study emphasized the importance of identifying critical storage reservoirs that
play a pivotal role in the network’s success. By reinforcing these critical edges and ensuring they
are reliable, operators can mitigate the most significant risks to the network. This approach
would allow for more stable long-term CCS operations and reduce the likelihood of costly
disruptions due to reservoir failures.

 Kansas: Statewide CCS Deployment Potential.
Kansas presents a strong case for the large-scale deployment of CCS technologies, owing to its
substantial industrial CO2 emissions and abundant geological storage capacity. The Kansas
Geological Survey collaborated with Montana State University to analyze the state’s CCS
potential, identifying 26 CO2 sources across seven industries, with a combined capturable
emissions rate of 33.76 MtCO2 per year.
The study identified 46 storage sites with a combined storage potential of approximately 2.1
GtCO2. These sites were ranked into three tiers based on their suitability for EOR operations and
geological storage. Tier 1 locations, with the highest suitability, were assigned an additional
EOR sales value of $25/MtCO2, in addition to the $35/Mt 45Q tax credit. Tier 2 and Tier 3
locations were assigned lower EOR values.
Scenarios run using SimCCS demonstrated that the deployment of CCS infrastructure in Kansas
is economically feasible, particularly when the 45Q tax credits are applied. Figure 620 presents
the infrastructure calculated by SimCCS for one scenario. The study explored both CAP (capture
all emissions) and PRICE (capture only profitable emissions) modes, concluding that Kansas
could capture up to 33.76 MtCO2 annually with the right infrastructure in place. However, under
more constrained economic scenarios, capturing 16.78 MtCO2 from the most profitable sources
was deemed optimal.

corner of the state in a multiphase project

 Four Corners Region: CO2 Transport and Environmental Justice
 Concerns
The Four Corners region presents unique challenges and opportunities for CCS deployment,
largely due to its complex land ownership and environmental justice (EJ) concerns. This study
focused on the development of CO2 transport infrastructure that accounts for the presence of
tribal lands and disadvantaged communities.
Using SimCCS, the study evaluated pipeline routing scenarios with and without EJ
considerations, as presented in Figure 621. It was found that incorporating EJ restrictions
resulted in a 10.7% increase in total pipeline length, raising transport costs by approximately
$0.80/MtCO2. Despite this increase, the study emphasized the importance of adhering to EJ
principles to ensure that pipeline infrastructure does not disproportionately impact vulnerable
communities.

Figure 621 Optimized pipelines in the Four Corners Region study without considering environmental justice
considerations
In addition to transport challenges, the study conducted a thorough risk assessment using
reservoir simulation data to evaluate the potential for CO2 leakage. The results showed that the
region’s geological formations are suitable for safe, long-term CO2 storage, provided that
appropriate monitoring and risk mitigation measures are in place.

 Conclusion
The scenario analyses conducted for the CUSP region provide valuable insights into the
opportunities and challenges of CCS deployment across diverse geological and industrial
landscapes. Each region presents unique factors that influence the economic and technical
feasibility of CCS, from the significant storage potential in California’s Southern San Joaquin
Basin to the phased approach pioneered by Kansas. By leveraging economic incentives such as
the 45Q tax credit, combined with advanced optimization tools like SimCCS, these studies
highlight the critical role that targeted CCS infrastructure can play in achieving regional and
national emissions reduction goals.

 Phase 3 – Model Development
As the CUSP project progressed from data collection to full-scale scenario analysis, it became
increasingly clear that new modeling capabilities were needed to address the challenges of
realistic CCS deployment planning. Existing single-period MILP formulations were insufficient
for representing phased infrastructure buildouts over decades. Computational bottlenecks limited
the scale of problems that could be solved to optimality, preventing tractable national-level
analyses or Monte Carlo ensembles. In addition, the ability to explore very large design spaces
efficiently was essential for robust design under uncertainty.
To address these challenges, the Analytics Working Group led a sustained research effort to
advance the state of CCS optimization modeling. This work resulted in multiple peer-reviewed
publications and major enhancements to the SimCCS modeling framework. The contributions in
this phase fall into three main categories:
• Multiphased MILP formulations that explicitly represent staged infrastructure deployment
 over time, enabling more realistic and cost-effective planning.
• Heuristic algorithms that generate near-optimal solutions orders of magnitude faster than
 exact MILP solvers, enabling national-scale studies and large scenario ensembles.
• A genetic algorithm (GA) specifically designed for the multi-capacity fixed-charge network
 flow problem (MC-FCNF), capable of efficiently exploring massive solution spaces and
 producing high-quality solutions under fixed runtime budgets.
Together, these contributions form the methodological backbone for risk-aware, large-scale CCS
infrastructure planning. The following subsections present each contribution in detail, including
mathematical formulations, algorithmic descriptions, experimental setups, and key results.

 Phased Deployment
Planning the large-scale deployment of CCS is challenging because it requires concurrently
selecting which CO2 sources to capture from, which locations to store the CO2, and where to
route the transportation pipelines (Jones et al. 2022). Large scale CCS projects will inevitably
experience variability in their economic conditions, source and reservoir availability, and project
objectives over their lifetimes. Many current CCS infrastructure modeling approaches assume a
static environment, where the infrastructure design is optimized based on a snapshot of available
sources, reservoirs, and their associated economic and capacity parameters that are assumed to
remain constant for the entire length of the project. While static models may rely on reasonable
assumptions for many applications, there are some where this static assumption is limiting:
 897

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 1. Sources or reservoirs may not be available throughout the entire project length, instead
 coming online after project initiation, or becoming inactive prior to project completion.
 2. Government policies, such as increased (or decreased) tax credits (e.g., continuation or
 increase in 45Q credits in the United States) or modified carbon taxes, that change during
 the lifetime of a project could lead to increased CCS participation from sources or
 reservoirs.
 3. Fluctuations in the price of oil could incentivize or disincentivize EOR fields to purchase
 CO2 from a CCS project over the life of the project thereby impacting CO2 sales prices.
 4. Financial constraints of the CCS project may require phased construction of the
 infrastructure over a significant period of time (e.g., 20 yr) instead of construction all at
 once.
 5. An increase (or decrease) over time in the target CO2 capture amount for a CCS project,
 due to meeting phased capture objectives.
None of these scenarios can be adequately addressed by a single-phase, static, infrastructure
design model without significant degradation in solution quality. In this effort, we proposed a
novel multiphased CCS infrastructure design model, formulated as a MILP, that concurrently
optimizes the design across multiple phases to construct a solution that is globally optimal for the
full project instead of locally optimal for individual phases. We discuss the theoretical
mechanism at play in the multiphased model's operation and show how it is able to solve more
scenarios than the single-phase model is able to solve. We also present an evaluation using real
CCS infrastructure data showing that the multiphased model is in fact able to determine cheaper
infrastructure designs than the single-phase model when solving the same problem.

 Model Formulation
In this section, we introduce the multiphased CCS infrastructure design model. We consider
input consisting of a set of CO2 emission sources, geologic storage reservoirs, candidate pipeline
components, and project phases. Sources are parameterized with phase-specific unit capture
costs and annual amounts of capturable CO2 emissions. Reservoirs are parameterized with phase-
specific unit injection costs and annual storage capacities, as well as total lifetime storage
capacities.
Candidate pipeline components are the set of possible pipeline locations that the model is
allowed to choose from when making deployment decisions. The candidate pipeline components
are generated by the existing SimCCS process of calculating paths in a weighted cost surface.
The weighted cost surface aggregates numerous properties from the underlying geography (e.g.,
population, land ownership, land cover, topography, rights-of-way) and produces a raster
quantifying the relative costs of building pipelines between the neighboring cells. Paths between
sources and reservoirs are then calculated and sparsified to produce the set of candidate pipeline
components. The result of this effort is pipeline network routing at the resolution of the raster
grid size. Pipelines component costs are represented as a set of linear functions (called trends) of
pipeline capacity versus cost. The costs of the distinct pipeline trends were obtained from the
National Energy Technology Laboratory (NETL) Transport Cost Model (NETL 2023). Using
pipeline trends instead of explicit pipeline capacities (i.e., diameters) reduces the number of
integer variables in the model. It is assumed that the capacity of the largest pipeline trend is
arbitrarily large. Pipeline construction costs are annualized by way of a capital recovery factor

 898

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

that accounts for project financing. The capital recovery factor includes the amount of time left
in the modelled project. In this way, all pipelines are paid off in the project's time period,
whether the pipeline opens in an early phase or a late one. The multiphased CCS infrastructure
design problem is formulated as a MILP below:

      ∑ 𝑎𝑖𝑡 ≥ 𝐺𝑡 , ∀𝑡 ∈ 𝑇                                                             (H)
 𝑖∈𝑆

Where constraint (A) restricts pipeline capacity by its minimum and maximum values.
Constraint (B) ensures that new and existing pipeline capacity is sufficient for the amount of CO2
to be transported. Constraint (C) enforces conservation of flow at each internal vertex. Constraint
(D) ensures that the amount of CO2 captured at each source is limited by the source's emission
rate. Constraint (E) ensures that capture amounts do not decrease between consecutive phases.
Constraint (F) limits lifetime storage for each reservoir by its maximum capacity. Constraint (G)
limits the annual storage amount in each reservoir to the phase's annual capacity of the reservoir.
Constraint (H) ensures each phase's total capture amount meets the phase's target. The version of
the model with Constraint (H) is called the CAP version. Constraint (H) can be omitted to form a
version of the model called the PRICE version that will only deploy cost negative (i.e.,
profitable) infrastructure. The PRICE version of the model is useful when considering scenarios
with price incentives for CCS projects (e.g., tax credits such as 45Q).

 Model Discussion
The multiphased model presented above will determine optimal values for the decision variables
that minimize the objective function. The model needs to be parameterized with accurate, user-
supplied, cost and capacity data. Determining accurate cost and capacity data for a specific CCS
sources and reservoirs is a complicated effort and case study specific. With appropriate input
data, the proposed multiphased model can be used to model all of the scenarios described earlier
by manipulating instance input parameters:
 1. Source or reservoir unavailability can be modelled by setting their capacities to zero in
 the phases they are unavailable in.
 2. Modifications to tax credits and carbon taxes can be modelled by subtracting the credit
 amount from the capture or storage costs. If the credit is source dependent (e.g.,
 California's Low Carbon Fuel Standard credit), then the credit should be subtracted from
 the capture costs of the sources that qualify for the credit.
 3. If the credit is reservoir dependent (e.g., 45Q), then the credit should be subtracted from
 the storage costs of the reservoirs that qualify for the credit. The model is not equipped to
 manage a credit that is both source and reservoir dependent.
 4. Proceeds from sales to EOR fields can be modelled by subtracting the unit (per metric
 ton) sales proceeds from the storage costs of each individual EOR field.
 5. Phased capture objectives can be modelled by modifying the phase-specific annual CO2
 capture target.
The multiphased model presented above is a generalization of an existing single-phase CCS
infrastructure design model. In the single-phase version of the model, the instance input
parameters and MILP decision variables are constant throughout the entire project length while
the objective of minimizing infrastructure cost remains the same. The infrastructure design for a
multiphase CCS project can be naively approximated by sequential solutions of the single-phase
model:

 901

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 1. Find optimal infrastructure to support phase 1.
 2. Mark opened infrastructure as purchased and find optimal additional infrastructure
 needed to support phase 2.
 3. Repeat for remaining phases.
The limitation of this iterative approach is that infrastructure deployed in each phase is done
without consideration given to future phases. This can lead to sub-optimal solutions for the full
project. Instead of designing infrastructure one phase at a time, the multiphased model
concurrently optimizes infrastructure for all phases. This results in infrastructure designs that are
globally optimal for the full project instead of locally optimal for the individual phases. The
multiphased model leverages three techniques for generating globally optimal solutions that
improve upon iterative single-phase solutions:
• As-needed Infrastructure Deployment. In single-phase models, any infrastructure that is
 opened needs to be opened during the entire (single-phased) project. Alternatively, in the
 multiphased model, infrastructure can open (and close) over the course of the project. This
 flexibility can lead to cost savings when infrastructure is only opened when necessary. Figure
 622 presents a scenario that illustrates this cost saving.

Figure 622 Consider the objective of capturing one unit per year for a two-year project. The single-phased and
multiphased solutions will both capture all emissions from the source and fill all capacity in both sinks. However,
the single-phased solution will deploy all sources and sinks at once, and build a one-capacity pipeline from src1 to
snk1 and one half-capacity pipeline from snk1 to snk2. Alternatively, the multiphased solution will build a one-
capacity pipeline from src1 to snk1 and fill snk1 in the one-year phase one followed by an additional one-capacity
pipeline from snk1 to snk2 to fill snk2 in the one-year phase two. This will result in a cheaper solution since pipeline
cost functions are subadditive (i.e., two one half-capacity pipelines are more expensive than a single one-capacity
pipeline.)

• Infrastructure Overprovisioning. The aggregate of optimal single-phased solutions does not
 allow for overprovisioning early phases in anticipation of future phases. Since the
 multiphased model concurrently optimizes all phases, a pipeline can be deployed in one
 phase with a larger capacity (i.e., diameter) than is necessary if a larger capacity will be
 required in a future phase. This can provide beneficial economies of scale by constructing a
 single large pipeline in an early phase instead of multiple smaller pipelines across multiple
 phases. Figure 623 presents a scenario that illustrates the power of overprovisioning in early
 phases.

 902

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 623 Suppose there are two available pipeline capacities: 1 unit per year and 2 units per year. Consider a two-
phased scenario with an objective of capturing one unit in the first one-year phase and two units in the second one-
year phase. Optimal single-phased solutions for each of the phases in isolation would result in a one-capacity
pipeline connecting the source to snk1 in phase 1 and a two-capacity pipeline connecting the source to snk 1 and one-
capacity pipeline connecting snk1 to snk2 in phase 2. This would require building two pipelines over the life of the
project between the source and snk1. Alternatively, the optimal multiphased solution would build a single two-
capacity pipeline between the source and snk1 initially in phase 1. This pipeline would be overprovisioned for phase
1 but would not require new construction in phase 2.

• Targeted Routing. Optimal pipeline routing for a single phase without consideration given to
 future phases will not necessarily result in an optimal solution across all phases. Instead, it
 may be advantageous to select a routing that is sub-optimal for the current phase but leads to
 cheaper pipeline networks in subsequent phases. By concurrently optimizing all phases, the
 multiphase model will find globally optimal pipeline routes across all phases. Figure 624
 presents a scenario that illustrates this advantage of concurrently optimizing pipeline routes
 across multiple phases.

Figure 624 Suppose pipeline costs are proportional to length. Consider a two-phased scenario with an objective of
capturing one unit in the first one-year phase and one unit in the second one-year phase. Optimal single-phased
solutions for each of the phases in isolation would result in a direct pipeline between the source and snk 1 and the
source and snk2 for a total pipeline length of 4.83. Alternatively, a cheaper pipeline network can be selected by using
the shared pipeline from src1 to the cell between snk1 and snk2, and then pipelines from that cell to snk 1 and snk2 for
a total pipeline length of 4.

 Heuristic Solvers
Deploying CCS infrastructure on a massive scale requires careful and comprehensive planning to
ensure investments are made in a cost-effective manner (Whitman et al. 2022). At its core,
designing CCS infrastructure is an optimization problem that aims to determine the most cost-
effective locations and quantities of CO2 to capture, route via pipeline, and inject for storage.
Designing CCS infrastructure can naturally be formulated as a MILP that aims to minimize total
cost, while capturing and injecting a target amount of CO2. The MILP is parameterized with a

 903

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

candidate pipeline network constructed from a weighted cost surface, and economic and capacity
data about the possible source and sink locations. We show in this research that designing CCS
infrastructure is a generalization of the well-studied NP-Hard fixed charge network flow (FCNF)
problem. This means that optimal algorithms for designing CCS infrastructure do not efficiently
scale as scenarios grow in size.
The intractability of designing CCS infrastructure impacts CCS infrastructure design studies in
three ways. First, CCS infrastructure studies are moving from local scale projects with tens of
sources and sinks to regional and national scale projects with thousands of sources and sinks. For
instances of this size, MILP implementations have not been successful at executing in a
reasonable time period (e.g., 40% gap after 72 hours). Second, many CCS infrastructure studies
explore impacts of minute changes to input parameters that arise due to uncertainty (e.g.,
reservoir specific storage potential or injectivity). Studies of this type require ensemble runs,
where thousands of differently parameterized instances are generated and solved, with results
feeding the generation of more instances. Finally, studies are being proposed that consider
continuous reservoir regions instead of discrete point locations. To solve these problems, the
infrastructure design algorithm will need to be run many sequential times where, between runs,
discrete reservoir locations are moved based on the previous iteration's solution. It is not possible
to rely on MILP formulations to solve these types of problems. New optimization techniques
need to be developed to address the problem of designing CCS infrastructure for massive
deployments.
In this research, we introduce the CCS Infrastructure Design (CID) problem and develop custom
optimization algorithms for it. We prove that CID is a generalization of the well-studied FCNF
problem and characterize its computational complexity. We then introduce three fast algorithms
for the CID problem. Finally, we evaluate the performance of the algorithms on realistic datasets
and find that they reduce running time compared to an optimal MILP, with a minimal increase in
solution costs. Reducing the time it takes to determine CCS infrastructure designs will support
national-level scenarios, undertaking risk and sensitivity assessments, and understanding the
impact of government policies (e.g., tax credits for CCS).

 Problem Formulation
Given a set of CO2 emitters (sources), geological reservoirs, and a candidate pipeline network,
the goal of the CCS Infrastructure Design (CID) problem is to determine, in a cost-minimal
fashion, which sources to capture from, which reservoirs to inject into, and which (and what
diameter) pipelines to build to capture a pre-determined system-wide quantity of CO2.
The sources and reservoirs are parameterized with an economic model consisting of fixed costs
to open locations (millions of dollars), and variable costs to utilize the locations (dollars per
metric ton of CO2 captured/injected). These costs vary based on the ease of injection at that
particular site. Candidate pipeline routes are constructed from a weighted cost surface. Pipelines
have construction and per-metric-ton utilization costs dependent on their geographic location and
the quantity of CO2 they transport. Pipelines can intuitively be represented as a number of
discrete pipeline sizes (i.e., diameters) and their associated costs and capacities. Pipeline costs
include construction and operation costs (e.g., pumping stations, maintenance). In a MILP
formulation, this representation requires an integer variable for each possible pipeline edge/size
pair, which results in a large number of variables and quickly leads to intractable formulations.

 904

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

To reduce the number of integer variables used in the MILP formulation, pipelines can be
represented as a smaller set of linear functions (called trends) of pipeline capacity versus cost.
The composition of these trends forms a pipeline capacity versus cost function that is increasing,
piecewise linear, and subadditive. An example of two trends approximating the non-linear
pipeline capacity versus cost function is presented in Figure 625. The pipeline costs that the
trends approximate were determined using the National Energy Technology Laboratory's CO2
Transport Cost Model. The increasing and subadditivity properties of the cost function enforces
that a pipeline of a given capacity is cheaper than multiple pipelines of smaller capacities or a
pipeline of a larger than necessary capacity. It is also assumed that the capacity of the largest
pipeline trend is arbitrarily large. Using pipeline trends instead of explicit diameters} allows for
simpler formulations compared to the discrete formulation while still ensuring that the cost
model is realistic. All fixed construction costs are annualized by way of a capital recovery factor
that accounts for project financing. The CID problem based on linearized pipelines is formulated
as an MILP is a similar fashion as previously presented.

Figure 625 Two linear trends approximating the cost of a pipeline given the transportation volume

 Computational Complexity
CID generalizes the Fixed Charge Network Flow (FCNF) problem: Consider a directed graph
with edge capacities and fixed edge costs. Purchasing an edge incurs its fixed cost and allows it
to host any amount of flow up to its capacity. A subset of the vertices is designated as sources
and have an associated amount of flow they are able to supply. Likewise, a subset of the vertices
is designated as sinks (analogous to reservoirs in the CID problem) and have an associated
amount of flow they demand. The goal of the FCNF problem is to determine a least-cost set of
edges that allows sufficient flow to be routed from the sources to the sinks to satisfy all of the
sink demand.
Theorem: 𝛾 ln |𝑉|-approximation algorithm for the FCNF problem, where 0 < 𝛾 < 1 is some
constant, unless P=NP.
Proof: This complexity result is via an approximation-preserving reduction from the Dominating
Set problem: Given a graph 𝐺 = (𝑉, 𝐸), find a minimum sized 𝑈 ⊆ 𝑉 such that for each vertex 𝑣
in 𝑉 ∖ 𝑈, there is some vertex 𝑢 in 𝑈 such that the edge (𝑢, 𝑣) is in 𝐸.

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Let 𝐺 = (𝑉, 𝐸) be an instance of Dominating Set where |𝑉| = 𝑛. 𝐺 reduces to an FCNF instance
𝐺′ = (𝑉′, 𝐸′) as follows: For each vertex 𝑣 in 𝑉, make a new vertex 𝑣𝑖𝑛 . Make a directed edge
with cost zero and capacity one from the new vertex to the original one (the dotted red edges in
Figure 626). For every edge 𝑒 = (𝑢, 𝑣) in 𝐸, make the directed edges (𝑢, 𝑣𝑖𝑛 ) and (𝑣, 𝑢𝑖𝑛 ) with
cost zero and capacity one (the solid black edges in Figure 626). Create a new vertex 𝑠 and for
each vertex 𝑣 in 𝑉, make the directed edge (𝑠, 𝑣) with cost one and infinite capacity (the dashed
green edges in Figure 626). Let the original vertices 𝑉 be the sinks and each have a demand of
one. Let 𝑠 be the single source and let its supply be |𝑉|. Figure 626 shows the reduction from
Dominating Set to FCNF.

Figure 626 Dominating Set reduction to the FCNF problem where each edge is weighted as (cost, capacity)
Suppose that 𝑈 ⊆ 𝑉 is a dominating set of 𝐺 with |𝑈| = 𝑘. For each vertex in 𝑉 ∖ 𝑈, associate it
with one neighbor that is in 𝑈. In this way, each vertex 𝑢 in 𝑈 is associated with a set of
neighbors 𝑁𝑢 that are in 𝑉 ∖ 𝑈. 𝑈 can now be translated into a source-sink flow of cost 𝑘 in 𝐺′.
For each vertex 𝑢 in 𝑈, push |𝑁𝑢 | + 1 units of flow from the source 𝑠 to 𝑢. One unit of that flow
will be consumed by 𝑢 and the additional |𝑁𝑢 | units of flow will be distributed to the neighbors
in 𝑁𝑢 . Consider a vertex 𝑣 in 𝑉 ∖ 𝑈. This vertex has been associated with a single neighbor
vertex 𝑢 that is in 𝑈. Since 𝑣 and 𝑢 are neighbors in 𝐺, the directed edges (𝑢, 𝑣𝑖𝑛 ) and (𝑣𝑖𝑛 , 𝑣)
are in 𝐺′ and form a path from 𝑢 to 𝑣. The capacity of this path is one, so one unit of flow can be
pushed to each vertex 𝑣 in 𝑉 ∖ 𝑈 from its associated neighbor vertex 𝑢 in 𝑈. Therefore, this flow
will satisfy all demand in 𝐺′ and its cost will be 𝑘 since the only costs incurred are the fixed unit
costs for sending flow to the nodes directly connected to source 𝑠 (i.e., the vertices in 𝑈).
Suppose there is a flow solution to 𝐺′ of cost 𝑘. This means that every vertex in 𝑉 receives one
unit of flow from source 𝑠. Let 𝑈 be the set of vertices receiving flow directly from source 𝑠.
Since the only costs incurred in the flow network are on vertices receiving flow directly from
source 𝑠, |𝑈| = 𝑘. Consider a vertex 𝑣 in 𝑉 ∖ 𝑈. Suppose that 𝑣 was able to forward flow to
another vertex in 𝑉′. This would require 𝑣 receiving more than one unit of flow, since 𝑣's
demand for one unit needs to be satisfied. There are only two directed edges into 𝑣: (𝑣𝑖𝑛 , 𝑣) and
(𝑠, 𝑣). Since 𝑣 is not in 𝑈, the directed edge (𝑠, 𝑣) is not carrying any flow. Since the capacity of
(𝑣𝑖𝑛 , 𝑣) is one, all of the flow carried on this edge must be used to satisfy 𝑣's demand. Therefore,
there is no excess flow available for 𝑣 to forward to another vertex in 𝑉′. This means that every
vertex in 𝑉 ∖ 𝑈 must be receiving flow from a neighbor that is in 𝑈, which means that 𝑈 is a
dominating set of 𝑉.
Since any dominating set in 𝐺 of size 𝑘 corresponds to a flow in 𝐺′ of cost 𝑘 and conversely,
inapproximability results the Dominating Set problem hold for the FCNF problem. It has been
shown that there exists a constant, 0 < 𝛾 < 1, such that the Dominating Set problem cannot be
 906

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

approximated within a factor of 𝛾 ln |𝑉| unless P=NP, thus this result holds for the FCNF
problem as well.
Corollary: The CID problem has the same inapproximability result as the FCNF problem.
Proof: CID generalizes the classic FCNF problem by allowing parallel edges representing
different pipeline sizes. Other apparent differences between CID and FCNF are not actually
generalizations of the FCNF model: Source and reservoir costs and capacities can be pushed to a
new edge between the original source/reservoir and a new node. Also, allowing only a subset of
the demand to be captured can be enforced with a new source node that feeds the original
sources and a new reservoir node connected to the original reservoirs with the required demand
(i.e., the target CO2 capture amount).
As such, CID cannot be easier to approximate than FCNF.

 Algorithms
Existing approaches to solving CCS infrastructure design type problems rely on exact
techniques, specifically solving MILPs like the ones detailed throughout this report. The running
time of MILP solvers does not scale linearly with linearly increasing input size. Large instances
(e.g., thousands of vertices and pipeline components) cannot be solved by MILPs in a reasonable
time, which motivates the search for sub-optimal techniques with better running time
performance. In this section, we present three algorithms for CID.

 Greedy Add
The first algorithm we introduce iteratively builds a solution by greedily selecting cheap (source,
reservoir) pairs, as well as the cheapest appropriately sized pipelines connecting them. This
algorithm is presented in Algorithm 1 and detailed below with references to the applicable lines
of Algorithm 1.
First, for each (source, reservoir) pair, the maximum amount of CO2 that is able to be transferred
between the pair is determined. This value is calculated as the minimum of the source's
uncaptured production, the reservoir's unused capacity, and the amount of the target capture
remaining (line 4).
Second, the (source, reservoir) pair's capture and storage costs are calculated. Fixed costs are
only included if the source or reservoir has not yet been opened (lines 6-11). Variable costs are
included based on the amount of CO2 that was determined to be transferred between the source
and reservoir (line 5).
Third, the cheapest path between the source and reservoir for the amount of CO2 that will be
transferred is calculated. To calculate the cheapest path, the pipeline network first needs to be
parameterized with costs that reflect the cost to transport that amount of CO2 along each pipeline
component. These costs need to take into account the following considerations:
 1. Unused pipeline capacity that has already been purchased.
 2. Upgrade costs associated with moving from one trend to a higher capacity trend.
 3. Changes to the variable costs for CO2 already being transported along that pipeline
 component associated with changing pipeline trends.

 907

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

 4. Cost savings associated with downsizing pipeline capacities due to redirecting CO2 (i.e.,
 pushing CO2 in the opposite direction of CO2 already being transported).
Parameterizing the pipeline network with costs is done in lines 13-27. Each pipeline component
𝑒 = (𝑢, 𝑣) is sequentially considered as a directed edge. Depending on the pipeline trend already
purchased and existing CO2 flow on 𝑒 or 𝑒′ = (𝑣, 𝑢), there are three possibilities for the new
pipeline's required volume and the existing pipeline's cost:
 1. 𝑒 is already hosting CO2 (lines 14-16). In this case, the new volume of CO2 on 𝑒 will be
 the existing volume plus the new amount being transported. The old pipeline cost is the
 old cost of 𝑒.
 2. 𝑒′ is already hosting CO2 (lines 17-19). Pipelines cannot transport CO2 in both directions.
 If 𝑒′ is already hosting CO2, adding flow in the opposite direction on 𝑒 represents
 redirecting CO2 that was traveling from 𝑣 to 𝑢. If 𝑒′ is hosting less CO2 than the amount
 being transported, the new volume of CO2 on 𝑒 will be the new amount minus the amount
 𝑒′ is currently hosting. If 𝑒′ is hosting more CO2 than the amount being transported, the
 new volume of CO2 on 𝑒′ would be the amount 𝑒′ is currently hosting minus the new
 amount. In either case, the magnitude of the difference is the new volume of CO2, so line
 18 captures both with the absolute value. In both cases, the old pipeline cost is the old
 cost of 𝑒′.
 3. Neither 𝑒 nor 𝑒′ is already hosting CO2 (lines 20-22). In this case, the new volume of CO2
 on 𝑒 will be the new amount being transported and there was no old pipeline cost.
The cost associated with using pipeline component 𝑒 is then calculated by first determining the
smallest trend that will fit the new volume of CO2 (line 24). A pipeline of sufficient capacity is
always available since the maximum capacity of the largest trend exceeds the target CO2 capture
amount. The new cost of the pipeline component is calculated as the fixed cost for the selected
trend plus the utilization cost as a factor of the new volume of CO2 (line 25). The cost of pipeline
component 𝑒 is set to be the new cost minus the old pipeline component cost (line 26). This is
the cost to use pipeline component 𝑒, factoring in already purchased pipeline infrastructure. A
consequence of this calculation is that the cost of 𝑒 can be negative when 𝑒′ is hosting CO2. If
redirecting CO2 results in the new cost of the pipeline component being lower than the old cost
of 𝑒′, the cost to use 𝑒 will be negative. Selecting 𝑒 in this case represents redirecting some of the
CO2 that was traversing 𝑒′, thereby enabling a smaller pipeline trend for the remaining CO2, less
utilization, and a cost savings. The cheapest path can then be calculated between the source and
reservoir (line 28). Since there can be negative edge weights in the network, and possibly
negative cycles, we implemented this step by setting the capacity of each edge to 1 and finding
the minimum-cost flow of value 1.
After the costs for each (source, reservoir) pair are calculated, the pair that captures, transports,
and injects CO2 for the lowest cost per metric ton is added to the solution (lines 31-35). When
the cheapest pair is selected, the infrastructure used to support the pair is updated for future
iterations (lines 38-63)}. For the selected source and reservoir, they are added to the solution and
their amounts captured and stored are updated (lines 39-40). The path between the source and
reservoir is added one edge at a time (lines 42-63). In a similar fashion as was done to
parameterize the costs for the pipeline network when finding cheapest paths, the new edge added
to the solution depends on whether or not that edge (or its reverse) was already in the solution. If
the edge was already in the solution, it will stay in the solution with a new volume of CO2 being
 908

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

the old volume plus the new amount being transported (lines 43-45). If the edge in the reverse
direction is already in the solution, the edge added to the solution and its volume of CO2 depends
on if the reverse edge was hosting more or less than the new amount of CO2 being transported
(lines 46-53). If neither the edge nor the reverse direction edge is already in the solution, the
edge is added with a volume of CO2 being the new amount being transported (lines 54-56).
This process then repeats until the target quantity of CO2 is captured. The running time for the
algorithm is driven by lines 2-36. The running time for the algorithm is 𝑂((|𝑆||𝑅|)2 (|𝐾||𝐶| +
𝑆ℎ𝑜𝑟𝑡𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑃𝑎𝑡ℎ)), where |𝑆| is the number of sources, |𝑅| is the number of reservoirs, |𝐾| is the
number of pipeline components, |𝐶| is the number of trends, and 𝑆ℎ𝑜𝑟𝑡𝑒𝑠𝑡𝑃𝑎𝑡ℎ is the running
time for the shortest path algorithm used. Line 2 repeats until the capture target is met by
maximizing the transfer between some (source, reservoir) pair at each iteration of the algorithm.
Since the transfer between each pair is maximized, it cannot be revisited in future iterations. This
means that line 2 cannot repeat more than |𝑆||𝑅| times. Line 3 repeats |𝑆||𝑅| times. Line 13-27
runs in |𝐾||𝐶| time and line 28 runs in whatever the running time is of the selected shortest path
algorithm. When there are a reasonable number of trends, the shortest path algorithm at line 28
will dominate the running time.

 Iterative Linear Program (LP)
The second algorithm we introduce iteratively solves LPs that result from removing all integer
variables from the MILP formulation of the CID problem. Removing integer variables allows the
resulting LPs to be solved optimally in polynomial running time. However, the integer variables
in the original MILP formulation provided the mechanism to charge the fixed cost based on the
binary decision of whether infrastructure was used or not. Each type of infrastructure entity (i.e.,
source, pipeline, or reservoir) in the CID problem has a fixed utilization cost 𝐹 and variable
utilization cost 𝑉. This means that the total cost for an entity is 𝐹𝑤 + 𝑉𝑥, where 𝑤 indicates if
the entity is in use and 𝑥 is the continuous amount of CO2 processed by the entity. To
approximate fixed costs with only continuous variables, entity costs are reformulated by
removing the fixed utilization component and changing the variable utilization coefficient from
 𝐹
𝑉 to 𝑥̂ + 𝑉, where 𝑥̂ is an estimate of what the value of 𝑥 will be when the LP is solved.
Therefore, the closer 𝑥 is to 𝑥̂, the closer the reformulated cost is to the true cost. This results in
the following LP, where 𝑎̂, 𝑝̂ , and 𝑏̂ are the estimated capture, transportation, and injection
amounts:

These constraints are similar to the standard capacity limiting constraints. Constraint I limits the
maximum capacity of a pipeline. Constraint J limits the amount captured at each source by its

capacity. An iterative scheme is used to generate estimated 𝑎̂, 𝑝̂ , and 𝑏̂ values: The estimated
values are all initially set to one and the LP is solved, resulting in solution values for 𝑎, 𝑝, and 𝑏.

iteration's 𝑎, 𝑝, and 𝑏 values. In this way, if an infrastructure entity's utilization remains identical
across iterations, its total cost will accurately reflect the correct fixed and variable costs, since

accurately reflect costs. Both of these procedures incentivize use of specific infrastructure based

 LP-Greedy Hybrid
The third algorithm we introduce is a hybrid of the first two algorithms. This algorithm is
presented in Algorithm 3 and detailed below. First, an initial solution is generated by Algorithm
2 (line 1). The unit cost to transfer the maximum amount of CO2 between each (source,
reservoir) pair in the solution is then calculated (lines 4-29). Calculating this cost is done in a
similar fashion to what was done in Algorithm 1 when finding the cheapest path for a (source,
reservoir) pair: First, the maximum amount of CO2 transferable between the (source, reservoir)
pair in the solution is calculated as the minimum of the CO2 captured at the source and injected
at the reservoir (line 5). Second, the capture and storage costs associated with that amount of
 914

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

CO2 is calculated as the sum of the utilization costs (line 6) and applicable fixed costs (lines 7-
12). Third, the shortest path in the solution between the (source, reservoir) pair is calculated by
first parameterizing a network with the cost savings of removing this pair from the solution (lines
14-23). This is done by considering each directed edge in the solution that is hosting more CO2
than the maximum transferable amount (lines 15-16). The cost of a new pipeline hosting the
original amount of CO2 minus the maximum transferable amount is calculated (lines 17-20). The
cost of this edge in the cost network is set to be the difference between the cost of the pipeline in
the solution and the new pipeline cost (line 21). The cheapest path for the (source, reservoir) pair
is calculated by finding the shortest path in the cost network (line 24). These capture, transport,
and storage costs and summed and the cost per metric ton of CO2 calculated and recorded (line
27).
Once the pairwise costs of each (source, reservoir) pair is calculated, the cheapest (per metric ton
of CO2) reservoir for each source is identified (lines 31-35) and the most expensive pair is
selected (line 36). The rationale for this step is that selecting the most expensive (source,
reservoir) pair from the list of all pairs will likely select a pair with high transportation cost (i.e.,
physically distant from each other) that would not actually pair together to transfer CO2 instead
of a pair that would reasonably pair together. Instead, the list of cheapest pairs will reflect more
likely pairings, of which we select the most expensive one for removal.
The most expensive of the cheapest, for each source, (source, reservoir) pairs is removed from
the solution (lines 38-59). A pair is removed from the solution by removing the maximum
transferable amount of CO2 from the source and reservoir (lines 38-46). The cost and volume of
CO2 on each edge in the cheapest path between the (source, reservoir) pair is then calculated and
updated (lines 48-59).
Finally, the cheapest replacement (source, reservoir) pairs are then added back to the solution
using Algorithm 1 (line 62). Before Algorithm 1 is run, the solution variables in it (𝑆′, 𝑅′, 𝐾′) are
set to be the 𝑆′, 𝑅′, and 𝐾′ values from this algorithm (line 61). This process is repeated for a
fixed number of iterations and improves the solution by replacing expensive (source, reservoir)
pairs with cheaper ones.

 Algorithm 3. LP-Greedy Hybrid

Solving CCS infrastructure design problems is fundamentally a computationally intractable
problem (formally, it is an NP-Hard optimization problem; Eardley et al. 2025). CCS
infrastructure design optimization is actually even NP-Hard to approximate within the natural
logarithm of the number of vertices in the graph. As such, finding optimal solutions to large
 916

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

instances is often computationally infeasible. The MILPs presented throughout this report are
solvable with specialized software, but do not scale to national-level CCS case studies. In this
Section, we introduce a novel genetic algorithm to solve CCS infrastructure design problems.
The novel contribution of our genetic algorithm is the representation of a flow solution by an
array of parameters that scale the fixed-costs for each edge in the network. This representation
ensures that each array corresponds to a valid flow, thereby eliminating the need for
computationally expensive repair functions that are required by other genetic algorithms for
similar fixed-charge flow network problems. By avoiding costly repair functions, the proposed
algorithm is able to efficiently find high-quality solutions to very large CCS infrastructure design
problem instances. The proposed genetic algorithm is inspired by slope scaling techniques
previously employed for the flow network problems. It is a matheuristic, as it employs
mathematical programming to calculate a flow solution from a LP parameterized with the fixed-
cost scaling arrays.

 Non-Integer LP
In this section, we introduce a LP that is a modification of the MILP presented in the
Background Section. Since it is an LP, this new formulation can be solved optimally in
polynomial time. This LP forms the foundation of the genetic algorithm discussed in later in this
report. Two components of the integer linear program (ILP) change to turn it into an appropriate
LP:
 1. The binary decision variables 𝑠𝑖 , 𝑟𝑗 , and 𝑝𝑘𝑐 are removed, thereby turning the model into
 an LP. Since the binary variables are removed, the fixed costs are then scaled and
 combined with the variable costs.
 2. New scaling parameters 𝑠𝑖𝑠 , 𝑟𝑗𝑠 , and 𝑝𝑘𝑐
 𝑠
 are introduced for component that will scale the
 fixed cost of each entity. These parameters form the representation of a flow solution in
 the genetic algorithm.

decision variable in the MILP.

The genetic algorithm described below works by varying the 𝑠𝑖𝑠 , 𝑟𝑗𝑠 , and 𝑝𝑘𝑐𝑠

and scoring the resulting optimal 𝛼𝑖 , 𝛽𝑗 , and 𝛿𝑘𝑐 values found by this true cost equation.

Genetic algorithms are a common evolutionary heuristic method used for searching and
optimization. Genetic algorithms manage a population of organisms that each correspond to a
solution to the problem. The population evolves over iterations of the algorithm using
evolutionary processes observed in nature including selection, crossover, and mutation
operations. Selection is the process of deciding which organisms of the population continue into
the next iteration (i.e., next generation). This is the mechanism that allows the algorithm to
prioritize organisms that correspond to better solutions to the problem and control the size of the
population. Crossover is the generation of a new organism from two existing organisms,
analogous to biological reproduction. Similarly, mutation is the slight modification of an
organism into a new one corresponding to a different solution. Crossover and mutation
operations are the mechanisms that allow the algorithm to search for new, and possibly better,
solutions.
A number of genetic algorithms have been developed to solve various versions of the fixed-
charge flow network problem. In these algorithms, organisms are broadly represented as either
individual edges, or predefined routes through the network. Representing organisms as
individual edges typically involves a binary variable for each edge indicating its availability for
use. Alternatively, representing organisms as predefined routes involves a binary variable for
each route in a set of predefined routes through the network. In the case of the individual edge
representation, generating the initial population, crossover operations, and mutation operations
often requires repairing the organism, as random sets of edges are unlikely to result in valid
flows. Using predefined routes simplifies repairing operations but may still require repair in the
 918

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

event of capacity constraint violations and is likely to result in suboptimal solutions due to the
limited set of routing options. The genetic algorithms that use these representations address the
issue by employing computationally expensive repair functions to make organisms correspond to
valid flows. Instead of representing an organism in this fashion, we represent it as an array of the
fixed-cost scaling parameters 𝑠𝑖𝑠 , 𝑟𝑗𝑠 , and 𝑝𝑘𝑐
 𝑠
 . Then, the solution corresponding to this organism
is the set of solution values 𝛼𝑖 , 𝛽𝑗 , and 𝛿𝑘𝑐 found by the LP described earlier. The result of this
representation is that we can guarantee the solution corresponding to any organism is a valid
flow, since the LP enforces that. This avoids costly repair functions and is the key to the
efficiency of our approach.
The motivation for using the fixed-cost scaling parameters as the organism representation is that
it allows control over the amount of fixed-costs incurred, while also removing the integer
variables from the optimal MILP. As the scaling parameter decreases to zero, the scaled fixed-
cost increases to infinity, thereby dissuading selection of that edge by the LP. Conversely, as the
scaling parameter increases to infinity, the scaled fixed-cost approaches zero, thereby
encouraging selection of that edge by the LP. The genetic algorithm is tasked with searching for
an organism of scaling parameters whose corresponding flow solution is as close to optimal for
the MILP as possible. Given that the genetic algorithm is using the fixed-cost scaling parameters
as a proxy for a solution instead of using a solution directly, an important question is whether or
not there exists a set of scaling parameters that yields an optimal flow solution. A proof that such
a set of scaling parameters is guaranteed to exist is presented later in this report. The key
components and workflow of the genetic algorithm are described below:

 Fitness Function
Genetic algorithms use fitness functions to rank and compare the population of organisms to aid
the selection process. Our fitness function first determines the solution for a given organism by
solving the LP to get the 𝛼𝑖 , 𝛽𝑗 , and 𝛿𝑘𝑐 solution values. After the 𝛼𝑖 , 𝛽𝑗 , and 𝛿𝑘𝑐 values are
determined, the solution's true cost in the context of the optimal ILP is calculated using the LP’s
true cost solution equation. This value is used as the fitness of the organism, where lower values
correspond to higher fitness.

 Selection Function
To keep the size of the population computationally manageable, a selection function is employed
to prune the population at each iteration. A selection function is also used to identify the
organisms for crossover operations. Our genetic algorithm implements a binary tournament
selection function in an effort to prioritize high fitness organisms, while not ignoring all low
fitness organisms. In binary tournament selection, two random organisms are selected, and the
one with the higher fitness is kept, while the other is discarded. This ensures that high-fitness
organisms are likely to remain in the population while maintaining the possibility for low-fitness
ones to survive as well. Binary tournament selection is repeated until the number of organisms in
the population is at the desired size.

 Crossover Function
A crossover function is used to generate a new child organism from two parent organisms
already in the population. Our crossover function first randomly selects two parent organisms

 919

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

from the existing population. A child organism is constructed by taking a random interval of the
scaling parameter array from the first parent, combined with the remaining values from the
second parent.

 Mutation Function
In order to mimic evolution and introduce another element of randomness into the search, a
mutation function is used to further alter child organisms. After a child organism is generated
with the crossover function, it may be randomly selected for mutation. During a mutation
operation, a number of scaling parameter values in the organism are selected and, with equal
probability, either incremented up or down a random amount between zero and one. Mutated
scaling parameter values are not allowed to go below a lower bound to avoid negative values and
divide by zero issues.

Using the functions described above, our algorithm operates as follows: First, an initial
population of organisms is randomly generated. Each organism in the initial population is
initialized as a scaling parameter array filled with a random value between 𝜖 > 0 and the average
value of the fixed-costs in the input instance. After the initial population of organisms are
created, the algorithm proceeds in an iterative fashion: At each iteration, the fitness of each
organism is first calculated as described above. While the population size is less than some
threshold, the crossover function is executed to generate child organisms. The child organisms
are also subject to randomized mutations from the mutation function. Once the population has
increased in size to the designated threshold, the selection function is run to reduce its size while
statistically discarding the lower fitness organisms. The algorithm keeps executing iterations
until the running time reaches a designated time limit.

 CPLEX Polishing
Once the time limit has been reached, the most fit organism's 𝛼𝑖 , 𝛽𝑗 , and 𝛿𝑘𝑐 solution values are
used as a warm start for IBM's CPLEX optimization software. CPLEX polishing is run for one
fifth of the total time limit resulting in the final flow values returned by the algorithm.

 Optimal Search Viability
The purpose of this section is to show that the genetic algorithm is capable of finding the optimal
solution of the ILP. This claim is not trivial, as the search space of the genetic algorithm is the
set of possible scaling parameter arrays, which are merely a proxy for solution values, the
property we are actually optimizing for. The original motivation for formulating the LP and
representing the organisms in the genetic algorithm as scaling parameter arrays follows from the
following false claim.
Claim: If each scaling parameter equals the optimal MILP solution value for that resource, then
the optimal flow found by the resulting LP is also an optimal flow for the ILP.
The rationale for this claim is that if each scaling parameter and 𝛼𝑖 , 𝛽𝑗 , and 𝛿𝑘𝑐 solution value
both equal the optimal MILP flow values, then the cost of the LP's objective function will equal
the optimal cost of the ILP's objective function. This claim is shown to be false with a simplified

 920

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

example in Figure 627 with only pipeline costs and capacities as fixed costs (𝑎𝑒 ), variable costs
(𝑏𝑒 ), capacities (𝑐𝑒 ), and a capture target of three. In this instance, the optimal ILP solution is to
set the amount of flow on 𝑒1 and 𝑒3 to two and the amount of flow on 𝑒2 and 𝑒4 to one for a total
cost of 20. Setting flow values for 𝑒1 and 𝑒3 to two and 𝑒2 and 𝑒4 to one yields the LP objective
of minimizing 7𝛿𝑒1 + 6𝛿𝑒2 . The optimal solution to this is to set the amount of flow on 𝑒1 and 𝑒3
to one and the amount of flow on 𝑒2 and 𝑒4 to two for a total cost of 21, thereby contradicting the
claim.

Figure 627 Counterexample to claim with only transportation costs and capacities having the displayed fixed costs
(𝑎𝑒 ), variable costs (𝑏𝑒 ), capacities (𝑐𝑒 ), and a capture target of three. In this instance, the optimal ILP solution is 20
with a flow of two units on 𝑒1 and 𝑒3 and one unit on 𝑒2 and 𝑒4 . The corresponding optimal LP solution is 21 with a
flow of one unit on 𝑒1 and 𝑒3 and two units on 𝑒2 and 𝑒4 .
Since the motivation claim is false, along with the fact that the scaling parameter arrays are only
proxies for the flow value solutions we seek, it remains to be shown that there actually exists a
set of scaling parameter values that will result in the genetic algorithm finding optimal flow
values for the ILP.

Theorem: For every problem instance, there exists a set of scaling parameter values such that the
optimal flow found by the resulting LP is also an optimal flow for the ILP.
