To demonstrate the efficiency and effectiveness of the genetic algorithm, an evaluation was
conducted using CCS data collected as part of the CUSP effort. The genetic algorithm was
implemented and integrated into SimCCS. Initial performance simulations guided the
parameterization of the genetic algorithm to have a population size of 10, and mutation and
crossover probability of both 50%. A mutation probability of 50% means that each organism has
a 50% chance of mutation, and a crossover probability of 50% means that 50% of the population
(without organism repetition) is crossed over with a random other organism in each iteration of
the genetic algorithm. All reported genetic algorithm values are the average of three runs. The
optimal MILP from the Background Section was implemented in SimCCS using CPLEX as well.
SimCCS was used as a standardized way to represent CCS data and for problem and solution
visualization. Timing was coded directly into SimCCS to ensure only the algorithm of interest
was being timed during simulation. Simulations were run on a machine with Ubuntu 20.04.5, an
Intel Xeon W-2255 processor running at 3.7 GHz, and 64 GB of RAM. SimCCS on this machine
used IBM's CPLEX optimization tool, version 22.1.1.0.
The genetic algorithm was tested on two CCS infrastructure design datasets. The first dataset
covers the state of California and consists of 190 sources with a total annual emission rate of
88.3$ MtCO2/yr, 102 sinks with a total lifetime storage capacity of 37.18 GtCO2, and 1,188
possible pipeline components (i.e., edges in the graph) with a total length of 17,940.88 km and
11 possible capacities on each edge. A map of this dataset is presented in Figure 628.

 923

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Figure 628 Carbon capture and storage dataset for the state of California consisting of sources (red), sinks (blue),
and possible pipeline routes
The second dataset covers the contiguous United States and consists of 2,746 sources with a total
annual emission rate of 532.61 MtCO2/yr, 1,202 sinks with a total lifetime storage capacity of
2,691.86 GtCO2, and 22,597 possible pipeline components with a total length of 424,674.41 km
and 11 possible capacities on each edge. This data was collected by Carbon Solutions, LLC apart
from the CUSP project as part of a study conducted by the Clean Air Task Force (Boston, MA).
Storage data was generated using the SCO2T geologic sequestration tool. A map of this dataset is
presented in Figure 629.

Figure 629 Carbon capture and storage dataset for the contiguous United States consisting of sources (red), sinks
(blue), and possible pipeline routes

 924

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

Candidate pipeline routes were generated in SimCCS using its candidate network generation
algorithms. The National Energy Technology Laboratory’s CO2 Transport Cost Model was used
by SimCCS to determine fixed construction and variable utilization costs for the 11 discrete
pipeline capacity options.
To assess the efficiency of the genetic algorithm, its solution cost was compared to the solution
cost found by CPLEX solving the optimal ILP, with both methods being allowed to run for set
running time periods. For the California dataset, those running time periods were 0.5, 1, 2, 4, and
8 hours. The target flow amount (𝑇) was set to 80 MtCO2/yr for all of the California scenarios.
For the contiguous United States dataset, the running time periods were 0.5, 1, 2, 4, 8 and 16
hours. The target flow amount was set to 500 MtCO2/yr for the contiguous United States
scenarios. Figure 630(a) presents each algorithm's solution cost over the running time periods for
the California dataset, and Figure 630(b) presents the same results for the contiguous United
States dataset. The cost of the best solution found by the genetic algorithm in the California
dataset was within 0.5% of the ILP's solution across all running times. Conversely, the cost of
the best solution found by the genetic algorithm in the contiguous United States dataset was 17%
lower than the ILP's solution after one hour, 7% lower after four hours, and 2% lower after 16
hours. This suggests that the genetic algorithm may have utility for very large problem instances.
The utility for small instances is likely limited, due to the speed of CPLEX.

 (a) (b)
Figure 630 Solution cost versus running time for the genetic algorithm and optimal ILP on (a) the California dataset
and (b) the contiguous United States dataset
Problem solvability is not only related to instance size, but also the amount of target flow being
found. To identify the impact that target flow amount has on solution quality, scenarios were run
on the contiguous United States dataset where the target flow amount was varied from 1
MtCO2/yr to 532 MtCO2/yr. The maximum annual capturable amount of CO2 for this dataset is
532.61 MtCO2/yr. Each algorithm was given two hours to solve each scenario. Figure 631
presents each algorithm's solution cost for the various target flow amounts. Table 94 presents the
specific solution cost values and the percent improvement of the genetic algorithm's solution
over the ILP's solution. Other than in very low and high target flow amount scenarios, the
genetic algorithm was fairly consistent in its improvement over the ILP. Interestingly, in the low
target flow amount scenario, the genetic algorithm performed the best relative to the ILP. This
suggests that the genetic algorithm could have utility in a very large problem instance, even if the
 925

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

target flow amount is quite small. This is likely a very realistic scenario, where a relatively small
target is sought amongst a very large space of options, and provides a compelling argument for
the utility of the genetic algorithm.

  Phase 4 – Readiness Indices and Mapping
A major effort of the Analytics Working Group was the development of a workflow for
determining Regional Readiness Indices and applying that workflow to CUSP data to generate
Regional Readiness Indices Maps. The outcome of this effort is described in detail in the Subtask
5.1 component of the final report.

Over the duration of the CUSP, the Analytics Working Group provided the computational,
methodological, and integrative foundation that enabled consistent, data-driven CCS analyses
across the western United States. The group’s work evolved from early-stage data
standardization and partner support to advanced model development and regional synthesis,
culminating in the generation of the CUSP Readiness Indices (Maps) described in Subtask 5.1 –
Development of Regional Readiness Indices.

 926

CUSP West Final Report – DOE Award DE-FE0031837

By establishing a unified modeling framework, the Analytics Working Group ensured that each
subtask’s outputs were interoperable and grounded in reproducible computational methods. The
adoption of standardized SimCCS data templates and cost specifications allowed state partners to
produce compatible datasets and comparable regional scenarios. These foundational efforts
supported extensive scenario analyses spanning California’s San Joaquin Basin, Kansas, Nevada,
the Four Corners region, and beyond—each revealing the diverse technical and economic
realities of CCS deployment across varying geological, policy, and industrial contexts.
Methodologically, the group advanced the state of CCS infrastructure modeling by developing
new formulations for multiphased build-out planning, risk-aware and repair-aware network
design, and heuristic optimization algorithms capable of scaling to national problem sizes. These
innovations improved the realism and tractability of CCS planning models, enabling assessment
of phased deployment, uncertainty in storage performance, and trade-offs between cost and
resilience. These advances were disseminated through peer-reviewed publications, expanding
their utility to the wider CCS research and policy community.
The culmination of these efforts is reflected in the regional readiness framework produced under
Subtask 5.1, which integrates geologic, economic, infrastructural, regulatory, and risk metrics
into composite readiness indices. These indices quantify where CCS deployment is most feasible
and identify barriers requiring further investment or policy action. Together, the readiness maps
and supporting analyses form a decision-support tool that bridges scientific modeling and
practical planning, providing a data-driven foundation for DOE, state agencies, and private
stakeholders to prioritize CCS projects effectively.
In total, the Analytics Working Group’s contributions position the CUSP region for informed,
risk-aware, and cost-effective carbon management. By unifying data, methods, and modeling
across jurisdictions, the group created a durable analytical framework that will continue to
support regional decarbonization initiatives well beyond the life of the CUSP project.
